knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the continuous single-resource allocation formulation; convexity of the component cost functions is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a total resource $X\ge 0$ and component cost functions $f_i:[0,X]\to\mathbb{R}$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, the continuous separable resource allocation problem is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\;F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=X,\qquad x_i\ge 0\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).
\]
The functions $f_i$ may be nonconvex on subsets of their domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate a nonnegative amount of a single resource to each of n activities, with the allocations summing to the available amount X, so as to minimize the sum of activity-specific costs. The component costs may be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i):x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=X,\ x_i\ge 0\ \forall i\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric search for the minimal root
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar Lipschitz equations on an interval, including the case where no root exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R be Lipschitz and suppose it has been evaluated at ordered trial points x_0<\cdots<x_n. On every [x_{i-1},x_i], construct a piecewise-linear function \phi_i satisfying \phi_i(x)\leq f(x) for all x in that interval. Choose the smallest index k for which \phi_k(x)=0 has a solution, and use the corresponding leftmost candidate \widetilde x_n as the next trial, thereby refining the minorants and the current root approximation. The procedure either determines the minimal root of f(x)=0 on [a,b], or, when no root exists there, determines a global minimizer of f. Regional local tuning may be used to accelerate the refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method builds Lipschitz piecewise-linear lower bounds on successive sampled intervals and samples at the earliest interval whose lower bound can reach zero. Repeated refinement targets the leftmost root; if the equation has no root on the interval, the same process instead determines a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The refinement determines }\min\{x\in[a,b]:f(x)=0\}\text{ when this set is nonempty, and otherwise determines a global minimizer of }f.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical box-bounded, continuously constrained global minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the general continuous global optimization problem is
\[
\min_{x\in D} f(x),\qquad
D:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:l\le x\le u,\ g_j(x)\le0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,m\},
\]
where $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ are continuous, $l,u$ are finite componentwise bounds, and $D$ is a nonempty proper subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general continuous global optimization problem minimizes a continuous scalar objective over a nonempty proper feasible subset of real n-space defined by finite componentwise bounds and finitely many continuous inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{f(x):x\in D\},\quad D=\{x:l\le x\le u,\ g_j(x)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for $D=\{x\in[a,b]\mid g(x)\leq0\}$, its accumulation-point set $D^*$, and the strict-margin set $D_\varepsilon$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D:=\{x\in[a,b]\mid g(x)\leq0\}$ and let $D^*$ be the set of accumulation points of $D$. A point $x^*\in D^*$ is an essential optimal solution if $f(x^*)\leq f(x)$ for every $x\in D^*$. For $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, define $D_\varepsilon:=\{x\in[a,b]\mid g(x)\leq-\varepsilon\}$. A point $x\in D_\varepsilon$ is $\varepsilon$-essential feasible, and a nonisolated feasible point $x^*$ is essential $(\varepsilon,\eta)$-optimal if $f(x^*)\leq f(x)+\eta$ for every $x\in D_\varepsilon$. For $\varepsilon=\eta=0$, this is a nonisolated feasible global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential optimality minimizes the objective over the accumulation points of the feasible set. Epsilon-essential feasibility requires a constraint margin of at least epsilon, and essential (epsilon, eta)-optimality compares a nonisolated feasible point within eta against every point having that margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in D^*\text{ is essential optimal}\iff f(x^*)\leq f(x)\ \forall x\in D^*;\quad x^*\text{ is essential }(\varepsilon,\eta)\text{-optimal}\iff x^*\text{ is nonisolated feasible and }f(x^*)\leq f(x)+\eta\ \forall x\in D_\varepsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Essential feasibility and optimality certificates from Q-gamma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The unspecified referenced assumption is retained symbolically as assumption (12.16).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under assumption (12.16): (i) if x^0 is feasible for Q_\gamma and g(x^0)>0, then x^0 is a nonisolated feasible solution of P and f(x^0)\le\gamma. Hence, if \max(Q_\gamma)>0, an optimizer \widehat x of Q_\gamma is nonisolated feasible for P and satisfies f(\widehat x)\le\gamma. (ii) If \bar x is nonisolated feasible for P, \gamma=f(\bar x)-\varepsilon, and \max(Q_\gamma)<\varepsilon, then \bar x is essential \varepsilon-optimal. If instead \gamma=f(b) and \max(Q_\gamma)<\varepsilon, then P is \varepsilon-essentially infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subject to the referenced assumption, a master-problem feasible point with positive g-value certifies a nonisolated feasible point whose objective is at most gamma. A sufficiently small master optimum at gamma equal to an incumbent value minus epsilon certifies essential epsilon-optimality; at gamma equal to f(b), it certifies epsilon-essential infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(x^0)>0\Rightarrow[x^0\text{ nonisolated feasible for }P,\ f(x^0)\le\gamma];\quad \max(Q_{f(\bar x)-\varepsilon})<\varepsilon\Rightarrow\bar x\text{ essential }\varepsilon\text{-optimal};\quad \max(Q_{f(b)})<\varepsilon\Rightarrow P\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-essentially infeasible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Utility-uniform improvement from an auxiliary stochastic-programming system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded, context-dependent result; the numbered systems, objective construction, and utility condition are defined outside this item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}. (a) If (y,\Pi) solves (12)\text{--}(15), then F(y)\leq F(x) for every u\in\mathcal C_m^J. When J=\varnothing, if a vector y satisfies F(y)\leq F(x) for every u\in\mathcal C_m, then there exists an r\times r matrix \Pi such that (y,\Pi) satisfies (12), (13), and (23). (b) If (y,\Pi) solves (12)\text{--}(15) and (16), then F(y)<F(x) for every u\in\mathcal C_m^J strictly convex on \operatorname{conv}\{z^i:1\leq i\leq r\}. (c) If it solves (12)\text{--}(15) and (17), the same strict inequality holds for every u\in\mathcal C_m^J that is not affine-linear on that convex hull. (d) If it satisfies (12)\text{--}(15) and (18), the strict inequality holds for every u\in\mathcal C_m^J satisfying (4).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The auxiliary system implies weak improvement uniformly over the specified convex utility class. Three separate supplementary conditions imply strict improvement for, respectively, strictly convex utilities, non-affine utilities, and utilities satisfying condition (4). Only for the unrestricted convex class is the stated converse asserted.
assumptions_latex: F,\mathcal C_m^J,z^1,\ldots,z^r\text{ and systems (12)--(18), (23) have their source-defined meanings}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (y,\Pi)\text{ satisfying (12)--(15)}\Longrightarrow \forall u\in\mathcal C_m^J,\ F(y)\leq F(x),\text{ with the stated separate strictness conclusions and only the stated }J=\varnothing\text{ converse.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate global optimality relative to the original problem's optimal value while permitting componentwise constraint tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), and let \(S_\delta\) denote the \(\delta\)-feasible set. A point \(x^\star\) is an \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-optimal solution if \(x^\star\in S_\delta\) and \(f(x^\star)\le f^\star+\varepsilon\), where \(f^\star\) is the optimal value of the original problem. In particular, when \(x^\star\in S\) and \(f^\star<\infty\), it is called an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is epsilon-delta optimal if it is feasible within the componentwise delta tolerances and its objective value is no more than epsilon above the original optimal value. If it is exactly feasible and the optimal value is finite, it is called epsilon-optimal.
assumptions_latex: f^\star\text{ is the optimal value of the original problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star\text{ is }(\varepsilon,\delta)\text{-optimal}\iff x^\star\in S_\delta\ \land\ f(x^\star)\le f^\star+\varepsilon;\qquad x^\star\in S,\ f^\star<\infty\Longrightarrow x^\star\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-optimal}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relief-subproblem method for obtaining either a global optimizer or a strictly improving feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\alpha_1\in f(S)\). At iteration \(k\), globally solve \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\varphi(\alpha_k,x)\), let \(x^{k+1}\) be an optimizer, and set \(\mu_k=\varphi(\alpha_k,x^{k+1})\). If \(\mu_k=0\), terminate with \(x^{k+1}\) as a solution of \((\mathrm{COP})\). Otherwise \(\mu_k<0\), \(x^{k+1}\in S\), and \(f(x^{k+1})<\alpha_k\); set \(\alpha_{k+1}=f(x^{k+1})\) and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible objective value, globally minimize the relief function. A zero minimum certifies a global solution; a negative minimum yields a feasible point with strictly smaller objective value, which becomes the next level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_k=0\Rightarrow x^{k+1}\text{ solves }(\mathrm{COP});\qquad \mu_k<0\Rightarrow x^{k+1}\in S,\ f(x^{k+1})<\alpha_k,\ \alpha_{k+1}=f(x^{k+1}).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The objective inequality is preserved in the direction printed in the extract, which differs from the usual additive minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After translation, suppose U is a compact convex subset of a hyperrectangle [a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}_+^n\times\mathbb{R}_+^m and C is a compact convex subset of \mathbb{R}_+^m. For \varepsilon>0, u=(x,y)\in U is \varepsilon-feasible if g(u)\le\varepsilon. A point \bar u=(\bar x,\bar y)\in U is (\varepsilon,\eta)-optimal if it is \varepsilon-feasible and \[f(u)\le f(\bar u)+\eta\qquad\text{for every \varepsilon-feasible }u.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the translated compact nonnegative domain, epsilon-feasibility permits a gap value no larger than epsilon. As extracted, an epsilon-feasible point is called epsilon–eta optimal when every epsilon-feasible point has objective value at most eta above its value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(\bar u)\le\varepsilon\quad\text{and}\quad f(u)\le f(\bar u)+\eta\ \forall u\in U\text{ with }g(u)\le\varepsilon.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for (MO); the final comparison class follows the extracted wording, which refers to ε-essential optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point $x\in\mathbb R^n$ is essential feasible for (MO) when $x\in[a,b]$ and $g(x)<0\le h(x)$. For $\eta>0$, an essential feasible $\bar x$ is essential $\eta$-optimal when $f(\bar x)\ge f(x)-\eta$ for every essential feasible $x$. For $\varepsilon>0$, $x$ is $\varepsilon$-essential feasible when $x\in[a,b]$ and $g(x)+\varepsilon\le0\le h(x)$. For $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, an $\varepsilon$-essential feasible $\bar x$ is $(\varepsilon,\eta)$-optimal when $f(\bar x)\ge f(x)-\eta$ for every $\varepsilon$-essential optimal solution $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential feasibility requires membership in the box, strict satisfaction of g(x)≤0, and h(x)≥0. Essential eta-optimality compares the objective with every essential feasible point. Epsilon-essential feasibility strengthens g(x)≤0 by margin epsilon. The extracted final definition compares an epsilon-essential feasible point with every epsilon-essential optimal solution up to objective tolerance eta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global epsilon-optimal solution and relative objective error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines additive approximate global optimality and, when the objective range and a positive lower bound on it are available, states the associated relative-error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), a feasible point \(\bar x\in D\) is globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal for \(\min\{f(x):x\in D\}\) if \[f(x)\ge f(\bar x)-\varepsilon\qquad\forall x\in D.\] If \(\min_D f\) and \(\max_D f\) exist, \(\Delta f:=\max_D f-\min_D f>0\), and \(0<M\le\Delta f\), then \[\frac{f(\bar x)-\min_D f}{\Delta f}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\Delta f}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{M}.\] For \(\varepsilon=0\), the defining inequality makes \(\bar x\) a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is globally epsilon-optimal if its objective value is no more than epsilon above the global minimum. When the objective range is positive and has a positive lower bound M, the relative objective error is at most epsilon divided by that range and hence at most epsilon divided by M. Zero tolerance gives exact global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \min_{x\in D}f(x)\text{ and }\max_{x\in D}f(x)\text{ exist for the relative-error statement}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in D,\ f(x)\ge f(\bar x)-\varepsilon;\qquad \frac{f(\bar x)-\min_D f}{\Delta f}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\Delta f}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{M}.

knowledge_statements.title: Local versus Global Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space definitions for constrained minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). A point \(x^\star\in C\) is a global minimizer when \(f(x^\star)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\). It is a local minimizer relative to \(C\) when there exists \(r>0\) such that \(f(x^\star)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\) satisfying \(d(x,x^\star)<r\). Every global minimizer is local, whereas a local minimizer need not be global.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimizer dominates every feasible point; a local minimizer only dominates feasible points in some neighborhood. Global minimality implies local minimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\Rightarrow x^\star\text{ is a local minimizer relative to }C.\)

notation.meaning: open metric ball of radius r about x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary nonconvex boundary for the reverse implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2+x\) on \(C=\mathbb R\), the equation \(f'(x)=4x(x^2-1)+1=0\) has three distinct real roots, and its leftmost and rightmost roots are strict local minimizers. The right-hand minimizer is not global because \(f(-x)=f(x)-2x<f(x)\) whenever \(x>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tilted double-well objective has a strict local well that is not globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_{\mathrm{loc}}\in C:\ x_{\mathrm{loc}}\text{ is strict local but not global}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Local and Strict Global Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict variants of the comparison domains defined by the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the seed's metric-space setting, \(x^\star\in C\) is a strict global minimizer if \(f(x^\star)<f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\setminus\{x^\star\}\). It is a strict local minimizer relative to \(C\) if some \(r>0\) satisfies \(f(x^\star)<f(x)\) for every \(x\in(C\cap B_r(x^\star))\setminus\{x^\star\}\). Every strict global minimizer is the unique global minimizer and is a strict local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict global and local minimizers use strict inequalities on the whole feasible set and on a feasible neighborhood, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ strict global}\Rightarrow x^\star\text{ unique global and strict local}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a robust minimizer under variance sequential compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines an existence result for robust global minimizers with the zero-modified-variance characterization of their minimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a metric space and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be bounded below, lower semicontinuous, and robust. If $f$ has the variance sequential compactness property, then there exist a robust global minimizer $x^*$ and a subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ such that
\[
x_{n_k}\to x^*,\qquad f(x_{n_k})\to f(x^*)=\inf_{x\in X}f(x).
\]
Moreover, a point $x^*\in X$ is a global minimizer with global minimum value $c^*=f(x^*)$ if and only if
\[
V_1(f,c^*)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-below, lower-semicontinuous robust function on a metric space attains its global infimum if it has the variance sequential compactness property; an associated subsequence converges to a robust minimizer with convergent objective values. A point is globally minimizing exactly when the modified variance at its attained value is zero.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to\mathbb R\text{ is bounded below, lower semicontinuous, and robust}
f\text{ has the variance sequential compactness property}
C\text{ is the set of continuity points of }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*,(x_{n_k}):\ x_{n_k}\to x^*,\quad f(x_{n_k})\to f(x^*)=\inf_{x\in X}f(x),\qquad [x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\iff V_1(f,f(x^*))=0].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular and critical points and finite critical-point enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable unconstrained optimization on a smooth manifold without boundary, or at an interior minimizer; the enumeration conclusion additionally requires finitely many critical points and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $f:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be differentiable. A point $p\in M$ is regular when $T_pf:T_pM\to\mathbb{R}$ is onto, and critical otherwise. Every interior global minimizer is critical. If the critical set is finite and a global minimizer exists, the global minimizers can be found by enumerating all critical points and comparing their objective values. This strategy may also enumerate many nonglobal local minima, local maxima, and saddle points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is regular when the differential of the objective is onto and critical otherwise. Every interior global minimizer is critical. If there are finitely many critical points and a minimum is attained, comparing the objective values at all critical points identifies the global minimizers, although many irrelevant extrema and saddle points may also be enumerated.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ has no boundary, or each minimizer under consideration is an interior point}
\operatorname{Crit}(f)\text{ is finite for the enumeration conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is regular}\iff T_pf\text{ is onto};\quad p\text{ is critical otherwise};\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{M}f\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f),\text{ subject to interiority, and exhaustive finite critical-point enumeration identifies the global minimizers.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a compactness property for sequences of continuity points whose associated modified variances vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let X be a metric space, let f:X\to\mathbb R, and let C be the set of continuity points of f. The function f has the variance sequential compactness property if, for every sequence (x_n)\subset X,
\[
\bigl((x_n)\subset C\ \text{and}\ V_1(f,f(x_n))\to0\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\text{there exists a convergent subsequence }(x_{n_k}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function has the variance sequential compactness property if every sequence of its continuity points whose modified variances tend to zero has a convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall(x_n)\subset X,\quad ((x_n)\subset C\land V_1(f,f(x_n))\to0)\Rightarrow\exists(x_{n_k})\text{ convergent}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential approximation through continuity points for a real-valued function on a topological space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space and let \(C\) be the set of continuity points of \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is approximatable if \(C\) is dense in \(X\) and, for every \(x_0\in X\), there is a sequence \(\{x_\alpha\}\subset C\) such that \(x_\alpha\to x_0\) and \(f(x_\alpha)\to f(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is approximatable when its continuity points are dense and every point can be approached by continuity points along which the function values converge to the value at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{C}=X\quad\text{and}\quad\forall x_0\in X\;\exists\{x_\alpha\}\subset C:\ x_\alpha\to x_0,\ f(x_\alpha)\to f(x_0)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modified variance with respect to a level
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines normalized squared deviation over a sublevel set. The source uses V rather than V_1 inside the limiting extension at c^*, so that notation is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \mu be a Q-measure on X and let H_c=\{x\in X:f(x)\le c\}. For \mu(H_c)>0, the modified variance of f with respect to c is
\[
V_1(f,c)=\frac{1}{\mu(H_c)}\int_{H_c}(f(x)-c)^2\,d\mu.
\]
At c=c^*, the definition is extended by
\[
V_1(f,c^*)=\lim_{c_n\downarrow c^*}V(f,c_n).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The modified variance at level c is the normalized integral of the squared deviation from c over the c-sublevel set. At c*, the source extends it by a decreasing-level limit and writes V, rather than V1, inside that limit.
assumptions_latex: c_n\downarrow c^*\text{ for the limiting extension}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V_1(f,c)=\frac{1}{\mu(H_c)}\int_{H_c}(f(x)-c)^2\,d\mu,\qquad V_1(f,c^*)=\lim_{c_n\downarrow c^*}V(f,c_n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topologically Robust Sets, Points, and Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of robustness used in robust-minimizer theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space. A set \(D\subset X\) is robust if \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}D)=\operatorname{cl}D\). A point \(x_0\in D\) is a robust point of \(D\) if \(x_0\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}D)\), equivalently if a net in \(\operatorname{int}D\) converges to \(x_0\). Thus, \(D\) is robust if and only if every point of \(D\) is robust. A function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is robust on \(X\) if \(f^{-1}(G)\) is robust for every open set \(G\subset\mathbb{R}\). It is robust at \(x_0\in X\) if, for every \(\epsilon>0\), \(x_0\) is a robust point of \(f^{-1}((f(x_0)-\epsilon,f(x_0)+\epsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is robust when the closure of its interior equals its closure. A point is robust when it is approachable by interior points. A real-valued function is robust when every open inverse image is robust, and it is robust at a point when inverse images of all epsilon-neighborhoods of its value are locally robust there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is robust}\iff\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}D)=\operatorname{cl}D\iff\forall x\in D,\ x\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{int}D)

knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Global Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive objective-gap definition with finite global infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\neq\varnothing\), let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\), and suppose \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\). For a tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), a point \(x_\varepsilon\in C\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-global solution when \(f(x_\varepsilon)\leq f^\star+\varepsilon\). Equivalently, its global objective gap satisfies \(0\leq f(x_\varepsilon)-f^\star\leq\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon=0\), this definition reduces to an attained global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-global solution is feasible and has objective value at most epsilon above the finite global infimum; zero tolerance gives an exact global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\varepsilon\text{ is epsilon-global}\iff x_\varepsilon\in C\text{ and }f(x_\varepsilon)-f^\star\leq\varepsilon.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Accuracy Need Not Imply Decision Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between additive objective error and distance to an exact optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=x^2/(1+x^4)\), one has \(f^\star=0\) and \(S^\star=\{0\}\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the set \(S_\varepsilon=\{x\in\mathbb R:f(x)\le\varepsilon\}\) is unbounded because \(f(x)\to0\) as \(|x|\to\infty\). Thus epsilon-globality alone supplies no bound on \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even arbitrarily small objective tolerance need not control distance to the optimizer set without a growth or error-bound condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall\varepsilon>0)\quad \sup_{x\in S_\varepsilon}\operatorname{dist}(x,S^\star)=+\infty.\)

notation.meaning: distance from x to the exact optimizer set

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Accuracy Need Not Imply Decision Accuracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Nesting of Epsilon-Global Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic set structure of additive near-optimality targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and define \(S_\varepsilon:=\{x\in C:f(x)\le f^\star+\varepsilon\}\). Then \(S_\varepsilon\neq\varnothing\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). If \(0\le\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\), then \(S_{\varepsilon_1}\subseteq S_{\varepsilon_2}\), and \(S_0\neq\varnothing\) exactly when the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-tolerance global solution sets always exist for a finite infimum, grow with tolerance, and the zero-tolerance set is nonempty exactly under attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\Rightarrow S_\varepsilon\neq\varnothing,\qquad \varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\Rightarrow S_{\varepsilon_1}\subseteq S_{\varepsilon_2}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Global Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued formulation of all attained global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty feasible set \(C\) and objective \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) and the global solution set \(S^\star:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\{x\in C:f(x)=f^\star\}\). The infimum is attained exactly when \(S^\star\neq\varnothing\). The solution is unique exactly when \(S^\star\) is a singleton; otherwise \(S^\star\) may contain finitely many points or an infinite, including continuum-valued, family of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global solution set contains every feasible point attaining the infimum. It may be empty, a singleton, finite, or an infinite continuum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^\star=\{x\in C:f(x)=f^\star\}\quad\text{and}\quad S^\star\neq\varnothing\iff f^\star\text{ is attained}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness Does Not Require Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse boundary for the strict-convexity uniqueness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[-1,1]\), the convex function \(f(x)=|x|\) is not strictly convex, yet \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\{0\}\). Thus strict convexity is sufficient but not necessary for uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex objective can have a unique minimizer without being strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is not strictly convex on }C\quad\text{and}\quad S^\star=\{0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness Does Not Require Strict Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of global solution sets in convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Then \(S^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is convex. If \(f\) is strictly convex on \(C\), then \(S^\star\) contains at most one point; consequently, any attained minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex problem has a convex optimizer set, and strict convexity makes any attained optimizer unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^\star\text{ is convex};\qquad f\text{ strictly convex}\Rightarrow |S^\star|\le1.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Geometry and Strict-Convex Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard existence and compactness theorem stated for the global optimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty compact subset of a topological space and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be lower semicontinuous and finite at some point. Then \(f\) attains a finite infimum on \(C\), and \(S^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is a nonempty compact subset of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous objective finite somewhere on a nonempty compact feasible set has a nonempty compact global solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite at some point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varnothing\neq S^\star\subseteq C\quad\text{and}\quad S^\star\text{ is compact}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-Copositivity Characterization of a Concave Quadratic Global Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality characterization for problem (1) under a negative-definite quadratic matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let Q\prec0 and let x^\star be feasible for (1). Define I(x^\star)=\{i:(Ax^\star)_i=b_i\} and u_i=b_i-(Ax^\star)_i>0 for i
otin I(x^\star). If a_i^T is row i of A, set B_i=-a_i(Qx^\star+c)^T-(Qx^\star+c)a_i^T, Q_0=Q, and Q_i=u_iQ-B_i. Define \Gamma=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:(Av)_i\leq0	ext{ whenever }(Ax^\star)_i=b_i\}, \Gamma_0=\{v\in\Gamma:(Av)_i\leq0\  orall i
otin I(x^\star)\}, and \Gamma_i=\{v\in\Gamma:(Av)_i\geq0,\ u_j(Av)_i\geq u_i(Av)_j\  orall j
otin I(x^\star)\}. Then x^\star is a global solution of (1) if and only if both of the following hold: (a) x^\star is a KKT point and Q_i is \Gamma_i	ext{-copositive for every }i\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\setminus I(x^\star); (b) v^T(Qx^\star+c)\leq0 for every v\in\Gamma_0 and Q_i is \Gamma_i	ext{-copositive for every }i\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\setminus I(x^\star).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a negative-definite quadratic program, the feasible point is globally optimal exactly when the stated KKT and directional conditions hold together with copositivity of the derived matrices on the active-set-dependent cones.
assumptions_latex: \Gamma,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_i\text{ are defined by the displayed active-set direction inequalities}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star\text{ is globally optimal}\iff\text{conditions (a) and (b), including every stated }\Gamma_i\text{-copositivity condition, hold}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact squared penalty for integer-valued equality constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an explicit sufficient penalty coefficient when all constraints are integer-valued equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(m=0\), each \(h_j:X\to\mathbb Z\), \(P(x)=\sum_{j=1}^l h_j(x)^2\), \(\underline f\le\min_{x\in X}f(x)\), and \(\bar f\ge v(\mathrm P)\). Then, for every \(\mu\ge\mu_0:=\bar f-\underline f\), every global minimizer \(x^*\) of \(\min_{x\in X}\{f(x)+\mu P(x)\}\) is a global minimizer of \(\mathrm P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite integer problem having only integer-valued equality constraints, the sum of squared equality residuals is an exact penalty whenever its coefficient is at least the difference between an upper bound on the constrained optimum and a lower bound on the objective over the full domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-system definition of model feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a model with decision domain \(X\), inequality functions \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and equality functions \(h_j:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\). Its feasible set is \(C:=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\leq0\ \text{for all }i,\ h_j(x)=0\ \text{for all }j\}\). The model is feasible if and only if \(C\neq\varnothing\), equivalently, if at least one point simultaneously satisfies every declared constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained model is feasible exactly when at least one point in its decision domain satisfies every inequality and equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The model is feasible}\iff C\neq\varnothing.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global minimization by convergent record values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the distinction between convergence to the minimizer set and convergence to a particular minimizer; the source leaves the additional hypotheses for record-point set convergence unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:A\to\mathbb R, let m=\min_{x\in A}f(x), and assume A_*:=\{x\in A:f(x)=m\}\ne\varnothing. For observations x_1,x_2,\ldots\in A, define y_{on}:=\min_{1\le i\le n}f(x_i) and let x_{on} be the least-index observation attaining y_{on}. Global minimization means constructing observations such that y_{on}\to m. Under the source's unspecified additional general hypotheses, \rho(x_{on},A_*):=\inf_{z\in A_*}\rho(x_{on},z)\to0. If A_* is not a singleton, y_{on}\to m does not in general imply convergence of x_{on} to a particular member of A_*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming the minimum is attained, a global minimizer attains the least feasible objective value. The record value after n observations is their best objective value, and its associated record point is the earliest observation attaining that value. The global minimization task is to make record values converge to the global minimum. The extract additionally asserts, under unspecified general hypotheses, that record points approach the set of all minimizers; without uniqueness they need not converge to one particular minimizer.
assumptions_latex: (A,\rho)\text{ is a metric space for the set-distance assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_{on}\to m;\quad\text{and, under additional unspecified hypotheses, }\rho(x_{on},A_*)\to0,\text{ but }|A_*|>1\text{ need not imply }x_{on}\to x_*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-phase local improvement and global certification scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generic global-optimization scheme with finite termination when its distinguished candidate set is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the feasible domain and let \(X\subseteq D\) contain a global minimizer. Assume that, for every \(z\in D\), a local phase can produce \(x\in X\) with \(f(x)\le f(z)\), and that a global phase applied to \(x\in X\) either certifies that \(x\) is globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal or returns \(z\in D\) with \(f(z)<f(x)\). Starting from \(z^0\in D\), alternate these phases until certification. Each unsuccessful cycle produces \(x^{k+1}\in X\) satisfying \(f(x^{k+1})<f(x^k)\). Hence, if \(X\) is finite, the scheme terminates after finitely many cycles at a globally \(\varepsilon\)-optimal point. If \(X\) is infinite, finite termination is not guaranteed; convergence to a global optimum requires an additional convergence property of the organized process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible point, first find a no-worse point in a distinguished set X. Then either certify that point as globally epsilon-optimal or obtain a strictly better feasible point and repeat. Every unsuccessful cycle strictly decreases the objective at points of X, so a finite X guarantees finite termination. For infinite X, the process may continue indefinitely unless additional assumptions ensure convergence to a global optimum.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq D\text{ contains at least one global minimizer}
\forall z\in D\ \exists x\in X:\ f(x)\le f(z)
\forall x\in X,\ \text{the global phase either certifies global }\varepsilon\text{-optimality or returns }z\in D\text{ with }f(z)<f(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{An unsuccessful cycle gives }f(x^{k+1})<f(x^k);\quad |X|<\infty\Longrightarrow\text{finite termination at a global }\varepsilon\text{-optimal point}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a constrained minimization problem with separately chosen nonnegative tolerances for its constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), define \(S_\delta:=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\leq\delta_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). A point \(x\in X\) is \(\delta\)-feasible exactly when \(x\in S_\delta\). A point \(x^\star\in S_\delta\) is \(\delta\)-optimal when \(f(x^\star)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in S_\delta\). The components \(\delta_i\) may differ, including zero tolerances for some constraints and positive tolerances for others.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given one nonnegative tolerance for each constraint, a point is delta-feasible when every constraint violation is at most its corresponding tolerance. A delta-optimal point globally minimizes the objective over this relaxed feasible set. Different constraints may use different tolerances, including zero or positive values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star\text{ is }\delta\text{-optimal}\iff x^\star\in S_\delta\ \land\ \forall x\in S_\delta,\ f(x^\star)\leq f(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a model with a nonempty decision domain \(X\), inequality functions \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), equality functions \(h_j:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\), and an objective function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is infeasible exactly when its constraints have no common satisfying point. Its feasible set is then empty, so the constrained objective has no minimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Optimal Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-infimum status for feasible minimization models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\neq\varnothing\) and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be finite at some feasible point. The minimization model has a finite optimal value when \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\). Finiteness of \(f^\star\) does not imply attainment: the global solution set \(S^\star:=\{x\in C:f(x)=f^\star\}\) may be empty. If \(S^\star\neq\varnothing\), every member of \(S^\star\) has objective value \(f^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible minimization model has finite optimal value when its infimum is a real number, whether or not any feasible point attains it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{finite optimal value}\iff -\infty<f^\star<+\infty.\)

notation.meaning: infimum of the objective over the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Infimum Without Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation property intrinsic to every finite, possibly unattained, infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\neq\varnothing\), let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and suppose \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb R\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(x_\varepsilon\in C\) such that \(f^\star\le f(x_\varepsilon)<f^\star+\varepsilon\). Consequently, a sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) exists with \(f(x_k)\to f^\star\), even when the infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite infimum has feasible points of arbitrarily small positive objective error and therefore a minimizing sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall\varepsilon>0)(\exists x_\varepsilon\in C)\quad f^\star\le f(x_\varepsilon)<f^\star+\varepsilon.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Optimal Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded-below status for feasible minimization models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\neq\varnothing\) and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). The minimization model is unbounded below when \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=-\infty\). Equivalently, for every real threshold \(M\) there exists \(x_M\in C\) such that \(f(x_M)<M\). Thus no finite global optimal value exists and no feasible point can be a global minimizer. This status concerns objective values and is distinct from infeasibility of the constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible minimization model is unbounded below when feasible objective values fall below every real threshold; it then has no finite global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=-\infty\iff (\forall M\in\mathbb{R})(\exists x_M\in C)\ f(x_M)<M.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Continuous Attainment Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weierstrass attainment theorem for compact feasible domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty compact subset of a metric space and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Then the infimum \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) is finite and attained: there exists \(x^\star\in C\) such that \(f(x^\star)=f^\star\). Moreover, the global solution set \(S^\star:=\{x\in C:f(x)=f^\star\}\) is a nonempty compact subset of \(C\). Uniqueness is not implied without an additional hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous real-valued objective on a nonempty compact feasible set attains its finite minimum, and its minimizer set is nonempty and compact.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty compact subset of a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\text{ is nonempty and compact}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Unbounded-Domain Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment on closed noncompact Euclidean feasible sets via coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be lower semicontinuous and coercive on \(C\), meaning \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\) whenever \(x_k\in C\) and \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\). Then \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) is finite and attained. The global minimizer set \(S^\star:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is nonempty and compact, even when \(C\) is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous coercive objective on a nonempty closed Euclidean feasible set attains its minimum and has a nonempty compact minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\text{ is nonempty and compact}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Finite Infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-value nonattainment for feasible minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\neq\varnothing\) and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). The model has an unattained finite infimum when \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\) but no \(x\in C\) satisfies \(f(x)=f^\star\). Equivalently, the global solution set is empty while, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(x_\varepsilon\in C\) with \(f(x_\varepsilon)<f^\star+\varepsilon\). Hence arbitrarily accurate positive-tolerance global solutions exist although no exact global solution exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum is finite but unattained when no feasible point reaches it, even though feasible points can approach it within every positive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad(\forall\varepsilon>0)(\exists x_\varepsilon\in C)\ f(x_\varepsilon)<f^\star+\varepsilon.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of finite nonattainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and epsilon-approximation characterization are mathematically precise and fit the terminal container, but the record supplies no inspectable source reference or specific definition locator.

children.title: Boundary-Approach Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonattainment caused by feasible sequences approaching an excluded boundary.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional boundary-approach example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=(0,1]\) and \(f(x)=x\), \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=0\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing\). Moreover, every minimizing sequence satisfies \(x_k\to0\in\overline C\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing x over (0,1] approaches the excluded endpoint zero without attaining the infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\star=0\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}_Cf=\varnothing\), and every minimizing sequence converges to \(0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Boundary Nonattainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary localization of bounded minimizing sequences under continuous extendability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), suppose \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) has a finite unattained infimum \(f^\star\), and suppose \(f\) extends continuously to \(\overline C\). Every bounded minimizing sequence has a subsequence converging to some \(\bar x\in\overline C\setminus C\), and every cluster point of that sequence satisfies \(\bar f(\bar x)=f^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a continuous extension to the closure, a bounded minimizing sequence accumulates only at excluded boundary points having the limiting optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_{k_j}\to\bar x\in\overline C\setminus C\), and every cluster point \(\bar x\) satisfies \(\bar f(\bar x)=f^\star\).

notation.meaning: continuous extension of the objective to the closure

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Point Characterization of Boundary Approach
Boundary-Approach Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment witnessed by convergence to an excluded boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\), and suppose \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\) is unattained. The model is in a boundary-approach regime when there exist \(\bar{x}\in\overline{C}\setminus C\) and a sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) such that \(x_k\to\bar{x}\) and \(f(x_k)\to f^\star\). Thus nonattainment is witnessed by feasible points approaching a finite excluded boundary point rather than escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary-approach regime occurs when a minimizing sequence converges to a finite point in the closure that is excluded from the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\exists\bar{x}\in\overline C\setminus C)(\exists(x_k)\subset C)\ x_k\to\bar{x}\ \text{and}\ f(x_k)\to f^\star.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequence-based classification of finite nonattainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequence condition is internally coherent and condition is an appropriate role for this regime leaf. However, the classification terminology and its exact scope require an authoritative source with a specific locator before acceptance.

children.title: Minimizing-Sequence Escape
children.top_down_role: Nonattainment associated with optimizing sequences leaving every bounded region.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical smooth example of finite nonattainment at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=[0,\infty)\) and \(f(x)=e^{-x}\), the infimum is zero and is not attained. A sequence is minimizing if and only if \(x_k\to+\infty\), so every minimizing sequence escapes every bounded subset of \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function exp(-x) on the nonnegative line approaches zero only as x escapes to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_Cf=0\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}_Cf=\varnothing\), and \(f(x_k)\to0\iff x_k\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Escape at Infinity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss-of-compactness characterization on closed Euclidean feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be lower semicontinuous with finite unattained infimum \(f^\star\). Then every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) satisfies \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\), equivalently, it eventually leaves every compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a closed Euclidean feasible set with a lower-semicontinuous objective, finite nonattainment forces every minimizing sequence to escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)\to f^\star\implies\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Lower-Semicontinuous Nonattainment Forces Escape
Minimizing-Sequence Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment witnessed by a sequence escaping every bounded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and unbounded, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\), and suppose \(f^\star:=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\) is unattained. A minimizing sequence escapes to infinity when \((x_k)\subset C\), \(f(x_k)\to f^\star\), and \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\). Equivalently, the sequence eventually leaves every bounded subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Such a sequence witnesses loss of compactness at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimizing sequence escapes when its objective values approach the finite infimum while its points eventually leave every bounded region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_k)\text{ escapes while minimizing}\iff f(x_k)\to f^\star\text{ and }\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The escape-to-infinity condition and its equivalence with eventually leaving every bounded Euclidean set are correct, and the selected content kind fits the terminal container. No inspectable source reference or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Model Information-Regularity-Geometry Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Classifies models by available representation, analytic regularity, observation model, and search-domain geometry.

children.title: Model-Access Regimes
children.top_down_role: Separates symbolic, evaluation-only, expensive, and uncertain access to objectives and constraints.

children.title: Symbolically Structured Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for algebraic and computational-graph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Symbolically Structured Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite expression-graph representation of objectives and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous optimization model on a domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is symbolically structured when every objective and constraint function is supplied as a finite directed acyclic expression graph. Its leaves are variables or known constants, and each internal vertex applies an identified primitive operation from a specified library. Thus function values and intermediate quantities are determined by recursively evaluating the graph, and the algebraic structure is available to the optimization method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symbolically structured model exposes each objective and constraint as a finite computational graph built from known constants, variables, and primitive operations.
assumptions_latex: The library of primitive operations and their domains is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_j(x)=v_{j,\mathrm{root}}(x)\) is represented by a finite expression graph for every model function \(f_j\).

notation.meaning: root value of the expression graph for function j

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of ordinary recursive expression-graph semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symbolic graph does not define a total function on \(D\) if a feasible evaluation applies a primitive outside its declared domain. A directed cycle is not an acyclic recursively evaluable expression and instead requires separately justified implicit-system semantics, including existence and uniqueness where needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Out-of-domain primitives or graph cycles invalidate ordinary recursive expression evaluation.
assumptions_latex: A symbolic representation is proposed on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Finite acyclicity and primitive-domain validity are required for the declared recursive semantics.}
knowledge_statements.title: Primitive-Domain and Cyclicity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact auxiliary-variable representation of an expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed acyclic expression graph with internal relations \(v_i=\phi_i((v_j)_{j\in\operatorname{pa}(i)})\), introduce an auxiliary variable \(z_i\) for every internal vertex and impose \(z_i=\phi_i((z_j)_{j\in\operatorname{pa}(i)})\). If every primitive is well-defined, projection onto the original variables and root values reproduces the graph-defined model exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning a variable and defining equation to each intermediate expression gives an exact lifted formulation.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
Every primitive is well-defined at represented feasible evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{x,z_{\mathrm{root}}}\{(x,z):z_i=\phi_i(z_{\operatorname{pa}(i)})\}=\{(x,f(x)):x\in D\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Graph Lifting

children.title: Deterministic Black-Box Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for repeatable evaluation-only models.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Black-Box Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeatable evaluation-only access to a continuous global objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A deterministic black-box model for \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) provides an evaluation oracle \(\mathcal O_f\) satisfying \(\mathcal O_f(x)=f(x)\) for every query \(x\in D\). Repeated evaluations at the same point return the same value. No symbolic expression, derivative, decomposition, or other internal representation of \(f\) is assumed available unless separately declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimizer can query exact, repeatable function values, but it is not given formulas, derivatives, or internal model structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_f(x)=f(x)\) and \(\mathcal O_f(x)\) is invariant across repeated queries at \(x\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1 General Problem Statement and Special Model Forms p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 General Problem Statement and Special Model Forms p. 3

children.title: Expensive-Evaluation Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for evaluation-budget-dominated global optimization.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Global Optimization: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Global Optimization: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box access in which evaluation expenditure is the designated primary resource, without requiring a particular hard-budget semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An expensive-evaluation model is an oracle model equipped with a declared evaluation-resource measure under which obtaining objective or constraint observations is the designated dominant computational cost. For queries \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\), this measure may be query count, \(N\), or an aggregate declared cost \(\sum_{i=1}^N c(x_i)\). A hard budget may restrict this resource but is not part of the definition. Expensiveness is orthogonal to whether observations are deterministic or noisy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expensive-evaluation models treat oracle evaluations as the primary resource; they may use query count or declared per-query costs, with or without a fixed budget, and may be deterministic or noisy.
assumptions_latex: An objective or constraint evaluation oracle is available.
A query-count or evaluation-cost resource measure is declared.
Evaluation expenditure is designated as the dominant resource for the model class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Performance and admissibility are assessed primarily through the declared evaluation resource, without implying deterministic observations or a mandatory fixed budget.

notation.meaning: Declared cost of an evaluation at x when nonuniform costs are modeled.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Cost-Dominated Access Regime
Expensive-Evaluation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box optimization classified by an explicit evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and assign each oracle query at \(x\in D\) a positive cost \(c(x)\). An expensive-evaluation model is a black-box optimization model equipped with a finite budget \(B>0\), for which an admissible algorithm may query points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) only when \(\sum_{i=1}^{N}c(x_i)\leq B\). Its output is computed from the resulting observations, and evaluation cost is the designated limiting resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expensive-evaluation model limits oracle queries by a finite cost budget, making evaluation expenditure the primary computational resource.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^{N}c(x_i)\leq B\) is required for every admissible evaluation sequence.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No inspectable citation supports identifying all expensive-evaluation models with a predetermined additive query-cost budget. This is a coherent budgeted subclass, but the exact scope requires a dedicated source.

children.title: Noisy Observation Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for uncertain or randomized evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Observation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized oracle access with point-dependent observation laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A noisy observation model supplies, at each queried \(x\in D\), a random observation \(Y(x,\xi)\) having a specified or unknown conditional law \(P_x\). For repeated queries, observations need not coincide. When the optimization target is the mean response, the objective is \(F(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\), provided the expectation exists; other declared distributional functionals may replace the mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A query returns a random value governed by a point-dependent distribution; the optimized quantity may be its expectation or another declared distributional functional.
assumptions_latex: For a mean-response objective, \(\mathbb E[|Y(x,\xi)|]<\infty\) for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(x,\xi)\sim P_x\), with \(F(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\) in the mean-response formulation.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 General Minimization Problem p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 General Minimization Problem p. 5

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive representation separating a declared target, systematic mean bias, and centered random error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integrable observation \(Y(x)\) and declared target \(F(x)\), define \[b(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x)]-F(x),\qquad \varepsilon(x)=Y(x)-\mathbb E[Y(x)].\] Then \[Y(x)=F(x)+b(x)+\varepsilon(x),\qquad \mathbb E[\varepsilon(x)]=0.\] Thus mean-unbiased observation, \(\mathbb E[Y(x)]=F(x)\), is an additional condition equivalent to \(b(x)=0\); repeated averaging targets \(\mathbb E[Y(x)]\), not an unidentified \(F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable observation decomposes into the declared target, systematic mean bias, and centered noise; unbiasedness is an extra assumption and averaging does not remove bias.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(x)=F(x)+b(x)+\varepsilon(x)\) with \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon(x)]=0\), and \(\mathbb E[Y(x)]=F(x)\) exactly when \(b(x)=0\).

notation.meaning: Systematic mean bias relative to the declared target.

knowledge_statements.title: Bias–Noise Decomposition of Observations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General scalar observation model for an inexact evaluation, without assuming Gaussian, additive, homoskedastic, or independent noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), an observation at \(x\in\mathcal X\) has latent objective value \(\phi=f(x)\). A stochastic observation model specifies the conditional distribution of the measured value \(y\) as \(p(y\mid x,\phi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The measured response at a selected location may be generated from a conditional distribution depending on both that location and the latent objective value there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\mid x,f(x)\sim p(\,\cdot\mid x,f(x)).

children.title: Smoothness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Separates differentiability levels relevant to global underestimation and exclusion.

children.title: Twice-Differentiable Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for curvature-based deterministic global models.

knowledge_statements.title: Twice-Differentiable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The continuously twice-differentiable finite-dimensional regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(U\) be an open neighborhood of \(D\). A model is twice-differentiable in the curvature-based sense when every objective and constraint function \(f_j:U\to\mathbb{R}\) belongs to \(C^2(U)\). Consequently, its gradient \(\nabla f_j(x)\) and symmetric Hessian \(\nabla^2 f_j(x)\) exist at every \(x\in U\), and the Hessian varies continuously on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every objective and constraint extends to a continuously twice-differentiable function near the search domain, so gradients and continuous Hessians are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_j\in C^2(U)\) for every objective or constraint function \(f_j\).

notation.meaning: open neighborhood of the search domain

source_refs.locator: Chapter 10. From Biconvex to General Twice Differentiable NLPs p. 309
Chapter 11. The alphaBB for Box Constrained Twice-Differentiable NLPs: Theory p. 315

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 10. From Biconvex to General Twice Differentiable NLPs p. 309
Chapter 11. The alphaBB for Box Constrained Twice-Differentiable NLPs: Theory p. 315

knowledge_statements.statement_title: C2 Regularity Does Not Give a Global Curvature Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniform Hessian bounds on an unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x^4\) belongs to \(C^2(\mathbb R)\), but \(f''(x)=12x^2\) is unbounded. Thus C2 regularity on an unbounded domain does not by itself provide a global Lipschitz constant for \(\nabla f\) or a finite uniform quadratic-remainder constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Although x^4 is C2 everywhere, its Hessian is unbounded, so uniform curvature bounds require compactness or a separate bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in C^2(\mathbb R)\quad\text{and}\quad\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|f''(x)|=\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: C2 Regularity Does Not Give a Global Curvature Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic expansion supplied by C2 regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\in C^2(U)\) and \([x,x+h]\subset U\), then \[f(x+h)=f(x)+
abla f(x)^Th+\int_0^1(1-t)h^T
abla^2f(x+th)h\,dt.\] Equivalently, for some \(	heta\in(0,1)\), \[f(x+h)=f(x)+
abla f(x)^Th+	frac12h^T
abla^2f(x+	heta h)h.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A C2 function admits an exact second-order Taylor expansion with an integral or intermediate-point Hessian remainder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x+h)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^Th+\tfrac12h^T\nabla^2f(x+\theta h)h\text{ for some }\theta\in(0,1).
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Taylor Formula

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded-Hessian Consequences on Compact Convex Subdomains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform gradient and Taylor-error controls derived from continuous curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subset U\) be compact and convex and let \(f\in C^2(U)\). With \(M=\max_{z\in K}\|
abla^2f(z)\|_2\), \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|\] and \[|f(y)-f(x)-
abla f(x)^T(y-x)|\le	frac M2\|y-x\|^2\] for all \(x,y\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous Hessian is bounded on a compact convex subdomain, making the gradient Lipschitz and uniformly bounding the quadratic Taylor error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f;K)\le M,\quad |f(y)-f(x)-\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)|\le\frac M2\|y-x\|^2.

notation.meaning: maximum Hessian spectral norm on K

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Hessian Consequences on Compact Convex Subdomains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity criterion requiring an additional convex-domain assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f\in C^2(U)\). Then \[f\text{ is convex on }U\iff \nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\quad\forall x\in U.\] If \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq\mu I\) for every \(x\in U\) and some \(\mu>0\), then \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For C2 functions on open convex domains, positive-semidefinite Hessians characterize convexity and a uniform positive lower bound gives strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ convex}\iff\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\ \forall x\in U.
knowledge_statements.title: Hessian Characterization of Convexity

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is C2 regularity, second-order Taylor structure, compact-convex Hessian bounds, and failure of global curvature boundedness on noncompact domains. The Hessian convexity criterion was deferred to Smooth Convex Models. AlphaBB, Newton methods, DC constructions, and derivative-oracle access were excluded as adjacent scopes.

children.title: First-Order Smooth Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for differentiable models without globally usable second-order structure.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Smooth Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuously differentiable models without an imposed second-order hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(U\) be an open neighborhood of \(D\). A model is first-order smooth when every objective and constraint function \(f_j:U\to\mathbb{R}\) belongs to \(C^1(U)\). Thus \(\nabla f_j(x)\) exists for all \(x\in U\) and is continuous on \(U\). No existence, continuity, or algorithmic availability of \(\nabla^2 f_j\) is included in this classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every model function has a continuous gradient near the domain, while no usable second-order structure is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_j\in C^1(U)\) for every objective or constraint function \(f_j\).

notation.meaning: open neighborhood of the search domain

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Gradient Need Not Be Lipschitz or Twice Differentiable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation of C1 regularity from Lipschitz-gradient and C2 regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=|x|^{3/2}\) belongs to \(C^1(\mathbb R)\), with \(f'(x)=\tfrac32\operatorname{sgn}(x)|x|^{1/2}\), but \(f'\) is not locally Lipschitz at \(0\) and \(f''(0)\) does not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function |x|^(3/2) is continuously differentiable but has neither a locally Lipschitz derivative nor a second derivative at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in C^1(\mathbb R)\setminus C^2(\mathbb R),\quad f'\text{ is not locally Lipschitz at }0.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Gradient Need Not Be Lipschitz or Twice Differentiable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local affine approximation supplied by C1 regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\in C^1(U)\), then for every \(x\in U\), \[f(x+h)=f(x)+
abla f(x)^Th+o(\|h\|)\quad(h	o0).\] Whenever \([x,x+h]\subset U\), the exact remainder is \[f(x+h)-f(x)-
abla f(x)^Th=\int_0^1[
abla f(x+th)-
abla f(x)]^Th\,dt.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable function has a first-order expansion with an exact remainder controlled by variation of its gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x+h)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^Th+o(\|h\|).
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Expansion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Continuity on Compact Convex Subdomains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-value regularity implied by bounded continuous gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset U\) be compact and convex and let \(f\in C^1(U)\). Then \(M=\max_{x\in K}\|\nabla f(x)\|<\infty\) and \[|f(x)-f(y)|\le M\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in K).\] Thus first-order smoothness makes function values Lipschitz on each compact convex subdomain, but does not necessarily make the gradient Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous gradient is bounded on a compact convex subdomain, making the function Lipschitz there, although the gradient itself need not be Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Lip}(f;K)\le\max_{x\in K}\|\nabla f(x)\|.
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Continuity on Compact Convex Subdomains

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz continuity of smooth functions on bounded robust subsets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A regularity implication for first-order smooth models on bounded search sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a bounded, robust set contained in an open convex set \(D_0\), and let \(f:D_0\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable. Then \(f\) is Lipschitz-continuous on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a bounded, robust set lies in an open convex set on which a function is continuously differentiable, then the function is Lipschitz-continuous on the bounded set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz-continuous on }D

children.title: Nonsmooth Continuous Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for continuous models with kinks or active-piece transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Continuous Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous models permitting failure of classical differentiability relative to the domain's affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) have nonempty relative interior, let \(A=\operatorname{aff}(D)\), and let \(V=A-A\). A model is nonsmooth continuous when every objective and constraint function \(f_j:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued and continuous on \(D\), while at least one \(f_k\) fails to be differentiable relative to \(A\) at some \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(D)\). Here relative differentiability means that there exists a linear map \(\ell:V\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(f_k(x+h)=f_k(x)+\ell(h)+o(\lVert h\rVert)\) as \(h\to0\) through vectors satisfying \(x+h\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every model function is finite-valued and continuous, but at least one fails to have a classical first-order derivative relative to the affine hull of the domain at an interior point.
assumptions_latex: Every model function is finite-valued on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_j\in C(D)\) for every \(j\), and some \(f_k\) is not differentiable relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(D)\) at some \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(D)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity Does Not Imply Local Lipschitzness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure boundary for bounded-slope generalized derivative models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=\sqrt{|x|}\) is finite and continuous on \(\mathbb R\) and is nondifferentiable at \(0\), but it is not locally Lipschitz there because \[\frac{|f(x)-f(0)|}{|x|}=|x|^{-1/2}\to\infty.\] Hence continuity and nonsmoothness alone do not guarantee bounded slopes or a Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square root of |x| is continuous and nonsmooth but not locally Lipschitz at zero, so continuity alone supplies no bounded-slope generalized derivative model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in C(\mathbb R)\text{ but }f\text{ is not locally Lipschitz at }0.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuity Does Not Imply Local Lipschitzness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical active-piece construction of a nonsmooth continuous function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(f_i:U\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be continuous. Then \(f=\max_i f_i\) is continuous. If every active \(f_i\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \[f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\nabla f_i(x)^Td,\qquad I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}.\] If two active gradients differ, this directional derivative is not linear in \(d\), so \(f\) is not classically differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite maxima preserve continuity, and a transition between active differentiable pieces with different gradients creates a kink.
assumptions_latex: For the directional-derivative conclusion, every active \(f_i\) is differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=\max_i f_i\in C(U),\quad f'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\nabla f_i(x)^Td.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Maximum Kinks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic compactness consequence of continuity, not a result specific to nonsmooth models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\) is nonempty and compact and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is continuous, then \(f\) is uniformly continuous and bounded and attains its minimum and maximum on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous function on a nonempty compact domain is uniformly continuous, bounded, and attains both extrema.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{D}f\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname*{argmax}_{D}f\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Domain Attainment

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Lipschitz control relative to a specified norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and fix a norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\). A function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is Lipschitz on \(D\) when there exists a finite constant \(L\geq0\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in D.\] A Lipschitz function model requires this condition for each designated objective or constraint, with its constant and norm either known or treated as model parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Function variation is bounded everywhere on the domain by a fixed constant times the distance between the two points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\neq y,\,x,y\in D}|f(x)-f(y)|/\lVert x-y\rVert\leq L<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable characterization using the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\) if and only if \(\|\nabla f(x)\|_*\le L\) for every \(x\in D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz function on an open Euclidean domain is differentiable almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is differentiable almost everywhere on }U.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Functions and Lipschitz Global Optimization Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Lipschitz continuity and the problem class in which the objective and constraint functions are Lipschitz continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Y\), with norms chosen on the argument and value spaces. The function \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous if there exists \(L\in(0,\infty)\) such that \(\|f(x)-f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in X\). Such an \(L\) is called a Lipschitz constant. A global optimization problem whose objective and constraint functions are Lipschitz continuous is called a Lipschitz global optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is Lipschitz continuous if a finite positive constant bounds the difference between any two function values by that constant times the difference between their arguments. That constant is a Lipschitz constant. A global optimization problem with Lipschitz objective and constraint functions is a Lipschitz global optimization problem.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ and }Y\text{ are equipped with the chosen norms}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall x,y\in X,\ \|f(x)-f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\right)\Longrightarrow f\text{ is Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant }L;\quad \text{Lipschitz objective and constraint functions define a Lipschitz global optimization problem.}
