knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental unconstrained optimality property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and pseudoconvex. If \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\), then \(x^*\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every stationary point of a differentiable pseudoconvex function is globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudoconvex Stationarity Is Globally Sufficient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Minima of Pseudoconvex Programs Are Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global property for pseudoconvex minimization over a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of an open convex set \(D\), and let differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be pseudoconvex. Every local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\) is a global minimizer over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudoconvexity rules out nonglobal local minima on convex feasible sets.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Local Minima of Pseudoconvex Programs Are Global

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Sufficiency with Quasiconvex Inequality Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global constrained certificate for a pseudoconvex objective and differentiable quasiconvex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and pseudoconvex, and let each differentiable \(g_i:D\to\mathbb R\) be quasiconvex. If \(x^*\) is feasible and multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\) satisfy \[\nabla f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0,\] then \(x^*\) globally minimizes \(f\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT conditions are globally sufficient for a pseudoconvex objective with differentiable quasiconvex inequality constraints.
assumptions_latex: Every \(g_i\) is differentiable and quasiconvex on \(D\).
Feasibility, stationarity, multiplier nonnegativity, and complementarity hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{f(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Sufficiency with Quasiconvex Inequality Constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict derivative-based variant of differentiable pseudoconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:D	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable. The function is strictly pseudoconvex if, for all distinct \(x,y\in D\), \[f(y)\le f(x)\Longrightarrow 
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)<0.\] Equivalently, \(
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\ge0\) implies \(f(y)>f(x)\) whenever \(x
e y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict pseudoconvexity makes every direction toward a distinct point of no greater value a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(y)\le f(x),\ x\ne y\Longrightarrow\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)<0.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Pseudoconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion of differentiable convex objectives in the pseudoconvex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and convex and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex, then \(f\) is pseudoconvex on \(D\). The converse fails: \(f(x)=x+x^3\) is pseudoconvex on \(\mathbb R\), because \(f'(x)=1+3x^2>0\), but it is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every differentiable convex function is pseudoconvex, while a strictly increasing nonconvex function disproves the converse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is pseudoconvex on }D.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable Convexity Implies Pseudoconvexity
Pseudoconvex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable generalized-convex minimization based on a first-order implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable. The function \(f\) is pseudoconvex on \(D\) if, for every \(x,y\in D\), \[\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\geq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(y)\geq f(x).\] Equivalently, \(f(y)<f(x)\) implies \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)<0\). A pseudoconvex model minimizes such a function over a convex subset of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudoconvexity makes every direction toward a lower value a strict descent direction at the current point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\geq0\) implies \(f(y)\geq f(x)\) for all \(x,y\in D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconvexity, pseudoconvexity, and polynomial special cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-convexity definitions, implications, exceptional polynomial classes, and recognition boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} is quasiconvex if \{x:f(x)\leq s\} is convex for every s\in\mathbb{R}. A differentiable f is pseudoconvex if \nabla f(x)^T(y-x)\geq0 implies f(y)\geq f(x) for all x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n. In general, convexity implies pseudoconvexity, which implies quasiconvexity, and neither converse holds. For quadratic polynomials and for homogeneous polynomials of even degree, the three notions coincide; in the quadratic case they are recognizable in polynomial time. For even polynomial degree greater than two, recognizing pseudoconvexity or quasiconvexity is computationally difficult.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasiconvexity means that every lower level set is convex. Pseudoconvexity means that a nonnegative directional derivative from x toward y forces the value at y to be at least the value at x. Convexity implies pseudoconvexity, which implies quasiconvexity, but the converses generally fail. The notions coincide for quadratic polynomials and homogeneous even-degree polynomials; quadratic recognition is polynomial-time, whereas recognition beyond degree two is difficult.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{convex}\implies\text{pseudoconvex}\implies\text{quasiconvex},\quad\text{with no general converses; the notions coincide for quadratics and homogeneous even-degree polynomials.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global certificate for differentiable inequality-constrained invex programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Suppose \(D\) is invex and \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are differentiable and invex with respect to the same map \(\eta\). If a feasible \(x^*\) and multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\) satisfy \[\nabla f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x^*)=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i(x^*)=0,\] then \(x^*\) is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KKT conditions are globally sufficient when the objective and constraints share the same invexity map.
assumptions_latex: The domain, objective, and all inequality functions use one common invexity map.
\(x^*\) is feasible and the displayed stationarity, nonnegativity, and complementarity conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Map Invex KKT Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit differentiable nonconvex invex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x+x^3\) on \(\mathbb R\) and define \[\eta(y,x)=\frac{f(y)-f(x)}{f'(x)}=\frac{y+y^3-x-x^3}{1+3x^2}.\] Since \(f'(x)>0\), this map is defined everywhere and \(f(y)-f(x)=f'(x)\eta(y,x)\), so \(f\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\). Yet \(f''(x)=6x\) changes sign, so \(f\) is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The increasing cubic-plus-linear function is invex for an explicit map but is not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\) but is not convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Invexity Strictly Extends Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is the Straight-Displacement Special Case
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between differentiable convexity and invexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex, then the inequality \[f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\] holds with \(\eta(y,x)=y-x\). Thus differentiable convexity is the straight-displacement invex special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiable convex functions are invex for the ordinary displacement map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies the invex inequality with \(\eta(y,x)=y-x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is the Straight-Displacement Special Case

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary Invex Points Are Global Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental unconstrained invex optimality result under an explicit eta convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be invex with respect to \(\eta\), and suppose differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \[f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\quad(x,y\in D).\] If \(\nabla f(x^*)=0\), then \(f(y)\ge f(x^*)\) for every \(y\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every stationary point of an invex function is globally minimizing.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and satisfies the displayed invex inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Invex Points Are Global Minima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak and KKT-based strong duality for a differentiable common-map invex inequality program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{f(x):x\in D,\ g_i(x)\le0\}\), consider the Wolfe dual \[\max_{u\in D,\lambda\ge0}\ f(u)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(u)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \nabla f(u)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla g_i(u)=0.\] If \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) are differentiable and invex with respect to one common map \(\eta\), every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \((u,\lambda)\) satisfy \(f(x)\ge f(u)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(u)\). If an optimal primal point admits KKT multipliers, its KKT pair is dual optimal and the values coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common invexity map gives weak Wolfe duality, while an optimal KKT pair gives strong duality and dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: The domain and all model functions use the same invexity map \(\eta\).
For strong duality, an optimal primal point with KKT multipliers exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^*\le p^*\); an optimal primal KKT pair satisfies \(d^*=p^*\) and attains the dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Map Invex Wolfe Duality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of invex functions sharing one displacement map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_r:D\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and invex with respect to the same map \(\eta\), and let \(a_k\ge0\). Then \(F=\sum_{k=1}^r a_kf_k\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\): \[F(y)-F(x)\ge \nabla F(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\qquad(x,y\in D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative linear combination of differentiable functions sharing one invexity map remains invex for that map.
assumptions_latex: \(f_k\) is differentiable and invex with respect to the same \(\eta\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k=1}^r a_kf_k\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Local Minima of Invex Functions Are Global
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global result obtained from first-order stationarity on an open invex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and invex with respect to \(\eta\), and let differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \[f(y)-f(x)\ge \nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\qquad(x,y\in D).\] Every local minimizer \(x^*\in D\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open invex domain, every local minimum of a differentiable invex function is global.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is open and invex with respect to \(\eta\).
\(f\) is differentiable and invex with respect to \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-fixed definition of differentiable invex models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\eta:D\times D\to\mathbb R^n\). The domain is invex with respect to \(\eta\) when \(x+t\eta(y,x)\in D\) for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). A differentiable \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is invex with respect to this same map when \(f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\) for all \(x,y\in D\). Here the second argument \(x\) is the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invexity replaces the straight displacement from x to y in the convex gradient inequality by a specified feasible displacement map.
assumptions_latex: The argument order of \(\eta(y,x)\) is fixed with \(x\) as base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x+t\eta(y,x)\in D,\qquad f(y)-f(x)\ge\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x).

notation.meaning: Invex displacement based at \(x\) and directed toward the comparison point \(y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Invexity Gives a Unique Stationary Minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict variant of stationary-point global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be invex with respect to \(\eta\), and let differentiable \(f:D	o\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f(y)-f(x)>
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\) whenever \(x
e y\). If \(
abla f(x^*)=0\), then \(f(y)>f(x^*)\) for every \(y
e x^*\). Hence \(x^*\) is the unique global minimizer and no other stationary point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every stationary point of a strictly invex function is its unique global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The strict invex inequality holds for distinct points.

Invex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable generalized-convex models defined relative to an invexity map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\eta:D\times D\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(x+t\eta(y,x)\in D\) for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). A differentiable function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is invex with respect to \(\eta\) if \[f(y)-f(x)\geq\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\] for every \(x,y\in D\). An invex model minimizes such a function on an \(\eta\)-invex feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invexity replaces straight-line displacements in the convex gradient inequality by a specified invexity map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)-f(x)\geq\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}\eta(y,x)\) for every \(x,y\in D\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines concave minimization over an explicitly represented closed convex set, its set-difference lifting, its quasiconcave extension, and the polyhedral specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be closed and convex, with each \(g_i\) convex, and let \(f\) be concave. Concave minimization is \[\min\{f(x):x\in D\}.\] It is equivalently \[\min\{t:(x,t)\in G\setminus H\},\qquad G=D\times\mathbb R,\quad H=\{(x,t):f(x)>t\},\] where \(H\) is convex. Requiring only that \(f\) be quasiconcave gives quasiconcave minimization; if \(D\) is polyhedral, the concave problem is linearly constrained concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concave minimization minimizes a concave objective over a closed convex set described by convex inequalities. It admits an equivalent lifted set-difference formulation. Quasiconcave minimization relaxes concavity to quasiconcavity, and a polyhedral feasible set yields the linearly constrained subclass.
assumptions_latex: D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\text{ is closed and convex}
f\text{ is concave; for the extension, }f\text{ is quasiconcave}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in D}f(x)=\min\{t:(x,t)\in(D\times\mathbb R)\setminus\{(x,t):f(x)>t\}\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for problem (P) and the sign-reversal representation connecting convex maximization with concave minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\) denote the global minimum value of problem \((P)\) over its feasible set \(D\). A point \(x^*\in D\) satisfying \(f(x^*)=v\) is a global optimal solution (global minimum), and \(X^*=\{x\in D:f(x)=v\}\) denotes the set of all such solutions. If \(v=-\infty\), then \((P)\) is unbounded. If \(g\) is convex and \(Y\) is convex, then maximizing \(g\) over \(Y\) is equivalent to minimizing the concave function \(-g\) over \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symbol v denotes the global minimum value of (P), and X* is the set of feasible points attaining it. The problem is called unbounded when v is minus infinity. Maximizing a convex function over a convex set is equivalently formulated as minimizing its concave negative over the same set.

children.title: Separable Concave Minimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of independent minimization on a coupled convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^2:x_1+x_2=1\}\) and \(\phi_1(u)=\phi_2(u)=-u^2\). Then \[\min_{x\in C}\bigl(\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\bigr)=-1,\] whereas \[\min_{u\in[0,1]}\phi_1(u)+\min_{u\in[0,1]}\phi_2(u)=-2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear coupling constraint can invalidate independent coordinate minimization despite objective separability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\sum_j\phi_j(x_j)=-1>-2=\sum_j\min_{u\in[0,1]}\phi_j(u)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling Can Prevent Coordinatewise Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise additive concave objectives on a common convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. If each \(\phi_j\) is concave on the projection of \(C\) onto coordinate \(j\), then a separable concave-minimization problem has the form \[\inf_{x\in C}\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j).\] Separability means that each summand depends on only one decision coordinate; it does not require the feasible set to be a Cartesian product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable concave-minimization problem minimizes a sum of univariate concave coordinate functions; feasibility may still couple the coordinates.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\phi_j\) is concave on the relevant coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective \(x\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j)\) is concave and additively separable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Additively Separable Concave Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Decomposition on Cartesian Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent coordinate minimization when feasibility contains no cross-coordinate coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\prod_{j=1}^n C_j\), where every \(C_j\) is nonempty, and suppose each scalar infimum is finite. Then \[\inf_{x\in C}\sum_{j=1}^n\phi_j(x_j)=\sum_{j=1}^n\inf_{u\in C_j}\phi_j(u).\] If every scalar infimum is attained, the global minimizer set equals \[\prod_{j=1}^n\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C_j}\phi_j(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Cartesian feasible set, an additively separable objective decomposes exactly into independent coordinate problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint infimum is the sum of the coordinate infima, with the stated product formula under attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Decomposition on Cartesian Feasible Sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex base optimization restricted by convex-function superlevel constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) be convex on \(C\). A reverse-convex program has the form \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\geq0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Each constraint retains a superlevel set of a convex function, equivalently excluding the convex strict sublevel set \(\{x\in C:g_i(x)<0\}\); the resulting feasible region is generally nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible region is \(C\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:g_i(x)\geq0\}\), equivalently the convex base with finitely many convex strict sublevel sets excluded.

children.title: Programs with Separated Nonconvexity
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for models with isolated or low-dimensional nonconvex components.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(G_i:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex in \(x\) for every fixed \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{F(x,y):G_i(x,y)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ (x,y)\in X\times Y\}\) has nonconvexity confined to the \(y\)-block.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a two-block formulation in which all failure of joint convexity is isolated in one block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A program has separated nonconvexity if it can be written as \[\inf_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}\ F(x,y)\quad\text{subject to}\quad G_i(x,y)\le 0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where, for each fixed \(y\in Y\), the functions \(x\mapsto F(x,y)\) and \(x\mapsto G_i(x,y)\) are convex on \(X\). Thus every fixed-\(y\) subproblem is convex, while nonconvex dependence may occur through \(y\) or through interactions between \(x\) and \(y\). The nonconvexity is low-dimensional when \(k=\dim Y\) is small relative to \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A program has separated nonconvexity when fixing a designated, often low-dimensional variable block leaves a convex optimization problem in all remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Programs with Separated Nonconvexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-block formulation is mathematically coherent and fits the navigation container, but no citation is supplied for the exact term or its proposed scope. An authoritative source is needed to distinguish this class from biconvex, partially convex, and low-dimensional nonconvex formulations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise strengthening of a gamma-valid cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded valid-cut result for the referenced linearly constrained quadratic construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(i=1,\ldots,n\), let \(y^i\in\operatorname{argmin}\{F(t_i e^i,y)\mid y\in M(t)\}\), and suppose \(f(y^i)\geq\gamma\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict convexity, coercivity, and compact sublevel sets of a quadratic restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent properties for a quadratic function restricted to an affine manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be quadratic and let \(H\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be an affine manifold. Then \(f|_H\) is strictly convex if and only if it is coercive on \(H\), meaning \[f(x)\to+\infty\quad\text{as }x\in H,\ \|x\|\to+\infty.\] These conditions are also equivalent to compactness of every sublevel set \(\{x\in H:f(x)\leq\eta\}\), \(\eta\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic function restricted to an affine manifold is strictly convex exactly when it is coercive there, equivalently when every real sublevel set of the restriction is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f|_H\text{ is strictly convex}\iff\left[f(x)\to+\infty\text{ as }x\in H,\ \|x\|\to+\infty\right]\iff\left[\forall\eta\in\mathbb{R},\ \{x\in H:f(x)\leq\eta\}\text{ is compact}\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-constraint quadratic optimization problem has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_1(x)\le 0,\] where \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\) and \(Q_i\in\mathbb{S}^n\) for \(i\in\{0,1\}\). No positive-semidefiniteness assumption is imposed in the general class. A trust-region problem is the subcase in which, for some \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(\rho\ge 0\), the single constraint is \(\lVert Ax-d\rVert_2^2\le\rho^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class minimizes a quadratic function subject to exactly one quadratic inequality. Indefinite matrices are allowed, and trust-region problems are an important subcase.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Constraint Quadratic Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact matrix certificate for the Euclidean-ball trust-region subcase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:\|x\|_2\le\Delta\}\) with \(\Delta>0\). A feasible \(x^*\) is globally optimal if and only if there exists \(\lambda^*\ge0\) such that \[(Q+\lambda^*I)x^*=-c,\qquad Q+\lambda^*I\succeq0,\qquad\lambda^*(\|x^*\|_2-\Delta)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region point is globally optimal exactly when a nonnegative multiplier gives stationarity, complementarity, and a positive-semidefinite shifted Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ optimal}\iff\exists\lambda^*\ge0\text{ satisfying shifted-PSD stationarity and complementarity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Global Optimality Conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Semidefinite Solution in the Regular One-Constraint Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tractability consequence of the S-lemma for rational regular instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational data, strict feasibility, and finite optimal value, the S-lemma converts lower-bound testing for a one-quadratic-constraint problem into a semidefinite feasibility condition involving one scalar multiplier. Standard semidefinite optimization algorithms therefore compute the optimal value to prescribed accuracy in time polynomial in the input size and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), subject to the usual quantitative regularity assumptions for bit-complexity guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular one-quadratic-constraint problems admit polynomial-time approximate solution through their exact semidefinite dual characterization.
assumptions_latex: Strict feasibility and finite optimal value hold.
The quantitative regularity required by the chosen SDP bit-complexity model holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\widehat v-v^*|\le\varepsilon\text{ is computable by an exact-duality SDP in polynomial time under the stated regularity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Time Semidefinite Solution in the Regular One-Constraint Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Lagrangian Dual Under Strict Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong duality for a finite-valued one-quadratic-constraint problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v^*=\inf\{f_0(x):f_1(x)\le0\}\), assume strict feasibility and \(v^*>-\infty\). Then \[v^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(f_0(x)+\lambda f_1(x)\bigr).\] Equivalently, \(\gamma\le v^*\) is certified by some \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \(f_0(x)-\gamma+\lambda f_1(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly feasible one-quadratic-constraint problem with finite value has no Lagrangian duality gap, and a scalar multiplier certifies lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_x(f_0(x)+\lambda f_1(x)).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Lagrangian Dual Under Strict Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Feasibility Is Essential to the Basic S-Lemma
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity boundary for the scalar-multiplier equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Without a point satisfying \(f_1(x)<0\), the implication \(f_1(x)\le0\Rightarrow f_0(x)\ge0\) need not admit \(\lambda\ge0\) with \(f_0+\lambda f_1\ge0\) globally. For \(f_1(x)=x^2\) and \(f_0(x)=x\), the implication holds on the feasible set \(\{0\}\), but \(x+\lambda x^2\) is negative for some \(x\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic S-lemma can fail without strict feasibility even when the quadratic implication is true.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{quadratic implication without strict feasibility}\not\Rightarrow\text{scalar S-lemma certificate}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Feasibility Is Essential to the Basic S-Lemma

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact implication certificate for one quadratic inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0,f_1\) be real quadratic functions and suppose there exists \(\bar x\) with \(f_1(\bar x)<0\). Then \[f_1(x)\le0\Rightarrow f_0(x)\ge0\quad\text{for all }x\] if and only if there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \[f_0(x)+\lambda f_1(x)\ge0\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility, nonnegativity of one quadratic over a quadratic sublevel set is equivalent to a scalar nonnegative-multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [f_1\le0\Rightarrow f_0\ge0]\iff\exists\lambda\ge0:\ f_0+\lambda f_1\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R^n.
knowledge_statements.title: S-Lemma Under Strict Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linearly constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax\le b,\] where \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Its feasible region \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is polyhedral. The program is convex when \(Q\succeq0\); it is a nonconvex quadratic program when \(Q\not\succeq0\), including the concave case \(Q\preceq0\) and the indefinite case in which \(Q\) has eigenvalues of both signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearly constrained quadratic program minimizes a quadratic objective over a polyhedron and is nonconvex when its quadratic matrix is not positive semidefinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Relative to the Feasible Affine Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correction of the full-space Hessian test for lower-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) is convex on a convex polyhedron \(P\) if \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd\ge0\) for every direction \(d\) parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\). Thus \(Q\not\succeq0\) does not by itself imply nonconvexity on a lower-dimensional feasible polyhedron; when \(P\) is full-dimensional, convexity on \(P\) is equivalent to \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic convexity must be tested along feasible affine-hull directions; global indefiniteness can be irrelevant on a lower-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q|_P\text{ convex}\iff d^{\mathsf T}Qd\ge0\text{ for all }d\in\operatorname{lin}(P-P).

notation.meaning: direction space parallel to the affine hull of P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient unboundedness certificates for noncompact polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), \(x\in P\), and \(d\ne0\) satisfy \(Ad\le0\). If \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\), or if \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd=0\) and \((Qx+c)^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(q(x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative quadratic recession curvature, or zero curvature with negative linear slope, certifies unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\ \lor\ [d^{\mathsf T}Qd=0\land(Qx+c)^{\mathsf T}d<0]\Rightarrow\inf_Pq=-\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Direction Unboundedness Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation complexity parameterized by negative eigenvalues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and complexity of an approximation algorithm for problem (1) when its quadratic matrix is indefinite and its feasible region is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose D is indefinite, the feasible region of (1) is compact, and t is the number of negative eigenvalues of D. Then there exists an algorithm that finds an \epsilon-approximate solution of (1) in O\!\left(\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right)^t\ell\right) steps, where \ell denotes the time required to solve a convex quadratic program of the same size as (1).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact indefinite quadratic problem has an approximation algorithm whose bound grows exponentially with the number of negative eigenvalues and includes the cost of solving a same-size convex quadratic program.
assumptions_latex: t\text{ is the number of negative eigenvalues of }D.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_\epsilon=O\!\left(\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right)^t\ell\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise necessary conditions for a box-constrained quadratic local minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary coordinate conditions for a local minimizer of problem (13), stated in the source notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If x^\star is a local minimum of (13), then for every i with D_{ii}\ge 0, either g_i(x^\star)>0 and x_i^\star=0, or g_i(x^\star)=0 and 0\le x_i^\star\le1, or g_i(x^\star)<0 and x_i^\star=1. For every i with D_{ii}<0, either g_i(x^\star)>0 and x_i^\star=0, or g_i(x^\star)<0 and x_i^\star=1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a local minimum, the gradient sign determines the active bound of each coordinate. Zero coordinate gradient is permitted only when the corresponding diagonal coefficient is nonnegative; a coordinate with negative diagonal coefficient must be at a bound with nonzero coordinate gradient.
assumptions_latex: x^\star\text{ is a local minimum of problem (13).}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient global-optimality test for an indefinite quadratic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A global and unique-global optimality criterion for the candidate \(\bar x\) in problem (13).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a_i=H_{ii}/(2y_i),\ i=1,\ldots,m. For the points covered by the theorem, (D\bar x+c)^T(x-\bar x)\ge0 and Q(x)-Q(\bar x)\ge (D\bar x+c)^T(x-\bar x)\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^m a_i(x_i-\bar x_i)\right). Define \alpha=\sum_{i=1}^m\left|a_i(x_i^U-x_i^L)\right|. If \alpha\le1, then \bar x is a global minimizer of (13); if \alpha<1, then it is the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stated first-order expression gives a lower bound on the objective difference. If the resulting scaled-width sum is at most one, the candidate is globally optimal; strict inequality guarantees unique global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha\le1\Rightarrow \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}(13),\qquad \alpha<1\Rightarrow \operatorname*{argmin}(13)=\{\bar x\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-scale-invariant approximate solution for quadratic optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative objective-gap definition of an approximate feasible solution to quadratic problem (1), together with its stated invariance property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x^\star be an optimum of (1). A feasible point x' is an \epsilon-approximate solution if there exists another feasible point x^\# such that Q(x')-Q(x^\star)\le\epsilon\left[Q(x^\#)-Q(x^\star)\right]. This definition is insensitive to translations or dilations of the objective function Q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is epsilon-approximate if its gap from the optimum is no more than epsilon times the gap of another feasible point. The definition is unchanged by translating or dilating the objective.
assumptions_latex: x^\star\text{ is an optimum of problem (1).}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'\text{ is }\epsilon\text{-approximate}\iff\exists x^\#\text{ feasible}:\ Q(x')-Q(x^\star)\le\epsilon\left[Q(x^\#)-Q(x^\star)\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A box-constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad \ell_i\le x_i\le u_i,\quad i=1,\ldots,n,\] where \(Q\in\mathbb{S}^n\) and all bounds are finite with \(\ell_i\le u_i\). The feasible set is the hyperrectangle \([\ell,u]\). The problem is a nonconvex quadratic program precisely when the objective is not convex on this box, in particular whenever a feasible direction of the box has negative quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class minimizes a quadratic function over finite componentwise bounds, forming a hyperrectangle; negative curvature along feasible directions makes the problem nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact minimization of a concave quadratic over a finite box is NP-hard. In particular, a weighted Max-Cut instance can be represented as minimizing the negative of its convex quadratic cut objective over \([0,1]^n\); vertex attainment makes the continuous box optimum equal to the binary optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even the concave box-quadratic subfamily is NP-hard, despite always having an optimal vertex.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x^*\) locally minimizes differentiable \(q\) on \([\ell,u]\), then \[\ell_i<x_i^*<u_i\Rightarrow
abla_iq(x^*)=0,\quad x_i^*=\ell_i<u_i\Rightarrow
abla_iq(x^*)\ge0,\quad x_i^*=u_i>\ell_i\Rightarrow
abla_iq(x^*)\le0.\] These conditions are sufficient for global optimality when \(q\) is convex on the box, in particular when \(Q\succeq0\), but not in general.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratically constrained quadratic program has the form \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\le0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where \(f_i(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\) and \(Q_i\in\mathbb{S}^n\) for every \(i=0,\ldots,m\). The QCQP is convex when \(Q_i\succeq0\) for all indices; otherwise the objective or at least one constraint can introduce nonconvexity. Linear inequalities are included by taking the corresponding \(Q_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP has a quadratic objective and finitely many quadratic inequalities; it is generally nonconvex when an objective or constraint matrix is not positive semidefinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Sufficiency in the Convex QCQP Subclass
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality certificate at the convex boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(Q_i\succeq0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\) and that some \(\bar x\) satisfies \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every constraint. A feasible \(x^*\) is globally optimal if and only if there exist \(\lambda_i\ge0\) such that \[\nabla f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla f_i(x^*)=0,\qquad\lambda_i f_i(x^*)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex QCQP satisfying Slater's condition, KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_i\succeq0\) for the objective and every constraint quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ globally optimal}\iff\exists\lambda\ge0\text{ satisfying KKT}.
knowledge_statements.title: KKT Sufficiency in the Convex QCQP Subclass

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted representation of a QCQP before relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(y=(1,x)\) and \(M_i=\begin{bmatrix}r_i&q_i^{\mathsf T}\\q_i&Q_i\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(f_i(x)=\langle M_i,Y\rangle\) with \(Y=yy^{\mathsf T}\). Hence the QCQP is exactly \[\min\ \langle M_0,Y\rangle\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\langle M_i,Y\rangle\le0,\ Y_{00}=1,\ Y\succeq0,\ \operatorname{rank}Y=1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QCQP has an exact linear matrix formulation over a positive-semidefinite rank-one lift.
assumptions_latex: The QCQP uses the quadratic functions in the accepted definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{QCQP}\equiv\text{PSD lifted formulation with }Y_{00}=1\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}Y=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate QCQP feasibility of an LPR solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines approximate feasibility through tolerances on the original quadratic constraints and lifted product identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For given \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\), a solution \((x,w)\) of LPR is \((\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\)-feasible for the QCQP when \[x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+c_i^{\mathsf T}x\le d_i+\varepsilon_1\quad\forall i,\qquad \lvert w_{st}-x_sx_t\rvert\le\varepsilon_2\quad\forall s,t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LPR solution is approximately feasible for the QCQP when each quadratic constraint exceeds its bound by at most epsilon 1 and each lifted product variable differs from the corresponding variable product by at most epsilon 2.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the extracted initialization, LP subproblem evaluation, incumbent pruning, selection, exhaustive subdivision, and termination rules without expanding the undefined symbols (SNP) and SP(M).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an \(n\)-simplex \(M_1\subset\mathbb R^n\) containing the projection of \(\Omega\) onto \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\) be the best available feasible solution and set \(\gamma=g_0(\bar x)\), or \(\gamma=+\infty\) if none is known; initialize \(\mathcal R=\mathcal S=\{M_1\}\). For each \(M\in\mathcal S\), compute the optimal value \(\beta(M)\) of \(SP(M)\), update the incumbent, and delete every \(M\in\mathcal R\) satisfying \(\beta(M)\ge\gamma\). If the remaining collection \(\mathcal R'\) is empty, terminate with \((\bar x,\bar y)\) solving \((SNP)\) when \(\gamma<+\infty\), or declare \((SNP)\) infeasible when \(\gamma=+\infty\). Otherwise choose \(M_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal R'}\beta(M)\), obtain a basic optimal solution of \(SP(M_k)\), subdivide \(M_k\) by bisection or radial subdivision under an exhaustive rule, replace \(M_k\) by the resulting partition, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with a simplex containing the projected set. Solve the specified LP subproblem on active simplices, update the incumbent, prune simplices whose values cannot improve it, select a simplex of minimum value, subdivide it exhaustively, and repeat. An empty active collection triggers the stated optimality or infeasibility return according to whether a finite incumbent exists.
assumptions_latex: M_1\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ contains the projection of }\Omega\text{ onto }\mathbb R^n
\gamma=g_0(\bar x)\text{ for the best available feasible solution, or }+\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R'=\varnothing\Longrightarrow\begin{cases}(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ solves }(SNP),&\gamma<+\infty,\\(SNP)\text{ is infeasible},&\gamma=+\infty.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity and subgradient of the Lagrangian dual function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Lagrangian dual-function theory; the source uses the multiplier domain \(\mathbb R_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(X\) is compact and \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are continuous on \(X\). Then \(\psi\) is defined and concave on \(\mathbb R_+^m\). If \(\bar x\in X\), \(\bar u\in\mathbb R_+^m\), and \(\psi(\bar u)=L(\bar x,\bar u)\), then \(-\bigl(f_i(\bar x)\bigr)_{i=1}^m\in\partial(-\psi)(\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain with continuous objective and constraint functions, the Lagrangian dual function is defined and concave. If its value at a multiplier is attained at x-bar, the negatives of the constraint values form a subgradient of the negative dual function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi\text{ is defined and concave on }\mathbb R_+^m,\qquad -\bigl(f_i(\bar x)\bigr)_{i=1}^m\in\partial(-\psi)(\bar u).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\). Suppose there exist \(\bar y\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(L(x,\bar y):=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\bar y_i g_i(x)\) is convex, \(\bar x\) minimizes \(L(\cdot,\bar y)\), and \(g_i(\bar x)\leq0\) and \(\bar y_i g_i(\bar x)=0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Then strong duality holds: \(\psi_X^*=f_X^{\natural}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral solution and hard-case construction for the trust-region subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact eigenvalue-based solution procedure, with the singular endpoint and uniqueness boundary stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q=Q^\top have eigenpairs (\lambda_i,u^i), ordered so that \lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_n, with \lambda_1 of multiplicity k. For \mu> -\lambda_1 define x(\mu)=-(Q+\mu I)^{-1}c and define \bar x=-\sum_{i=k+1}^n\frac{\langle c,u^i\rangle}{\lambda_i-\lambda_1}u^i. If \langle c,u^i\rangle\ne0 for some i\le k, or if \langle c,u^i\rangle=0\ (i\le k) and \|\bar x\|>r, find the unique \mu^*>-\lambda_1 satisfying \|x(\mu^*)\|=r by bisection; then x^*=x(\mu^*) is the unique global solution. If \langle c,u^i\rangle=0\ (i\le k) and \|\bar x\|=r, then \mu^*=-\lambda_1 and x^*=\bar x is the unique global solution. If \langle c,u^i\rangle=0\ (i\le k) and \|\bar x\|<r, set \mu^*=-\lambda_1 and choose \alpha\in\mathbb R^k with \sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i^2=r^2-\|\bar x\|^2; every x^*=\bar x+\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i u^i is globally optimal, and the solution is not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonalize the quadratic matrix. Outside the hard case, solve the secular norm equation by bisection and obtain the unique optimizer. At the singular endpoint, the limiting vector is uniquely optimal when its norm equals the radius; when its norm is smaller, add any minimum-eigenspace component of the required length, producing nonunique optimizers.
assumptions_latex: (\mathrm{TRS})\text{ and its nonconvex spectral setting are as defined in the surrounding section}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}x^*=-(Q+\mu^*I)^{-1}c\text{ is the unique global solution},&\mu^*>-\lambda_1,\ \|x(\mu^*)\|=r,\\x^*=\bar x\text{ is the unique global solution},&\langle c,u^i\rangle=0\ \forall i\le k,\ \|\bar x\|=r,\\x^*=\bar x+\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i u^i\text{ is globally optimal and nonunique},&\langle c,u^i\rangle=0\ \forall i\le k,\ \|\bar x\|<r,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i^2=r^2-\|\bar x\|^2.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duality theorem for one quadratic constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong duality, dual attainment, convexifying multipliers, and exact primal optimality characterizations for QPA and QPB.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let E be the subspace parallel to H and L(x,y)=f(x)+yg(x). (i) For QPA, condition (S) implies v(\mathrm{QPA})=\sup_{y\geq0}\inf_{x\in H}L(x,y). If also v(\mathrm{QPA})>-\infty, then there exists  ar y\geq0 such that L(\cdot, ar y) is convex on H and v(\mathrm{QPA})=\min_{x\in H}L(x, ar y)=\max_{y\geq0}\inf_{x\in H}L(x,y). For this  ar y,  ar x\in H solves QPA iff \langle
abla f( ar x)+ ar y
abla g( ar x),uangle=0\  orall u\in E,\  ar y g( ar x)=0,\ g( ar x)\leq0. Condition (T) with D=\mathbb R_+ is sufficient for v(\mathrm{QPA})>-\infty. (ii) For QPB, if H is a subspace, v(\mathrm{QPB})>-\infty, and either g is homogeneous and takes both positive and negative values on H or f and g are both homogeneous, then v(\mathrm{QPB})=\min_{x\in H}L(x, ar y)=\max_{y\in\mathbb R}\inf_{x\in H}L(x,y) for some  ar y\in\mathbb R with L(\cdot, ar y) convex on H. For this  ar y,  ar x\in H solves QPB iff \langle
abla f( ar x)+ ar y
abla g( ar x),uangle=0\  orall u\in H and g( ar x)=0. (iii) In the equality case, condition (T) implies the duality identity v(\mathrm{QPB})=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}\inf_{x\in H}L(x,y), with the supremum restrictable to multipliers for which L(\cdot,y) is convex on H. If the dual has an optimizer  ar y, then  ar x\in H is primal-optimal iff \langle
abla f( ar x)+ ar y
abla g( ar x),uangle=0\  orall u\in E.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility gives strong duality for the one-inequality quadratic problem. If its value is finite, an optimal multiplier makes the Lagrangian convex, and stationarity, complementarity, and feasibility exactly characterize global optimizers. For the equality problem on a subspace, the stated finiteness and homogeneity alternatives give strong duality, dual attainment, and an exact stationarity-and-feasibility characterization. In the theorem's equality-case third part, a strictly convex Lagrangian multiplier also gives strong duality, and stationarity characterizes the primal optimizer when the dual optimum is attained.
assumptions_latex: f,g\text{ are quadratic functions on }\mathbb R^n
H\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is affine and }E\text{ is its parallel subspace}
\text{The case-specific conditions (S), (T), finiteness, homogeneity, and sign hypotheses hold as stated}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The corresponding strong-duality, dual-attainment, convexity, and iff optimality conclusions in parts (i)--(iii) hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Random-order greedy sparsification of a violated PSD cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heuristic sparsification of a violated PSD separating vector in a QCQP matrix relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(v\in\mathbb R^q\) with \(v^T\widetilde Xv<0\), \(\widetilde X\in\mathbb S^q\), and \(p_{NZ},p_{VIOL}\in[0,1]\), set \(\delta=-v^T\widetilde Xv\,p_{VIOL}\), \(s=\lfloor q p_{NZ}\rfloor\), and \(w=v\). Visit the coordinates in a random permutation. At each coordinate, form \(z\) by setting that coordinate of the current \(w\) to zero, and accept \(w\leftarrow z\) if \(-z^T\widetilde Xz>\delta\). Output \(w\) only if \(\operatorname{nnz}(w)<s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a violated PSD-cut vector, the procedure visits coordinates in random order and deletes a coordinate whenever the resulting vector retains more than the prescribed minimum violation. It outputs the vector only if the strict nonzero-count threshold is met.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{nnz}(w)<\lfloor q p_{NZ}\rfloor\Longrightarrow w\text{ is output and }-w^T\widetilde Xw>-v^T\widetilde Xv\,p_{VIOL}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States convergence under continuity, tight cellwise convex minorants, and the extracted sequential consistency condition; the extract does not define the precise convergence mode.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-quadratic-constraint programs and their Lagrangian duals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the inequality and equality models, multiplier domains, dual values, and strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H\subseteq\mathbb R^n be an affine manifold, f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Q^0x\rangle+\langle c^0,x\rangle, and g(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Q^1x\rangle+\langle c^1,x\rangle+d_1. Define \mathrm{QPA}:\inf\{f(x):x\in H,\ g(x)\leq0\} and \mathrm{QPB}:\inf\{f(x):x\in H,\ g(x)=0\}. Set L(x,y)=f(x)+yg(x), with D=\mathbb R_+ for QPA and D=\mathbb R for QPB. Then \sup_{y\in D}L(x,y)=f(x) for feasible x and +\infty otherwise, so v(P)=\inf_{x\in H}\sup_{y\in D}L(x,y). The dual value is d(P)=\sup_{y\in D}\inf_{x\in H}L(x,y), and strong duality means v(P)=d(P). With \inf\varnothing=-\infty, the dual supremum may be restricted to multipliers for which L(\cdot,y) is convex on H.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratic program over an affine manifold with one quadratic inequality or equality, the inequality multiplier is nonnegative and the equality multiplier is unrestricted. Maximizing the Lagrangian over the multiplier reproduces the constrained objective; reversing infimum and supremum defines the dual. Strong duality is equality of the primal and dual values. Multipliers whose Lagrangian is nonconvex on the affine manifold contribute minus infinity to the dual inner problem and may be omitted.
assumptions_latex: H\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is an affine manifold}
Q^0,Q^1\in\mathbb S^n,\quad c^0,c^1\in\mathbb R^n,\quad d_1\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v(P)=\inf_{x\in H}\sup_{y\in D}L(x,y),\quad d(P)=\sup_{y\in D}\inf_{x\in H}L(x,y),\quad \text{strong duality}\iff v(P)=d(P).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix optimality certificate for one quadratic inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient global-optimality certificate for QPA on the full space under condition (S).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H=\mathbb R^n and assume condition (S). Then \bar x\in\mathbb R^n solves QPA iff there exists \bar y\in\mathbb R_+ such that Q^0+\bar yQ^1\succeq0,\ (Q^0+\bar yQ^1)\bar x+c^0+\bar yc^1=0, and \langle Q^1\bar x+2c^1,\bar x\rangle+2d_1\leq0. If Q^0\not\succ0, the last inequality is replaced by \langle Q^1\bar x+2c^1,\bar x\rangle+2d_1=0.

If the objective Hessian is not positive definite, the feasibility condition must hold with equality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional two-block form with affine and bilinear expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilinear program has objective and constraint functions of the form \[\phi_i(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}B_i y+a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i^{\mathsf T}y+c_i,\qquad i=0,\ldots,m,\] with \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(y\in Y\subseteq\mathbb R^p\), \(B_i\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_i\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(c_i\in\mathbb R\). Each \(\phi_i\) is affine in either block when the other is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear program contains pairwise products between two variable blocks and is affine in either block separately.
assumptions_latex: All coefficients have the displayed real dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonaffine cross-block term is bilinear and every fixed-block expression is affine.
knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indefinite Joint Curvature of a Nonzero Bilinear Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-curvature boundary for a pure cross-block term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}By\), \[\nabla^2q=\begin{bmatrix}0&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}.\] If \(B\ne0\), this matrix has positive and negative eigenvalues. Thus \(q\) is separately affine but neither jointly convex nor jointly concave on a full-dimensional open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero bilinear form has indefinite joint curvature despite separate affinity.
assumptions_latex: The joint domain contains a full-dimensional open convex subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}By\) is separately affine and jointly neither convex nor concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Joint Curvature of a Nonzero Bilinear Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure bilinear objective over a Cartesian product of compact polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are nonempty compact polytopes, then both \(\min_{x\in P,y\in Q}x^{\mathsf T}By\) and \(\max_{x\in P,y\in Q}x^{\mathsf T}By\) are attained at some \((v,w)\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\times\operatorname{vert}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure bilinear objective over a product of compact polytopes has an optimal vertex pair.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is exactly \(P\times Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each extremum has an optimizer in \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\times\operatorname{vert}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Pair Attainment over Product Polytopes

Part I. Biconvex and Bilinear Problems

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A biconvex program has the form \[\inf_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}\ f(x,y)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x,y)\le0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where \(X\) and \(Y\) are convex, and each of \(f\) and \(g_i\) is convex in \(x\) for every fixed \(y\in Y\) and convex in \(y\) for every fixed \(x\in X\). Joint convexity is not required. Consequently, fixing either block yields a convex optimization subproblem in the remaining block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biconvex program is convex in either of two variable blocks when the other block is fixed, though it need not be jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Biconvex Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190
Part I. Biconvex and Bilinear Problems

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic block-coordinate method for two-block biconvex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From a feasible \((x^k,y^k)\), choose \(x^{k+1}\) as a global minimizer of the feasible \(x\)-section with \(y=y^k\), then choose \(y^{k+1}\) as a global minimizer of the feasible \(y\)-section with \(x=x^{k+1}\). Then \[f(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\leq f(x^{k+1},y^k)\leq f(x^k,y^k).\] If these values are bounded below, the objective-value sequence converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact alternating minimization produces nonincreasing objective values; a lower bound ensures convergence of the values, not necessarily of the iterates or to a global optimum.
assumptions_latex: Both block subproblems are feasible and attain global minima at every iteration.
Objective-value convergence additionally requires a finite lower bound along the iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\leq f(x^k,y^k)\), and boundedness below implies convergence of \(f(x^k,y^k)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Alternating Convex Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise Optimality Is Not Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for alternating minimization and blockwise certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x,y)=(xy-1)^2\) on \([-1,1]^2\), \(f\) is convex in each block separately. The point \((0,0)\) is coordinatewise globally minimizing because \(f(x,0)=f(0,y)=1\) for all \(x,y\), but it is not globally minimizing because \(f(1,1)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinatewise minimum of a biconvex objective can be strictly suboptimal globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\) is coordinatewise minimizing but not globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Optimality Is Not Global Optimality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Sections of a Biconvex Feasible Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sectionwise geometry induced by biconvex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:g_i(x,y)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(X,Y\) are convex and every \(g_i\) is separately convex. Then \(S_y=\{x:(x,y)\in S\}\) and \(S^x=\{y:(x,y)\in S\}\) are convex for every fixed opposite block, although \(S\) need not be jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every one-block feasible section is convex, but the full feasible set need not be convex.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is convex in either block with the other fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_y\) and \(S^x\) are convex for all fixed blocks.

notation.meaning: Feasible sections in the two blocks

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Sections of a Biconvex Feasible Set

children.title: Convex–Concave Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for opposing curvature across blocks or components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global certificate under the minimizer–maximizer convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point exactly when \[f(x^*,y)\leq f(x^*,y^*)\leq f(x,y^*)\qquad\forall x\in X,\ \forall y\in Y.\] It then certifies optimality for both orders and equality of their values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two global saddle inequalities certify minimax and maximin optimality.
assumptions_latex: The minimizer controls \(x\) and the maximizer controls \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities are necessary and sufficient for a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Inequality Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure Without Concavity in the Maximizing Block
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature boundary for minimax equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=Y=[0,1]\) and \(f(x,y)=(x-y)^2\), \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)=\tfrac14>0=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}f(x,y).\] Here \(f\) is convex rather than concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping maximizing-block concavity can create a strict minimax gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_x\max_y f>\max_y\min_x f\).
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Concavity in the Maximizing Block

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained two-block saddle convention; constrained variants require separately specified feasible correspondences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex–concave minimax program is \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}f(x,y),\] where \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex sets, \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) is convex for every fixed \(y\), and \(y\mapsto f(x,y)\) is concave for every fixed \(x\). This definition alone does not assert minimax equality or attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex–concave minimax program is convex in the minimizing block and concave in the maximizing block.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is real-valued and has the stated blockwise curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizing and maximizing blocks have opposing curvature roles.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Minimax Program

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuous compact form of the minimax theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be nonempty compact convex sets and let \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Then \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}f(x,y),\] and a saddle point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity, compact convex domains, and opposing block curvature imply minimax equality and saddle-point attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_X\max_Y f=\max_Y\min_X f\), with an attained saddle point.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Convex–Concave Minimax Equality

assumptions_latex: The objective and constraint functions have the stated blockwise curvature on \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is convex in the minimizing block and concave in the opposing block.

notation.meaning: convex and concave variable blocks, respectively

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the two-block minimax sense: convex in the minimizing block and concave in the maximizing block.

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex-concave program in the two-block minimax sense has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\ \sup_{y\in Y}\ f(x,y),\] where \(X\) and \(Y\) are convex, \(x\mapsto f(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every fixed \(y\in Y\), and \(y\mapsto f(x,y)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every fixed \(x\in X\). In constrained variants, admissible functions preserve convex feasible sections for the minimizing block and concave-compatible sections for the maximizing block. Joint convexity of \(f\) is neither required nor generally meaningful across the opposing roles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the minimax sense, a convex-concave program has an objective convex in the minimizing variables and concave in the maximizing variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unconstrained convex-concave minimax formula is coherent, but the immutable container describes opposing curvature across blocks or components and does not itself fix the minimax convention. The sentence about concave-compatible feasible sections is not a precise mathematical condition. The cited source must be inspected to determine the intended convention before selecting a reliable replacement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algorithm for an unconstrained multiaffine objective on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multiaffine objective in \(n\) scalar variables on a box, evaluation at all \(2^n\) vertices is exact. If one evaluation costs \(T_p\), exhaustive enumeration takes \(O(2^nT_p)\) time and can use \(O(n)\) working memory beyond the incumbent and input storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Box-vertex enumeration is exact but exponential in the number of scalar variables.
assumptions_latex: The only feasible-set restriction is the box.
Objective values admit exact or certified comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact optimization is possible in \(O(2^nT_p)\) time.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Vertex Enumeration Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-Box Vertex Reduction Fails under Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the box vertex theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([0,1]^2\) with the additional constraint \(x+y=1\), the bilinear objective \(xy\) has maximum \(1/4\) at \((1/2,1/2)\), which is not a vertex of the ambient box. Thus coupled constraints invalidate unrestricted ambient-box vertex reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled constraints can force a multilinear optimum away from all ambient-box vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ambient-box vertex enumeration is not generally exact for coupled constrained models.

notation.meaning: Bilinear special case used for the boundary example

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Box Vertex Reduction Fails under Coupling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiple-block programs whose defining expressions are affine in each block separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multilinear program over \(X_1\times\cdots\times X_k\) has objective and constraint functions that are multiaffine: fixing all blocks except \(x^{(j)}\) leaves an affine function of \(x^{(j)}\). In finite dimensions such expressions are finite sums of constant, affine, and cross-block multilinear terms. Degree-two cross-block terms are bilinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilinear program is affine in each variable block separately but may contain products spanning several blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(X_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_j}\) is nonempty for every block.
All defining expressions are finite multiaffine expressions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every defining expression is affine in each block with the other blocks fixed.

notation.meaning: The j-th variable block and domain

knowledge_statements.title: Multilinear Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Attainment of Multiaffine Functions on Boxes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical box-domain extremum theorem for a multiaffine objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{j=1}^n[\ell_j,u_j]\) be a nonempty compact box and let \(p:B\to\mathbb R\) be affine in each scalar coordinate with the others fixed. Then \[\min_Bp=\min_{v\in\operatorname{vert}(B)}p(v),\qquad \max_Bp=\max_{v\in\operatorname{vert}(B)}p(v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiaffine function on a compact box attains both extrema at box vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is affine in every scalar coordinate separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both extrema are attained at vertices of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Attainment of Multiaffine Functions on Boxes

children.title: Power-Product Program Family
children.top_down_role: Power-product models extending the convex geometric-programming regime.

children.title: Convexifiable Posynomial Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for the convex geometric-programming boundary.

assumptions_latex: The objective and inequality functions are posynomials, while equality constraints are monomial equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The logarithmic change \(x_j=e^{y_j}\) converts the geometric program into a convex optimization problem.

notation.meaning: positive monomial coefficients and real exponent vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the standard logarithmic convexification of posynomial-form geometric programs on the positive orthant.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every posynomial be \(p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{a_{kj}}\), with \(c_k>0\), and let every monomial have one such term. Under \(x_j=e^{y_j}\), a constraint \(p(x)\le1\) is equivalent to \[\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\exp\!\left(a_k^{\mathsf T}y+\log c_k\right)\right)\le0,\] which is convex in \(y\). A monomial equality becomes affine after taking logarithms. Applying the same logarithm to a positive posynomial objective yields an equivalent convex objective because the logarithm is strictly increasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-variable geometric programs with posynomial inequalities and monomial equalities become convex after taking logarithms of variables and the positive objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexifiable Posynomial Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

children.title: General Signomial Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for nonconvex signomial models.

assumptions_latex: The domain is the strictly positive orthant \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\).
Each signomial is a finite sum of generalized monomials with real coefficients and real exponents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Allowing coefficients of either sign yields the general signomial-program class, which is not generally convex after logarithmic substitution.

notation.meaning: nonzero real coefficients and real exponent vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses generalized real exponents on positive variables and permits mixed coefficient signs.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A signomial on the positive orthant is a function \[s(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{a_{kj}},\] where \(c_k\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\) and \(a_{kj}\in\mathbb{R}\). A general signomial program minimizes one signomial subject to finitely many signomial inequalities and equalities over \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\). Unlike a posynomial, a signomial may have coefficients of both signs. After \(x_j=e^{y_j}\), it becomes a signed sum of exponentials, so the logarithmic transformation does not in general produce a convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general signomial program uses finite sums of real-power monomials with coefficients of either sign on positive variables and is generally nonconvex after logarithmic substitution.
knowledge_statements.title: General Signomial Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Conditions for a Signomial Term
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient convexity conditions for one signed power-product term on its positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^N x_i^{p_i}\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^N\). If \(c>0\), then \(s\) is convex if either all \(p_i<0\), or exactly one exponent \(p_k>0\), all remaining exponents are negative, and \(\sum_{i=1}^N p_i\ge1\). If \(c<0\), then \(s\) is convex if all \(p_i>0\) and \(0\le\sum_{i=1}^N p_i\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the positive orthant, a positive-coefficient power product is convex when all exponents are negative, or when exactly one is positive, the others are negative, and their sum is at least one. A negative-coefficient power product is convex when all exponents are positive and their sum is between zero and one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[c>0\land((\forall i,\ p_i<0)\lor(\exists!k:\ p_k>0,\ \forall i\ne k,\ p_i<0,\ \sum_i p_i\ge1))\bigr]\lor\bigl[c<0\land(\forall i,\ p_i>0)\land0\le\sum_i p_i\le1\bigr]\implies s\text{ is convex}.
