children.title: Domain-Sensitive Power Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for power models whose validity depends on sign and domain restrictions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Points Can Destroy Finiteness or Real-Valuedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary zero and sign failures for real power atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The atom \(x^{-1}\) is not finite at \(x=0\), and the real atom \(x^{1/2}\) is undefined for \(x<0\). Thus a nominal constraint such as \(-1\le x\le1\) does not itself provide a valid common domain for either expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero can be singular for negative powers, while negative values can be invalid for fractional powers.
assumptions_latex: Power atoms are interpreted as finite, single-valued real functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\notin\operatorname{dom}(x^{-1})\) and \(( -\infty,0)\cap\operatorname{dom}_{\mathbb R}(x^{1/2})=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Points Can Destroy Finiteness or Real-Valuedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power Identities Depend on the Admitted Real Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of formal exponent laws when negative bases and principal real roots are mixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the nonnegative principal square root, take \(x=-1\). Then \[(x^2)^{1/2}=1\neq-1=x^{2(1/2)}.\] Hence \((x^a)^b=x^{ab}\) is not valid on arbitrary real domains without compatible base restrictions and branch conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponent-composition identities can fail on negative bases, so reformulations must preserve the declared real domain and branch.
assumptions_latex: The outer exponent \(1/2\) denotes the nonnegative real square root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^2)^{1/2}\ne x\), so unrestricted use of \((x^a)^b=x^{ab}\) is invalid.
knowledge_statements.title: Power Identities Depend on the Admitted Real Domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for algebraic substitutions involving power atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two power-model formulations have expression maps \(F\) and \(\widetilde F\), feasible effective domains \(E\) and \(\widetilde E\), and a change of variables \(T\). They are optimization-equivalent if \(T:E\to\widetilde E\) is bijective and \(F(x)=\widetilde F(T(x))\) for every \(x\in E\). Formal equality away from excluded zeros, signs, or branches is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-model reformulation is valid only when it preserves values and the complete feasible effective domain.
assumptions_latex: Every power atom has a declared finite, single-valued real domain.
The proposed transformation and its inverse are defined on the respective feasible effective domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T:E\leftrightarrow\widetilde E\text{ bijective and value-preserving}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\inf_{x\in E}F(x)=\inf_{z\in\widetilde E}\widetilde F(z).

notation.meaning: feasible effective domains of the two formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Preserving Reformulation Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Real Domains of Scalar Power Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponent-by-exponent domain classification under a declared standard real-power convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a=p/q\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}\) be in lowest terms with \(q>0\), and define \(x^{p/q}\) using the real \(q\)-th root. If \(q\) is odd, its finite real domain is \(\mathbb R\) for \(p>0\) and \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) for \(p<0\). If \(q\) is even, its domain is \([0,\infty)\) for \(p>0\) and \((0,\infty)\) for \(p<0\). This includes nonzero integers as \(q=1\). For irrational \(a\), the canonical definition \(x^a=\exp(a\log x)\) has domain \((0,\infty)\); when \(a>0\), it has the continuous finite extension \(0^a=0\). The value of \(0^0\) is convention-dependent and must be declared explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced-rational denominator parity, exponent sign, and the treatment of zero determine the finite real domain of a scalar power.
assumptions_latex: Rational exponents are reduced to \(p/q\) with \(q>0\).
Even roots use the nonnegative real branch.
Irrational powers use \(\exp(a\log x)\) on positive bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}_{\mathbb R}(x^{p/q})=\begin{cases}\mathbb R,&q\text{ odd},\ p>0,\\\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},&q\text{ odd},\ p<0,\\[0,\infty),&q\text{ even},\ p>0,\\(0,\infty),&q\text{ even},\ p<0.\end{cases}

notation.meaning: nonzero rational exponent in lowest terms with positive denominator

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Real Domains of Scalar Power Atoms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective Domain Is the Common Atom Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-level construction from the declared domains of constituent power atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a finite optimization model on a declared set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) contains power occurrences \(h_k(x)^{a_k}\) with declared finite, single-valued real domains \(D_k\), then its effective domain is \[E=X\cap\bigcap_k\{x:h_k(x)\in D_k\}.\] Every objective value, constraint value, equivalence claim, and feasibility statement for the model is restricted to \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The valid model domain is the intersection of the declared search set with every power atom's real domain.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many power occurrences appear.
Each occurrence has a declared finite, single-valued real domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E=X\cap\bigcap_k h_k^{-1}(D_k).

notation.meaning: effective domain of the complete power model

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Domain Is the Common Atom Domain

assumptions_latex: Every power atom is assigned a real exponent and an explicit real-valued domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D=\{x\in X:x_j\in D_{a}\text{ for every occurring atom }x_j^{a}\}\).

notation.meaning: Largest prescribed real domain on which the power atom is single-valued and finite
Effective domain of the complete model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued power models with explicit sign, zero, and exponent-dependent domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain-sensitive power model is an optimization problem whose expressions contain atoms \(x_j^a\), with each atom interpreted only on a specified set \(D_a\subseteq\mathbb R\) where it is real, single-valued, and finite. For \(a\in\mathbb Z\), one may take \(D_a=\mathbb R\), excluding zero when \(a<0\). For nonintegral rational or irrational powers, the chosen real branch and sign restrictions must be stated explicitly; the universally valid convention \(D_a=(0,\infty)\) is always admissible. The feasible set is intersected with all such atom domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power model is domain-sensitive when every real power carries explicit sign and zero restrictions, and feasibility includes the common domain of all power atoms.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Sensitive Power Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the domain-sensitive power-model container and is mathematically plausible, but no source supports the exponent-dependent real-domain conventions or the treatment of branches and sign restrictions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Domain Curvature of a Real Power Atom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential and curvature classification on the strictly positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\mathbb R\), the atom \(p_a(x)=x^a=\exp(a\log x)\) on \((0,\infty)\) satisfies \(p_a'(x)=ax^{a-1}\) and \(p_a''(x)=a(a-1)x^{a-2}\), yielding the usual exponent-based monotonicity and curvature classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the positive domain, a real power has an unambiguous derivative and exponent-based curvature classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_a''\ge0\text{ for }a\le0\text{ or }a\ge1,\qquad p_a''\le0\text{ for }0\le a\le1.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Domain Curvature of a Real Power Atom

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns sign, zero, branch, effective-domain, and domain-preserving-reformulation issues. Its exponent-by-exponent domain convention remains unresolved. The proposed positive-domain curvature claim is sound but deferred as misplaced: positive-domain atom properties, posynomial convexification, and general signomial structure belong to adjacent scopes.

children.title: Single-Ratio Fractional Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for one-ratio continuous models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X} f(x)/g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minimization form with one everywhere-positive denominator.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-ratio fractional program has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)},\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the feasible set and \(g(x)>0\) throughout \(X\). Positivity makes the quotient finite whenever \(f\) and \(g\) are finite and fixes the direction of inequalities after multiplication by \(g(x)\). A maximization problem with the same single quotient is included by replacing \(f\) with \(-f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-ratio fractional program optimizes one quotient of a numerator by a denominator that remains strictly positive over the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Ratio Fractional Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-subproblem method for an attained continuous single-ratio minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(x_k\in\arg\min_{x\in X}(f(x)-\lambda_k g(x))\) and set \(\lambda_{k+1}=f(x_k)/g(x_k)\). Under the stated compactness and continuity assumptions, \(\lambda_1\ge v^*\); unless equality terminates the method, \((\lambda_k)_{k\ge1}\) decreases to \(v^*\). A zero residual \(f(x_k)-\lambda_k g(x_k)=0\) certifies that \(x_k\) is globally ratio-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dinkelbach's method solves exact subtractive subproblems and converges monotonically to the optimal ratio after its first update.
assumptions_latex: Every parametric subproblem is solved globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_k\to v^*,\qquad \phi(\lambda_k)=0\Longleftrightarrow \lambda_k=v^*.

notation.meaning: global minimizer of the current subtractive subproblem

knowledge_statements.title: Dinkelbach Iteration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration bound for convex sublevel feasibility bisection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\ell\le v^*\le u\), decide at each midpoint \(\alpha\) whether \(f(x)-\alpha g(x)\le0\) is feasible on \(X\). Feasibility replaces \(u\) by \(\alpha\); infeasibility replaces \(\ell\) by \(\alpha\). After \(k\) exact tests the bracket width is \((u-\ell)2^{-k}\), so width at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\lceil\log_2((u-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact sublevel-feasibility bisection halves the value bracket at every test.
assumptions_latex: A finite valid bracket \([\ell,u]\) is known.
Every feasibility test is decided correctly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\ge\left\lceil\log_2\frac{u-\ell}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\Longrightarrow u_k-\ell_k\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Value Bisection Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-feasibility structure for a standard single-ratio subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is convex, \(f\) is convex and nonnegative on \(X\), and \(g\) is positive and concave on \(X\), then \(f/g\) is quasiconvex. For \(\alpha\ge0\), \[\{x\in X:f(x)/g(x)\le\alpha\}=\{x\in X:f(x)-\alpha g(x)\le0\},\] a convex set; negative sublevels are empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative convex numerator divided by a positive concave denominator is quasiconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is concave and strictly positive on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f/g\text{ is quasiconvex on }X.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Fractional Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniform ratio transformations at zeros or sign changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g\) vanishes at a feasible point, the quotient may be undefined or unbounded nearby. If \(g\) changes sign, multiplication by \(g(x)\) does not preserve a uniform inequality direction. The subtractive sublevel equivalence and positive-perspective reformulations therefore require restriction to sign-definite regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Denominator zeros or sign changes invalidate the standard positive-denominator equivalences.
assumptions_latex: The feasible domain contains a zero of \(g\) or points at which \(g\) has opposite signs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{f/g\le\alpha\}=\{f-\alpha g\le0\}\text{ need not hold globally}.
knowledge_statements.title: Denominator-Sign Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear reformulation when the original polyhedron is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{(c^Tx+c_0)/(d^Tx+d_0):Ax\le b\}\), assume the polyhedron is nonempty and bounded and \(d^Tx+d_0>0\) throughout it. With \(t=(d^Tx+d_0)^{-1}\) and \(y=tx\), the problem is equivalent to \[\min c^Ty+c_0t\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ay\le bt,\ d^Ty+d_0t=1,\ t\ge0.\] Boundedness excludes transformed feasible points with \(t=0\), and optimizers recover by \(x=y/t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Charnes–Cooper converts a bounded positive-denominator linear-fractional problem into an equivalent linear program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(P)=\operatorname{val}(P_{CC}),\qquad x=y/t.
knowledge_statements.title: Charnes–Cooper Linear-Fractional Reformulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric characterization of a positive-denominator single-ratio minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)/g(x)\) and \(\phi(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}(f(x)-\lambda g(x))\). If \(g>0\) on \(X\), then \(\phi(\lambda)\ge0\) for \(\lambda\le v^*\) and \(\phi(\lambda)<0\) for \(\lambda>v^*\). If the ratio minimum is attained, then \(\phi(v^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal ratio is the threshold where the subtractive value function changes from nonnegative to negative; attainment makes it a zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^*=\sup\{\lambda:\phi(\lambda)\ge0\},\qquad \phi(v^*)=0\text{ under attainment}.
knowledge_statements.title: Subtractive Value Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the quadratic-over-quadratic subclass of single-ratio fractional programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-ratio problem \(\sup\{f(x)/g(x):x\in S\}\) is called a quadratic fractional program if \(f\) and \(g\) are quadratic functions and \(S\) is a convex polyhedron, with \(g(x)>0\) on the fractional-program domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic fractional program is a single-ratio problem whose numerator and denominator are quadratic, whose feasible set is a convex polyhedron, and whose denominator is positive on the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in S}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\text{ is a quadratic fractional program.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave fractional program and nonconcavity boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the curvature conditions for concave fractional programming and records that the resulting ratio objective is generally not concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and \(S=\{x\in C:h_k(x)\leq0,\ k=1,\ldots,m\}\). A single-ratio problem \(\sup_{x\in S}f(x)/g(x)\) is a concave fractional program if \(f\) is concave on \(C\), while \(g\) and every \(h_k\) are convex on \(C\); if \(g\) is not affine, also require \(f(x)\geq0\) on \(S\). The fractional-program denominator is positive on its domain. Even under these conditions, \(f/g\) is generally not concave, so the problem is generally nonconcave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex domain, a concave fractional program has a concave numerator and convex denominator and constraint functions. If the denominator is nonaffine, the numerator must be nonnegative on the feasible set. Despite these assumptions, the ratio is generally not concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in S}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\text{ is a concave fractional program, but }\frac{f}{g}\text{ is generally nonconcave.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the affine-over-affine subclass of single-ratio fractional optimization over a polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-ratio problem is called a linear fractional program when its numerator and denominator are affine and its feasible set is a convex polyhedron. A standard form is \[\sup\left\{\frac{c^Tx+\alpha}{d^Tx+\beta}:Ax\leq b,\ x\geq0\right\},\] where \(c,d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), with \(d^Tx+\beta>0\) on the fractional-program domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear fractional program has an affine numerator and affine denominator over a convex polyhedron, with the denominator positive on the domain.
assumptions_latex: S=\{x:Ax\leq b,\ x\geq0\}\text{ is a convex polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup\left\{\frac{c^Tx+\alpha}{d^Tx+\beta}:Ax\leq b,\ x\geq0\right\}\text{ is a linear fractional program.}

source_witnesses.locator: FRACTIONAL PROGRAMMING / 10.1. Introduction / Definition 10.1-extra-3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a constrained continuous optimization problem with one ratio objective and a denominator of constant positive sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g,h_1,\ldots,h_m:C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(S=\{x\in C:h_k(x)\leq0,\ k=1,\ldots,m\}\), and suppose \(g(x)>0\) for every \(x\in C\). Then \(\sup\{f(x)/g(x):x\in S\}\) is called a single-ratio fractional program. If \(g(x)<0\) throughout \(C\), replacing \((f,g)\) by \((-f,-g)\) yields an equivalent ratio with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing one ratio over a constrained set is a single-ratio fractional program when its denominator is positive throughout the domain. A denominator that is negative throughout can be normalized by negating both numerator and denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in S}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\text{ is a single-ratio fractional program.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records two scalar formulations using multiple ratios and their stated relationship to the corresponding multi-objective fractional problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_i(x)=f_i(x)/g_i(x)\) with \(g_i(x)>0\) for \(x\in S\). Two multi-ratio formulations are \(\sup_{x\in S}\min_{1\leq i\leq p}q_i(x)\) and \(\sup_{x\in S}\sum_{i=1}^p q_i(x)\). The first is sometimes called a generalized fractional program. Both are related to the multi-objective fractional problem \(\max\{(q_1(x),\ldots,q_p(x)):x\in S\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive denominators, several ratios can be combined by maximizing their minimum or their sum. The max-min formulation is sometimes called a generalized fractional program, and both formulations are related to the vector-valued multi-objective fractional problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in S}\min_i q_i(x)\text{ and }\sup_{x\in S}\sum_i q_i(x)\text{ are multi-ratio formulations; the former is sometimes called a generalized fractional program.}

children.title: Extremal-Ratio Programs
children.top_down_role: Fractional programs aggregating component ratios through an extremal operator.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i,g_i:X\to\mathbb R\) with \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X}\max_{i\in I} f_i(x)/g_i(x)\), or dually \(v^*=\sup_{x\in X}\min_{i\in I} f_i(x)/g_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite worst-ratio minimization and best-guaranteed-ratio maximization.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extremal-ratio program aggregates finitely many well-defined ratios by an extremum. Its minimax form is \[\inf_{x\in X}\max_{i\in I}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)},\] and its maximin form is \[\sup_{x\in X}\min_{i\in I}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}.\] Every denominator satisfies \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\). Thus each indexed quotient is defined on the common feasible domain, while the extremal operator selects the worst or best component at each feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extremal-ratio program minimizes the largest, or maximizes the smallest, member of a finite family of positive-denominator ratios.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremal-Ratio Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold Bisection for Convex Fractional Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasiconvex method for nonnegative-threshold worst-ratio minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(X\) is convex, each \(f_i\) is convex, and each \(g_i\) is positive and concave on \(X\). For fixed \(t\geq0\), the system \(f_i(x)-t g_i(x)\leq0\) is convex and its feasibility is monotone in \(t\). If \(0\leq L\leq v^*\leq U\), bisection returns a value bracket of width at most \(\varepsilon\) after \(\lceil\log_2((U-L)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) convex-feasibility tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard convex-fractional assumptions and a nonnegative value bracket, worst-ratio minimization admits threshold bisection.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i\) is convex and every \(g_i\) is positive and concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(\lceil\log_2((U-L)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) convex-feasibility tests produce an \(\varepsilon\)-wide value bracket.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Bisection for Convex Fractional Components

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph and hypograph representations for the two seed variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\), then \[\inf_{x\in X}\max_i\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}=\inf_{x,t}\{t:x\in X,\ f_i(x)-t g_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\},\] and \[\sup_{x\in X}\min_i\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}=\sup_{x,t}\{t:x\in X,\ f_i(x)-t g_i(x)\geq0\ \forall i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One common threshold gives exact epigraph and hypograph formulations of worst- and best-component ratio objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i(x)>0\) for every \(x\in X\) and every index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The threshold inequalities are equivalent to \(t\geq\max_i f_i/g_i\) and \(t\leq\min_i f_i/g_i\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Reformulations of Extremal Ratios

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multi-objective fractional program and efficient solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the vector-ratio model class and Pareto efficiency for maximization; no denominator sign or nonvanishing assumptions are supplied in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multi-objective fractional program has the form \(\max_{x\in S}\bigl(f_1(x)/g_1(x),\ldots,f_p(x)/g_p(x)\bigr)\). Writing its objective components as \(F_i\), a point \(\bar x\in S\) is efficient (Pareto-optimal) if there is no \(x\in S\) such that \(F_i(x)\ge F_i(\bar x)\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,p\), with strict inequality for at least one index. The set of efficient points is \(E\), and \(F(E)\) is the efficient frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-objective fractional program maximizes a vector of p ratios over a feasible set. A feasible point is Pareto-efficient when no other feasible point is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in at least one. The efficient points form E, and their objective images form the efficient frontier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in E\iff\nexists x\in S:\ \bigl(\forall i,\ F_i(x)\ge F_i(\bar x)\bigr)\land\bigl(\exists j,\ F_j(x)>F_j(\bar x)\bigr),\qquad F(E)\text{ is the efficient frontier.}

children.title: Sum-of-Ratios Programs
children.top_down_role: Fractional programs whose objective combines several ratio terms additively.

notation.meaning: Numerator and denominator of ratio i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted finite sum; fixed real weights can be absorbed into the numerators.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sum-of-ratios program has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)},\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the index set is finite, and every denominator obeys \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\). The numerators, denominators, and feasible set may be nonconvex. A weighted objective \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f_i(x)/g_i(x)\) is included by absorbing each fixed real weight \(w_i\) into its numerator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum-of-ratios program optimizes a finite sum of quotient terms whose denominators are positive throughout the common feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Ratios Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating sums of ratios from independent single-ratio problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[0,1]\), take \(r_1(x)=x\) and \(r_2(x)=1-x\), both representable with denominator one. Then \[\min_{x\in X}(r_1(x)+r_2(x))=1,\qquad \min_Xr_1+\min_Xr_2=0.\] Thus a shared decision generally prevents separate optimization of the ratio terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing each ratio independently and summing the results generally gives the wrong value.
assumptions_latex: All component ratios share the same decision vector and feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_X\sum_i r_i\) need not equal \(\sum_i\min_Xr_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Decisions Prevent Componentwise Decoupling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lift for minimization of a finite sum of positive-denominator ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g_i(x)>0\) on \(X\), then \[\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}=\inf_{x\in X,t\in\mathbb R^m}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m t_i:f_i(x)-t_i g_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\right\}.\] Whenever the lifted optimum is attained, an optimal solution satisfies \(t_i=f_i(x)/g_i(x)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One epigraph variable per component gives an exact lifted sum-of-ratios model.
assumptions_latex: Every denominator is strictly positive on the common feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and lifted infima agree, with componentwise equality at any attained lifted optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Componentwise Epigraph Lift

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a multi-ratio fractional program seeking the supremum of an additive collection of ratios over a convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, and suppose the displayed ratios are well-defined on \(S\). The multi-ratio fractional program is
\[
\sup\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}:x\in S\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous sum-of-ratios program seeks the supremum of the sum of p ratios f_i(x)/g_i(x) over a convex feasible region S in R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{f_i(x)}{g_i(x)}:x\in S\right\}

children.title: Multiple-Ratio Systems
children.top_down_role: Models containing several coupled ratio objectives or constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) specifies admissible simultaneous ratio values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is feasible exactly when }x\in X\text{ and }R(x)\in Y\).

notation.meaning: Admissible set for simultaneous ratio values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued ratio systems before choosing a sum or extremal scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiple-ratio system is specified by the vector mapping \[R(x)=\left(\frac{f_1(x)}{g_1(x)},\ldots,\frac{f_m(x)}{g_m(x)}\right),\qquad x\in X,\] with \(g_i(x)>0\) for every \(i\) and \(x\in X\). Feasibility imposes a joint condition \(R(x)\in Y\), where \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\); equivalently, it may impose finitely many predicates \(\Phi_k(R(x),x)\leq0\). An objective may depend on \(x\) and the entire vector \(R(x)\), without requiring a sum or extremal scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-ratio system constrains or optimizes the vector of several positive-denominator ratios jointly, without prescribing a particular scalar aggregation.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Ratio Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed vector-ratio formulation is coherent, but the exact boundary of the class, including arbitrary joint predicates and objectives depending on the entire ratio vector, is not supported by a source and is not sufficiently canonical to validate without one.

children.title: Multiplicative Programs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for products of structured factors.

assumptions_latex: Each factor \(h_i:X\to\mathbb R\) is finite on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^*=\inf_{x\in X}\prod_{i=1}^{m}h_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products of structured factors with an explicitly stated common domain.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiplicative program optimizes an objective containing a finite product of factor functions, in the canonical form \[\inf_{x\in X}H(x),\qquad H(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}h_i(x).\] The feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) lies in the common domain of all factors. Factor signs and possible zeros are part of the model specification; positivity is required only when a logarithmic representation is invoked. Product constraints, such as \(\prod_{i=1}^{m}h_i(x)\leq c\), belong to the same class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicative program optimizes or constrains a finite product of structured factors defined on a common feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative Convex Factors Need Not Have a Convex Product
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary distinguishing convex factors from log-convex factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[0,1]\), \(h_1(x)=x^2\) and \(h_2(x)=(1-x)^2\) are nonnegative and convex, but \(H(x)=x^2(1-x)^2\) is not convex because \(H(0)=H(1)=0\) while \(H(1/2)=1/16\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even two nonnegative convex factors can have a nonconvex product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonnegativity and convexity of all factors do not imply convexity of their product.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Convex Factors Need Not Have a Convex Product

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical curvature-preserving subclass of multiplicative programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex and let \(h_i:X\to(0,\infty)\) be log-convex for \(i=1,,m\). Then \(H=\prod_i h_i\) is log-convex and therefore convex on \(X\), with \(\log H=\sum_i\log h_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product of positive log-convex factors is log-convex and convex.
assumptions_latex: Every factor is strictly positive and log-convex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\prod_i h_i\) is log-convex, hence convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Products of Positive Log-Convex Factors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic factorization of a finite product into binary product equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m h_i(x)\), introduce \(z_1=h_1(x)\) and \(z_j=z_{j-1}h_j(x)\) for \(j=2,\ldots,m\). The exact lifted system satisfies \(z_m=H(x)\), and its projection onto \((x,z_m)\) is the graph of \(H\). Replacing a product equality by an outer relaxation generally yields only a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any finite product has an exact chain lift using binary product equations.
assumptions_latex: Every factor is finite on the common domain.
All binary product equations are imposed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted system projects exactly to \(z_m=\prod_i h_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Recursive Product Lift

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-product characterization of a quadratic function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-and-inertia characterization of quadratic functions representable as products of two affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x)=c^Tx+\tfrac12x^TQx with Q=Q^T, and define \widetilde Q=\begin{bmatrix}Q&c\\c^T&0\end{bmatrix}. Then f can be decomposed into a product of two affine functions if and only if (i) \operatorname{rank}(\widetilde Q)-1\leq\operatorname{rank}(Q)\leq2 and (ii), when \operatorname{rank}(Q)=2, Q has one negative and one positive eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic function factors into two affine functions exactly when the stated augmented-matrix rank condition holds and a rank-two quadratic matrix has one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a product of two affine functions}\iff\left(\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde Q)-1\leq\operatorname{rank}(Q)\leq2\right)\land\left(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=2\Rightarrow Q\text{ has one negative and one positive eigenvalue}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parametric LP Algorithm via a Piecewise-Quadratic Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the stated linear multiplicative-program formulation and its parameterized linear program ${\rm P1}(\eta)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First compute $\underline{\eta}=\min\{d_2^Tx+d_{20}:x\in X\}$, solve ${\rm P1}(\underline{\eta})$, and retain an optimal basis $B_0$. Then increase $\eta$ over $[\underline{\eta},\infty)$, obtaining intervals $[\eta_k,\eta_{k+1}]$ and bases $B_k$ that are optimal throughout their associated intervals, together with the induced piecewise-quadratic function $G$. For each interval choose $\eta^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in[\eta_k,\eta_{k+1}]}G(\eta)$; choose $\eta^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{G(\eta^0),\ldots,G(\eta^t)\}$ and return $x^*=x^*(\eta^*)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute the smallest feasible value of the linear parameter expression, trace the optimal bases of the parameterized linear program from that value upward, and construct the resulting piecewise-quadratic function. Minimize this function on each basis interval, select the best interval minimizer, and return its associated solution.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is the feasible set used in }\underline{\eta}=\min\{d_2^Tx+d_{20}:x\in X\}
\text{The stated minima and associated solutions exist.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*=x^*(\eta^*),\quad \eta^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in\{\eta^0,\ldots,\eta^t\}}G(\eta)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cutting-Plane Algorithm for a Convex Multiplicative Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm 3.3, including initialization, vertex selection, primal-dual linear-program solves, termination test, and cutting update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute bounds \(\underline y\) and \(\bar y\) for \(y^*\), set \(Y_0=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^p:\underline y\le y\le\bar y\}\), and initialize \(k=0\). Select \(y^k\in\operatorname{argmin}\{\prod_{j=1}^p y_j:y\in V(Y_k)\}\). Solve \(\mathrm{DL}(y^k)\) for a basic optimal solution \(z^k\), and obtain an optimal solution \((x^k,t^k)\) of its dual \(\mathrm{PL}(y^k)\). If \(t^k=0\), set \(x^*=x^k\) and terminate. Otherwise define \(l_k(y)=(z^k)^Tb-(z^k)^TBy\), set \(Y_{k+1}=Y_k\cap\{y\in\mathbb{R}^p:l_k(y)\le0\}\), increment \(k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound the reduced variable, choose a vertex minimizing the coordinate product, solve the associated primal-dual linear programs, and terminate when the residual is zero. Otherwise add the generated linear cut and repeat.
assumptions_latex: The bounds \(\underline y\) and \(\bar y\) contain the target \(y^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(t^k=0\), the procedure returns \(x^*=x^k\); otherwise it replaces \(Y_k\) by \(Y_k\cap\{y:l_k(y)\le0\}\) and continues.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex and g-Vertex by Maximal Active Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ordinary vertices through active polytope constraints and extends this notion using active maximizer indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X=\{x\mid a_j^Tx\ge b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,k\} and J(x)=\{j\mid a_j^Tx=b_j\}. A point x\in X is a vertex when J(x) is inclusion-maximal among \{J(y):y\in X\}; for polytopes this is equivalent to the usual extreme-point definition. If M(x)=\{i'\mid f_i(x)=g(x)\}, with M(x)\cap J(x)=\varnothing, then x is a g\text{-vertex} when J(x)\cup M(x) is inclusion-maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polytope, a point is a vertex when no feasible point has a strictly larger set of active defining inequalities; this is equivalent to being an extreme point. A g-vertex is defined analogously by requiring maximality of the union of the active constraints and the indices of component functions attaining g.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a }g\text{-vertex}\iff \nexists y\in X:\ J(x)\cup M(x)\subsetneq J(y)\cup M(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical-Point Attainment for Locally Stable Active Minimax Indices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes minimizers through maximal active-index sets for a finite, point-dependent minimax family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let g(x)=\max_{i\in I(x)}f_i(x), where the component functions are continuous and pseudoconcave on a convex region X, each I(x) is finite, and X' is a compact subset of the ambient region. Define M(x)=\{i\in I(x)\mid f_i(x)=g(x)\}. Suppose that for every x\in X there is a neighborhood U_x such that M(y)\subseteq M(x) for every y\in U_x. If \min_{x\in X}g(x) is attained at an interior point of X', then it is attained at a point whose M-set is inclusion-maximal over X'. Moreover, if x is an interior minimizer in X' and M(x)\subseteq M(y) for some y\in X', then y is also a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite point-dependent minimax family whose active-index set can only decrease locally, an attained interior minimum on the compact set occurs at a point with a maximal active-index set. Any point whose active-index set contains that of an interior minimizer is also a minimizer.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is convex and }X'\subseteq X\text{ is compact}
f_i\text{ is continuous and pseudoconcave on }X
\forall x\in X\ \exists U_x\ni x\ \forall y\in U_x:\ M(y)\subseteq M(x)
\min_{x\in X}g(x)\text{ is attained at an interior point of }X'
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^\star\in X':\ g(x^\star)=\min_{x\in X}g(x)\ \land\ \nexists y\in X':M(x^\star)\subsetneq M(y);\quad [x\in\operatorname{int}(X')\cap\operatorname*{argmin}g,\ M(x)\subseteq M(y)]\Rightarrow y\in\operatorname*{argmin}g.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A semi-infinite minimax program has the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{t\in T}f(x,t),\] where the decision vector \(x\) is finite-dimensional and \(T\) is an infinite index set. Its epigraph form is \[\inf_{x,\tau}\{\tau:x\in X,\ f(x,t)\leq\tau\text{ for every }t\in T\}.\] When the supremum is not attained, \(\sup\) rather than \(\max\) is essential; the epigraph equivalence still holds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-restriction method with exact worst-index separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(T_k\subset T\), globally solve \[L_k=\min_{x\in X}\max_{t\in T_k}f(x,t)\] and let \(x_k\) be an optimizer. Compute \(U_k=\sup_{t\in T}f(x_k,t)\). Then \(L_k\le v^*\le U_k\). Thus \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\) certifies that \(x_k\) is \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal. If the gap is larger, an exact maximizer, when one exists, or a declared approximate maximizer may be added, with its separation error included in subsequent bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exchange methods alternate finite minimax restrictions and worst-index separation; their lower–upper gap is a global value certificate.
assumptions_latex: Every finite restricted problem is solved globally.
The separation value is exact; any approximate separation error is explicitly included in the upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\le v^*\le U_k\), and \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow\phi(x_k)-v^*\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exchange Restriction and Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Danskin-type certificate for compact-index convex minimax optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex semi-infinite minimax point is optimal exactly when active component gradients balance the feasible-set normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(T\) is compact.
Every component is convex and differentiable in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\phi(x)\iff0\in\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla_xf(x^*,t):t\in T(x^*)\}+N_C(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Index First-Order Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonattained Suprema Defeat Exact Finite Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for exact discretization of an infinite index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{0\}\), \(T=(0,1)\), and \(f(0,t)=t\). Then \(\sup_{t\in T}f(0,t)=1\), whereas \(\max_{t\in S}f(0,t)<1\) for every finite \(S\subset T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonattained supremum can make every finite index restriction strictly inexact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{t\in T}f(0,t)=1>\max_{t\in S}f(0,t)\) for every finite \(S\subset T\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Suprema Defeat Exact Finite Restriction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity of the supremum objective under compact continuous indexing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(T\) be compact metric spaces and let \(f:X\times T\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Then \(\phi(x)=\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)\) is continuous, every active set \(T(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{t\in T}f(x,t)\) is nonempty and compact, and \(\min_{x\in X}\phi(x)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint continuity on compact decision and index sets makes the worst-case objective continuous and ensures attainment of both extrema.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\in C(X)\), \(T(x)\ne\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\phi(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Index Regularity and Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex semi-infinite minimax specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f(\cdot,t)\) is convex on \(C\) for every \(t\in T\), then \(\phi(x)=\sup_{t\in T}f(x,t)\) is convex on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of an arbitrary family of convex functions is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi=\sup_{t\in T}f(\cdot,t)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Preservation by Suprema

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-valued dual representation for compact convex semi-infinite minimax programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, let \(T\) be compact Hausdorff, and let \(f:C\times T\to\mathbb R\) be continuous with \(f(\cdot,t)\) convex for every \(t\). Then \[\min_{x\in C}\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal P(T)}\min_{x\in C}\int_T f(x,t)\,d\mu(t),\] and the maximum over regular Borel probability measures is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact convex semi-infinite minimax has an attained probability-measure dual under continuity and convexity in the decision variable.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous and \(f(\cdot,t)\) is convex for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal P(T)}\min_{x\in C}\int_Tf(x,t)\,d\mu(t)\), with an optimal \(\mu\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient convergence conditions for nested finite restrictions of a compact continuous semi-infinite minimax problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(T\) be compact metric spaces, let \(f:X\times T\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let finite sets \(T_k\subseteq T_{k+1}\) have dense union in \(T\). Define \(\phi_k(x)=\max_{t\in T_k}f(x,t)\), \(\phi(x)=\max_{t\in T}f(x,t)\), and \(L_k=\min_X\phi_k\). Then \(\phi_k\uparrow\phi\) uniformly and \(L_k\uparrow v^*=\min_X\phi\). If \(x_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_X\phi_k\) and \(U_k=\phi(x_k)\), then \(0\le U_k-L_k\le\|\phi-\phi_k\|_\infty\to0\), and every cluster point of \((x_k)\) is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested finite restrictions with dense index union close the certified minimax gap and have only globally optimal cluster points.
assumptions_latex: The finite restrictions are nested with dense union, and each restricted problem is solved globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_k\to\phi\) uniformly, \(L_k\uparrow v^*\), \(U_k-L_k\to0\), and every cluster point of \((x_k)\) minimizes \(\phi\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical-Point Attainment for Compact-Index Concave Minimax Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract writes the maximization set once as Y although the declared compact index set is I; the statement uses the declared set I.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X\subset\mathbb{R}^m be a polytope, let I\subset\mathbb{R}^n be compact, and let f:X\times I\to\mathbb{R} be continuous. Define g(x)=\max_{y\in I}f(x,y). If x\mapsto f(x,y) is concave on X for every y\in I, then the minimum of g over X is attained at a critical point, in the sense of a point with a maximal active-maximizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous minimax objective over a compact index set, if every indexed component is concave in the decision variable and the feasible set is a polytope, then the minimum is attained at a critical point with a maximal set of active maximizers.
assumptions_latex: f(\cdot,y)\text{ is concave on }X\quad(\forall y\in I)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^\star\in X:\ g(x^\star)=\min_{x\in X}g(x)\ \land\ x^\star\text{ is a critical point}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximin program has the form \[\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{t\in T}f(x,t),\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(T\) are nonempty. For each decision \(x\), the inner infimum is its worst indexed value, and the outer problem selects the decision with the largest such guarantee. If \(T=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(f_i(x)=f(x,i)\), the inner value is \(\min_{i=1,\ldots,m}f_i(x)\). This definition alone does not assert equality with the reversed quantity \(\inf_{t\in T}\sup_{x\in X}f(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximin program chooses a decision maximizing its worst indexed payoff; no equality with the reversed minimax order is implied.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) be concave. Then \[G(x)=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\] is concave on \(X\). Consequently, maximizing \(G\) over \(X\) has a convex hypograph formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite pointwise minimum of concave payoffs is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=\min_i f_i\) is concave on \(X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order relation between maximin and reversed minimax values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every real-valued function \(f:X\times T\to\mathbb R\) on nonempty sets, \[\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{t\in T}f(x,t)\leq\inf_{t\in T}\sup_{x\in X}f(x,t),\] whenever the two sides are well-defined as extended-real values. Equality requires additional structural assumptions and is not part of the maximin definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximin value never exceeds the reversed minimax value, but equality is not automatic.
assumptions_latex: The displayed extended-real values are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_x\inf_t f(x,t)\leq\inf_t\sup_x f(x,t)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted formulation for finitely many payoff components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(f_i(x)=f(x,i)\), then \[\sup_{x\in X}\min_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)=\sup_{x,t}\{t:x\in X,\ t\leq f_i(x)\text{ for every }i\}.\] Under attainment, an optimal decision \(x^*\) corresponds to \(t^*=\min_i f_i(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximin problem has an exact hypograph formulation using one guaranteed-payoff variable bounded by every component.
assumptions_latex: \(T=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is finite and every \(f_i\) is real-valued on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise-minimum and hypograph formulations have the same supremum, with the stated correspondence when the optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Maximin Hypograph Formulation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC decompositions of finite maximin and minimax objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit DC representations for extrema of finitely many composed facility-attraction functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_j:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R_+\) be convex. For the maximin objective \(F(x)=\min_{1\le j\le n}q_j(h_j(x))\), assume every \(q_j\) is convex and decreasing with \(|q'_{j,+}(0)|<\infty\). Choose suitable \(K_j\) and define the convex functions \(g_j=q_j\circ h_j+K_jh_j\). Then \(F=G-H\), where \(G=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j\) and \(H=\max_{1\le j\le n}\left(K_jh_j+\sum_{i\ne j}g_i\right)\). For the minimax objective \(F(x)=\max_{1\le j\le n}q_j(h_j(x))\), if every \(q_j\) is concave and increasing with \(|q'_{j,+}(0)|<\infty\), suitable convex functions \(g_j=K_jh_j-q_j\circ h_j\) yield \(F=G-H\), where \(G=\max_{1\le j\le n}\left(K_jh_j+\sum_{i\ne j}g_i\right)\) and \(H=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximin of convex decreasing composed terms and a finite minimax of concave increasing composed terms both admit explicit difference-of-convex decompositions when their right derivatives at zero are finite.
assumptions_latex: h_j:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R_+\text{ is convex for }j=1,\ldots,n
K_j\text{ is chosen sufficiently large to make the stated }g_j\text{ convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)=G(x)-H(x)\quad\text{with convex }G,H\text{ in both the finite maximin and minimax cases}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nested extremal-aggregate program places two or more ordered extremal operators inside its objective or constraints. A representative form is \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{i\in I}\inf_{j\in J_i}f_{ij}(x).\] The ordering is part of the model: the inner value \(\inf_{j\in J_i}f_{ij}(x)\) is formed separately for each \(i\), after which the outer supremum is taken. Interchanging the two operators generally defines a different function and a different optimization problem unless additional interchange conditions are established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested extremal program optimizes an ordered composition of minima, maxima, infima, or suprema; changing their order generally changes the model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the coordinatewise order on the nonnegative orthant and, separately, its restriction to a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set H\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n is conormal if x\in H implies x+\mathbb{R}_+^n\subseteq H. A set H\subseteq[a,b] is conormal in [a,b] if a\leq x\leq x'\leq b and x\in H imply x'\in H; equivalently, a\leq x\leq x'\leq b and x'\notin H imply x\notin H. Moreover, H\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n is conormal if and only if \mathbb{R}_+^n\setminus H is normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conormal set contains every nonnegative point coordinatewise above each of its points. Within a box, membership is upward closed, equivalently nonmembership is downward closed. In the nonnegative orthant, a set is conormal exactly when its complement is normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is conormal}\iff \mathbb{R}_+^n\setminus H\text{ is normal}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Radial Projection onto the Upper Boundary of a Normal Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of the upper-boundary intersection along rays from the lower box vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\subseteq[a,b]\) be a compact normal set with nonempty interior. For every \(z\in[a,b]\setminus\{a\}\), the segment from \(a\) to \(z\) meets \(\partial^+G\) at the unique point \(\pi_G(z)=a+\lambda(z-a)\), where \(\lambda=\max\{\alpha>0:a+\alpha(z-a)\in G\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact normal set with nonempty interior inside a box, every nontrivial ray from the lower vertex has a unique intersection with the set's upper boundary. The intersection is obtained by taking the largest positive scaling that remains in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\pi_G(z)\in\partial^+G\cap[a,z],\qquad \pi_G(z)=a+\left(\max\{\alpha>0:a+\alpha(z-a)\in G\}\right)(z-a)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An epsilon-eta approximate procedure for discrete monotonic optimization based on S-adjusted box reduction and adaptive branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\varepsilon,\eta>0\), initialize the box collection with \([a,b]\), and set \(\gamma\) either to \(f(\bar x)-\eta\) for an available essential feasible point \(\bar x\), or to \(\gamma_0=f(b)\). For each active box \(M\), compute \(\operatorname{red}_\gamma^S M=[p^M,q^M]\), delete empty boxes and boxes with \(g(p^M)>-\varepsilon\), and set \(\beta(M)=g(p^M)\). If no boxes remain, report \(\varepsilon\)-essential infeasibility when \(\gamma=\gamma_0\), or report \(\bar x\) as essentially \((\varepsilon,\eta)\)-optimal when \(\gamma=f(\bar x)-\eta\). Otherwise select a box minimizing \(\beta\), construct the prescribed upper-S-adjusted test point \(y^k\), update the incumbent and target when \(g(y^k)\le-\varepsilon\), and otherwise split the selected box adaptively through \((p^k,y^k)\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The discrete SIT algorithm reduces and filters boxes at a target objective level, searches the most promising surviving box for an essentially feasible discrete point, updates the incumbent and target when one is found, and otherwise branches. Exhaustion yields the stated essential-infeasibility or approximate-optimality status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R_k'=\varnothing\Rightarrow\begin{cases}(\mathrm{DMO})\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-essentially infeasible},&\gamma=\gamma_0,\\ \bar x\text{ is essentially }(\varepsilon,\eta)\text{-optimal},&\gamma=f(\bar x)-\eta.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm for obtaining a multiplicatively epsilon-optimal solution of the monotonic maximization reformulation and a corresponding original-variable solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\varepsilon>0\), initialize \(T_1=\widetilde T_1=\{b\}\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(z^k\in\arg\max_{z\in\widetilde T_k}\Phi(z)\), compute the radial projection \(y^k=\pi_G(z^k)\), and find \(x^k\in D\) with \(y_i^k\le f_i(x^k)/g_i(x^k)\) for all \(i\). Set \(\widetilde y_i^k=f_i(x^k)/g_i(x^k)\) and update the incumbent \(\bar y^k\) and \(CBV=\Phi(\bar y^k)\). Choose \(T'_k\subseteq T_k\cap\{z:z>y^k\}\) containing \(z^k\), and replace every \(z\in T'_k\) by \(z^{*i}=z-(z_i-y_i^k)e^i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Remove improper vertices, vertices with \(\Phi(z)<(1+\varepsilon)CBV\), and vertices \(z\not\ge a\). If no vertex remains, return \(\bar y^k\) and its corresponding \(\bar x^k\); otherwise iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm repeatedly selects the best current polyblock vertex, projects it radially onto the upper boundary of the feasible normal set, recovers and updates a feasible incumbent, splits dominated vertices coordinatewise, and prunes improper or insufficiently promising vertices. When the vertex set becomes empty, the incumbent image and original-variable points are epsilon-optimal.
assumptions_latex: \pi_G(z)\text{ and a corresponding }x\in D\text{ satisfying }\pi_G(z)_i\le f_i(x)/g_i(x)\text{ can be computed}
\Phi\text{ is increasing on the relevant order interval}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone-monotonicity and constancy along lineality fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of monotonicity relative to a closed convex cone and its consequence on fibers parallel to the cone's lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) a closed convex cone, and \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is \(K\)-monotonic on \(X\) if \[x,x'\in X,\quad x'-x\in K\implies f(x')\ge f(x).\] Equivalently, for each \(x\in X\) and \(u\in K\), the map \(\theta\mapsto f(x+\theta u)\) is nondecreasing over the feasible nonnegative parameters \(\{\theta\ge0:x+\theta u\in X\}\). If \(L=K\cap(-K)\) and \(Q\) satisfies \(\ker Q=L\), then \[x,x'\in X,\quad Qx=Qx'\implies f(x)=f(x').\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is K-monotonic on X when movement between feasible points in a K-direction cannot decrease its value. It is consequently constant on every fiber whose directions lie in the lineality space of K.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a closed convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'-x\in K\implies f(x')\ge f(x),\qquad Qx=Qx'\implies f(x)=f(x')

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone Monotonicity and the Rank Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines monotonicity relative to a closed convex cone, the associated rank property, and invariance along the cone's lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone. The function \(f\) is monotonic on \(\Omega\) with respect to \(M\) if \(f(x+u)\geq f(x)\) for all \(x\in\Omega\) and \(u\in M\). If, in addition, \(M\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(\Omega)\) and \(\dim M^*=k\), then \(f\) has the rank-\(k\) property on \(\Omega\). For the lineality space \(L=M\cap(-M)\), one has \(\dim L=n-k\) and \(f(x+u)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in\Omega\) and \(u\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is monotonic with respect to a closed convex cone when movement in any cone direction cannot decrease its value. When the cone lies in the recession cone of the domain and its dual has dimension k, this is called the rank-k property. The function is then constant along the cone's lineality directions, whose dimension is n-k.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a closed convex cone}
M\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(\Omega)\text{ and }\dim M^*=k\text{ for the rank-property conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim L=n-k\quad\text{and}\quad f(x+u)=f(x)\quad\forall x\in\Omega,\ \forall u\in L,\qquad L=M\cap(-M).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Application-specific box-search procedure for problem (DL).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal P_1=\{[a,b]\}\), \(\mathcal R_1=\varnothing\), and let \(r=\bar z\) when a feasible \((\bar x,\bar z)\) is available, or \(r=0\) otherwise. At iteration \(k\), apply \(S\)-adjusted reductions and delete \([p,q]\) if \(\varphi(p,r)-\lVert q\rVert^2\geq0\). For each remaining box \(M\), solve \(\operatorname{LP}(M,r)\), deleting \(M\) if the LP is infeasible or \(\mu(M)=r\), and use any successfully adjusted LP solution with \(z^M>r\) to update the current best value. Form \(\mathcal S_k=\mathcal R_k\cup\mathcal P_k^*\), reset \(r\) to the current best value, and delete boxes satisfying \(\mu(M)<r\). If no box remains, report infeasibility when \(r=0\), and otherwise report the incumbent attaining \(r\) as optimal. Otherwise, bisect a box in \(\arg\max_{M\in\mathcal R_{k+1}}\mu(M)\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the full box, the algorithm repeatedly applies S-adjusted reductions, solves an LP bound on each surviving box, updates the feasible incumbent, prunes non-improving boxes, and bisects a surviving box with maximal bound. When no box remains, it declares infeasibility if the current best value is zero and otherwise returns the incumbent as optimal.
assumptions_latex: r=\bar z\text{ if a feasible }(\bar x,\bar z)\text{ is available, and }r=0\text{ otherwise}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R_{k+1}=\varnothing\Rightarrow\left[(r=0\Rightarrow(\mathrm{DL})\text{ is infeasible})\land(r\neq0\Rightarrow r\text{ and an incumbent attaining }r\text{ are optimal})\right];\quad \mathcal R_{k+1}\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow\text{bisect a maximizer of }\mu\text{ and continue}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PA Algorithm for GQCM with Convex Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization, support subproblems, optimality test, incumbent update, and polyhedral cutting step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be monotone with respect to \(\mathbb R_+^r\), let \(\bar y\in E\) be feasible, and define \(C=\{y\mid F(y)\ge F(\bar y)\}\). After translating by \(y^0\in E\) with \(F(y^0)>F(\bar y)\), initialize \(P_1\) as the simplex with vertex set \(\{0,-e^1/\alpha,\ldots,-e^r/\alpha\}\), where \(\alpha>0\) satisfies \(F(\alpha w)=F(\bar y)\) and \(w=(-1,\ldots,-1)^T\). At iteration \(k\), solve \(\mu(t)=\max\{\langle t,y\rangle:y\in E\}=\max\{\langle t,g(x)\rangle:x\in D\}\) for every new nonzero \(t\in V_k\), and choose \(t^k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{t\in V_k}\mu(t)\). If \(\mu(t^k)\le1\), terminate with \(\bar y\) optimal. Otherwise set \(y^k=y(t^k)\); if \(F(y^k)<F(\bar y)\), reset \(\bar y=y^k\) and update \(C=\{y\mid F(y)\ge F(\bar y)\}\). Compute \(\theta_k=\sup\{\theta\mid F(\theta y^k)\ge F(\bar y)\}\), set \(P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\{t\mid\langle t,y^k\rangle\le1/\theta_k\}\), construct its vertex set, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PA method repeatedly solves convex support problems at vertices of a polytope. A maximum support value at most one certifies that the incumbent is optimal; otherwise the method may improve the incumbent and cuts the polytope using the incumbent level set.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is monotone with respect to }\mathbb R_+^r.
\bar y\in E\text{ is feasible and }C=\{y\mid F(y)\ge F(\bar y)\}.
t\in(\mathbb R_+^r)^\circ=-\mathbb R_+^r\text{ in the support subproblems}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu(t^k)\le1\Rightarrow\bar y\text{ is optimal};\qquad \mu(t^k)>1\Rightarrow P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\{t\mid\langle t,y^k\rangle\le1/\theta_k\}\text{ and the iteration continues}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Box-search procedure on [a,b] that incorporates robust branch-and-bound for the level subproblem Q_gamma into successive incumbent transcending.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). If no feasible solution is known, set \(\gamma=f(b)\); otherwise let \(\bar x\) be the best available nonisolated feasible solution and set \(\gamma=f(\bar x)-\varepsilon\). Initialize \(\mathcal P_1=\{[a,b]\}\), \(\mathcal R_1=\varnothing\). At each iteration, validly reduce the active boxes, delete empty reductions, compute for each reduced box \(M=[p',q']\) an upper bound \(\beta(M)\) on \(g\) over its feasible points satisfying \(\beta(M)\leq\min_j\{u_j(q')-v_j(p')\}\), and delete boxes with \(\beta(M)<0\). Add surviving boxes to the retained collection. If the retained collection is empty, return \(\bar x\) as essentially \(\varepsilon\)-optimal when \(\gamma=f(\bar x)-\varepsilon\), or report essential infeasibility when \(\gamma=f(b)\). Otherwise choose \(M_k=[p^k,q^k]\) maximizing \(\beta(M)\). If \(\beta(M_k)<\varepsilon\), return the corresponding essential \(\varepsilon\)-optimality result, or report \(\varepsilon\)-essential infeasibility when \(\gamma=f(b)\). If \(\beta(M_k)\geq\varepsilon\), set \(\lambda_k=\max\{\alpha\mid f(p^k+\alpha(q^k-p^k))\leq\gamma\}\) and \(x^k=p^k+\lambda_k(q^k-p^k)\). When \(g(x^k)>0\), update \(\bar x\) to the prescribed intersection with \(g(x)=0\) if \(g(p^k)<0\), and otherwise to \(p^k\). Finally bisect \(M_k\) by standard bisection or another rule consistent with \(M\mapsto\beta(M)\), retain the other boxes, and iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The robust SIT procedure initializes a target level from either the upper corner or a known nonisolated incumbent. It reduces and bounds boxes, removes boxes that cannot help, selects a box with maximal bound, applies the two distinct stopping tests, updates the incumbent from the prescribed segment construction when possible, and otherwise bisects the selected box and continues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure follows the stated reduction, deletion, selection, stopping, incumbent-update, and subdivision rules; an empty retained collection yields essential infeasibility, whereas }\beta_k<\varepsilon\text{ yields }\varepsilon\text{-essential infeasibility in the no-incumbent branch.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-set representation of the canonical increasing-function form under semicontinuity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the canonical monotonic program \max\{f(x)\mid g(x)\le 0\le h(x),\ x\in[a,b]\}, where f,g,h are increasing, f and h are upper semicontinuous, and g is lower semicontinuous. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a canonical monotonic program, the stated monotonicity and semicontinuity assumptions make the lower feasible set compact and normal and the upper feasible set compact and conormal, so the problem is maximization over their intersection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal Sets in the Nonnegative Orthant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, trivial cases, and the stated coordinate-hyperplane closure construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(G\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is normal if \(x\in G\) and \(0\le x'\le x\) imply \(x'\in G\), equivalently if \([0,x]\subseteq G\) for every \(x\in G\). The sets \(\varnothing\), \(\{0\}\), and \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) are trivial normal sets. If \(G\) is normal, then for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(G\cup\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:x_i=0\}\) is normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of the nonnegative orthant is normal when it contains every nonnegative point coordinatewise dominated by one of its points. The empty set, the origin, and the whole orthant are trivial normal sets. Adjoining a coordinate hyperplane in the orthant preserves normality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublevel-Set Representation of Closed Normal Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward normality and closedness of increasing-function sublevel sets, with the converse under closedness and nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is increasing and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), then \(G=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:g(x)\le\alpha\}\) is normal. If, additionally, \(g\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(G\) is closed. Conversely, if \(G\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is closed and normal with nonempty interior, then there exist a lower-semicontinuous increasing function \(g:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(G=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:g(x)\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel sets of increasing functions are normal and are closed when the function is lower semicontinuous. Conversely, every closed normal set with nonempty interior is a sublevel set of a lower-semicontinuous increasing function.
assumptions_latex: \text{for the converse, }G\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\text{ is closed and normal with }\operatorname{int}G\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:g(x)\le\alpha\}\text{ is normal and, under lower semicontinuity, closed; every stated }G\text{ has such a representation}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-point test and boxwise upper bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the definitions and standing hypotheses for the monotonic-optimization subproblem Q_gamma and the component functions u_j and v_j.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=[p,q]\). (i) If \(g(p)>0\) and \(f(p)<\gamma\), then \(p\) is a nonisolated feasible solution with \(f(p)<\gamma\). (ii) If \(f(q)>\gamma\), let \(x(M)=p+\lambda(q-p)\), where \(\lambda=\max\{\alpha\mid f(p+\alpha(q-p))\leq\gamma\}\), and define \(z^i=q+(x_i(M)-q_i)e^i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). Then \(\beta(M)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\min_{1\leq j\leq m}\{u_j(z^i)-v_j(p)\}\) is an upper bound for \(g(x)\) over all \(x\in[p,q]\) satisfying \(f(x)\leq\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated monotonic-optimization subproblem, the conditions g(p)>0 and f(p)<gamma make p a nonisolated feasible solution. When f(q)>gamma, the specified segment boundary point and coordinate substitutions produce an upper bound on g over the portion of the box satisfying f(x)<=gamma.
assumptions_latex: \text{The standing definitions and hypotheses for }Q_\gamma,u_j,v_j\text{ apply.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ is a nonisolated feasible solution with }f(p)<\gamma;\qquad \sup_{\substack{x\in[p,q]\\f(x)\leq\gamma}}g(x)\leq\beta(M)=\max_i\min_j\{u_j(z^i)-v_j(p)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Boundary and Pareto Points of a Conormal Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The lower-boundary notion is radial from the lower corner of the box; the Pareto notion uses coordinatewise minimality against points of H.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H\subseteq[a,b] be conormal. A point y\in[a,b] is a lower boundary point of H if y\in\operatorname{cl}H and there exist no x\in H and \lambda<1 such that x=a+\lambda(y-a). The set of all such points is denoted \partial^-H. A point y\in\operatorname{cl}H is a Pareto point, or lower extreme point, if (\forall x\in H)(x\leq y\Rightarrow x=y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower boundary point is a closure point of a conormal set for which the ray from the box's lower corner does not encounter the set earlier. A Pareto or lower extreme point has no distinct point of the set coordinatewise below it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial^-H=\{y\in[a,b]\cap\operatorname{cl}H:\nexists x\in H,\ \lambda<1,\ x=a+\lambda(y-a)\},\qquad y\text{ is Pareto}\iff(\forall x\in H)(x\leq y\Rightarrow x=y).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization obtained by quotienting out the lineality space of the ordering cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(K\subseteq\operatorname{rec}X\) be a closed convex cone with lineality space \(L\), and let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) have rank \(r\) and satisfy \(\ker Q=L\). A function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is \(K\)-monotonic on \(X\) if and only if there exists \(F:Q(X)\to\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)=F(Qx)\quad\forall x\in X\] and \[y,y'\in Q(X),\quad y'-y\in Q(K)\implies F(y')\ge F(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When K lies in the recession cone of X, a function is K-monotonic exactly when it factors through a linear map whose kernel is the lineality space of K, and the induced function is monotonic with respect to the projected cone Q(K).
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\operatorname{rec}X\text{ is a closed convex cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is }K\text{-monotonic on }X\iff \exists F:Q(X)\to\mathbb R:\ f=F\circ Q\text{ on }X\text{ and }F\text{ is }Q(K)\text{-monotonic}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Increasing, Strictly Increasing, and Decreasing Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise order definitions on the nonnegative orthant, together with algebraic examples stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is increasing if \(0\le x\le x'\) implies \(f(x)\le f(x')\); it is strictly increasing if \(x<x'\) implies \(f(x)<f(x')\). It is decreasing if \(-f\) is increasing. Polynomials with nonnegative coefficients and posynomials \(\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_{ij}}\) with \(c_j\ge0\) and \(a_{ij}\ge0\) are increasing; this includes Cobb–Douglas functions with nonnegative exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on the nonnegative orthant is increasing when it preserves coordinatewise order, strictly increasing when strict coordinatewise order produces a strict value inequality, and decreasing when its negative is increasing. Polynomials and posynomials with nonnegative coefficients and exponents are increasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\le x\le x'\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(x'),\qquad x<x'\Rightarrow f(x)<f(x')\text{ in the strictly increasing case}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical deterministic method for a compact normal/conormal monotonic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For compact normal \(G\subseteq[\ell,u]\), closed conormal \(H\subseteq[\ell,u]\), and continuous componentwise nondecreasing \(f\), outer polyblock approximation maintains a polyblock \(P_k\supseteq G\). A selected proper vertex \(v^k\in H\) gives the upper bound \(f(v^k)\); its radial projection \(p^k\) onto the upper boundary of \(G\) gives a feasible incumbent when \(p^k\in H\). Replacing \(v^k\) by the standard coordinate cut vertices preserves an outer cover. With exact projections and standard exhaustive proper-vertex selection, incumbent bounds increase to and vertex bounds decrease to \(\max_{G\cap H}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer polyblock approximation successively cuts an outer cover of the normal set and obtains convergent bounds, using the conormal set to test relevant vertices and projected incumbents.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is nonempty, compact, and normal relative to \([\ell,u]\).
\(H\) is closed and conormal relative to \([\ell,u]\), and \(G\cap H\ne\varnothing\).
Radial projections are exact and proper vertices are selected exhaustively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_k\le v^*\le U_k,\qquad L_k\uparrow v^*,\quad U_k\downarrow v^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical monotonic program is \[\sup\{f(x):x\in G\cap H\},\] where \(f\) is componentwise nondecreasing on \([\ell,u]\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Monotonic Program and Increasing Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the displayed canonical monotonic model, componentwise monotonicity, and closure under pointwise minimum and maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical monotonic optimization problem is \[\max\{f(x):g(x)\le 0\le h(x),\ x\in\mathbb R_+^n\},\] where \(f,g,h\) are increasing on \(\mathbb R_+^n\). A function \(\phi:\mathbb R_+^n\to\mathbb R\) is increasing if \(x\le x'\) componentwise implies \(\phi(x)\le\phi(x')\). If \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) are increasing, their pointwise minimum and maximum are increasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical monotonic program maximizes an increasing function on the nonnegative orthant subject to inequalities involving increasing functions. Increasing means nondecreasing under componentwise order, and pointwise minima and maxima preserve this property.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Box-constrained maximization with difference-of-monotonic objective and constraint functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A monotonic optimization problem is a problem of the form \max\{f(x)\mid g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in[a,b]\}, where [a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}^n and f,g_1,\ldots,g_m are dm functions on [a,b].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotonic optimization problem maximizes a difference-of-monotonic function over a box subject to finitely many difference-of-monotonic inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{f(x)\mid g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in[a,b]\}\text{ is a monotonic optimization problem.}
