children.title: Low-Dimensional Nonconvexity
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for models whose global difficulty is confined to few variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective and constraint nonconvexity confined to a common low-rank image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(P:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^k\) have rank at most \(k\). A model has nonconvexity confined to \(Px\) when \(f(x)=g_0(x)+h_0(Px)\) and its inequalities are \(g_i(x)+h_i(Px)\le0\), where every \(g_i\) is convex on \(X\) and the \(h_i\) may be nonconvex. For fixed \(y\), the model restricted to \(X\cap\{x:Px=y\}\) is convex in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained model has low-dimensional nonconvexity when all arbitrary objective and constraint dependence passes through one low-rank image.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is convex and each arbitrary \(h_i\) depends only on \(Px\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{For fixed }y,\text{ the fiber model on }X\cap\{x:Px=y\}\text{ is convex}.

notation.meaning: Low-rank map carrying all nonconvex dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Level Low-Dimensional Nonconvexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension Alone Does Not Imply Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a structural dimension parameter and an algorithmic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(\operatorname{rank}P\le k\) confines nonconvex dependence to at most \(k\) coordinates but, without assumptions on \(P(X)\), the functions \(h_i\), and their representations or oracles, implies neither polynomial-time global optimization nor a uniform convergence rate. Even \(k=1\) permits arbitrary univariate nonconvex dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few nonconvex coordinates are a structural property, not by themselves a tractability theorem.
assumptions_latex: Only the low-rank dependence condition is imposed.
No regularity, encoding, or oracle assumptions are imposed on the low-dimensional functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}P\le k\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{uniform tractability or convergence}.

notation.meaning: Dimension bound for the nonconvex image.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Alone Does Not Imply Tractability

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All objective nonconvexity is confined to the \(k\)-dimensional image variable \(Px\), while directions in \(\ker P\) retain convex dependence.

notation.meaning: Low-rank linear map selecting the nonconvex coordinates

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rank-factorized dependence is a standard precise model of low-dimensional nonconvexity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-level definition using a low-rank linear image; constraints may require an analogous decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) has \(k\)-dimensional nonconvexity relative to \(P\) if
\[
f(x)=g(x)+h(Px)\qquad(x\in X),
\]
where \(g\) is convex and \(P\) has rank at most \(k\). Thus the possibly nonconvex term depends only on \(y=Px\in P(X)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k\). In particular, on every affine fiber \(\{x\in X:Px=y\}\), the restriction of \(f\) differs from the convex function \(g\) by the constant \(h(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective has low-dimensional nonconvexity when its nonconvex component depends only on a low-rank linear image of the variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Dimensional Nonconvexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-factorized formulation is coherent and fits the container, but it is a particular formalization of low-dimensional nonconvexity rather than a uniquely standard definition. A dedicated source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Hidden-Structure Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Transformations revealing convex, monotone, homogeneous, or lifted structure.

children.title: Hidden Convexity
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for nonconvex presentations equivalent to convex regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient global certificate transported through an exact hidden-convexity map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under an exact hidden-convexity representation \(f=\phi\circ T\) with convex image \(Y=T(X)\), let \(y^*=T(x^*)\). If some \(g\in\partial\phi(y^*)\) satisfies \(\langle g,y-y^*\rangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in Y\), then \(x^*\) globally minimizes \(f\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transformed convex subgradient variational inequality certifies global optimality of the corresponding original point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x).

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of the transformed objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Transported Convex Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convexification through a surjective, possibly noninjective transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to Y\) be surjective, with \(Y\) convex, and suppose \(f=\phi\circ T\) for a convex function \(\phi:Y\to\mathbb R\). Then \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\phi(y)\). Every original minimizer maps to a transformed minimizer, and every preimage of a transformed minimizer is an original minimizer. For a prescribed surjection \(T\), such a factorization requires \(f\) to be constant on every fiber \(T^{-1}(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hidden convexity may use an exact quotient rather than a bijection, provided the objective is fiber-constant and induces a convex function on a convex image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\phi(y).

notation.meaning: Convex objective induced on the image.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Hidden Convexity

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a feasible set and \(T:X\to Y\) is a bijection onto a convex set \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\).
There exists a convex function \(\phi:Y\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f=\phi\circ T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The apparently nonconvex problem is exactly equivalent to a convex optimization problem, with optimal values and minimizers transported by \(T\) and \(T^{-1}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact convexification by an invertible change of variables is a standard hidden-convexity formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact hidden convexity under a bijective transformation, excluding relaxation-only convexifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The problem \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) has hidden convexity through \(T\) if \(Y=T(X)\) is convex and a convex function \(\phi:Y\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(f(x)=\phi(Tx)\) for all \(x\in X\). Then
\[
\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}\phi(y).
\]
Moreover, \(x^*\) is globally optimal for the original problem if and only if \(T(x^*)\) is globally optimal for the transformed convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hidden convexity occurs when an invertible transformation turns both the feasible region and objective into an equivalent convex problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Convexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Exact convexification by a bijection is mathematically coherent and fits hidden convexity, but the proposed definition needs a dedicated authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Hidden-Monotonicity Reformulation
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for exposing order structure through transformations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of dominance conclusions under a merely nondecreasing transformed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is componentwise nondecreasing and \(u\le y\), then only \(F(u)\le F(y)\) follows. Even when \(u\ne y\), strict improvement need not hold: a constant \(F\) makes every feasible point optimal. Excluding a dominated point by strict objective improvement requires strict increase along at least one improved coordinate relevant to that comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak monotonicity permits dominated optimizers when the transformed objective is flat.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is componentwise nondecreasing but need not be strictly increasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\le y,\ u\ne y\ \not\Rightarrow\ F(u)<F(y).
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Monotonicity Dominance Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of an exact hidden-monotonicity reformulation to the lower nondominated frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a bijection, let \(f=F\circ T\), and suppose \(Y\) is nonempty and compact while \(F\) is continuous and componentwise nondecreasing. If \(\operatorname{Min}(Y)\) denotes the points \(y\in Y\) for which no distinct \(u\in Y\) satisfies \(u\le y\), then \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)=\min_{y\in Y}F(y)=\min_{y\in\operatorname{Min}(Y)}F(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous nondecreasing transformed objective on a compact image attains its minimum on the Pareto-minimal frontier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}f(x)=\min_{y\in\operatorname{Min}(Y)}F(y).

notation.meaning: Pareto-minimal points of the transformed feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto-Minimal Reduction

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is feasible and \(T:X\to Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a bijection.
The product order on \(Y\) is used, and \(f=F\circ T\) for a componentwise nondecreasing function \(F:Y\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformation exposes monotonicity: dominance in transformed coordinates certifies objective dominance, while bijectivity preserves the optimization problem exactly.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: order-preserving objective factorization is the defining mechanism of hidden monotonicity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact order-revealing change of variables for minimization under the product order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hidden-monotonicity reformulation of \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) consists of a bijection \(T:X\to Y\) and a componentwise nondecreasing function \(F\) such that \(f(x)=F(Tx)\). Hence
\[
\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(y).
\]
For any \(y^1,y^2\in Y\), the relation \(y^1\leq y^2\) componentwise implies \(F(y^1)\leq F(y^2)\); therefore a feasible point dominated by another feasible point cannot be a uniquely better minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible transformation reveals hidden monotonicity when coordinatewise dominance in the transformed space implies objective dominance.
knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Monotonicity Reformulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-revealing factorization is internally consistent, but hidden-monotonicity terminology and its exact scope require a dedicated source with a specific locator.

children.title: Homogeneous Lifted Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for higher-dimensional representations exposing simpler global structure.

children.title: Homogenized Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations exposing homogeneous structure through added scaling variables or coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of affine equivalence when normalization is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Homogenization is automatically equivalent to the affine model on \(t=1\). A homogeneous feasible set may additionally contain nonzero points \((x,0)\), which have no affine representative \(x/t\) and encode leading-form directions at infinity. Consequently, deleting \(t=1\), or imposing another normalization not intersecting every relevant feasible ray, can introduce feasible points or optima absent from the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Points with t=0 show why an unnormalized homogeneous model need not be equivalent to the original affine problem.
assumptions_latex: A polynomial model has been homogenized.
The homogeneous formulation is considered outside the affine chart \(t=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Homogenization without a valid affine normalization need not preserve the feasible set or optimum.}

notation.meaning: Hyperplane containing projective points at infinity.

knowledge_statements.title: Points-at-Infinity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact degree-d homogenization and affine-chart recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d}c_\alpha x^\alpha\), define \(p^{\mathrm h}(x,t)=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d}c_\alpha x^\alpha t^{d-|\alpha|}\). Then \(p^{\mathrm h}(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda^d p^{\mathrm h}(x,t)\), \(p^{\mathrm h}(x,1)=p(x)\), and, for \(t\ne0\), \(p^{\mathrm h}(x,t)=t^d p(x/t)\). Polynomial objectives and constraints are therefore represented exactly when the affine chart \(t=1\) is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Completing every term to a common degree with a new coordinate produces a homogeneous polynomial that recovers the original on the chart t=1.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a real polynomial of degree at most \(d\).
The normalization \(t=1\) is retained for exact affine recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(x)=p^{\mathrm h}(x,1),\qquad p^{\mathrm h}(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda^d p^{\mathrm h}(x,t).
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Homogenization
Homogenized Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic homogenization by one scalar coordinate and recovery on the chart \(t=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the degree-two homogeneous polynomial
\[
q^{\mathrm h}(x,t)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2t c^{\mathsf T}x+d t^2
=\begin{pmatrix}x\\t\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}
\begin{pmatrix}Q&c\\c^{\mathsf T}&d\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\t\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It satisfies \(q^{\mathrm h}(\alpha x,\alpha t)=\alpha^2q^{\mathrm h}(x,t)\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(q(x)=q^{\mathrm h}(x,1)\). Thus affine quadratic objective and constraint expressions admit exact homogeneous representations on the chart \(t=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a homogenizing coordinate converts an affine quadratic polynomial into a homogeneous quadratic form that agrees with it when the new coordinate equals one.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric, \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) for \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
The affine chart \(t=1\) is used to recover the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic polynomial is represented exactly on the affine chart by a homogeneous quadratic form in one additional variable.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: augmentation by a homogenizing coordinate is the standard exact homogenization of a quadratic polynomial

children.title: Lifted Representations
children.top_down_role: Higher-dimensional representations exposing simpler global structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection, fiberwise value recovery, and the attainment boundary for optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq X\times Y\) and \(F:L\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xL\) and \(f(x)=\inf\{F(x,y):(x,y)\in L\}\) for every \(x\in S\). Then \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{(x,y)\in L}F(x,y)\). Every attained lifted optimum projects to an original optimizer. Conversely, an original optimizer \(x^*\) has an optimal lifted extension exactly when its fiber infimum is attained by some \(y^*\) with \(F(x^*,y^*)=f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact lift recovers feasibility by projection and objective values by fiberwise minimization; optimizer lifting additionally requires fiber attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{(x,y)\in L}F(x,y),\quad x^*\text{ extends optimally iff its fiber infimum is attained}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Lift and Optimizer-Recovery Conditions

assumptions_latex: The original feasible set equals the projection \(S=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ (x,y)\in L\}\).
The lifted objective \(F:L\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(f(x)=\inf\{F(x,y):(x,y)\in L\}\) for every \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimization over the original model and its lift has the same optimal value; attained fiber minima permit recovery of optimizers in both directions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: extended formulations represent a set by projection and an objective by fiberwise minimization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extended formulation defined by projection and fiberwise objective recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A lifted representation of \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\) is a set \(L\subseteq X\times Y\) and function \(F:L\to\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
S=\operatorname{proj}_x L,
\qquad
f(x)=\inf\{F(x,y):(x,y)\in L\}.
\]
Then
\[
\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{(x,y)\in L}F(x,y).
\]
If the relevant infima are attained, an optimal lifted pair projects to an original optimizer, and an original optimizer can be extended by a fiber minimizer to an optimal lifted pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted formulation adds variables so that projection recovers the feasible set and fiberwise minimization recovers the original objective exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection and fiberwise-minimization formulation is mathematically consistent and fits lifted representations, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Univariate Envelope Duality
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for bounded-domain univariate envelope families.

children.title: Univariate Convex Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Tight convex underestimating structures for bounded-domain univariate functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex envelope is the pointwise greatest convex underestimator of \(f\) on \(I\), equivalently the lower boundary of the convex hull of its epigraph.

notation.meaning: Convex envelope of the univariate function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous functions on compact intervals; closed convex-envelope formulation.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Convex Envelopes p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex envelope of \(f\) on \(I\) is
\[
(\operatorname{vex}_I f)(x)=
\sup\{g(x):g:I\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is convex and }g(u)\leq f(u)\text{ for all }u\in I\}.
\]
It is convex, satisfies \(\operatorname{vex}_I f\leq f\), and dominates every convex underestimator of \(f\). Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{vex}_I f)=\operatorname{clconv}(\operatorname{epi}f).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The univariate convex envelope is the largest convex function below the original function on the interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Convex Envelopes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Convex Envelopes p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Point Mixture Formula for the Convex Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-dimensional representation for finite continuous data on a compact interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. For every \(x\in[a,b]\), \[(\operatorname{vex}_{[a,b]}f)(x)=\min\{\lambda f(u)+(1-\lambda)f(v):u,v\in[a,b],\ \lambda\in[0,1],\ x=\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\}.\] The minimum is attained. Thus an envelope value is supported by a contact point or by a chord joining two graph points whose abscissae bracket \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value of a continuous univariate convex envelope is attained using at most two graph points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vex}_{[a,b]}f(x)=\min_{x=\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v}\{\lambda f(u)+(1-\lambda)f(v)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Point Mixture Formula for the Convex Envelope

children.title: Univariate Concave Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Tight concave overestimating structures for bounded-domain univariate functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The concave envelope is the pointwise least concave overestimator of \(f\), and it is the negative convex envelope of \(-f\).

notation.meaning: Concave envelope of the univariate function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign duality between univariate concave overestimation and convex underestimation.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Convex Envelopes p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The concave envelope of \(f\) on \(I\) is
\[
(\operatorname{cav}_I f)(x)=
\inf\{h(x):h:I\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is concave and }h(u)\geq f(u)\text{ for all }u\in I\}.
\]
It is concave, majorizes \(f\), and is bounded above by every concave overestimator. Its sign-dual relation to the convex envelope is
\[
\operatorname{cav}_I f=-\operatorname{vex}_I(-f).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The least concave overestimator of a function equals the negative convex envelope of the function with reversed sign.
knowledge_statements.title: Univariate Concave Envelopes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Convex Envelopes p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Point Mixture Formula for the Concave Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-dimensional representation for finite continuous data on a compact interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. For every \(x\in[a,b]\), \[(\operatorname{cav}_{[a,b]}f)(x)=\max\{\lambda f(u)+(1-\lambda)f(v):u,v\in[a,b],\ \lambda\in[0,1],\ x=\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\}.\] The maximum is attained. Thus an envelope value is supported by a contact point or by a chord joining two graph points whose abscissae bracket \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every value of a continuous univariate concave envelope is attained using at most two graph points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cav}_{[a,b]}f(x)=\max_{x=\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v}\{\lambda f(u)+(1-\lambda)f(v)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Point Mixture Formula for the Concave Envelope

children.title: McCormick Bilinear Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for bounded bilinear convex-hull relaxations.

assumptions_latex: The auxiliary variable satisfies \(w=xy\) on the original bilinear graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four McCormick inequalities describe exactly the convex hull of the bounded bilinear graph and therefore give its tightest convex relaxation in \((x,y,w)\)-space.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper bounds for the first factor
Lower and upper bounds for the second factor

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex hull of one bilinear graph over a rectangular domain.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Convex Envelopes p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex hull of
\[
\{(x,y,w):x\in[x^L,x^U],\ y\in[y^L,y^U],\ w=xy\}
\]
is defined by the bound constraints together with
\[
\begin{aligned}
w&\geq x^L y+y^L x-x^L y^L,\\
w&\geq x^U y+y^U x-x^U y^U,\\
w&\leq x^U y+y^L x-x^U y^L,\\
w&\leq x^L y+y^U x-x^L y^U.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first two affine functions form the convex envelope of the bilinear term, and the last two form its concave envelope on the rectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four affine McCormick inequalities give the exact convex hull of a bilinear product over finite factor bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: McCormick Bilinear Envelopes

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Convex Envelopes p. 45

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary of the four standard McCormick planes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The four standard McCormick inequalities depend on the factor bounds from which they are derived and describe the bilinear graph hull only on that rectangle. Reusing them on a larger domain can exclude points satisfying \(w=xy\), while without finite bounds the standard bounded-rectangle formulation is unavailable. If either factor interval has zero width, the product is affine and the relaxation coincides with its graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: McCormick planes require valid finite factor bounds, may be invalid outside their derivation rectangle, and become exact when either factor is fixed.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation is intended for the graph \(w=xy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Hull validity is relative to the finite derivation rectangle.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Bound Requirement and Domain Dependence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative strength of the bilinear envelopes on a finite rectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_x=x^U-x^L\) and \(\Delta_y=y^U-y^L\). For \(w=xy\), \[\max\bigl(xy-\operatorname{vex}(xy)\bigr)=\max\bigl(\operatorname{cav}(xy)-xy\bigr)=\frac{\Delta_x\Delta_y}{4},\] while the maximum separation between the concave and convex envelope surfaces is \(\Delta_x\Delta_y/2\). Thus restricting either interval tightens the relaxation, and fixing either factor makes it exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each side of the McCormick relaxation has maximum error one quarter of the product of factor widths; its total maximum width is one half of that product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E_{\mathrm{lower}}=E_{\mathrm{upper}}=\Delta_x\Delta_y/4,\qquad E_{\mathrm{width}}=\Delta_x\Delta_y/2.

notation.meaning: convex and concave envelopes on the rectangle

knowledge_statements.title: Exact McCormick Envelope Gaps

children.title: Multilinear Envelope Families
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for direct and recursively composed multilinear relaxations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Size of the Direct Vertex Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-size boundary for direct multilinear convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nondegenerate \(n\)-factor box, the direct vertex extended formulation has one nonnegative mixing variable for each of the \(2^n\) box vertices and \(n+2\) linking and normalization equalities. Direct vertex enumeration therefore has exponential representation size in \(n\); degeneracy may permit duplicate lifted vertices to be removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact direct vertex formulation is exponential in the number of multilinear factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\lambda}=2^n.
knowledge_statements.title: Size of the Direct Vertex Formulation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Representation of a Multilinear Graph Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct finite convex-hull representation for one multilinear monomial on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), \(m(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\), and let \(V(B)\) be the vertices of \(B\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}\{(x,m(x)):x\in B\}=\operatorname{conv}\{(v,m(v)):v\in V(B)\}.\] Equivalently, \[x=\sum_{v\in V(B)}\lambda_vv,\quad w=\sum_{v\in V(B)}\lambda_vm(v),\quad \sum_v\lambda_v=1,\quad\lambda_v\geq0\] is an extended formulation of the hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a multilinear monomial graph over a box is generated by the lifted box vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a nonempty box with finite coordinate bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(G_m)=\operatorname{conv}\{(v,m(v)):v\in V(B)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Recursive Convexification on the Unit Box
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Special regime in which recursive bilinear convexification of one multilinear monomial is exact after projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) on \([0,1]^n\). Choose any binary factorization tree, introduce an auxiliary variable for each partial product, give every auxiliary its exact bound \([0,1]\), and impose the four McCormick inequalities at every bilinear node. The projection onto \((x,w)\), where \(w\) is the root product, is \[0\le w,\qquad w\le x_i\ (i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad w\ge \sum_{i=1}^n x_i-(n-1),\] which equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,w):x\in[0,1]^n,\ w=\prod_i x_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a single multilinear monomial on the unit box, recursive McCormick relaxation is exact for every binary factorization tree.

Every bilinear node receives its complete McCormick hull.

If \(R_T\) is the resulting convex lifted relaxation, then \[G_m\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}(R_T),\qquad \operatorname{conv}(G_m)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}(R_T).\] Equality need not follow from validity alone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\) and \(m(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\). The direct multilinear envelope is the convex set \(\operatorname{conv}(G_m)\), where \(G_m=\{(x,w):x\in B,\ w=m(x)\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cost of One Forward Relaxation Pass
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-size cost of generic forward propagation, exclusive of nonconstant primitive solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite acyclic expression graph \(G=(V,E)\) supplied in topological order, one forward interval-and-relaxation pass visits every node and edge once. If each primitive enclosure and relaxation rule has constant evaluation cost, the pass requires \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time and \(O(|V|)\) stored node data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward relaxation pass is linear in expression-graph size when primitive rules have constant cost.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and acyclic and a topological order is available.
Each primitive propagation rule has constant cost and bounded-size output.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic consistency on shrinking boxes for a fixed finite acyclic expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a continuous factorable function \(f\) be represented by a fixed finite acyclic expression graph. Suppose every primitive relaxation rule is valid and locally gap-consistent: its propagated convex-concave gap tends uniformly to zero whenever its child gaps and input interval widths tend to zero. Then, on every nested sequence of admissible input boxes \(B_k\) shrinking to a point, the propagated root relaxations satisfy \[\sup_{x\in B_k}\bigl(f_k^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)-f_k^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\bigr)\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite acyclic factorable relaxation becomes locally exact on shrinking boxes when every primitive rule is valid and locally gap-consistent.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
All primitives remain defined on the considered boxes.
Every primitive relaxation rule is valid and locally gap-consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\Longrightarrow\sup_{x\in B_k}(f_k^{\mathrm{cc}}-f_k^{\mathrm{cv}})\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primitive Choice Can Change Relaxation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expression representation affects propagated relaxation strength even when the represented function is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(x\in[-1,1]\), the function \(f(x)=x^2\) has the exact convex underestimator \(x^2\) when treated as a square primitive. If it is represented as a product of two bounded copies, the generic McCormick product inequalities are imposed, and the copies are then identified, the propagated convex underestimator is \[\max\{-2x-1,2x-1\}=2|x|-1,\] which is strictly below \(x^2\) for \(-1<x<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square primitive can yield a strictly stronger relaxation than generic bilinear propagation of the same algebraic function.
assumptions_latex: The generic product rule uses bounds \([-1,1]\) for both factor copies before they are identified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 2|x|-1\le x^2\text{ on }[-1,1],\qquad 2|x|-1<x^2\text{ for }-1<x<1.
knowledge_statements.title: Primitive Choice Can Change Relaxation Strength

Then this invariant holds at every node. At the root \(r\) representing \(f\), \[r^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\le f(x)\le r^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\] throughout the input box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leaf validity and conditionally valid primitive rules inductively certify the propagated root under- and overestimators.

Leaves satisfy their relaxation and interval invariants.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g^{\mathrm{cv}}\le g\le g^{\mathrm{cc}}\) on a convex set \(B\), with \(g^{\mathrm{cv}}\) convex and \(g^{\mathrm{cc}}\) concave. If \(\phi\) is convex and nondecreasing on a common range enclosure, then \(\phi\circ g^{\mathrm{cv}}\) is a convex underestimator of \(\phi\circ g\). If \(\phi\) is convex and nonincreasing, then \(\phi\circ g^{\mathrm{cc}}\) is a convex underestimator. Dually, a concave nondecreasing outer function is composed with \(g^{\mathrm{cc}}\) for an overestimator, and a concave nonincreasing outer function is composed with \(g^{\mathrm{cv}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sign of an outer primitive's monotonicity determines whether its lower or upper inner relaxation is used.

children.title: Smooth Curvature Underestimators
children.top_down_role: Convex underestimation driven by derivative and curvature information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate underestimator formed by joining endpoint quadratic minorants to a central parabola under Lipschitz control of the first derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f'$ be Lipschitz continuous on $[x_{i-1},x_i]$ with constant $K$, let $m\ge K$, and let $\psi_i$ be the endpoint-based quadratic minorant. Suppose $x_{i-1}\le y'_i\le y_i\le x_i$ and $\pi_i(x)=\tfrac12mx^2+b_ix+c_i$ satisfies
\[
\psi_i(y'_i)=\pi_i(y'_i),\quad \psi_i'(y'_i)=\pi_i'(y'_i),\quad
\psi_i(y_i)=\pi_i(y_i),\quad \psi_i'(y_i)=\pi_i'(y_i).
\]
Define
\[
\theta_i(x)=\begin{cases}
\psi_i(x),&x\in[x_{i-1},y'_i]\cup[y_i,x_i],\\
\pi_i(x),&x\in[y'_i,y_i].
\end{cases}
\]
Then the matching conditions make $\theta_i$ continuously differentiable on $[x_{i-1},x_i]$, and the Lipschitz-derivative construction gives
\[
f(x)\ge\theta_i(x)\qquad\forall x\in[x_{i-1},x_i].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a valid Lipschitz overestimate for the derivative, a central parabola matched in value and derivative to the endpoint quadratic minorant at two junctions yields a continuously differentiable piecewise-quadratic lower bound over the interval.
assumptions_latex: \psi_i\text{ is the associated endpoint-based quadratic minorant}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta_i\in C^1([x_{i-1},x_i])\quad\text{and}\quad f(x)\ge\theta_i(x)\quad\forall x\in[x_{i-1},x_i]

assumptions_latex: \(\alpha_i\ge0\) are chosen so that the displayed underestimator is convex on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_B=\min_{x\in B}f_\alpha(x)\) is a valid lower bound for \(\min_{x\in B}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical diagonal quadratic AlphaBB correction for a twice-differentiable objective on a box.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 11. The alphaBB for Box Constrained Twice-Differentiable NLPs: Theory p. 315

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), define \[f_\alpha(x)=f(x)-\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i(x_i-\ell_i)(u_i-x_i).\] Because every factor \((x_i-\ell_i)(u_i-x_i)\) is nonnegative on \(B\), one has \(f_\alpha(x)\le f(x)\). If \(\alpha_i\ge0\) make \(\nabla^2 f(x)+2\operatorname{Diag}(\alpha)\) positive semidefinite for every \(x\in B\), then \(f_\alpha\) is convex. Consequently, solving the convex problem \(L_B=\min_{x\in B}f_\alpha(x)\) gives \(L_B\le\min_{x\in B}f(x)\), with equality of the correction at every vertex of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AlphaBB subtracts a nonnegative separable quadratic from the objective and chooses its coefficients to make the result convex, yielding a box-valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained AlphaBB

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 11. The alphaBB for Box Constrained Twice-Differentiable NLPs: Theory p. 315

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform AlphaBB Gap and Subbox Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case vertical error of the classical separable correction and its shrinkage criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f_\alpha(x)=f(x)-\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i(x_i-\ell_i)(u_i-x_i)\) with \(\alpha_i\ge0\), \[0\le f(x)-f_\alpha(x)\le\frac14\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i(u_i-\ell_i)^2\qquad(x\in B).\] Hence, along boxes \(B_k\), the underestimators converge uniformly to \(f\) whenever \(\sum_i\alpha_i^{(k)}(u_i^{(k)}-\ell_i^{(k)})^2\to0\); bounded alpha parameters and componentwise widths tending to zero are sufficient in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The AlphaBB error is bounded by one quarter of the alpha-weighted squared box widths and vanishes uniformly under the stated shrinking-box condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|f-f_\alpha\|_{\infty,B}\le\frac14\sum_i\alpha_i(u_i-\ell_i)^2\), with uniform consistency under the displayed limit condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform AlphaBB Gap and Subbox Consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality Handling by Two Convex Underestimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer convex relaxation of smooth equality constraints within constrained AlphaBB.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equalities \(h_k(x)=0\) on a box \(B\), let \(h_k^{\mathrm{cv}}\le h_k\) and \((-h_k)^{\mathrm{cv}}\le-h_k\) be convex AlphaBB underestimators. Replacing each equality by \[h_k^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\le0,\qquad (-h_k)^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\le0\] gives a convex outer relaxation because every point satisfying \(h_k(x)=0\) satisfies both inequalities. Combined with convex underestimators of the objective and original inequalities, the relaxation optimum is a valid lower bound; infeasibility of the combined relaxation certifies that the original box contains no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear equality is relaxed safely by underestimating both it and its negative and imposing both resulting convex inequalities.
assumptions_latex: Valid convex underestimators of \(h_k\) and \(-h_k\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two-inequality system is a convex outer relaxation of \(h_k=0\).

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a nonempty bounded box and \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\in C^2(B)\).
Convex underestimators \(f^{\mathrm{cv}}\le f\) and \(g_j^{\mathrm{cv}}\le g_j\) are available on \(B\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-wise convexification of a box-bounded nonlinear program using AlphaBB-type underestimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x):x\in B,\ g_j(x)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\). Construct convex AlphaBB-type underestimators \(f^{\mathrm{cv}}\le f\) and \(g_j^{\mathrm{cv}}\le g_j\) on \(B\), and solve \[L_B=\min\{f^{\mathrm{cv}}(x):x\in B,\ g_j^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}.\] If \(x\) is feasible for the original problem, then \(g_j^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\le g_j(x)\le0\), so the relaxed feasible region contains the original one. Hence \(L_B\) is a valid lower bound whenever the original feasible region is nonempty; infeasibility of the relaxation certifies infeasibility within \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Underestimating both objective and inequality functions produces a convex feasible superset whose optimum lower-bounds the constrained nonconvex problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient AlphaBB convexity certificate based on a positive-semidefinite interval enclosure of the shifted Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) have continuous second derivatives on \(B=[\mathbf x^L,\mathbf x^U]\), and let the real symmetric interval matrix \([H_f]\) satisfy
\[
H_f(\mathbf x)\in[H_f]\qquad\text{for every }\mathbf x\in B.
\]
Define
\[
[H_{\mathcal L}]=[H_f]+2\Delta=[H_f]+2\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_i).
\]
If every matrix represented by \([H_{\mathcal L}]\) is positive semidefinite, then \(\mathcal L\) is convex on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every matrix in an interval enclosure of the shifted AlphaBB Hessian is positive semidefinite, then the AlphaBB function is convex throughout the box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L\text{ is convex on }B

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient Hessian condition for convexity of the diagonally shifted AlphaBB function on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=[\mathbf x^L,\mathbf x^U]\), and let \(\mathcal L\) be the twice-differentiable AlphaBB function satisfying
\[
H_{\mathcal L}(\mathbf x)=H_f(\mathbf x)+2\Delta=H_f(\mathbf x)+2\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_i).
\]
Then \(\mathcal L\) is convex on \(B\) if and only if
\[
H_f(\mathbf x)+2\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_i)\succeq0\qquad\text{for every }\mathbf x\in B.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The AlphaBB function is convex on the box exactly when its shifted Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point of the box.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\subset\mathbb R^n\) be convex, \(c\in B\), and \(f\in C^2(B)\). If \[mI\preceq
abla^2f(z)\preceq MI\qquad(z\in B),\] then every \(x\in B\) satisfies \[f(c)+
abla f(c)^{\mathsf T}(x-c)+ rac m2\|x-c\|_2^2\le f(x)\le f(c)+
abla f(c)^{\mathsf T}(x-c)+ rac M2\|x-c\|_2^2.\]

assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^1(B)\), where \(B\subset\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(c\in B\).
Each derivative satisfies \(\partial_i f(z)\in[\underline g_i,\overline g_i]\) for every \(z\in B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed interval expression encloses \(f(x)\) for every \(x\in B\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order interval Taylor enclosure on a convex box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(x\in B\), the segment \(c+t(x-c)\), \(0\le t\le1\), lies in \(B\). If \(\partial_i f(z)\in[\underline g_i,\overline g_i]\) throughout \(B\), then the integral first-order Taylor formula gives the enclosure \[f(x)\in f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^n[\underline g_i,\overline g_i](x_i-c_i),\] where multiplication and addition are interval operations. Equivalently, selecting the lower and upper endpoint of each product interval yields computable functions \(L_c(x)\) and \(U_c(x)\) satisfying \(L_c(x)\le f(x)\le U_c(x)\) for every \(x\in B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform derivative intervals inserted into the first-order Taylor formula give explicit lower and upper bounds throughout a convex box.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional-order remainder control from Hölder continuity of the highest retained derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\) and its induced multilinear operator norms. Let \(B\) be convex, \(c\in B\), \(p\ge1\), and suppose \(D^pf\) is Hölder continuous with exponent \(\beta\in(0,1]\): \[\|D^pf(x)-D^pf(y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L\|x-y\|^\beta\qquad(x,y\in B).\] Then the degree-\(p\) Taylor polynomial satisfies \[|f(x)-T_p(x;c)|\le \frac{L\Gamma(\beta+1)}{\Gamma(p+\beta+1)}\|x-c\|^{p+\beta}\qquad(x\in B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hölder continuity of the highest retained derivative yields a certified Taylor remainder of order p plus beta.
assumptions_latex: \(D^pf\) is Hölder continuous with constant \(L\) and exponent \(\beta\in(0,1]\) in the specified induced norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed two-sided remainder bound of order \(p+\beta\) holds throughout \(B\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T_p(x;c)=\sum_{k=0}^p D^kf(c)[x-c]^k/k!\), where \(D^kf(c)[x-c]^k\) denotes evaluation of the \(k\)-linear derivative on \(k\) copies of \(x-c\). If \(\|D^{p+1}f(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M_{p+1}\) for all \(z\in B\), then every \(x\in B\) satisfies \[|f(x)-T_p(x;c)|\le\frac{M_{p+1}}{(p+1)!}\|x-c\|^{p+1}.\] Thus the Taylor polynomial plus and minus this term gives certified upper and lower bounds, and restricting \(B\) reduces the worst-case remainder according to its radius about \(c\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded polynomial RLT using multi-indices that permit repeated powers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bounded variables \(\ell_i\le x_i\le u_i\), choose an order \(d\) and introduce \(y_\alpha\) for retained monomials \(x^\alpha=\prod_i x_i^{\alpha_i}\) with \(|\alpha|\le d\), setting \(y_0=1\) and \(y_{e_i}=x_i\). Form products of valid nonnegative constraint and bound factors whose expanded degree is at most \(d\); expand and replace each \(x^\alpha\) by \(y_\alpha\). Every original feasible point satisfies the resulting linear system under \(y_\alpha=x^\alpha\), so its projection is a polyhedral outer relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RLT lifts repeated-power monomials and linearizes products of valid bounded factors to form a polyhedral outer relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Every multiplied factor is nonnegative on the original feasible set.
All required variable bounds are finite and valid.
Every monomial produced by a retained product is represented at order \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xR_d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-index RLT Construction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lift-size growth with variable count and relaxation order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The number of multi-index monomials in \(n\) variables of total degree at most \(d\) is \(\binom{n+d}{d}\). Thus even before product-generated inequalities are counted, a dense order-\(d\) RLT lift has combinatorial size when both \(n\) and \(d\) vary; polynomial size in \(n\) follows only for fixed \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense order-d RLT lift contains a binomial number of monomial variables and becomes combinatorial when the order varies.
assumptions_latex: All monomials of total degree at most \(d\) are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{n,d}=\binom{n+d}{d}\), which is polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \(d\) but not jointly polynomial in unrestricted \(n,d\).

notation.meaning: Number of retained monomials through degree d

knowledge_statements.title: RLT Monomial Growth

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and strength boundaries of RLT relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: RLT bound-factor inequalities require valid finite bounds. An invalid bound can exclude an original feasible point—for example, applying the false upper bound \(x\le1\) to the feasible set \(F=\{2\}\) destroys containment—while an infinite bound supplies no finite bound factor. Algebraically equivalent lifted formulations can also generate different RLT systems because they expose different products before linearization. Validity therefore requires certified factors, and strength is not invariant under reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RLT needs valid finite bounds, and its strength can change under equivalent reformulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Invalid factor bounds can destroy containment, and equivalent formulations need not yield identical RLT projections.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound Dependence and Reformulation Sensitivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength ordering for cumulatively constructed RLT levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(R_{d+1}\) retains every variable and constraint of \(R_d\), then \(\operatorname{proj}_xR_{d+1}\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xR_d\). Hence the corresponding minimization lower bounds satisfy \(L_{d+1}\ge L_d\). This nesting alone does not imply finite exactness or asymptotic convergence for an arbitrarily selected family of products.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative RLT levels cannot weaken the bound, but nesting alone gives no exactness guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Every lower-level constraint is retained at the next level.
The same original objective is compared across levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xR_{d+1}\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xR_d\Rightarrow L_{d+1}\ge L_d\).
review_flags: No generic finite-exactness claim is made for continuous polynomial problems or incompletely generated hierarchies.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-based lifted linear relaxation truncated at a prescribed product degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a relaxation degree \(d\). Introduce \(y_S\) for each retained monomial \(x^S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\) with \(|S|\le d\), taking \(y_{\{i\}}=x_i\). Multiply selected original linear constraints and bound factors \((x_i-\ell_i)\ge0\), \((u_i-x_i)\ge0\) so that the resulting products have degree at most \(d\); expand them and replace every retained monomial by its \(y_S\). Linearize polynomial objective and constraints by the same substitution. The resulting linear system is satisfied by every original feasible point under \(y_S=x^S\), so its projection is an outer relaxation and its linear optimum supplies a valid bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RLT lifts bounded products to new variables and linearizes products of valid constraints, producing a linear outer relaxation at a selected degree.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Convex Underestimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maximum-of-affine representation, defined on Euclidean space and used as an underestimator on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_k^T x+b_k\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\) and \(k=1,\ldots,N\). Define \[p(x)=\max_{1\le k\le N}(a_k^T x+b_k),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\] Then \(p\) is convex and piecewise affine, its epigraph is the polyhedron \[\operatorname{epi}p=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:t\ge a_k^T x+b_k,\ k=1,\ldots,N\},\] and \(p(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\). If \(a_k\in\partial f(z_k)\) and \(b_k=f(z_k)-a_k^Tz_k\) at points \(z_k\in C\), the subgradient inequality makes each affine function a valid minorant on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum of globally defined affine functions is a polyhedral convex function; when every affine piece minorizes the target on the domain, their maximum is a valid underestimator there.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex.
For \(k=1,\ldots,N\), the affine function \(x\mapsto a_k^T x+b_k\) satisfies \(a_k^T x+b_k\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(p(x)=\max_{1\le k\le N}(a_k^T x+b_k)\) is polyhedral convex and satisfies \(p(x)\le f(x)\) on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Epigraph of the globally defined function p

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-x^2\) on \([-1,1]\), the tangent at \(0\) is \(\ell(x)=0\), but \(\ell(x)>f(x)\) for every \(x\ne0\). Thus tangents to an arbitrary nonconvex target need not be global affine minorants, and their maximum need not be a valid lower model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangents are global minorants for convex functions, not for arbitrary nonconvex targets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=-x^2,\ \ell(x)=0\Rightarrow\ell(x)>f(x)\) for \(x\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and optimization-bound strengthening when valid affine pieces are added.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_N(x)=\max_{1\le k\le N}(a_k^Tx+b_k)\), with every affine piece minorizing \(f\) on \(C\). Adding another valid affine minorant gives \(p_N(x)\le p_{N+1}(x)\le f(x)\) on \(C\). Consequently, for every fixed \(R\subseteq C\), \(\inf_Rp_N\le\inf_Rp_{N+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a valid affine piece strengthens a maximum-of-affine underestimator and cannot lower its optimization bound.
assumptions_latex: Every affine piece is a valid minorant on \(C\).
The optimization comparison uses the same set \(R\subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_N\le p_{N+1}\le f\) on \(C\), and \(\inf_Rp_N\le\inf_Rp_{N+1}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Cut Enrichment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Polyhedral Approximation of a Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform finite maximum-of-affine approximation on compact interior sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be finite and convex on an open convex set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(C\subset U\) be compact. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), finitely many affine supports \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_N\) exist such that \[p(x)=\max_{1\le k\le N}\ell_k(x)\le f(x)\quad(x\in U),\qquad 0\le f(x)-p(x)\le\varepsilon\quad(x\in C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact interior set, a finite maximum of affine supports uniformly approximates a finite convex function from below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), a polyhedral convex \(p\) exists with \(0\le f-p\le\varepsilon\) on \(C\).

assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq B\subset\mathbb R^n\) is the feasible region of a minimization problem.

A convex function \(\varphi\) satisfies \(\varphi(x)\le f(x)\) on \(F\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2.5 Relaxation (Successive Outer Approximation) Strategies p. 31

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex outer approximation of \(F\) is a convex, tractably represented set \(R\) satisfying \(F\subseteq R\subseteq B\). If \(\varphi:R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex and \(\varphi(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\), then \[L_R=\inf_{x\in R}\varphi(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}\varphi(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}f(x).\] Thus \(L_R\) is a valid global lower bound. For two approximations \(F\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_2\) using the same \(\varphi\), their bounds satisfy \(L_{R_1}\ge L_{R_2}\), so set inclusion orders relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a convex objective underestimator over a tractable convex superset gives a valid lower bound; smaller supersets give no weaker bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Outer Approximations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.5 Relaxation (Successive Outer Approximation) Strategies p. 31

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary on conclusions obtainable from an outer approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F\subseteq R\), \(R=\varnothing\) implies \(F=\varnothing\), but a point of \(R\) need not belong to \(F\), and \(R\ne\varnothing\) does not imply \(F\ne\varnothing\). For example, \(F=\varnothing\subset R=[0,1]\). An outer-relaxation solution is therefore generally a lower-bound witness, not an original-feasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty outer approximation certifies infeasibility, but a feasible relaxation point need not be originally feasible.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combination rule for independently valid convex outer approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\subseteq R_1\) and \(F\subseteq R_2\), where \(R_1,R_2\) are convex, then \(R_1\cap R_2\) is a convex outer approximation of \(F\). For the same objective underestimator \(\varphi\), \[\inf_{x\in R_1\cap R_2}\varphi(x)\ge\max\{\inf_{x\in R_1}\varphi(x),\inf_{x\in R_2}\varphi(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting compatible convex outer approximations preserves validity and cannot weaken the lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The same underestimator \(\varphi\) is used in all comparisons.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Strengthening

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for increasingly tight convex outer sets to recover the exact value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be compact, \(f:B\to\mathbb R\) continuous, and \(F\subseteq B\) nonempty and closed. If \(R_1\supseteq R_2\supseteq\cdots\) are nonempty closed convex sets satisfying \(F\subseteq R_k\subseteq B\) and \(\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}R_k=F\), then \(L_k:=\min_{x\in R_k}f(x)\) is nondecreasing and \(L_k\uparrow\min_{x\in F}f(x)\). Every accumulation point of minimizers \(x_k\in\arg\min_{R_k}f\) is a minimizer over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested closed convex outer approximations on a compact domain converge in value when their intersection is exact.
assumptions_latex: The \(R_k\) are nested, nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\uparrow\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient Conditions for the Convex Extension Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions based on convex monotone aggregation, coordinate restrictions, radial scaling, and recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\) be defined on \(\mathbb R_+^{\sum_{i=1}^n d_i}\), let \(r>0\), and define \[G=\{\mathbf z:g(\mathbf z_1,\ldots,\mathbf z_n)\ge r\},\quad G_i=\{(\mathbf0,\ldots,\mathbf z_i,\ldots,\mathbf0)\in G\},\] and \(g_i(\mathbf z_i)=g(\mathbf0,\ldots,\mathbf z_i,\ldots,\mathbf0)\). Suppose functions \(h_i:\mathbb R_+^{d_i}\to\mathbb R\) and a convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) satisfy: \(g(\mathbf z)\le f(h_1(\mathbf z_1),\ldots,h_n(\mathbf z_n))\); \(f(\mathbf y_1)>f(\mathbf y_2)\) whenever \(\mathbf y_1\ge\mathbf y_2\) and \(\mathbf y_1\ne\mathbf y_2\); \(g_i(\mathbf z_i)=f(0,\ldots,h_i(\mathbf z_i),\ldots,0)\); for every \(i\), \(h_i(\mathbf0)=0\) and \(\lambda h_i(\mathbf z_i/\lambda)\ge h_i(\mathbf z_i)\) for all \(\lambda\in(0,1]\); and \[h_i(\mathbf z_i)\le0\implies(\mathbf0,\ldots,\mathbf z_i,\ldots,\mathbf0)\in0^+\!\left(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{chull}(G_i))\right).\] Then \(G\) satisfies the convex extension property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The superlevel set G satisfies the convex extension property if g is bounded above by a convex, strictly componentwise-increasing aggregation of block functions; the aggregation agrees with every coordinate restriction; each block function vanishes at zero and obeys the stated radial scaling inequality; and nonpositive block values generate recession directions of the corresponding closed convex hulls.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is convex, and }\mathbf y_1\ge\mathbf y_2,\ \mathbf y_1\ne\mathbf y_2\Rightarrow f(\mathbf y_1)>f(\mathbf y_2).
\forall i:\ h_i(\mathbf0)=0\text{ and }\forall\lambda\in(0,1],\ \lambda h_i(\mathbf z_i/\lambda)\ge h_i(\mathbf z_i).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ satisfies the convex extension property.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of convex extension, its equivalent closed-convex-hull characterization, and the stated consequence when it replaces Assumption 4.4 in the surrounding construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) satisfy Assumption 4.3. The convex extension property holds if every \(\mathbf z\in Y\) admits \[\mathbf z=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\mathbf v_i+\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_i\mathbf w_i,\] where \(\mathbf v_i\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{chull}(Y_i))\), \(\mathbf w_i\in0^+(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{chull}(Y_i)))\), \(\lambda_i,\mu_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\). The property is equivalent to \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{chull}(Y))=\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\operatorname{chull}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^nY_i\right)\right).\] In the surrounding construction, if this property replaces Assumption 4.4, then \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf z}(X))=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{chull}(Y)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Y satisfying Assumption 4.3, the convex extension property requires every point of Y to be a convex combination of points from the closed convex hulls of the component sets plus a nonnegative combination of directions from their recession cones. It is equivalent to equality of the closed convex hull of Y and the closed convex hull of the union of the component sets. In the surrounding construction, using this property in place of Assumption 4.4 yields equality between the closure of the projected set and the closed convex hull of Y.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the projection consequence, the convex extension property replaces Assumption 4.4 in the surrounding construction.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall\mathbf z\in Y,\ \mathbf z=\sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf v_i+\sum_i\mu_i\mathbf w_i\text{ with the stated conditions}\right]\iff\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{chull}(Y))=\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\operatorname{chull}\!\left(\bigcup_iY_i\right)\right).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-feasible matrix certificate for an SDP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p^*=\inf\{c^Tx:F_0+\sum_i x_iF_i\succeq0\}\), any \(Z\succeq0\) satisfying \(\langle F_i,Z\rangle=c_i\) for all \(i\) certifies \(p^*\ge-\langle F_0,Z\rangle\). If the SDP projects to an outer relaxation, the same value bounds the original minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite dual matrix satisfying coefficient matching certifies an SDP lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The primal SDP uses the displayed sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*\ge-\langle F_0,Z\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Dual Lower-Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for interpreting solver values and certificates at an SDP interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an SDP has a strictly feasible primal matrix pencil and finite primal value, its dual has the same value and attains it; the symmetric conclusion holds under dual strict feasibility and finite dual value. If all feasible matrices lie in a proper face of the positive-semidefinite cone, ambient Slater feasibility fails, so standard attainment and zero-gap conclusions require facial reduction or a relative-interior formulation. Absence of a dual certificate in the unreduced formulation is not an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility supports SDP strong duality; facial degeneracy requires reduction or relative-interior analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Appropriate primal or dual Slater regularity yields zero gap and opposite-side attainment; without it these conclusions are not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.title: SDP Slater and Facial-Degeneracy Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General solver-facing form of an SDP outer relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spectrahedron has the form \(S=\{x:F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i\succeq0\}\). A semidefinite-representable set is a projection \(R=\{x:\exists z,\ F_0+\sum_i x_iF_i+\sum_jz_jG_j\succeq0,\ Hx+Jz=h\}\). Both are convex. If every original feasible point admits such a lift, then \(R\) is a convex outer relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectrahedra and projections of spectrahedra provide the general semidefinite relaxation interface.
assumptions_latex: All matrix coefficients are real symmetric.
Every original feasible point has a feasible lift when outer validity is claimed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is convex and contains the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectrahedral and Semidefinite-Lift Representation

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and a quadratic formulation is lifted with a symmetric matrix variable \(X\).
Every replaced quadratic expression is linear in \((x,X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(X=xx^T\) by the displayed positive-semidefinite constraint yields a convex outer relaxation.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the semidefinite lifting interface.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order matrix lifting for quadratically represented nonconvex problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce \(X=xx^T\), so each quadratic form satisfies \(x^TQx=\langle Q,X\rangle\). The equality \(X=xx^T\) is nonconvex because it imposes rank one. Its standard semidefinite outer relaxation is \[\begin{pmatrix}1&x^T\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\] equivalently \(X-xx^T\succeq0\) by the Schur complement. Replace every quadratic occurrence by the corresponding linear expression in \((x,X)\), retain valid linear constraints, and impose the positive-semidefinite condition. Every original point lifts feasibly with \(X=xx^T\); dropping rank therefore produces a convex feasible superset and a valid lower bound for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic products are lifted into a matrix, and the rank-one equality is relaxed to a positive-semidefinite block constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Relaxation Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable lower-bound certificate exported by a nonpolyhedral conic relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p^*=\inf\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ Gx+h\in K\}\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. If \(s\in K^*\) and \((y,s)\) satisfy \(c-A^Ty-G^Ts=0\), then \(c^Tx\ge b^Ty-h^Ts\) for every primal-feasible \(x\). If the conic problem is a valid outer relaxation, this bound transfers to the original minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified dual-cone multiplier satisfying stationarity certifies a transferable lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The conic problem is a valid outer relaxation whenever transfer to the original problem is claimed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*\ge b^Ty-h^Ts\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Lower-Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity boundary for importing exact values or infeasibility conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weak duality needs no constraint qualification. If the cone is represented in its linear span, primal Slater feasibility \(Ax=b\), \(Gx+h\in\operatorname{ri}K\), together with a finite primal value and the standard conic regularity hypotheses, yields zero duality gap and dual attainment. Without relative-interior or facial regularity, a conic problem may have a gap or unattained optimum, and a linear image of a closed cone need not be closed. Numerical failure or absence of a dual certificate alone therefore does not certify infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior regularity supports strong duality; its absence prevents automatic certificate or infeasibility conclusions.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without an appropriate Slater or facial regularity condition, zero gap and attainment are not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Duality and Closure Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Native nonsymmetric-cone encodings used by nonpolyhedral relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed exponential cone \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ ve^{u/v}\le w\}\), \(e^x\le t\) is equivalent to \((x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the power cone \(K_\alpha=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ u^\alpha v^{1-\alpha}\ge|w|\}\) represents weighted geometric-mean inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponential and power inequalities can be exported through their native closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e^x\le t\iff(x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}\), while weighted geometric-mean inequalities are representable by \(K_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential- and Power-Cone Interfaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Native nonpolyhedral conic representation of norm and rotated quadratic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Lorentz cone \(\mathcal Q^{m+1}=\{(t,u):\|u\|_2\le t\}\) represents \(\|Ax+b\|_2\le c^Tx+d\) as \((c^Tx+d,Ax+b)\in\mathcal Q^{m+1}\). The rotated Lorentz cone \(\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}=\{(s,t,u):s\ge0,\ t\ge0,\ 2st\ge\|u\|_2^2\}\) represents corresponding convex quadratic-over-product constraints. Affine inverse images and finite intersections of these cones are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norm and rotated convex-quadratic constraints have direct second-order-cone representations.
assumptions_latex: All affine expressions have compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed constraints are affine conic constraints over \(\mathcal Q\) or \(\mathcal Q_r\).
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Interface

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be a closed convex nonpolyhedral cone, such as a second-order, exponential, or power cone. A conic outer relaxation has the lifted form \[R_K=\{x\in B:\exists z,\ A(x,z)+b\in K,\ Cx+Dz\le d\}.\] It is valid for an original feasible set \(F\) when every \(x\in F\) has some \(z\) satisfying the displayed constraints. Because affine inverse images, intersections, and projections preserve convexity, \(R_K\) is convex and contains \(F\). Minimizing a conic-representable objective underestimator over \(R_K\) therefore supplies a valid lower bound for the original minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted affine constraint in a tractable nonpolyhedral cone defines a convex outer approximation whenever every original feasible point has a valid lift.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural Interval Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural interval evaluation of a real expression over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite expression in variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants, and elementary operations, and let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\) be an interval box. Its natural interval extension \([E](X)\) is obtained by replacing every variable \(x_i\) by \(X_i\), every constant by its point interval, and every operation by an inclusion-preserving interval counterpart, following the expression tree. Whenever all interval operations are defined, inclusion isotonicity gives \[\{E(x):x\in X\}\subseteq [E](X).\] Repeated occurrences of a variable are evaluated independently, so the enclosure need not equal the exact range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct interval evaluation encloses every expression value on the box, but repeated variables may make the enclosure wider than the exact range.
assumptions_latex: \(E(x)\) and all interval operations used in \([E](X)\) are defined on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(X)\subseteq [E](X)\).

notation.meaning: natural interval evaluation of expression E on X
exact range of E over X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of natural interval evaluation for a fixed expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every primitive interval operation used by a fixed expression \(E\) is inclusion isotone and \(X\subseteq Y\), then \([E](X)\subseteq[E](Y)\). Consequently, subdivision cannot enlarge a child's natural enclosure relative to its parent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed expression tree, evaluating a smaller box produces an interval contained in the evaluation of a larger box.
assumptions_latex: The same expression tree and inclusion-isotone primitive extensions are used on both boxes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\subseteq Y\Longrightarrow[E](X)\subseteq[E](Y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion Isotonicity Under Box Restriction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency of natural extensions away from singularities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the primitive interval extensions in a finite expression \(E\) are continuous at the encountered point intervals and remain defined near \(x^*\). If boxes \(X_k\) contain \(x^*\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(X_k)\to0\), then \(\operatorname{wid}([E](X_k))\to0\), and both endpoints converge to \(E(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural interval evaluations collapse to the point value on boxes shrinking to a nonsingular point.
assumptions_latex: Every primitive interval extension is continuous at the encountered point intervals.
No singular or undefined operation is approached.
knowledge_statements.title: Shrinking-Box Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Expressions Can Have Different Natural Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntax dependence caused by repeated-variable dependency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[0,1]\), the algebraically identical expressions \(E_1(x)=x-x^2\) and \(E_2(x)=x(1-x)\) have natural evaluations \([E_1](X)=[-1,1]\) and \([E_2](X)=[0,1]\), while their exact common range is \([0,1/4]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraically equivalent formulas can yield different natural interval enclosures.
assumptions_latex: Ordinary real interval arithmetic is used on \(X=[0,1]\).
