knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a box, let \(c\in X\), and let \(f\) be continuously differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\). If \([\nabla f](X)=G_1\times\cdots\times G_n\) contains \(\nabla f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), the centered first-order enclosure is \[C_f(X;c)=f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^n G_i(X_i-c_i).\] It satisfies \[f(X)\subseteq C_f(X;c).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable function, its value at a box center plus an interval-gradient remainder encloses its complete range on the box.
knowledge_statements.title: Centered Enclosures

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Exactness of the Centered Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness boundary for first-order centered enclosures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf T}x+\beta\) on a box \(X\) and \([\nabla f](X)=\{a\}\), then for every \(c\in X\), \[C_f(X;c)=f(c)+a^{\mathsf T}(X-c)=f(X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The centered first-order enclosure gives the exact box range of an affine function when its gradient is represented exactly.
assumptions_latex: The gradient enclosure is the singleton \(\{a\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Exactness of the Centered Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shrinking-box consistency of centered enclosures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_k\) be boxes with \(c_k\in X_k\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(X_k)\to0\). If the interval gradient enclosures \([\nabla f](X_k)\) are uniformly bounded, then \(\operatorname{wid}(C_f(X_k;c_k))\to0\). If additionally the boxes converge to the singleton \(\{x^*\}\), both endpoints converge to \(f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On shrinking boxes with uniformly bounded derivative enclosures, a centered range enclosure collapses to the point value.
assumptions_latex: The hypotheses of the accepted centered-enclosure seed hold for every \(X_k\).
The interval gradient enclosures are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{wid}(C_f(X_k;c_k))\to0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Width Consistency

children.title: Slope Enclosures
children.top_down_role: Range enclosures using slope information to reduce interval dependency.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a box and \(c\in X\).
\(f\) admits the displayed slope representation for every \(x\in X\).
\([S_f](c,X)\) encloses a valid slope vector for each \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq S_f^{\mathrm{rng}}(X;c)\).

notation.meaning: interval enclosure of point-to-center slope vectors
range interval induced by the slope enclosure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range enclosure based on point-to-center slopes.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a box and let \(c\in X\). A slope enclosure \([S_f](c,X)=S_1\times\cdots\times S_n\) has the property that, for every \(x\in X\), there exists \(s(c,x)\in[S_f](c,X)\) satisfying \[f(x)-f(c)=s(c,x)^{\mathsf T}(x-c).\] Its associated range enclosure is \[S_f^{\mathrm{rng}}(X;c)=f(c)+\sum_{i=1}^n S_i(X_i-c_i),\] and it satisfies \[f(X)\subseteq S_f^{\mathrm{rng}}(X;c).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enclosing a valid point-to-center slope vector for each point in the box yields an interval enclosing the function's range on that box.
knowledge_statements.title: Slope Enclosures

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Interval Methods for Global Optimization p. 47

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness for affine target functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf T}x+\beta\), the singleton slope enclosure \([S_f](c,X)=\{a\}\) is valid for every \(c\in X\), and \(S_f^{\mathrm{rng}}(X;c)=f(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singleton slope vector produces the exact box range of an affine function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_f^{\mathrm{rng}}(X;c)=f(X)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Exactness of Slope Enclosures

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of point-to-center slopes from derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a convex neighborhood of \(X\), then for \(c,x\in X\), \[f(x)-f(c)=s(c,x)^{\mathsf T}(x-c),\qquad s(c,x)=\int_0^1\nabla f(c+t(x-c))\,dt.\] Consequently, every interval vector containing all gradients on \(X\) is a valid slope enclosure, although a directly computed slope enclosure can be narrower.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating the gradient along the center-to-point segment gives an exact slope vector and shows that every interval-gradient enclosure induces a slope enclosure.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f(c)=s(c,x)^{\mathsf T}(x-c)\) and \(s(c,x)\in[\nabla f](X)\) for every valid interval-gradient box.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Induced Slope Representation

children.title: Affine Enclosures
children.top_down_role: Range enclosures retaining affine dependence across uncertain quantities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-arithmetic enclosures retaining correlations through shared noise symbols.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An affine form is \(\widehat z=z_0+\sum_{i=1}^m z_i\varepsilon_i\), where one common noise vector satisfies \(\varepsilon\in[-1,1]^m\). Its concretization is \(\gamma(\widehat z)=\{z_0+\sum_i z_i e_i:e\in[-1,1]^m\}\), and therefore \(\gamma(\widehat z)=[z_0-\sum_i|z_i|,z_0+\sum_i|z_i|]\). A collection of affine forms encloses jointly uncertain quantities when every admissible joint realization is represented using the same noise vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine enclosures represent jointly uncertain quantities by affine functions of shared bounded noise symbols, retaining their linear dependence.
assumptions_latex: The noise symbols are interpreted jointly and shared consistently by all affine forms.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Form Enclosures

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Cancellation of Shared Affine Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical dependency advantage of shared affine forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If both occurrences of an uncertain quantity use the same affine form \(\widehat x\), coefficientwise affine arithmetic gives \(\widehat x-\widehat x=0\). Independently intervalizing its range \([\underline x,\overline x]\) instead gives \([\underline x-\overline x,\overline x-\underline x]\), which is nondegenerate when \(\underline x<\overline x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared noise symbols preserve exact linear cancellation that occurrence-independent interval evaluation loses.
assumptions_latex: Both occurrences denote the same affine form with identical shared noise symbols.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x-\widehat x=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Cancellation of Shared Affine Dependence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound propagation rules preserving affine dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For affine forms \(\widehat x=x_0+\sum_i a_i\varepsilon_i\) and \(\widehat y=y_0+\sum_i b_i\varepsilon_i\), addition and scalar multiplication are represented exactly by coefficient arithmetic. For their joint same-noise product, a valid affine enclosure is \[\widehat p=x_0y_0+\sum_i(x_0b_i+y_0a_i)\varepsilon_i+\rho\varepsilon_{m+1},\qquad \rho=\Bigl(\sum_i|a_i|\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_i|b_i|\Bigr),\] because the new noise symbol encloses the discarded quadratic remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine operations propagate exactly, while a nonlinear product can be enclosed by its affine part plus a fresh bounded remainder symbol.
assumptions_latex: The original forms share one vector \(\varepsilon\in[-1,1]^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\widehat x(e)\widehat y(e):e\in[-1,1]^m\}\subseteq\gamma(\widehat p)\).

notation.meaning: absolute bound on the discarded quadratic remainder

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Propagation and Nonlinear Remainders
Affine Enclosures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine lower and upper range models on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) on a box \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\), an affine enclosure is a pair \((\ell,u)\) of affine functions \(\ell(x)=a^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) and \(u(x)=b^{\mathsf T}x+\beta\) such that \[\ell(x)\leq f(x)\leq u(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] It induces the scalar interval enclosure \[f(X)\subseteq\left[\min_{x\in X}\ell(x),\ \max_{x\in X}u(x)\right],\] whose endpoints are obtained by selecting coordinate bounds according to the signs of the affine coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globally valid affine lower and upper functions enclose the function and give easily computed scalar range bounds on a box.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\) and \(u\) are affine and satisfy \(\ell\leq f\leq u\) pointwise on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\subseteq[\min_X\ell,\max_Xu]\).

notation.meaning: affine lower and upper enclosure functions
coefficient vectors of the affine functions

children.title: Lipschitz Minorants
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for distance-based global lower models.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Minorants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-based global lower models from sampled values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((D,d)\) be a metric space and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. For any sampled point \(y\in D\), define \(m_y(x)=f(y)-L d(x,y)\). The Lipschitz inequality implies \(m_y(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in D\). Hence, for sampled points \(y_1,\ldots,y_k\), \[m_k(x)=\max_{1\leq j\leq k}\{f(y_j)-L d(x,y_j)\}\leq f(x).\] Therefore \(\inf_{x\in R}m_k(x)\) is a valid global lower bound for \(f\) on every nonempty region \(R\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each sample generates a distance cone below a Lipschitz function; their maximum remains a valid global minorant and supplies regional lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_k\leq f\) on \(D\), and \(\inf_Rm_k\leq\inf_Rf\) for every nonempty \(R\subseteq D\).

notation.meaning: maximum of the available sample minorants

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Lipschitz Global Optimization p. 14
Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.4 Lipschitz Global Optimization p. 14

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform approximation and lower-bound convergence under dense sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty sample set \(Y\subseteq D\), define \(m_Y(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}\{f(y)-Ld(x,y)\}\), \(d(x,Y)=\inf_{y\in Y}d(x,y)\), and \(h_Y=\sup_{x\in D}d(x,Y)\). If \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \[0\leq f(x)-m_Y(x)\leq2L\,d(x,Y)\leq2Lh_Y.\] Thus \(h_{Y_k}\to0\) implies uniform convergence of \(m_{Y_k}\) to \(f\) and convergence of their infima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-envelope error is at most twice the Lipschitz constant times the distance to the samples, so dense sampling makes the minorant uniformly exact.
assumptions_latex: The displayed fill distance is finite when a finite uniform bound is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|f-m_Y\|_\infty\leq2Lh_Y\).

notation.meaning: distance from x to the sample set

knowledge_statements.title: Fill-Distance Error Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Underestimated Lipschitz Constant Invalidates the Minorant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp validity boundary for distance-cone lower models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Using an uncertified \(\widetilde L<L\) can destroy the minorant property. On \(D=[0,1]\), let \(f(x)=-x\), sample \(y=0\), and use \(0\leq\widetilde L<1\). The claimed cone is \(m(x)=-\widetilde Lx\), but \(m(1)=-\widetilde L>-1=f(1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slope smaller than the true Lipschitz modulus can put the purported lower cone above the function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(1)>f(1)\), so \(m\) is not a valid minorant.
knowledge_statements.title: Underestimated Lipschitz Constant Invalidates the Minorant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise optimality of the sampled Lipschitz cone envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonempty sample data \((y_j,v_j)\) satisfy \(|v_i-v_j|\leq Ld(y_i,y_j)\). Then \[m(x)=\sup_j\{v_j-Ld(x,y_j)\}\] is \(L\)-Lipschitz, interpolates every sample, and every \(L\)-Lipschitz function \(g\) with \(g(y_j)=v_j\) satisfies \(g(x)\geq m(x)\). Hence \(m\) is the pointwise smallest sample-consistent \(L\)-Lipschitz extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The supremum of the lower Lipschitz cones is the smallest Lipschitz function consistent with the sampled values.
assumptions_latex: The sample values are pairwise \(L\)-Lipschitz consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(y_j)=v_j\) and \(m\leq g\) for every sample-consistent \(L\)-Lipschitz extension \(g\).
knowledge_statements.title: Extremal Sample-Consistent Lower Extension

children.title: Lagrangian Global Bounds

assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\), and the primal feasible set is nonempty.
\(q(\lambda,\mu)\) is evaluated as a global infimum over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(\lambda,\mu)\leq p^*\), hence \(\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,\mu\in\mathbb R^q}q(\lambda,\mu)\leq p^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality bounds for globally minimized Lagrangian subproblems.

source_refs.locator: 6. Duality in Global Optimization p. 167

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[p^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,q)\},\] without assuming convexity. For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^q\), define \[L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jh_j(x),\qquad q(\lambda,\mu)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda,\mu).\] The weak-duality bounds are \[q(\lambda,\mu)\leq p^*,\qquad \sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,\mu\in\mathbb R^q}q(\lambda,\mu)\leq p^*.\] A duality gap may remain in the nonconvex case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a possibly nonconvex minimization problem, globally minimizing the Lagrangian at nonnegative inequality multipliers gives a valid lower bound, and optimizing over the multipliers preserves that bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Global Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 6. Duality in Global Optimization p. 167

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Lagrangian Duality Gap in a Nonconvex Finite Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of strong Lagrangian duality without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{a,b,c\}\), impose the equality \(h(x)=0\), and set \((h(a),f(a))=(0,1)\), \((h(b),f(b))=(-1,0)\), and \((h(c),f(c))=(1,0)\). The only feasible point is \(a\), so \(p^*=1\). For \(\mu\in\mathbb R\), \[q(\mu)=\min\{1,-\mu,\mu\}=-|\mu|,\] and therefore \(d^*=\sup_{\mu}q(\mu)=0<p^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex equality-constrained finite problem can have a strict Lagrangian duality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\{a,b,c\}\) with the displayed objective and equality-constraint values.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Lagrangian Duality Gap in a Nonconvex Finite Problem

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity and Supergradients of the Global Lagrangian Dual Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties of Lagrangian global lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(\lambda,\mu)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g(x)+\mu^{\mathsf T}h(x)\bigr)\), the extended-real function \(q\) is concave on \(\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q\), even when the primal functions are nonconvex. If \(q(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R\) and the infimum is attained at \(x_{\lambda,\mu}\), then \((g(x_{\lambda,\mu}),h(x_{\lambda,\mu}))\) is a supergradient of \(q\) at \((\lambda,\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangian dual function is concave; a finite attained global Lagrangian minimum supplies a multiplier-space supergradient.
assumptions_latex: The infimum defining \(q\) is interpreted in the extended-real sense.
For the supergradient conclusion, \(q(\lambda,\mu)\) is finite and \(x_{\lambda,\mu}\in\arg\min_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda,mu)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\text{ is concave, and }(g(x_{\lambda,\mu}),h(x_{\lambda,\mu}))\in\partial^+q(\lambda,mu)\text{ under the stated finiteness and attainment conditions}.

notation.meaning: superdifferential of the concave dual function
global minimizer of the Lagrangian subproblem

knowledge_statements.title: Concavity and Supergradients of the Global Lagrangian Dual Function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian dual lower bounds and weak duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian-dual construction for the stated constrained global minimization problem. Without compactness, the relevant minima must be replaced by infima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\) be convex and compact, let \(f,h_1,\ldots,h_m\) be lower semicontinuous on \(X\), and suppose \(S=\{x\in X:h_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\neq\varnothing\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i h_i(x)\) and \(g(\lambda)=\min_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\). Then \(g\) is concave, every \(g(\lambda)\) is a lower bound on \(f^*=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\), and \(g^*=\sup_{\lambda\geq0}g(\lambda)\leq f^*\). If compactness is removed, the corresponding minima are replaced by infima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing the Lagrangian over the base set produces a concave dual function. Every nonnegative multiplier gives a valid primal lower bound, and the supremum of these bounds cannot exceed the primal optimum. Without compactness, infima replace minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is concave},\qquad g(\lambda)\leq f^*\ \forall\lambda\geq0,\qquad g^*=\sup_{\lambda\geq0}g(\lambda)\leq f^*.

children.title: Global-Optimization Duality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Optimization Duality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic weak-duality interface encompassing nonconvex dual constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a minimization problem have value \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). A global-optimization dual family consists of an index set \(Y\) and functions \(D_y:F\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(D_y(x)\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in F\) and \(y\in Y\). Define \(d(y)=\inf_{x\in F}D_y(x)\) and \(d^*=\sup_{y\in Y}d(y)\). Then weak duality gives \[d(y)\leq d^*\leq p^*.\] The construction has strong global duality precisely when \(d^*=p^*\); otherwise \(p^*-d^*\) is its global duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any parameterized family of global minorants defines a dual lower-bound problem; equality with the primal value is strong global duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in F}D_y(x)\leq\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: dual-family global minorant indexed by y
best lower bound furnished by the family

children.title: GOP Primal–Relaxed Dual Family
children.top_down_role: Decomposition family for biconvex and related structured global programs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General GOP iteration coordinating primal upper bounds, relaxed-dual lower bounds, valid underestimators, and feasibility cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \begin{array}{ll}\text{Step 0:}&\text{Initialize storage parameters and choose }y^1.\\\text{Step 1:}&k\gets1;\ \text{solve the primal at }y=y^k,\text{ form the Lagrangian using optimal multipliers, and update the best upper bound.}\\&\text{If the primal is infeasible, solve a relaxed primal and use its solution to generate a feasibility cut for the relaxed dual.}\\\text{Step 2:}&\text{Add constraints from earlier iterations that are valid underestimators for the current region.}\\\text{Step 3:}&\text{Solve the relaxed dual as linear subproblems and store all feasible solutions.}\\&\text{Select the best stored value as the lower bound and its associated point as }y^{k+1}.\\\text{Step 4:}&\text{Check convergence between the bounds; set }k\gets k+1\text{ and return to Step 2 if continuing.}\end{array}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize storage parameters and a starting point y^1. Set k = 1, solve the primal problem at y^k, form the Lagrangian from its optimal multipliers, and update the best upper bound. If the primal is infeasible, solve a relaxed primal and generate a feasibility cut for the relaxed dual. Add previously generated constraints that are valid underestimators on the current region. Solve the relaxed dual as linear subproblems, store all feasible solutions, and use the best stored value as the lower bound and its associated point as y^(k+1). Check convergence between the bounds; otherwise increment k and return to the underestimator step.
assumptions_latex: y^1\text{ and the storage parameters are initialized}
\text{When the primal is feasible, its optimal multipliers are available for forming the Lagrangian}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each iteration updates an upper bound and a relaxed-dual lower bound and tests their convergence.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower bound supplied by the Lagrangian linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of the original and linearized Lagrangian minima at iteration k.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathbf{x}^k solve the k-th primal subproblem and define \ell_k(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y}^d)=L(\mathbf{x}^k,\mathbf{y}^d,\lambda^k,\mu^k)+\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}L(\mathbf{x}^k,\mathbf{y}^d,\lambda^k,\mu^k)^T(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^k). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Microcluster specialization of the primal–relaxed-dual GOP procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Application-specific GOP procedure for microcluster potential-energy minimization using coordinate boxes, stored Lagrange functions, and pair-potential convexification parameters. The stopping conditions are reported algorithmic declarations, not independently established convergence guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \((X^0,Y^0,Z^0)\), coordinate bounds, iteration counter \(K=0\), a convergence tolerance \(\epsilon\), the best primal value \(P^{\mathrm{UBD}}\), and stored relaxed-dual solutions. At iteration \(K\): solve the primal problem at \((X^K,Y^K,Z^K)\) and update \(P^{\mathrm{UBD}}\) if its value decreases; retain predecessor-node Lagrange functions and inherit the parent-node box; update
\[
\alpha_{ij}=\max_{r_{ij}}\begin{cases}
-\dfrac{v'(r_{ij})}{2r_{ij}},&r_{\min}\le r_{ij}\le r_0,\\
0,&r_0\le r_{ij}\le r_1,\\
-\dfrac{v''(r_{ij})}{2},&r_1\le r_{ij}\le r_{\max};
\end{cases}
\qquad
r_{ij}=\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2+(z_i-z_j)^2};
\]
eliminate the appropriate relaxed-dual cases when a current connected coordinate is at a bound; and, for each remaining bound combination \(B\), solve
\[
\min_{X,Y,Z,\mu_B}\mu_B
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\mu_B\ge L_k(x^{B_x^k},y^{B_y^k},z^{B_z^k},X,Y,Z),\quad k=1,\ldots,K,
\]
subject to the current coordinate box and \(X_1=Y_1=Z_1=Y_2=Z_2=Z_3=0\). Select the lowest-valued stored relaxed-dual solution as the reported \(R^{\mathrm{LBD}}\), use its \((X,Y,Z)\) as the next current point, and delete it from storage. Stop and declare rigorous convergence when \(P^{\mathrm{UBD}}-R^{\mathrm{LBD}}<0\); otherwise stop and declare \(\epsilon\)-convergence when \(P^{\mathrm{UBD}}-R^{\mathrm{LBD}}<\epsilon\); otherwise increment \(K\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The microcluster GOP procedure alternates primal evaluations with relaxed-dual subproblems. It updates the incumbent primal value, carries forward predecessor Lagrange functions and coordinate boxes, recomputes convexification parameters from the pair potential, removes cases invalidated by coordinates at their bounds, and solves the remaining relaxed-dual problems. The lowest stored relaxed-dual solution supplies the reported lower-bound value and next point and is then deleted. The procedure reports rigorous convergence for a negative bound gap and epsilon-convergence for a gap below the chosen tolerance.
assumptions_latex: x_i^l\le x_i\le x_i^u\ (i=2,\ldots,N),\quad y_i^l\le y_i\le y_i^u\ (i=3,\ldots,N),\quad z_i^l\le z_i\le z_i^u\ (i=4,\ldots,N)
P^{\mathrm{UBD}}\text{ denotes the smallest primal value found, while }R^{\mathrm{LBD}}\text{ is selected from the stored relaxed-dual solutions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^{\mathrm{UBD}}-R^{\mathrm{LBD}}<0\Rightarrow\text{the procedure declares rigorous convergence};\qquad 0\le P^{\mathrm{UBD}}-R^{\mathrm{LBD}}<\epsilon\Rightarrow\text{the procedure declares }\epsilon\text{-convergence}

Then (i) the solution of the relaxed-dual problem in Step 3 of GOP is always a valid underestimator of the solution of problem (3.1), and (ii) GOP terminates at a global optimum of problem (3.1).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Major steps of the regional branch-and-bound version of GOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the tolerance $\epsilon$, global bounds $(f^U,f^L)$, bounds $(\mathbf x^L,\mathbf x^U)$, a starting point $\mathbf y^1$, and the iteration and node indices. At iteration $K$, construct the current region $R_C$ from the Lagrange functions and qualifying constraints along the current node's ancestry. Solve the primal problem at $\mathbf y^K$; if it is feasible, record $K\in F$ and set $f^U\leftarrow\min\{f^U,P^K(\mathbf y^K)\}$, while if it is infeasible, solve a relaxed primal problem and record $K\in I$. Store $\mathbf y^K$, $\boldsymbol\lambda^K$, and $\boldsymbol\mu^K$. Form the current Lagrange function, identify connected variables and functions $g_i^K(\mathbf y)$, tighten variable bounds over $R_C$ when possible, and bound each $g_i^K$. If $g_i^K(\mathbf y)\geq0$ throughout $R_C$, fix $x_i$ at $x_i^L$; if $g_i^K(\mathbf y)\leq0$ throughout $R_C$, fix $x_i$ at $x_i^U$; remove such indices from the connected set. For each remaining bound combination, solve the corresponding relaxed-dual subproblem subject to $\mathbf y\in Y$, the sign-dependent qualifying constraints, and $(\mathbf y,\mu_B)\in R_C$. Retain a child when $\mu_B^\star<f^U-\epsilon$ and fathom it when $\mu_B^\star\geq f^U-\epsilon$. Select the retained child with minimum $\mu_B^j$, set its point as $\mathbf y^{K+1}$, and update $f^L$ to that minimum value. Stop if $\left|(f^U-f^L)/f^U\right|<\epsilon$; otherwise increment $K$ and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm alternates regional primal solves with derivative-based variable fixing and regional relaxed-dual subproblems, fathoms children whose lower estimate is within ε of the incumbent, selects the surviving child with the smallest lower estimate, and stops at the stated relative-gap test.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon,\ f^U,\ f^L,\ \mathbf x^L,\ \mathbf x^U,\text{ and }\mathbf y^1\text{ are initialized.}
F\text{ records feasible-primal iterations and }I\text{ records infeasible-primal iterations.}
\text{Each relaxed-dual subproblem uses the current region and the qualifying constraints induced by its bound combination.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|\frac{f^U-f^L}{f^U}\right|<\epsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{STOP; otherwise continue from the retained child having the minimum relaxed-dual value.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through the y-dependence of coefficients in the x-linearization of the iteration Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that L is differentiable in \mathbf{x} and define \[\mathbf{g}^k(\mathbf{y})=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}L(\mathbf{x}^k,\mathbf{y},\lambda^k,\mu^k),\qquad g_i^k(\mathbf{y})=\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{x}^k,\mathbf{y},\lambda^k,\mu^k).\] The corresponding linearization is \[L(\mathbf{x}^k,\mathbf{y},\lambda^k,\mu^k)+\sum_{i=1}^n g_i^k(\mathbf{y})(x_i-x_i^k).\] A variable x_i is connected when g_i^k(\mathbf{y}) depends on \mathbf{y}, and \[I_c^k=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:g_i^k(\mathbf{y})\text{ depends on }\mathbf{y}\}.\] If the stated primal KKT stationarity conditions hold at (\mathbf{x}^k,\mathbf{y}^k,\lambda^k,\mu^k), then g_i^k(\mathbf{y}^k)=0 for every i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coefficient g_i^k(y) is the x_i derivative of the iteration Lagrangian at x^k. A primal variable is connected exactly when this coefficient depends on y; the connected indices form I_c^k. At a point satisfying the stated primal KKT stationarity conditions, all coefficients vanish at y^k.
assumptions_latex: L\text{ is differentiable with respect to }\mathbf{x}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I_c^k=\{i:g_i^k(\mathbf{y})\text{ depends on }\mathbf{y}\},\qquad \mathrm{KKT}\Rightarrow g_i^k(\mathbf{y}^k)=0\ \forall i.

knowledge_statements.title: Biconvex GOP Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical two-block setting for GOP primal–relaxed-dual decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constrained problem belongs to the biconvex GOP regime when it can be written as \[\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in X\times Y,\ g_r(x,y)\leq0,\ r=1,\ldots,m\},\] where \(X\) and \(Y\) are convex sets and, for every fixed \(y\in Y\), the functions \(f(\cdot,y)\) and \(g_r(\cdot,y)\) are convex on \(X\), while for every fixed \(x\in X\), the functions \(f(x,\cdot)\) and \(g_r(x,\cdot)\) are convex on \(Y\). Joint convexity is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconvex GOP regime is convex in either variable block when the other is fixed, but need not be jointly convex.
assumptions_latex: All displayed objective and constraint functions are finite on their stated block domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is blockwise convex in \(x\) and \(y\), though it may be globally nonconvex in \((x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blockwise Convexity Does Not Imply Joint Convexity or Coordinatewise Globality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of the defining biconvex property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=Y=[-1,1]\), let \(f(x,y)=xy\). Each one-block restriction is affine and hence convex, but the Hessian \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is indefinite. Moreover, \((0,0)\) minimizes each one-block restriction when the other block is fixed at zero, whereas \(f(0,0)=0>-1=\min_{X\times Y}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biconvex function need not be jointly convex, and a coordinatewise minimum need not be globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is biconvex but not jointly convex, and \((0,0)\) is coordinatewise minimizing but not globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Convexity Does Not Imply Joint Convexity or Coordinatewise Globality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blockwise convexity conditions for the GOP iteration Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions (B) imposed on the iteration-specific Lagrange function in the biconvex GOP regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration k, the Lagrange function L(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\lambda^k,\mu^k) satisfies Conditions (B) when (i) L(\cdot,\mathbf{y}^d,\lambda^k,\mu^k) is convex in \mathbf{x} for every fixed discretized \mathbf{y}^d, and (ii) L(\mathbf{x}^k,\cdot,\lambda^k,\mu^k) is convex in \mathbf{y}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At iteration k, Conditions (B) require convexity in x for each fixed discretized y-value and convexity in y when x is fixed at x^k.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf{y}^d\text{ ranges over the discretized values of }\mathbf{y}.
\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^k\text{ is fixed in the second condition.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\mathbf{y}^d,\ L(\cdot,\mathbf{y}^d,\lambda^k,\mu^k)\text{ is convex in }\mathbf{x},\qquad L(\mathbf{x}^k,\cdot,\lambda^k,\mu^k)\text{ is convex in }\mathbf{y}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic GOP variant is a global minimization problem of the form \[\min_{x\in X}\ x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+c_0^{\mathsf T}x+d_0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\leq0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and is described by explicit variable bounds and affine constraints. This is a quadratic program when \(m=0\) and a quadratically constrained quadratic program when \(m>0\). The model may be nonconvex when the symmetric part of \(Q_0\) or of a constraint matrix \(Q_i\) is not positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic GOP variants globally minimize a quadratic objective over bounds and affine constraints, optionally with quadratic constraints; non-positive-semidefinite quadratic parts can make the model nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Regime for Quadratic GOP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature conditions separating a standard convex QCQP regime from quadratic nonconvexity on the working domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_i=(Q_i+Q_i^{\mathsf T})/2\). The quadratic function \(x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\) is convex on \(\mathbb R^n\) if and only if \(S_i\succeq0\). Hence, when \(X\) is convex and \(S_i\succeq0\) for the objective and every inequality function, the displayed QCQP is a convex optimization problem. More generally, if \(X\) has nonempty relative interior in its affine hull, convexity of a quadratic on \(X\) requires nonnegative curvature on every direction parallel to that affine hull; a negative-curvature direction there makes the quadratic nonconvex on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-semidefinite symmetric quadratic parts give a standard convex QCQP; relevant negative curvature on a full relative-dimensional domain makes a quadratic nonconvex there.
assumptions_latex: For the affine-hull necessity statement, \(\operatorname{ri}X\neq\varnothing\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_i\succeq0\) for the objective and all inequality quadratics implies convexity of the QCQP.

notation.meaning: symmetric part of the quadratic matrix Q_i

knowledge_statements.title: GOP Master Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph master formed from finitely many valid relaxed-dual cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*=\inf_{y\in Y}\phi(y)\), and suppose each generated cut \(q_k:Y\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(q_k(y)\leq\phi(y)\) for every \(y\in Y\). The finite GOP lower master is represented by \[M_K=\inf_{y\in Y,\,\theta\in\mathbb R}\{\theta:\theta\geq q_k(y),\ k=1,\ldots,K\}=\inf_{y\in Y}\max_{1\leq k\leq K}q_k(y).\] Consequently \(M_K\leq p^*\), and adding a valid cut cannot decrease \(M_K\). Disjunctive cut domains may be encoded with integer variables, producing a mixed-integer master without changing weak validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A GOP master minimizes the epigraph of accumulated valid cuts, giving a monotone global lower bound; disjunctions can yield a mixed-integer formulation.
assumptions_latex: The displayed infima are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_K\leq M_{K+1}\leq p^*\).

notation.meaning: value of the K-cut lower master

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MILP representation of the best nodewise relaxed-dual solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded representation for the current GOP node at iteration K.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be the current node at iteration \(K\), and let \(R_C\) define its associated region. If \(\underline g_i^K\) and \(\overline g_i^K\) are lower and upper bounds on \(g_i^K(y)\) over \(Y\), then the best solution among the relaxed-dual subproblems at that iteration is obtained by solving
\[\min_{y,\mu_B,t^K,\alpha^K}\ \mu_B\]
subject to
\[\mu_B\geq \sum_{i=1}^{NI_c^K}t_i^K+\sum_{i=1}^{NI_c^K}x_i^L g_i^K(y)+L_0^K(y,\lambda^K,\mu^K),\]
\[t_i^K\geq \alpha_i^K(x_i^U-x_i^L)\underline g_i^K,\]
\[t_i^K\geq (x_i^U-x_i^L)\bigl(g_i^K(y)-(1-\alpha_i^K)\overline g_i^K\bigr),\]
\[\alpha_i^K\underline g_i^K\leq g_i^K(y)\leq (1-\alpha_i^K)\overline g_i^K,\qquad i=1,\ldots,NI_c^K,\]
\[t^K\in\mathbb R^{NI_c^K},\quad \alpha^K\in\{0,1\}^{NI_c^K},\quad y\in Y,\quad (y,\mu_B)\in R_C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At iteration K, the best relaxed-dual solution associated with the current node C can be obtained as the optimum of the displayed mixed-integer linear program.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is the current node to be partitioned at iteration }K.
R_C\text{ is the set of constraints defining the region associated with }C.
\underline g_i^K\leq g_i^K(y)\leq\overline g_i^K\quad\text{for all }y\in Y\text{ and }i=1,\ldots,NI_c^K.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{An optimal solution of the displayed MILP yields the best solution among the iteration-}K\text{ relaxed-dual subproblems.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign-based fixing and elimination of GOP master binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded simplification of the iteration-K GOP MILP master formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each applicable index \(i\) at iteration \(K\),
\[\bigl(\forall y\in Y,\ g_i^K(y)\geq0\bigr)\Longrightarrow \alpha_i^K\text{ may be fixed to }0,\]
\[\bigl(\forall y\in Y,\ g_i^K(y)\leq0\bigr)\Longrightarrow \alpha_i^K\text{ may be fixed to }1.\]
If
\[\forall y\in Y,\quad g_i^K(y)=0,\]
then \(\alpha_i^K\) vanishes from the MILP formulation (3.66)--(3.72).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If g_i^K is nonnegative everywhere on Y, its associated binary variable may be fixed to zero; if it is nonpositive everywhere, the variable may be fixed to one. If g_i^K is identically zero on Y, that binary variable disappears from the master formulation.
assumptions_latex: \alpha_i^K\text{ is the binary variable associated with }g_i^K\text{ in formulation (3.66)--(3.72).}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall y\in Y,\ g_i^K(y)\geq0)\Rightarrow \alpha_i^K\text{ may be fixed to }0;\quad (\forall y\in Y,\ g_i^K(y)\leq0)\Rightarrow \alpha_i^K\text{ may be fixed to }1;\quad (\forall y\in Y,\ g_i^K(y)=0)\Rightarrow \alpha_i^K\text{ is eliminated.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\) and a feasible candidate \(\hat x\in F\). Let \(L:F\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(L(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). If \[L(\hat x)=\inf_{x\in F}L(x)\qquad\text{and}\qquad L(\hat x)=f(\hat x),\] then \[f(\hat x)=p^*.\] Thus the touching lower model is a certificate of global optimality for \(\hat x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is certified globally optimal when a globally valid lower model is minimized at that point and touches the objective there.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Optimality from Convex First-Order Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex specialization of the global lower-model criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Assume the subdifferential sum rule \(\partial(f+\delta_F)(\hat x)=\partial f(\hat x)+N_F(\hat x)\), as holds under standard relative-interior qualification. Then \[\hat x\in\arg\min_{x\in F}f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\partial f(\hat x)+N_F(\hat x).\] Equivalently, some \(s\in\partial f(\hat x)\) satisfies \(s^{\mathsf T}(x-\hat x)\geq0\) for every \(x\in F\). For differentiable \(f\), this becomes \(\nabla f(\hat x)^{\mathsf T}(x-\hat x)\geq0\) for all \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and the standard subdifferential qualification, the normal-cone first-order condition exactly characterizes global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The displayed subdifferential sum rule holds at \(\hat x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial f(\hat x)+N_F(\hat x)\iff\hat x\in\arg\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvex Stationarity Is Not a Global Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of first-order sufficiency outside the convex regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(F=[-1,1]\), let \(f(x)=x^3\). At \(\hat x=0\), \(f'(0)=0\), but \(f(-1)=-1<0=f(0)\). Thus unconstrained first-order stationarity at an interior point does not certify global optimality without convexity or another globally valid lower-model argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary point of a nonconvex function need not be globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0)=0\) but \(0\notin\arg\min_{x\in F}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential-weighted barycenters converge to the unique global minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains the source's inherited standing conditions without attempting to reconstruct assumptions absent from the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the previously specified conditions, suppose that \(f\) has a unique global minimizer \(x^0\) on \(S\). Then, for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\), \[\frac{\int_S x_i e^{-k f(x)}\,dx}{\int_S e^{-k f(x)}\,dx}\longrightarrow x_i^0\qquad (k\to+\infty).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the inherited standing conditions, if f has a unique global minimizer x⁰ on S, then every coordinate of the barycenter formed with weights exp(−k f(x)) converges to the corresponding coordinate of x⁰ as k tends to infinity.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ has a unique global minimizer }x^0\text{ on }S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad \frac{\int_S x_i e^{-k f(x)}\,dx}{\int_S e^{-k f(x)}\,dx}\to x_i^0\quad\text{as }k\to+\infty.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent certification from matching global lower and feasible upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with global value \(p^*\), let \(\hat x\) be feasible, set \(U=f(\hat x)\), and let \(L\) be a certified lower bound satisfying \(L\leq p^*\). Then \[L\leq p^*\leq U,\qquad 0\leq U-p^*\leq U-L.\] Hence \(U=L\) certifies exact global optimality. For a prescribed absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the test \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\) certifies that \(\hat x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal, meaning \(f(\hat x)-p^*\leq\varepsilon\). Both bounds must refer to the same feasible problem and objective convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible upper bound minus a certified global lower bound controls incumbent suboptimality; zero gap gives exact global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(L\leq p^*\) is a valid global lower bound for the same minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\) implies \(f(\hat x)-p^*\leq\varepsilon\); in particular, \(U=L\) implies exact global optimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicitly normalized relative-tolerance companion to the accepted absolute-gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\leq p^*\leq U<+\infty\), where \(U=f(\hat x)\) for a feasible incumbent. For any declared scale \(s>0\), \[\frac{U-L}{s}\leq\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{U-p^*}{s}\leq\varepsilon_{\rm rel}.\] One scale-safe convention is \(s=\max\{1,|U|,|L|\}\). Normalization by \(|U|\) alone is undefined when \(U=0\), so the normalization is part of the certificate specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative gap certificate requires an explicit positive normalization; a scale bounded away from zero remains meaningful at zero-valued objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(L\leq p^*\) is a finite valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((U-L)/s\leq\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\Rightarrow(U-p^*)/s\leq\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Aware Relative Bound-Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.title: Region-Exclusion Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe pruning certificate for a subregion in deterministic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) over a feasible set \(F\subseteq X\), and let \(R\subseteq X\) be a search region. A region-exclusion certificate consists of either a verified assertion \(F\cap R=\varnothing\), or a valid lower bound \(L_R\leq\inf\{f(x):x\in F\cap R\}\), together with an incumbent \(\hat x\in F\) having value \(U=f(\hat x)\). Given tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the region may be discarded when \(F\cap R=\varnothing\) or \(L_R\geq U-\varepsilon\), because it cannot contain a feasible point improving the incumbent by more than \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A region is safely removed when certified infeasible or when its valid lower bound cannot improve the incumbent beyond the chosen tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(L_R\) is a certified lower bound on \(F\cap R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) contains no feasible point \(x\) satisfying \(f(x)<U-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound for region R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of certified regional bounds and feasible incumbent values for safe exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exclusion comparison is unsound if either input lacks its stated validity. For \(\min\{x:x\in[0,1]\}\), the false estimate \(L_R=1\) and feasible value \(U=1\) would exclude \(R=[0,1]\), although \(x=0\) improves the incumbent. For \(\min\{x^2:x\in[1,2]\}\), the valid regional bound is \(L_R=1\), but treating the infeasible point \(0\) as an incumbent with \(U=0\) would authorize exclusion without possessing any feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invalid regional bound or an infeasible alleged incumbent can make the pruning comparison discard relevant regions.
assumptions_latex: Regional exclusion is attempted by comparing a claimed regional lower bound with a claimed incumbent value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Safe bound-based exclusion requires both \(L_R\leq\inf_{x\in F\cap R}f(x)\) and an incumbent \(\hat x\in F\) with \(U=f(\hat x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General global infeasibility witnesses based on certified positive residual bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), let \(F=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\leq0,\ h_j(x)=0\}\), and define \[v(x)=\max\{0,g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x),|h_1(x)|,\ldots,|h_p(x)|\}.\] If a certified scalar \(\ell\) satisfies \(0<\ell\leq\inf_{x\in X}v(x)\), then \(F=\varnothing\). More generally, if \(X\subseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^K R_k\) and each region has a certified bound \(0<\ell_k\leq\inf_{x\in X\cap R_k}v(x)\), then \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive certified lower bound on feasibility violation, globally or over every region of an exhaustive finite cover, proves global infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: All displayed lower bounds are rigorously valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Residual and Exhaustive-Cover Infeasibility Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incomplete Regional Exclusion Does Not Prove Global Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage requirement for aggregating regional infeasibility certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[0,1]\) and impose the equality \(x=1\). The region \(R=[0,1/2]\) is certified infeasible, but \(R\) does not cover \(X\), and the original problem is feasible at \(x=1\). Thus any aggregation of regional infeasibility certificates proves global infeasibility only when the certified regions cover the entire domain under consideration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified infeasibility of tested regions does not imply global infeasibility unless those regions exhaust the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\cap F=\varnothing\) but \(F=\{1\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Regional Exclusion Does Not Prove Global Infeasibility
Global Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive lower-bound certificate for an empty nonlinear feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty domain and define \(F=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ h_j(x)=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}\). Define the aggregate violation \(v(x)=\max\{0,g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x),|h_1(x)|,\ldots,|h_p(x)|\}\). A verifiable number \(\ell\) satisfying \(\ell\leq\inf_{x\in X}v(x)\) is a global infeasibility certificate whenever \(\ell>0\). Indeed, every feasible point would have violation zero, contradicting the positive certified lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive certified lower bound on aggregate constraint violation proves that no point satisfies all constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized S-Lemma certificates for quadratic-system inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded inconsistency certificates for quadratic inequality, equality, and homogeneous systems on affine manifolds or subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be quadratic. (i) If H is affine and \exists x^*\in H with g(x^*)<0, then \{x\in H:f(x)<0,\ g(x)\leq0\}=\varnothing if and only if \exists\bar y\in\mathbb{R}_+ such that f(x)+\bar y g(x)\geq0 for every x\in H. (ii) If H is affine, g is homogeneous or g(x)=\langle x,Q^1x\rangle+\langle c^1,x\rangle+d_1 with Q^1 nonsingular, and g takes both positive and negative values on H, then \{x\in H:f(x)<0,\ g(x)=0\}=\varnothing if and only if \exists\bar y\in\mathbb{R} such that f(x)+\bar y g(x)\geq0 for every x\in H. (iii) If H is a subspace and f and g are homogeneous, then \{x\in H\setminus\{0\}:f(x)\leq0,\ g(x)\leq0\}=\varnothing if and only if \exists(y_1,y_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2 such that y_1f(x)+y_2g(x)>0 for every x\in H\setminus\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the respective strict-feasibility, sign-change, nonsingularity, and homogeneity assumptions, inconsistency of each quadratic system is equivalent to a globally valid scalar or conic linear-combination certificate.
assumptions_latex: \text{Case (ii): }H\text{ is affine; }g\text{ is homogeneous or }g(x)=\langle x,Q^1x\rangle+\langle c^1,x\rangle+d_1\text{ with }Q^1\text{ nonsingular; }g\text{ takes both signs on }H
\text{Case (iii): }H\text{ is a subspace and }f,g\text{ are homogeneous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\{x\in H:f(x)<0,\ g(x)\leq0\}=\varnothing\iff\exists\bar y\in\mathbb{R}_+:\forall x\in H,\ f(x)+\bar y g(x)\geq0;\\&\{x\in H:f(x)<0,\ g(x)=0\}=\varnothing\iff\exists\bar y\in\mathbb{R}:\forall x\in H,\ f(x)+\bar y g(x)\geq0;\\&\{x\in H\setminus\{0\}:f(x)\leq0,\ g(x)\leq0\}=\varnothing\iff\exists(y_1,y_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2:\forall x\in H\setminus\{0\},\ y_1f(x)+y_2g(x)>0.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidefinite Form of the S-Lemma Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix representation of global nonnegativity in the strictly feasible S-lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q_k(x)=x^{\mathsf T}A_kx+2a_k^{\mathsf T}x+c_k\), the condition \(q_0(x)+\lambda q_1(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is equivalent to \[\begin{pmatrix}A_0+\lambda A_1&a_0+\lambda a_1\\(a_0+\lambda a_1)^{\mathsf T}&c_0+\lambda c_1\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] Consequently, under \(q_1(\bar x)<0\), the implication \(q_1\le0\Rightarrow q_0\ge0\) is decidable by feasibility of this LMI with \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar S-lemma certificate is equivalent to one positive-semidefinite block-matrix constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic implication is equivalent to feasibility of the displayed LMI for some \(\lambda\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Form of the S-Lemma Certificate
Single-Quadratic-Constraint Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly feasible inhomogeneous S-lemma over a real finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\in\{0,1\}\), let \(q_k(x)=x^{\mathsf T}A_kx+2a_k^{\mathsf T}x+c_k\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(A_k\) is symmetric. Suppose there exists \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(q_1(\bar x)<0\). Then the quadratic implication \[q_1(x)\leq0\ \Longrightarrow\ q_0(x)\geq0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n\] holds if and only if there exists a scalar \(\lambda\geq0\) such that \[q_0(x)+\lambda q_1(x)\geq0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n.\]

children.title: S-Lemma Quadratic Tractability Consequences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded quadratic minimax exactness theorem over a closed set, with nonnegative or unrestricted scalar multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be quadratic, let W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be closed, and define L(x,y)=f(x)+yg(x). Let D\subseteq\mathbb{R} be closed and \gamma:=\inf_{x\in W}\sup_{y\in D}L(x,y)>-\infty. Assume either D=\mathbb{R}_+ and \exists x^*\in W with g(x^*)<0, or D=\mathbb{R} and \exists a,b\in W with g(a)<0<g(b). Assume also that every a,b\in W satisfying g(a)<0<g(b) obey \sup_{y\in D}\inf_{x\in\{a,b\}}L(x,y)\geq\gamma. Then there exists \bar y\in D such that \inf_{x\in W}L(x,\bar y)=\gamma, and consequently \inf_{x\in W}\sup_{y\in D}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in D}\inf_{x\in W}L(x,y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratic Lagrangian on a closed set, the stated strict sign condition and two-point lower-bound condition guarantee an attained dual value equal to the primal minimax value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\bar y\in D:\inf_{x\in W}L(x,\bar y)=\gamma,\qquad \inf_{x\in W}\sup_{y\in D}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in D}\inf_{x\in W}L(x,y).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete spectral solution structure, including singular interior solutions and the hard case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First test whether \(A\succeq0\), \(Ay=-b\) is solvable, and some solution has norm at most \(r\); any such feasible solution is optimal with \(\lambda=0\). Otherwise seek \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(A)\}\), where \(A+\lambda I\succ0\), and solve the monotone secular equation \[\|(A+\lambda I)^{-1}b\|_2=r,\qquad y=-(A+\lambda I)^{-1}b.\] In the hard case \(\lambda=-\lambda_{\min}(A)>0\), if \(b\in\operatorname{Range}(A+\lambda I)\), take \(y_0=-(A+\lambda I)^\dagger b\) and choose \(z\in\ker(A+\lambda I)\) with \(\|y_0+z\|_2=r\); then \(y_0+z\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trust-region problem is solved by an interior singular-system test, a regular secular equation, or a minimum-eigenspace hard-case construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The applicable construction produces a point satisfying the necessary and sufficient global optimality conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(y)=y^{\mathsf T}Ay+2b^{\mathsf T}y+\gamma\), with \(A\in\mathbb S^n\), and let \(r>0\). If the trust-region problem \(p^*=\min\{q(y):\|y\|_2\leq r\}\) has a finite value, then \[p^*=\max_{\lambda\geq0,\,\tau\in\mathbb R}\left\{\tau:\begin{pmatrix}A+\lambda I&b\\b^{\mathsf T}&\gamma-\lambda r^2-\tau\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\] Thus the nonconvex quadratic problem has no duality gap with this convex semidefinite formulation, and an optimal value can be computed by semidefinite optimization to prescribed numerical accuracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic minimax equalities on a line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional quadratic exactness result for nonnegative and unrestricted scalar multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be quadratic and L(x,y)=f(x)+yg(x). For every affine line \Gamma\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, \inf_{x\in\Gamma}\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}_+}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}_+}\inf_{x\in\Gamma}L(x,y). If g|_\Gamma is not affine, then also \inf_{x\in\Gamma}\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\inf_{x\in\Gamma}L(x,y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any two quadratic functions, their scalar Lagrangian satisfies minimax equality on every affine line when the multiplier is nonnegative. With an unrestricted multiplier, the same holds provided the constraint quadratic is not affine on that line.
assumptions_latex: g|_\Gamma\text{ is not affine}\quad\text{for the unrestricted-multiplier conclusion}

children.title: Multiple-Constraint Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on direct S-Lemma exactness when several quadratic constraints are present.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictly Feasible Box Implication Without Scalar Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of multi-constraint scalar S-procedure exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(q_0(x)=x_1x_2\) and impose \(q_1=-x_1\leq0\), \(q_2=x_1-1\leq0\), \(q_3=-x_2\leq0\), and \(q_4=x_2-1\leq0\). The system is strictly feasible at \((1/2,1/2)\), and its feasible set is \([0,1]^2\), where \(q_0\geq0\). Nevertheless, no \(\lambda_i\geq0\) make \(q_0+\sum_{i=1}^4\lambda_iq_i\) globally nonnegative, because the multiplier terms are affine and cannot change the indefinite quadratic part \(x_1x_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even strict feasibility does not make the scalar S-procedure lossless for several quadratic inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_i\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,4)\Rightarrow q_0\geq0\), but no nonnegative scalar-multiplier certificate exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Feasible Box Implication Without Scalar Multipliers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate notion whose general exactness fails beyond one quadratic constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For quadratic functions \(q_0,q_1,\ldots,q_m\), the nonnegative scalar S-procedure certifies \[q_i(x)\leq0\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\Longrightarrow q_0(x)\geq0\] when there exist scalars \(\lambda_i\geq0\) such that \(q_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iq_i(x)\geq0\) for every \(x\). It is lossless on a class when every valid implication in that class admits such multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multi-constraint scalar S-procedure seeks one nonnegative scalar multiplier per constraint whose weighted sum makes the conclusion globally nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global nonnegativity of \(q_0+\sum_i\lambda_iq_i\) is sufficient for the quadratic implication.

Multiple-Constraint Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of scalar S-procedure exactness with two constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^2\), set \(q_0(x)=2x_1x_2\), \(q_1(x)=-x_1\), and \(q_2(x)=-x_2\). The system is strictly feasible because \(q_1(1,1)<0\) and \(q_2(1,1)<0\), and \[q_1(x)\leq0,\ q_2(x)\leq0\ \Longrightarrow\ q_0(x)\geq0.\] Nevertheless, no \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\geq0\) make \(q_0+\lambda_1q_1+\lambda_2q_2\) globally nonnegative: its quadratic part \(2x_1x_2\) is indefinite and cannot be altered by the affine multiplier terms. Thus the single-constraint S-lemma does not extend verbatim to multiple quadratic inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two strictly feasible affine-quadratic constraints can imply a quadratic inequality even though no nonnegative scalar multipliers certify it globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implication holds, but \(q_0+\lambda_1q_1+\lambda_2q_2\not\geq0\) globally for every \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\geq0\).

children.title: Degenerate Quadratic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exactness boundaries associated with singular or otherwise degenerate quadratic structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Single-Constraint Failure Without Strict Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of the scalar S-lemma guarantee on a lower-dimensional feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(q_1(x)=x_1^2\) and \(q_0(x)=x_1x_2\). The constraint \(q_1(x)\leq0\) forces \(x_1=0\), so it implies \(q_0(x)\geq0\). Strict feasibility is impossible. For every \(\lambda\geq0\), however, \(q_0(x)+\lambda q_1(x)=x_1x_2+\lambda x_1^2\) takes negative values, so no nonnegative scalar multiplier gives a globally nonnegative certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a quadratic constraint collapses the feasible set and has no strict feasible point, a valid implication may lack the usual scalar S-lemma certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_1\leq0\Rightarrow q_0\geq0\), but \(q_0+\lambda q_1\not\geq0\) globally for every \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Single-Constraint Failure Without Strict Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Slater Is Loss of Guarantee, Not Automatic Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp interpretation of degeneracy in the single-constraint S-lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If no point satisfies \(q_1(x)<0\), the ordinary strict-feasibility S-lemma cannot be invoked. This absence does not itself determine certificate existence: the preceding degenerate example has no scalar certificate, whereas \(q_1(x)=x^2\) and \(q_0(x)=x^2\) satisfy both the implication and the global certificate \(q_0\geq0\) with \(\lambda=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of strict feasibility removes the general S-lemma guarantee but does not imply that every degenerate instance lacks a certificate.
assumptions_latex: The ordinary S-lemma is being used in the sign convention \(q_1\leq0\Rightarrow q_0\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists x:q_1(x)<0\) invalidates the standard guarantee but is neither sufficient nor necessary evidence of certificate failure in a particular instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Slater Is Loss of Guarantee, Not Automatic Failure
Degenerate Quadratic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the inhomogeneous S-lemma without strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(q_1(x)=x^2\) and \(q_0(x)=x\). The constraint \(q_1(x)\leq0\) forces \(x=0\), so \(q_1(x)\leq0\) implies \(q_0(x)\geq0\). However, strict feasibility fails, and for every \(\lambda\geq0\) the polynomial \(q_0(x)+\lambda q_1(x)=x+\lambda x^2\) takes a negative value: for \(\lambda=0\), take any \(x<0\); for \(\lambda>0\), take \(x=-1/(2\lambda)\). Hence the usual scalar certificate need not exist in a degenerate single-constraint regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without strict feasibility, a valid single-quadratic implication may have no nonnegative scalar S-lemma multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_1\leq0\Rightarrow q_0\geq0\), but no \(\lambda\geq0\) makes \(q_0+\lambda q_1\geq0\) globally.

knowledge_statements.title: Box Subdivision Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Longest-side bisection of axis-aligned boxes with a maximum-diameter refinement rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a bounded nondegenerate axis-aligned box \(B_0=[\ell,u]\subset\mathbb R^n\) and a tolerance \(\delta>0\). Maintain a finite family of leaf boxes initially equal to \(\{B_0\}\). While some leaf has diameter greater than \(\delta\), select a leaf \(B=[a,b]\) of maximum diameter, choose \(j\in\operatorname*{argmax}_i(b_i-a_i)\), set \(m_j=(a_j+b_j)/2\), and replace \(B\) by the two boxes obtained by imposing respectively \(x_j\leq m_j\) and \(x_j\geq m_j\). The leaves always cover \(B_0\) and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Under continued refinement by this rule, the maximum leaf diameter tends to zero; consequently the tolerance test is reached after finitely many subdivisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly bisecting a maximum-diameter box across one of its longest sides preserves a disjoint covering and drives the maximum leaf diameter to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(B_0\) is a bounded nondegenerate axis-aligned box in \(\mathbb R^n\).
At each refinement, a leaf of maximum diameter is selected and one of its longest coordinate intervals is bisected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The leaf boxes cover \(B_0\), have pairwise disjoint interiors, and satisfy \(\max_k\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\) under continued refinement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient coordinatewise condition for a nested box branch to shrink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let B_k=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i^k,b_i^k] be nested nonempty axis-aligned boxes. Then \operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0 if and only if b_i^k-a_i^k\to0 for every i. Hence repeatedly bisecting only the first coordinate along a nested branch of [0,1]^2 leaves the second width equal to 1 and the diameter bounded below by 1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested box diameters vanish exactly when every coordinate width vanishes; unfair coordinate refinement can leave a nonshrinking branch.
assumptions_latex: Diameter is measured in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinatewise width decay is necessary and sufficient for \operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Relaxation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick convex-hull relaxation for one bilinear term on a rectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and \(w=xy\), where \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\). The convex hull of the bilinear graph in \((x,y,w)\)-space is described by \[w\geq\ell_xy+\ell_yx-\ell_x\ell_y,\qquad w\geq u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y,\] \[w\leq u_xy+\ell_yx-u_x\ell_y,\qquad w\leq\ell_xy+u_yx-\ell_xu_y.\] Replacing a bilinear equality by these inequalities gives an outer relaxation on the rectangle. If the remaining objective and constraints are convex in the lifted variables, the resulting formulation is a convex relaxation. For minimization, any globally solved relaxation supplies a valid regional lower bound, and the maximum bilinear-envelope discrepancy tends to zero as the two interval widths tend to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The four McCormick inequalities give the exact convex hull of one bilinear graph on a rectangle. They provide an outer relaxation and, when the rest of the lifted model is convex, a convex regional lower-bounding problem.
assumptions_latex: The variables retain the bounds \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\).
Convexity of the complete relaxation additionally requires the remaining lifted objective and constraints to be convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The McCormick system equals the convex hull of the bilinear graph; a globally minimized outer relaxation has value no greater than the original rectangular subproblem, and its bilinear-envelope discrepancy vanishes under rectangular refinement.

Then 0\le xy-\underline m(x,y)\le\frac{(u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)}4 and 0\le\overline m(x,y)-xy\le\frac{(u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)}4. Each upper constant is attained at the rectangle midpoint.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Subdivision Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Longest-edge bisection of nondegenerate simplices with maximum-diameter leaf selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a nondegenerate simplex \(S_0=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_n\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) and a tolerance \(\delta>0\). Maintain a finite family of leaf simplices initially equal to \(\{S_0\}\). While some leaf has diameter greater than \(\delta\), select a leaf \(S=\operatorname{conv}(V)\) of maximum diameter, choose a longest edge \([v_i,v_j]\), and set \(m=(v_i+v_j)/2\). Replace \(S\) by \(S_i=\operatorname{conv}((V\setminus\{v_i\})\cup\{m\})\) and \(S_j=\operatorname{conv}((V\setminus\{v_j\})\cup\{m\})\). The children cover \(S\), meet on a common face, and have disjoint interiors. Continued longest-edge refinement with maximum-diameter leaf selection drives the maximum leaf diameter to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bisecting a maximum-diameter simplex at a longest-edge midpoint produces two face-compatible children and drives the global mesh diameter to zero under continued refinement.
assumptions_latex: \(S_0\) is a nondegenerate simplex in \(\mathbb R^n\).
At every refinement, a leaf of maximum diameter and one of its longest edges are selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The leaves cover \(S_0\), have pairwise disjoint interiors, and satisfy \(\max_k\operatorname{diam}(S_k)\to0\) under continued refinement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Volume and Face Structure of Simplex Midpoint Bisection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric invariants of one edge-midpoint simplex bisection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_n\} be a nondegenerate n-simplex, let [v_i,v_j] be an edge, and set m=(v_i+v_j)/2. Replacing v_i and v_j respectively by m produces nondegenerate simplices S_i,S_j with S=S_i\cup S_j, \operatorname{int}(S_i)\cap\operatorname{int}(S_j)=\varnothing, and \operatorname{vol}_n(S_i)=\operatorname{vol}_n(S_j)=\frac12\operatorname{vol}_n(S). Their intersection is the common face spanned by m and the vertices outside the bisected edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-midpoint bisection divides a simplex into two face-compatible, equal-volume nondegenerate simplices.
assumptions_latex: m is the midpoint of an edge of S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_i and S_j form an interior-disjoint cover of S and each has half its volume.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit geometry of nested simplices generated by point subdivisions with infinitely many bisections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(M_k)_{k\geq1}$ be nested $p$-simplices such that $M_{k+1}$ is a child of $M_k$ obtained by subdivision through $\omega^k\in M_k$. Let $\Delta=\{k:M_k\text{ is bisected}\}$ be infinite and set $M_\infty=\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}M_k$. If $\mathbb N\setminus\Delta$ is finite, then $M_\infty$ is a singleton. Otherwise, at least one cluster point of $\{\omega^k:k\notin\Delta\}$ is a vertex of $M_\infty$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nested p-simplices whose children are produced by point subdivisions, suppose bisection occurs infinitely often. If only finitely many steps are not bisections, the limiting intersection is a single point. Otherwise, at least one cluster point of the subdivision points from the non-bisection steps is a vertex of the limiting simplex.
assumptions_latex: M_{k+1}\text{ is a child of }M_k\text{ obtained by subdivision through }\omega^k\in M_k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathbb N\setminus\Delta|<\infty\Rightarrow M_\infty\text{ is a singleton};\qquad |\mathbb N\setminus\Delta|=\infty\Rightarrow\exists\text{ a cluster point of }\{\omega^k:k\notin\Delta\}\text{ that is a vertex of }M_\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(n\)-dimensional pseudomanifold is a simplicial complex \(K\) such that: (i) every simplex of \(K\) is a face of an \(n\)-simplex of \(K\); (ii) every \((n-1)\)-simplex of \(K\) is a face of at least one and at most two \(n\)-simplices of \(K\); and (iii) any two \(n\)-simplices can be joined by a finite sequence of \(n\)-simplices in which consecutive members share an \((n-1)\)-simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An n-dimensional pseudomanifold is a pure n-dimensional simplicial complex whose codimension-one simplices belong to one or two n-simplices and whose n-simplices are connected through shared codimension-one faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is pure of dimension }n,\quad 1\leq \#\{\text{incident }n\text{-simplices}\}\leq 2\text{ for each }(n-1)\text{-simplex, and the }n\text{-simplices are facet-connected.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limit Geometry of a Simplex Filter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accumulation structure of vertices and subdivision points in nested simplex subdivisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_k=[u^{k1},\ldots,u^{kn}]\), \(k\ge1\), be a simplex filter such that \(S_{k+1}\) is a child of \(S_k\) under subdivision through \(v^k\in S_k\). Then: (i) for each \(i\), the sequence \(\{u^{ki}\}_{k\ge1}\) has an accumulation point \(u^i\), and \(S_\infty:=\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}S_k=\operatorname{conv}\{u^1,\ldots,u^n\}\); (ii) \(\{v^k\}_{k\ge1}\) has an accumulation point \(v\in\{u^1,\ldots,u^n\}\); and (iii) if, for infinitely many \(k\), the subdivision is a bisection whose ratio is at least some \(\alpha>0\), then an accumulation point of \(\{v^k\}\) is a vertex of \(S_\infty=[u^1,\ldots,u^n]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nested filter of child simplices, each indexed vertex sequence has an accumulation point, and the convex hull of the resulting points is the limiting intersection. The subdivision-point sequence has an accumulation point among those limiting points. If bisections with ratios bounded below by a positive alpha occur infinitely often, an accumulation point of the subdivision points is a vertex of the limiting simplex.
assumptions_latex: S_{k+1}\text{ is a child of }S_k\text{ under subdivision through }v^k\in S_k
\exists\alpha>0\text{ such that bisections of ratio at least }\alpha\text{ occur for infinitely many }k\quad\text{for part (iii)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i,\ \{u^{ki}\}_{k\ge1}\text{ has an accumulation point }u^i,\quad S_\infty=\operatorname{conv}\{u^1,\ldots,u^n\};\quad \{v^k\}\text{ has an accumulation point in }\{u^1,\ldots,u^n\};\quad \text{under the condition in (iii), an accumulation point is a vertex of }S_\infty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithmic procedure; no convergence or global-optimality guarantee is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a search domain \(\mathcal D\), an initial sampled triangulation, size tolerance \(\delta\), entropy threshold \(\beta\), and a termination criterion, initialize \(\mathcal W\) with all simplices and compute their entropies. For a selected \(\mathcal S_c\in\mathcal W\), if \(\operatorname{size}(\mathcal S_c)<\delta\), remove it from \(\mathcal W\), add it to \(\mathcal P\), and remove its unshared vertices from \(\mathcal V\). Otherwise, if \(E_{\mathcal S_c}\ge\beta\), split it, add the new sampled vertex to \(\mathcal V\), remove the parent from \(\mathcal W\), and add its children to \(\mathcal T\). After the current pending-list scan, append \(\mathcal T\) to \(\mathcal W\), empty \(\mathcal T\), and recompute entropies using the updated \(f_{\max}\), \(f_{\min}\), and threshold \(t\). When the stopping test is reached, stop if \(\mathcal T\cup\mathcal W=\varnothing\) or the prescribed termination criterion holds, and report \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: TRIOPT scans pending simplices in a triangulation. Simplices below the size tolerance are reported and have their unshared sampled vertices removed. Larger simplices are split only when their entropy meets the threshold; their children are queued until the current scan ends. Entropies are then recomputed from the updated sample-value extrema and function threshold. The reported list consists of simplices regarded by the procedure as potentially enclosing an optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal V\subseteq\mathcal D\text{ is an initial sample admitting a triangulation}
E_j\text{ is computable for every pending simplex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Upon termination, return }\mathcal P\text{ as the simplices regarded as potentially enclosing }\mathbf x^*.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Based Relaxation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz lower bound computed from simplex vertex values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_n\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a compact simplex, and let \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm, with \(L\geq0\). Define \[L_S=\min_{0\leq i\leq n}f(v_i)-L\operatorname{diam}(S).\] Then \[L_S\leq\min_{x\in S}f(x)\] and \[0\leq\min_{x\in S}f(x)-L_S\leq L\operatorname{diam}(S).\] Hence the absolute error of this regional lower bound tends to zero whenever the simplex diameter tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex values and a Lipschitz constant give a valid simplex lower bound whose absolute error is at most the Lipschitz constant times the simplex diameter.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a compact simplex in \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(f:S\to\mathbb R\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_S\leq\min_{x\in S}f(x)\) and \(0\leq\min_{x\in S}f(x)-L_S\leq L\operatorname{diam}(S)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Lipschitz underestimator formed from every simplex vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_n\} and let f:S\to\mathbb R be L-Lipschitz. Define q_S(x)=\max_{0\le i\le n}\{f(v_i)-L\|x-v_i\|_2\} and \widehat L_S=\min_{x\in S}q_S(x). Then q_S(x)\le f(x) for every x\in S, so \widehat L_S\le\min_S f. Moreover, \widehat L_S\ge\min_i f(v_i)-L\operatorname{diam}(S), so the all-vertex cone bound dominates the seed's crude diameter bound and has error at most L\operatorname{diam}(S).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of all vertex-centered downward Lipschitz cones is a valid pointwise underestimator and yields a bound at least as strong as the crude vertex-diameter bound.
assumptions_latex: f is L-Lipschitz on S in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_i f(v_i)-L\operatorname{diam}(S)\le\widehat L_S\le\min_{x\in S}f(x).

notation.meaning: Maximum of the vertex-centered downward Lipschitz cones.
Lower bound obtained by globally minimizing q_S over S.

knowledge_statements.title: Conical Subdivision Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary ray subdivision of a pointed simplicial search cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_n\}\) be a pointed simplicial cone with linearly independent generators. Select two generators \(r_p,r_q\), set \(s=r_p+r_q\), and form \[K_p=\operatorname{cone}((R\setminus\{r_q\})\cup\{s\}),\qquad K_q=\operatorname{cone}((R\setminus\{r_p\})\cup\{s\}),\] where \(R=\{r_1,\ldots,r_n\}\). Replace \(K\) by these children, compute a valid lower bound on each child intersected with the prescribed radial domain, and prune children whose bounds fail the incumbent test. Stop when every active directional cell has angular diameter at most \(\delta\), returning the best feasible incumbent and the surviving cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplicial cone can be split by inserting a sum ray, after which child bounds guide pruning and angular refinement.
assumptions_latex: The searched radial domain is prescribed and bounded where required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=K_p\cup K_q\), the child interiors are disjoint, and certified child bounds permit safe pruning.
