knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal control scheme for MULTL; the referenced non-dominance rule and subdivision inequality are treated as previously defined primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(k=1\), \(f_{\min}(k)=\min\{f(a),f(b)\}\), and \(q(k)=Q(k)=p(k)=0\). In each local phase, store \(f_{\min}^{\mathrm{prec}}=f_{\min}(k)\), fix \(p'=p(k)\), perform \(N\) restricted searches with \(p''=\max\{p'-1,q(k)\}\), and then one search through groups \(q(k),\ldots,\max\{p',q(k)\}\); each search subdivides the non-dominated hyperintervals satisfying (4.8) and increments \(k\). Restart the local phase with the new record whenever \(f_{\min}(k)\le f_{\min}^{\mathrm{prec}}-0.01|f_{\min}^{\mathrm{prec}}|\). If this decrease fails but \(p(k)<Q(k)\) or \(q(k)=Q(k)\), repeat the local phase with the old record. If all three conditions fail, enter the global phase. There, store the current record, fix \(p'=p(k)\), and repeatedly search through groups \(q(k),\ldots,r'\), where \(r'=\left\lceil(q(k)+\max\{p',q(k)\})/2\right\rceil\), for at most \(2^{N+1}\) passes, returning immediately to the local phase after a sufficient record decrease. After those passes, search through all groups up to \(\max\{p',q(k)\}\); return to the local phase after sufficient decrease, and otherwise update \(p'\) and repeat the global phase with the stored record.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MULTL initializes from the two endpoint values and alternates local and global searches over indexed groups of non-dominated hyperintervals. Every selected interval must satisfy the prescribed subdivision test. The local phase makes N restricted passes and one broader pass. A relative record improvement of at least one percent triggers a fresh local phase; without that improvement, local search continues while the incumbent interval is not smallest or all diagonals are equal, and otherwise global search begins. The global phase makes at most 2^(N+1) middle-range passes followed by a full-range pass, returning to local search after sufficient improvement and otherwise repeating globally with the stored record.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ has endpoints }a,b\text{ and a current nonredundant partition into indexed hyperinterval groups }q(k),\ldots,Q(k).
p(k)\text{ indexes the group containing the current record hyperinterval }D_{\min}(k).
\text{Non-dominance and the subdivision condition (4.8) are defined for the current partition.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated switching rules recursively generate the MULTL sequence of partition refinements and objective evaluations.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an interval-valued enclosure of a scalar function over every box and the additional nesting property called isotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal B_n\) be the set of all \(n\)-dimensional boxes and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). A map
\[
F^f:\mathcal B_n\to\mathcal B_1
\]
is an inclusion function for \(f\) if
\[
\forall B\in\mathcal B_n,\qquad \{f(x):x\in B\}\subseteq F^f(B).
\]
Writing \(F_\ell^f(B)\) and \(F_u^f(B)\) for the lower and upper endpoints of \(F^f(B)\), the inclusion function is isotone if
\[
\forall B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B_n,\qquad B_1\subseteq B_2\Longrightarrow F^f(B_1)\subseteq F^f(B_2).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inclusion function maps every n-dimensional box to an interval containing all values attained by the scalar function on that box. Its lower and upper interval endpoints are denoted separately. It is isotone when nested input boxes always produce nested enclosing intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall B\in\mathcal B_n,\ \{f(x):x\in B\}\subseteq F^f(B);\qquad F^f\text{ is isotone iff }B_1\subseteq B_2\Rightarrow F^f(B_1)\subseteq F^f(B_2).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=x^2\) and \(X=[-r,r]\) with \(r>0\). The unique zero \(x^*=0\) is multiple, and the interval derivative is \(F'(X)=[-2r,2r]\), which contains the singular value \(0\). Consequently, an interval Newton formula requiring division by \(F'(X)\) is not a regular contraction, and an interior-inclusion test designed to certify a simple zero cannot establish simple-root uniqueness at \(x^*\). Subdivision alone does not remove the singularity from every box containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the multiple root of x squared, every enclosing interval derivative contains zero, so regular interval Newton inversion and simple-root certification break down.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Jacobian Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete enclosure-overestimation example distinguishing failure to verify uniform regularity from an actual singular Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(u,v)=(e^u\cos v,e^u\sin v)\) on \(X=[-\delta,\delta]\times[0,2\pi]\), where \(\delta>0\). Then \(\det F'(u,v)=e^{2u}>0\) at every point of \(X\), but the natural entrywise interval enclosure of \(F'(X)\) contains the zero matrix and hence singular matrices. Therefore failure to verify regularity of this interval hull does not imply a singular realized Jacobian; Newton tests requiring a uniformly regular enclosure are merely inconclusive. Subdivision or a sharper structured enclosure may restore certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Jacobian can be nonsingular everywhere even though its entrywise interval hull contains singular matrices, making regular Newton tests inconclusive through overestimation alone.
assumptions_latex: [J](X) is the natural entrywise interval enclosure of F'(X).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \det F'(u,v)>0\ \forall(u,v)\in X,\qquad 0_{2\times2}\in[J](X).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Propagation from Bounds on a Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termwise domain reduction for a separable sum constraint over a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $B$ be a box and let $p_1,\ldots,p_t$ be real-valued functions on $B$. For each $k\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$: if $\sum_{j=1}^t p_j(x)\ge c$, $p_j(x)\le\bar p_j$ for every $j$ and $x\in B$, and $\bar c\ge\sum_{j=1}^t\bar p_j$, then $p_k(x)\ge c-\bar c+\bar p_k$. Similarly, if $\sum_{j=1}^t p_j(x)\le c$, $\widehat p_j\le p_j(x)$ for every $j$ and $x\in B$, and $\widehat c\le\sum_{j=1}^t\widehat p_j$, then $p_k(x)\le c-\widehat c+\widehat p_k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For points satisfying a sum constraint, bounds on all summands imply a valid bound on each individual summand.
assumptions_latex: x\in B\text{ satisfies the applicable sum constraint}.
p_j(x)\le\bar p_j\ \forall j,\ x\in B,\quad \bar c\ge\sum_{j=1}^t\bar p_j,\text{ in the lower-bound case}.
\widehat p_j\le p_j(x)\ \forall j,\ x\in B,\quad \widehat c\le\sum_{j=1}^t\widehat p_j,\text{ in the upper-bound case}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k(x)\ge c-\bar c+\bar p_k\quad\text{or, respectively,}\quad p_k(x)\le c-\widehat c+\widehat p_k.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial polyblock \(P_0\supseteq G\). At iteration \(k\), select a proper vertex \(v^k\) maximizing \(f\), project it radially to \(y^k\in\partial^+G\), and update the incumbent when \(y^k\in H\). Replace \(v^k\) by the vertices \(v^k-(v_i^k-y_i^k)e_i\), discard dominated or infeasible vertices, and obtain \(P_{k+1}\supseteq G\). Stop when the best remaining vertex value exceeds the incumbent value by at most \(\varepsilon\); return the incumbent as an \(\varepsilon\)-global maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer polyblocks shrink around the normal feasible set. Vertex objective values give upper bounds, while feasible radial projections update the incumbent until the gap is small.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-approximation procedure for problem (MO), subject to its standing order and feasibility assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(P_1=[a,b]\). Given a polyblock \(P_k\supseteq G\) with proper vertex set \(T_k\), set \(T'_k=T_k\cap H\). If \(T'_k=\varnothing\), stop and declare infeasibility. Otherwise choose \(z^k\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in T'_k}f(x)\). If \(z^k\in G\), return \(z^k\) as an optimal solution of \((\mathrm{MO})\). If \(z^k\notin G\), compute \(x^k=\pi_G(z^k)\) and set \(P_{k+1}=P_k\cap\bigl([a,b]\setminus(x^k,b]\bigr)\). Then \(G\subseteq P_{k+1}\subseteq P_k\setminus\{z^k\}\), and the procedure is repeated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the bounding box, maximize the increasing objective over the proper vertices that lie in H. An empty such vertex set gives the algorithm's infeasibility stopping condition. A selected vertex in G is optimal; otherwise its projection onto G defines a smaller outer polyblock that retains G and removes the selected vertex.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\subseteq P_{k+1}\subseteq P_k\setminus\{z^k\}\text{, with the stated infeasibility and optimality stopping rules}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an incumbent-dependent box contraction and records the associated boundary-retention observation in the stated monotonic-optimization setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma\in f(G\cap H)\), \([p,q]\subseteq[a,b]\), and \(S_\gamma(p,q):=\{x\in[p,q]:g(x)\leq0\leq h(x),\ f(x)\geq\gamma\}\). If \(S_\gamma(p,q)\neq\varnothing\), a box \([p',q']\subseteq[p,q]\) that contains at least one point of \(S_\gamma(p,q)\) is called a \(\gamma\)-valid reduction of \([p,q]\) and is denoted \(\operatorname{red}_\gamma[p,q]\). In the stated monotonic-optimization setting, if \(g(q)\geq0\), then every \(x\in S_\gamma(p,q)\) has a point \(x'\in[x,q]\) such that \(g(x')=0\leq h(x')\) and \(f(x')\geq f(x)\geq\gamma\). These boundary points equivalently satisfy \(g(x')\leq0\leq h_\gamma(x')\), where \(h_\gamma(y):=\min\{g(y),h(y),f(y)-\gamma\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gamma-valid reduction is a smaller box retaining at least one point that satisfies the constraints and reaches the incumbent threshold. Under the stated monotonic assumptions and g(q) nonnegative, every such point can be associated with a qualifying point on the boundary g=0.
assumptions_latex: \text{The boundary observation additionally assumes }g(q)\geq0\text{ and the stated monotonic-optimization setting.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [p',q']\subseteq[p,q],\quad [p',q']\cap S_\gamma(p,q)\neq\varnothing;\qquad g(q)\geq0\Rightarrow \forall x\in S_\gamma(p,q)\ \exists x'\in[x,q]:g(x')=0\leq h(x'),\ f(x')\geq f(x)\geq\gamma.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite normal and conormal hulls in an order interval \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(V\subseteq[a,b]\), its polyblock is \(P=V^{\downarrow}=\bigcup_{z\in V}[a,z]\). A vertex \(z\in V\) is proper if no \(z'\in V\setminus\{z\}\) satisfies \(z'\geq z\); such vertices are precisely the Pareto points of \(P\), and \(P=(\operatorname{pvert}P)^{\downarrow}\). Dually, for finite \(T\subseteq[a,b]\), its copolyblock is \(Q=T^{\uparrow}=\bigcup_{z\in T}[z,b]\). A vertex \(z\in T\) is proper if no distinct \(z'\in T\) satisfies \(z'\leq z\), and \(Q=(\operatorname{pvert}Q)^{\uparrow}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyblock is the normal hull of a finite vertex set, while a copolyblock is the conormal hull of a finite vertex set. Each is completely determined by its proper vertices; proper polyblock vertices are its Pareto points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\bigcup_{z\in V}[a,z]=(\operatorname{pvert}P)^{\downarrow},\qquad Q=\bigcup_{z\in T}[z,b]=(\operatorname{pvert}Q)^{\uparrow}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides endpoint infeasibility tests and coordinatewise contractions that retain every solution of the gamma-threshold system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_\gamma(x):=\min\{g(x),h(x),f(x)-\gamma\}\) and \(S:=\{x\in[p,q]:g(x)\leq0\leq h_\gamma(x)\}\). (i) If \(g(p)>0\) or \(h_\gamma(q)<0\), then \(S=\varnothing\). (ii) If \(g(p)\leq0\), define \(q'=p+\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i(q_i-p_i)e^i\), where \(\alpha_i:=\sup\{\alpha\in[0,1]:g(p+\alpha(q_i-p_i)e^i)\leq0\}\). Then \(S\subseteq[p,q']\). (iii) If \(g(p)\leq0\leq h_\gamma(q)\), define \(p'=q'-\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i(q_i'-p_i)e^i\), where \(\beta_i:=\sup\{\beta\in[0,1]:h_\gamma(q'-\beta(q_i'-p_i)e^i)\geq0\}\). Then \(S\subseteq[p',q']\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Endpoint evaluations may certify that the threshold system has no solution. Otherwise, coordinatewise maximal steps contract first the upper and then the lower corner while retaining every original solution.
assumptions_latex: \text{The order-monotonicity hypotheses of the stated polyblock setting hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(p)>0\lor h_\gamma(q)<0\Rightarrow S=\varnothing;\quad g(p)\leq0\Rightarrow S\subseteq[p,q'];\quad g(p)\leq0\leq h_\gamma(q)\Rightarrow S\subseteq[p',q'].

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-polyblock reduction algorithm for monotonic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a polyblock \(P_1\supseteq G\cap H\) with proper vertex set \(V_1\), together with an available feasible incumbent \(\bar x^1\) and \(CBV=f(\bar x^1)\); use \(CBV=-\infty\) if no feasible point is known. At iteration \(k\), form \(\bar P_k=\operatorname{red}_{CBV}P_k\) and \(\bar V_k=\operatorname{pvert}(\bar P_k)\). If \(\bar V_k=\varnothing\), declare infeasibility when \(CBV=-\infty\), and otherwise return the incumbent as optimal. Otherwise reset \(b=\bigvee\bar V_k\), choose \(z^k\in\arg\max\{f(x):x\in\bar V_k\}\), and return \(z^k\) as optimal if \(g(z^k)\leq0\). If not, compute \(x^k=\pi_G(z^k)\), update the feasible incumbent and \(CBV\), set \(P_{k+1}=\bar P_k\setminus(x^k,b]\), compute its proper vertices by the polyblock vertex-update rule, increment \(k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from an outer polyblock and an optional feasible incumbent, repeatedly reduce the polyblock, select its objective-maximizing proper vertex, apply the stated termination tests, and otherwise project the vertex onto G, update the incumbent, remove the resulting upper orthant, and recompute the proper vertices.

CBV=f(\bar x^1)\text{ for a known feasible incumbent, or }CBV=-\infty

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The all-discrete case has finite termination; the mixed case additionally requires uniform separation of the remaining coordinates from the lower box boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(s=n\), the discrete polyblock algorithm is finite. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every coordinate is discrete, the discrete polyblock algorithm terminates finitely. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyblock search specialized to a discrete monotonic optimization problem through S-adjusted reductions and discrete projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a polyblock \(P_0\supseteq G\cap H\) with proper vertices \(T_0\), an incumbent value \(\gamma_0\) (or \(-\infty\) if none exists), and \(S_0^*=\{x\in S^*\mid f(x)>\gamma_0\}\). At iteration \(k\): apply \(\operatorname{red}_{\gamma_k}^S[a,v]\) to every \(v\in T_k\), deleting empty reductions and vertices with \(f(v)\le\gamma_k\); if no vertices remain, certify infeasibility when \(\gamma_k=-\infty\), otherwise certify the incumbent optimal. Select \(v^k\in\arg\max_{v\in T_k}f(v)\); if \(v^k\in G\cap S^*\), return it as optimal. Otherwise form an adjusted projection \(\widetilde v^k\) into or toward \(G\cap S_k^*\), replace vertices strictly above \(\widetilde v^k\) by the coordinate-cut vertices, remove dominated or improper vertices, update the incumbent, \(\gamma_{k+1}\), and \(S_{k+1}^*\), and repeat.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Formula for Gamma-Valid Box Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes the reduced box using coordinatewise threshold values and gives the exact empty-versus-nonempty cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_\gamma(x):=\min\{g(x),h(x),f(x)-\gamma\}\). Define \(q'=p+\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i(q_i-p_i)e^i\) and \(p'=q'-\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i(q_i'-p_i)e^i\), with \(\alpha_i:=\sup\{t\in[0,1]:g(p+t(q_i-p_i)e^i)\leq0\}\) and \(\beta_i:=\sup\{t\in[0,1]:h_\gamma(q'-t(q_i'-p_i)e^i)\geq0\}\). Equivalently, the source expresses these values using its scalar threshold operator \(N\). Then \(\operatorname{red}_\gamma[p,q]=\varnothing\) if \(g(p)>0\) or \(h_\gamma(q')<0\), whereas \(\operatorname{red}_\gamma[p,q]=[p',q']\) if \(g(p)\leq0\) and \(h_\gamma(q')\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute maximal admissible coordinatewise movements for the upper and lower corners. The reduction is empty if either endpoint test fails; otherwise it is the box between the resulting corners.
assumptions_latex: \text{The coordinatewise suprema and the source's scalar threshold operator }N\text{ are interpreted as in the preceding reduction lemma.}
\text{The order-monotonicity hypotheses of gamma-valid reduction hold.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{red}_\gamma[p,q]=\begin{cases}\varnothing,&g(p)>0\lor h_\gamma(q')<0,\\[p',q'],&g(p)\leq0\land h_\gamma(q')\geq0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyblock vertex update after upper-orthant removal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric update used by polyblock outer approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq[a,b]\) be a polyblock with proper vertex set \(V\), and let \(x\in[a,b]\) satisfy \(V_*:=\{z\in V:x<z\}\neq\varnothing\). Then \(P':=P\setminus(x,b]\) is a polyblock with vertex set \[T'=(V\setminus V_*)\cup\{z^i=z+(x_i-z_i)e^i:z\in V_*,\ i=1,\ldots,n\}.\] Let \(V_*^+:=\{y\in V:x\leq y\}\). Its proper vertex set is obtained from \(T'\) by removing improper elements; for every \(z\in V_*\) and \(y\in V_*^+\), if \(J(z,y):=\{j:z_j>y_j\}=\{i\}\), then \(z^i\) is improper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing the upper orthant above x from a polyblock replaces each proper vertex strictly above x by coordinate-cut candidates. The proper vertices are obtained by removing candidates identified as improper by the singleton-coordinate test.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq[a,b]\text{ is a polyblock with proper vertex set }V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P'=P\setminus(x,b]\text{ is a polyblock with vertex set }T',\quad J(z,y)=\{i\}\Rightarrow z^i\text{ is improper}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a feasible incumbent \(x^0\in D\). At iteration \(k\), set \(\gamma_k=f(x^k)+\delta\) and invoke a complete global feasibility oracle for \(D_k=D\cap\{x:f(x)\ge\gamma_k\}\). If the oracle returns \(y^k\in D_k\), set \(x^{k+1}=y^k\) and repeat. If it certifies \(D_k=\varnothing\), stop and return \(x^k\). The empty-level certificate implies \(f(x)<f(x^k)+\delta\) for every \(x\in D\), so the returned incumbent is globally \(\delta\)-optimal in objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly seek a feasible point improving the incumbent by a fixed amount. Failure of a complete level-feasibility query certifies global objective accuracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive Incumbent Transcending scheme for essential optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Master-problem iteration for the monotonic reformulation, with conditional essential-optimality and essential-infeasibility outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\eta>0\), set \(\gamma_0=f(b)\), and initialize \(\gamma\leftarrow\gamma_0\). Repeatedly solve \(Q_\gamma\). If \(\max(Q_\gamma)>0\), obtain an essential feasible point \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(f(\widehat x)\le\gamma\), set \(\gamma\leftarrow f(\widehat x)+\eta\), and repeat. If \(\max(Q_\gamma)\le0\), then no essential feasible point \(x\) satisfies \(f(x)\le\gamma\). If \(\gamma=f(\widehat x)+\eta\) for a previously found essential feasible point, return \(\widehat x\) as essential \(\eta\)-optimal; if \(\gamma=\gamma_0\), declare Q essentially infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the cutoff at f(b) and repeatedly solve the cutoff master problem. A positive master optimum supplies an essential feasible incumbent and updates the cutoff to its value plus eta. A nonpositive optimum terminates: it certifies the previous incumbent as essential eta-optimal or, at the initial cutoff, declares essential infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \text{The master-problem implications used in Proposition 12.1 apply to each }Q_\gamma
Q_\gamma\text{ is solved globally at each iteration}

Choose $\varepsilon,
\eta>0$ and initialize $\gamma=\gamma_0:=f(a)-\eta$. Call $(SP_\gamma)$. Whenever it returns a nonisolated feasible point $\bar x$ with $f(\bar x)\leq\gamma$, reset $\gamma\leftarrow f(\bar x)-\eta$ and repeat. Otherwise stop. If $\gamma=f(\bar x)-\eta$ for a nonisolated feasible point $\bar x$, then $\bar x$ is essential $(\varepsilon,\eta)$-optimal; if $\gamma=
\gamma_0$, then $(P)$ has no $\varepsilon$-essential feasible solution. If $f(D)$ is compact, the scheme is finite.

Compactness of the feasible objective image and positive eta ensure finite termination.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive incumbent-transcending algorithm for monotonic optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-tolerance SIT procedure using gamma-valid reduction, lower-bound pruning, adaptive branching, and incumbent updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set $\gamma_0=f(b)$ and choose $\varepsilon,\eta>0$. Initialize $\mathcal P_1=\{[a,b]\}$ and $\mathcal R_1=\varnothing$. If an essential feasible incumbent $\bar x$ is known, set $\gamma=f(\bar x)-\eta$; otherwise set $\gamma=\gamma_0$. At iteration $k$, replace every $M\in\mathcal P_k$ by $\operatorname{red}_\gamma M$, deleting empty reductions. For each surviving reduced box $M=[p,q]$, compute a lower bound $\beta(M)$ of $g$ over $\{x\in[p,q]:k_\gamma(x)\ge0\}$ attained at some $z\in[p,q]$, and delete $M$ when $\beta(M)>-\varepsilon$. Add surviving boxes to the reserve. If the reserve is empty, terminate: $\gamma=\gamma_0$ certifies $\varepsilon$-essential infeasibility, while $\gamma=f(\bar x)-\eta$ certifies that $\bar x$ is essential $(\varepsilon,\eta)$-optimal. Otherwise select $M_k=[p^k,q^k]$ minimizing $\beta(M)$ and an attaining point $z^k$. If $k_\gamma(z^k)\ge0$, set $y^k=z^k$; otherwise take $y^k$ where $[z^k,q^k]$ meets $k_\gamma(x)=0$. If the resulting test sends $y^k$ to the incumbent step, treat it as essential feasible with $f(y^k)\ge\gamma$, set $\bar x\leftarrow y^k$, and restart with the updated threshold. Otherwise split $M_k$ into two subboxes by adaptive branching through $(z^k,y^k)$ and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SIT algorithm repeatedly reduces boxes, prunes boxes whose attainable lower bound cannot meet the epsilon feasibility margin, selects the box with smallest bound, and either obtains a threshold-improving essential feasible incumbent or adaptively bisects the selected box. An empty reserve certifies epsilon-essential infeasibility when no incumbent was available, or essential (epsilon, eta)-optimality of the incumbent otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R_k'=\varnothing\Rightarrow\begin{cases}(MO)\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-essentially infeasible},&\gamma=\gamma_0,\\ \bar x\text{ is essential }(\varepsilon,\eta)\text{-optimal},&\gamma=f(\bar x)-\eta.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: SIT implementation using box reduction, lower bounds, pruning, incumbent handling, and adaptive bisection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose $\varepsilon,\eta>0$, set $\gamma_0=f(a)-\eta$, $\mathcal P_1=\{[a,b]\}$, $\mathcal R_1=\varnothing$, $\gamma=\gamma_0$, and $k=1$. Reduce each $M\in\mathcal P_k$ to a subbox preserving $\min\{g(x)\mid f(x)\leq\gamma,
 x\in M\}$, compute a lower bound $\beta(M)$ for $g$ over the relevant points, require $\beta(M)<+\infty\Rightarrow\{x\in M\mid f(x)\leq\gamma\}\neq\varnothing$, and delete boxes satisfying $\beta(M)>-\varepsilon$. Add surviving boxes to the reserve. If the reserve is empty, terminate with $\varepsilon$-essential infeasibility when $\gamma=\gamma_0$, or with essential $(\varepsilon,\eta)$-optimality of the current nonisolated incumbent $\bar x$ when $\gamma=f(\bar x)-\eta$. Otherwise select $M_k$ minimizing $\beta$, and choose $x^k,y^k\in M_k$ satisfying $f(x^k)\leq\gamma$ and $g(y^k)-\beta(M_k)=o(\lVert x^k-y^k\rVert)$. If $g(x^k)<-\varepsilon$, treat $x^k$ as a nonisolated feasible solution and initialize or improve $\bar x$ as specified. Bisect $M_k$ at $v^k=(x^k+y^k)/2$ along an index $j_k\in\arg\max_j|y_j^k-x_j^k|$, replace it by the two subboxes, increment $k$, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm reduces and bounds boxes, prunes boxes whose bounds exclude epsilon-essential feasibility, and terminates with an infeasibility or approximate-optimality certificate when no boxes remain. Otherwise it selects the lowest-bound box, tests paired points, handles any strictly margin-feasible incumbent, and adaptively bisects along the largest coordinate discrepancy.
assumptions_latex: \beta(M)\text{ is a lower bound of the prescribed kind}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each iteration either terminates with the stated essential-infeasibility or essential-optimality conclusion, or continues after incumbent handling and adaptive bisection.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic certified partition workflow for compact DC minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a finite active partition \(\mathcal P_k\) of a compact feasible set, a feasible incumbent \(U_k\), and valid bounds \(L(B)\leq\inf_{x\in B}f(x)\). Discard cells satisfying \(L(B)\geq U_k\), subdivide a remaining cell into finitely many covering cells, compute their bounds and feasible trial values, and stop with an \(\varepsilon\)-global incumbent when \(U_k-\min_{B\in\mathcal P_k}L(B)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the feasible region, lower-bound each cell, prune cells that cannot improve the incumbent, and stop when the certified global gap reaches tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is nonempty and compact.
Active cells cover every feasible point not already safely fathomed.
Every \(L(B)\) is a valid finite regional lower bound.
Every incumbent value is attained at a feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U_k-\min_{B\in\mathcal P_k}L(B)\leq\varepsilon\Longrightarrow U_k-\min f\leq\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: Valid lower bound on cell B.
Best feasible value through iteration k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regional consistency condition required for asymptotic partition convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every infinite nested selected-cell sequence \(B_k\) has \(\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\) and satisfies \[0\leq\inf_{x\in B_k}f(x)-L(B_k)\leq\eta(\operatorname{diam}(B_k)),\qquad \eta(t)\to0\text{ as }t\downarrow0.\] Then \(\inf_{B_k}f-L(B_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regional DC bounds are consistent when their error is controlled by a modulus vanishing with cell diameter.
assumptions_latex: \(L(B)\) is a valid finite lower bound on every active cell.
Every infinite nested selected-cell sequence has vanishing diameter.
The displayed error estimate holds for a function \(\eta\) with \(\eta(t)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in B_k}f(x)-L(B_k)\to0.

notation.meaning: Cells along an infinite nested selected sequence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cellwise DC Minorant from a Convex Majorant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical regional convex lower model used by DC partition search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=g-h\) on a convex cell \(B\), with \(g\) and \(h\) convex. If the affine function \(a_B\) satisfies \(a_B(x)\geq h(x)\) on \(B\), then \(\underline f_B=g-a_B\) is convex and satisfies \(\underline f_B\leq f\) on \(B\). Therefore \(L(B)=\inf_{x\in B}\underline f_B(x)\) is a valid regional lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine majorant of the subtracted convex component produces a convex cellwise lower model.
assumptions_latex: \(a_B\) is an affine majorant of \(h\) on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \underline f_B=g-a_B\text{ is convex and }\underline f_B\leq f\text{ on }B.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the DC partition search, suppose cells are selected by best bound, every infinite selected nested sequence has vanishing diameter and consistent bounds, and feasible trial values on such a sequence approach the objective value at its feasible limit. If the algorithm does not terminate earlier, then the global active lower bounds and incumbent values converge to the global minimum; consequently every positive absolute-gap tolerance is eventually attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Best-bound DC partitioning converges globally when refinement is exhaustive, cell bounds are consistent, and feasible sampling tracks refined cells.
assumptions_latex: The assumptions of DC Partition Search hold and \(f\) is continuous on the compact feasible set.
A cell attaining the least active lower bound is selected at every nonterminal iteration.
Every infinite selected nested-cell sequence has vanishing diameter and consistent regional bounds.
Feasible trial values generated along every such sequence converge to the objective at its feasible limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Convex Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional DC representation of an objective and finitely many inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\). A DC program has the form \(\min_{x\in X}\{g_0(x)-h_0(x):g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Introducing \(t\in\mathbb R\) gives the epigraph formulation \[\min_{x\in X,\,t\in\mathbb R} t-h_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_0(x)\leq t,\quad g_i(x)-h_i(x)\leq0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] For every feasible \(x\) of the original problem, choosing \(t=g_0(x)\) gives the same objective value, while every feasible \((x,t)\) of the epigraph problem satisfies \(t-h_0(x)\geq g_0(x)-h_0(x)\). Hence the two problems have the same infimum, and whenever an optimum is attained their optimal \(x\)-components coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Express the objective and each inequality as a difference of two convex functions. An epigraph variable for the positive convex objective component produces a formulation with the same optimal value and the same optimal x-components when optima exist.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i,h_i:X\to\mathbb R\) are finite-valued convex functions for \(i=0,1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and epigraph formulations have the same infimum; when an optimum is attained, their minimizing \(x\)-components coincide.

notation.meaning: convex components of inequality constraint i
epigraph variable for the positive convex objective component

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact inequality-only representation of a DC equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex \(g,h\), \[g(x)-h(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g(x)-h(x)\leq0,\quad h(x)-g(x)\leq0.\] Both inequalities are DC constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC equality is exactly equivalent to its two opposite DC inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are finite convex functions on a common domain.

children.title: Relaxation-Strength Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrarily Weak and Inconsistent Equivalent DC Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition-dependent relaxation failure on fixed and shrinking intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\equiv0\) on \(B=[-r,r]\), write \(f(x)=Mx^2-Mx^2\). The endpoint secant majorant of \(h(x)=Mx^2\) is \(a_B(x)=Mr^2\), so \(\underline f_B(x)=Mx^2-Mr^2\) and \(\min_B f-\min_B\underline f_B=Mr^2\). On the fixed interval \(r=1\), this gap is arbitrarily large as \(M\to\infty\). On shrinking intervals, choosing \(M=r^{-2}\) keeps the gap equal to one even as \(r\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent DC decompositions can make a bound arbitrarily weak, and changing the decomposition with the cell can prevent consistency even on shrinking cells.
assumptions_latex: The subtracted convex quadratic is replaced by its endpoint secant majorant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_B f-\min_B\underline f_B=Mr^2;\quad M=r^{-2}\Longrightarrow\text{gap}=1.

notation.meaning: Scaling of the common convex quadratic.
Affine secant majorant of the subtracted component.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrarily Weak and Inconsistent Equivalent DC Decompositions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restriction Monotonicity with a Fixed DC Lower Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength improvement under spatial restriction when the lower model is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(B'\subseteq B\) and the same valid lower model \(\underline f_B\leq f\) is used on both cells, then \[\inf_{x\in B'}\underline f_B(x)\geq\inf_{x\in B}\underline f_B(x).\] Hence domain restriction cannot weaken a fixed relaxation; parent-child bound monotonicity may fail only when the model, its decomposition, or its parameters are changed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking a cell strengthens a fixed lower model, whereas rebuilding the model can reverse bound monotonicity.
assumptions_latex: \(\underline f_B\) is a valid lower model on \(B\) and is reused on \(B'\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{B'}\underline f_B\geq\inf_B\underline f_B.
knowledge_statements.title: Restriction Monotonicity with a Fixed DC Lower Model

assumptions_latex: \(B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a compact convex cell with diameter \(d(B)\).
\(f=g-h\) on \(B\), with \(g\) convex and \(h\) convex and Lipschitz with constant \(M_B\).
\(\ell_B\) is an affine minorant of \(-h\) on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation error is bounded by \(0\leq f(x)-\underline f_B(x)\leq2M_Bd(B)\) for every \(x\in B\), so diameter reduction forces consistency, whereas nonshrinking cells need not yield exact bounds.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of h on B

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency boundary for cellwise DC convex relaxations under Lipschitz control.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\ell_B(x)\leq-h(x)\) on \(B\) and that \(\ell_B\) touches \(-h\) at some \(z_B\in B\). Then \(\underline f_B=g+\ell_B\) is convex and satisfies \(\underline f_B\leq f\) on \(B\). Since both \(h\) and the touching affine support have slopes bounded in norm by \(M_B\), \[0\leq f(x)-\underline f_B(x)\leq2M_Bd(B),\qquad x\in B.\] Thus nested cells with \(d(B_k)\to0\) have vanishing relaxation error. Without shrinking diameters or uniform local slope control, the relaxation gap may remain positive, so pruning based on asymptotic exactness is unjustified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DC lower bounds become exact on shrinking cells under local Lipschitz control; without shrinking or slope control, a persistent relaxation gap can defeat global certification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contour coverage by connected augmented components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting a finite connected cover by contours through all global touching points ensures that every augmented connected component meets every contour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous between topological spaces. Let $K=\bigcup_{i=1}^mK_i$, where each $K_i$ is closed and connected, each $\pi_f(K_i)$ is closed in the contour space $X_f$, and every $f$-contour intersects $K$. Let $\Gamma\subseteq X$ contain every global touching point of $f$ with $K$, and define $Z:=K\cup\bigcup_{x\in\Gamma}C_x(f)$. Then, for every connected component $T$ of $Z$, every $f$-contour has nonempty intersection with $T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If K meets every contour and has finitely many closed connected pieces with closed contour-space images, augmenting K by contours through all global touching points makes every connected component of the augmented set meet every contour.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton leaves and their elementary incidence properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Newton leaves, Newton trajectories, and their basic set-theoretic structure, including the possible failure of connectedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, F\in C(B,\mathbb{R}^n), and let V\leq\mathbb{R}^n have dimension k. The k-Newton leaf is \mathcal F_V(F,B):=\{x\in B:F(x)\in V\}=F^{-1}(V)\cap B; a 1-Newton leaf is a Newton trajectory. Moreover, \mathcal F_{\{0\}}(F,B)=\operatorname{Zero}(F,B), \mathcal F_{\mathbb R^n}(F,B)=B, V\subseteq W\Rightarrow\mathcal F_V\subseteq\mathcal F_W, and \mathcal F_V\cap\mathcal F_W=\mathcal F_{V\cap W}. For every x\in B\setminus\operatorname{Zero}(F,B), the unique Newton trajectory through x is \mathcal F_{\langle F(x)\rangle}; distinct Newton trajectories intersect exactly in \operatorname{Zero}(F,B). Newton leaves need not be connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous map from B into R^n, the k-Newton leaf associated with a k-dimensional linear subspace V is the inverse image of V in B; a one-dimensional leaf is a Newton trajectory. Zero- and n-dimensional leaves are respectively the zero set and B. Inclusion and intersection of subspaces induce the corresponding inclusion and intersection of leaves. Every nonzero point lies on exactly one Newton trajectory, distinct trajectories meet precisely at zeros, and leaves may be disconnected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F_V(F,B)=F^{-1}(V)\cap B,\quad V\subseteq W\Rightarrow\mathcal F_V\subseteq\mathcal F_W,\quad \mathcal F_V\cap\mathcal F_W=\mathcal F_{V\cap W}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a trajectory-based method for locating solutions of a global optimization problem or an associated system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trajectory method constructs a finite family $K$ of curves on $M$ such that one or all solutions are known a priori to lie on curves in $K$, or there is good reason to suspect that some or all solutions lie on them. These curves are often solution trajectories of first- or second-order ordinary differential equations, but other curve constructions are also permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trajectory method constructs finitely many curves on the search space on which one or all solutions are known, or plausibly expected, to lie. The curves are often trajectories of first- or second-order ordinary differential equations, but they need not be.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is a finite family of curves on }M\text{ intended to contain, or plausibly pass through, some or all solutions; its curves need not be ODE trajectories.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular Newton leaves and extraneous singularities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes Newton leaves as zero sets of projected maps and records their regularity, singularity, transversality, and local zero-incidence conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V\leq\mathbb R^n have dimension k and let A_V have rows forming a basis of V^\perp, so \ker A_V=V. Then \mathcal F_V(F,B)=\{x\in B:A_VF(x)=0\}. If F is differentiable and \operatorname{rank}(A_VDF(x))=n-k for every x\in\mathcal F_V(F,\mathbb R^n), this leaf is a closed k-dimensional submanifold, called regular. A point x\in\mathcal F_V(F,B) with \operatorname{rank}(A_VDF(x))<n-k is an extraneous singularity; equivalently, for any basis v_1,\ldots,v_k of V, \operatorname{rank}[DF(x),v_1,\ldots,v_k]<n. The extraneous-singularity set is closed. If x\in\mathcal F_V\cap\mathcal F_W is not extraneously singular for \mathcal F_{V\cap W}, the two leaves intersect transversally at x; in particular this holds at nondegenerate zeros. Around every nondegenerate zero x^*, there is a neighborhood U such that each connected leaf component meeting U contains x^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton leaf is the zero set of the projected map A_V F, where A_V has kernel V. Full rank of its derivative makes the leaf a regular k-dimensional closed submanifold. Rank loss defines an extraneous singularity and has an equivalent augmented-matrix test; such singularities form a closed set. Nonsingular intersections are transverse, and every leaf component sufficiently near a nondegenerate zero must pass through that zero.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is differentiable for the rank and manifold assertions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F_V(F,B)=\{x\in B:A_VF(x)=0\},\qquad \operatorname{rank}(A_VDF(x))=n-k\Rightarrow\mathcal F_V\text{ is a regular }k\text{-manifold}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fiber connectivity under a global homeomorphic completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes connectivity of a level-set fiber by connectivity of its image in complementary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $F:D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k<n$, and suppose there is $G:D\to\mathbb{R}^{n-k}$ such that $H:=(F,G):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is a global homeomorphism. For every $x_0\in D$, the fiber $F^{-1}(F(x_0))$ is connected if and only if $H(D)\cap\bigl(\{F(x_0)\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-k}\bigr)$ is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a map F can be completed by complementary coordinates G to a global homeomorphism H, then the fiber of F through any point x0 in D is connected exactly when the corresponding coordinate slice of H(D) is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^{-1}(F(x_0))\text{ is connected}\iff H(D)\cap\bigl(\{F(x_0)\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-k}\bigr)\text{ is connected}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contours and the contour space of a map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines connected components of fibers, their induced equivalence relation, and the quotient projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a topological space, $Y$ a set, and $f:X\to Y$. For each $x\in X$, the $f$-contour at $x$, denoted $C_x(f)$, is the connected component containing $x$ of $f^{-1}(\{f(x)\})$. Define $R_f\subseteq X\times X$ by $xR_fy\iff C_x(f)=C_y(f)$. The quotient space $X_f:=X/R_f$ is the contour space of $f$, and $\pi_f:X\to X_f$ is its canonical projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contour at x is the connected component containing x in its level fiber. Points with the same contour are equivalent, and the resulting quotient is the contour space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_x(f):=\operatorname{ConnComp}_x\!\left(f^{-1}(\{f(x)\})\right),\quad xR_fy\iff C_x(f)=C_y(f),\quad X_f:=X/R_f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global and local touching through contour projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines boundary contact simultaneously in the original space and the contour-space quotient; the apparent source typo is interpreted as local touching of the set $A$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a topological space, $A\subseteq X$, $Y$ a set, $f:X\to Y$, and $x\in X$. The map $f$ touches $A$ globally at $x$ if $x\in\pi_f^{-1}(\partial\pi_f(A))\cap\partial A$. It touches $A$ locally at $x$ if, for every neighborhood $V$ of $x$, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ with $U\subseteq V$ such that $f|_U$ touches $A\cap U$ globally at $x$, using the contour projection of $f|_U$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global touching occurs when x lies both on the boundary of A and over the boundary of A's image in contour space. Local touching means that this global condition holds for a suitable smaller neighborhood inside every neighborhood of x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ touches }A\text{ globally at }x\iff x\in\pi_f^{-1}(\partial\pi_f(A))\cap\partial A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the graph of zeros linked through connected leaf components and records its monotonicity with leaf dimension and its search interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let B\subseteq\mathbb R^n and F\in C(B,\mathbb R^n). For k=0,\ldots,n, define \Gamma^k(F,B) with vertex set \operatorname{Zero}(F,B), joining distinct u,v exactly when some connected component of a k-Newton leaf contains both. If 0\leq l\leq k\leq n, then \Gamma^l(F,B) is a spanning subgraph of \Gamma^k(F,B); \Gamma^0 is edgeless and \Gamma^n is complete. Connectivity of \Gamma^k means that finitely many k-leaf components can be traversed successively through already discovered zeros to cover all zeros. If \Gamma^k is disconnected for some k>0, no single connected Newton-trajectory component contains all zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The k-th Newton-leaf graph has the zeros of F as vertices and links two distinct zeros when they lie in one connected component of a k-dimensional Newton leaf. These graphs gain edges as k increases; the zero-dimensional graph is edgeless and the n-dimensional graph is complete. Graph connectivity characterizes whether all zeros can be explored through a finite chain of leaf components, while disconnection rules out one Newton-trajectory component containing every zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(\Gamma^k)=\operatorname{Zero}(F,B),\quad \{u,v\}\in E(\Gamma^k)\iff u\neq v\text{ and }u,v\text{ share a component of a }k\text{-Newton leaf}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Positive Definiteness Ensures Newton-Leaf Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient matrix condition for connectivity of a k-Newton leaf on \mathbb{R}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal{F}_V(F,\mathbb{R}^n) be a k\text{-Newton leaf for }F, and let A_V be a matrix associated with V. If the (n-k)\times(n-k) matrix A_V\,DF(x)\,DF(x)^t\,A_V^t is uniformly positive definite on \mathbb{R}^n, then \mathcal{F}_V(F,\mathbb{R}^n) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-Newton leaf of F on R^n is connected if the associated (n-k)-by-(n-k) matrix A_V DF(x) DF(x)^T A_V^T is uniformly positive definite on R^n.
assumptions_latex: A_V\text{ is a matrix associated with }V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal{F}_V(F,\mathbb{R}^n)\text{ is connected}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The final fixed-point assertion is retained in its open-set and closure variants, resolving the extract's damaged parenthetical syntax by its explicit respective wording.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let U\subset\mathbb R^n be bounded and open, and suppose \partial U is contained in a free component of an (n-1)-Newton leaf \mathcal F_V(F,\mathbb R^n). knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Descent Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized descent alternating value-nonincreasing local minimization with attempts at strict interbasin escape.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(y_0\in X\), set \(x_0=\mathcal L(y_0)\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), call \(\mathcal E(x_k)\). If it returns \(y_k\in X\) with \(f(y_k)<f(x_k)\), set \(x_{k+1}=\mathcal L(y_k)\); then \(f(x_{k+1})\leq f(y_k)<f(x_k)\). If it certifies that \(\{z\in X:f(z)<f(x_k)\}=\varnothing\), stop and output \(x_k\) as a global minimizer. If it fails without that certificate, stop or continue according to the prescribed search policy, but regard \(x_k\) only as an uncertified incumbent. Thus generalized descent requires strict improvement between accepted local minima, while global optimality requires a complete escape certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized descent alternates value-nonincreasing local optimization with attempts to enter a strictly better basin. Failure establishes global optimality only when the escape procedure certifies that no lower-valued feasible point exists.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
The local minimization operator \(\mathcal L:X\to X\) returns a local minimizer and satisfies \(f(\mathcal L(y))\leq f(y)\) for every \(y\in X\).

At a local minimizer \(x\), the escape operator \(\mathcal E\) returns either a point \(y\in X\) with \(f(y)<f(x)\), a valid certificate that no such point exists, or an explicitly uncertified failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every successful outer iteration strictly decreases the accepted local-minimum value; global optimality follows only from a valid certificate that no point in \(X\) has value below the incumbent.

notation.meaning: escape operator based at an accepted local minimizer
accepted local minimizer at iteration k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Descent over Finitely Many Local-Minimum Levels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successful-transition bound when generalized descent can accept only finitely many distinct local-minimum objective levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{f(x):x\text{ is an eligible local minimizer}\}\) have \(m<\infty\) distinct values. If each successful generalized-descent transition accepts \(x_{k+1}\) only when \(f(x_{k+1})<f(x_k)\), then any run contains at most \(m-1\) successful transitions. This bound does not imply that an unsuccessful escape attempt is a global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only m eligible local-minimum levels, strict generalized descent can make at most m minus one successful transitions; an ensuing failed escape is still uncertified unless it excludes every lower-valued feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(V=\{f(x):x\text{ is an eligible local minimizer}\}\) has \(m<\infty\) distinct values.

Each of conditions (16), (17), and (18) separately gives the corresponding conclusion for its associated utility subclass.

The penalty must be designed using theoretical analysis or a heuristic safeguard because a poor construction can create false local minima.

children.title: Local-to-Global Transitions
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms governing movement from local improvement into broader exploration.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in X\) is a local minimizer returned by a local solver.
The escape test is complete for the strict sublevel set below \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition from local to global status occurs exactly when the strict lower sublevel set is empty: \(S_x=\varnothing\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in X}f(z)\).

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Local, Global, epsilon-Global Minima p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S_x=\{z\in X:f(z)<f(x)\}\). Then \[x\in X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in X}f(z)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S_x=\varnothing.\] Hence an escape procedure converts the local conclusion at \(x\) into a global conclusion precisely when it searches \(S_x\) completely and certifies emptiness. More generally, if it certifies \(f(z)\geq f(x)-\varepsilon\) for every \(z\in X\), then \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-global, meaning \(f(x)\leq\min_{z\in X}f(z)+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer becomes globally certified exactly when no feasible point has lower value; excluding values more than epsilon lower yields epsilon-global certification.

children.title: Trajectory Stagnation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Path structures that trap or stall trajectory-based global search.

assumptions_latex: The trajectory rule generates trial points only in a subset \(R\subseteq X\).
A better basin contains a nonempty relatively open set \(V\subseteq X\setminus\overline R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No generated trajectory point enters \(V\); therefore a local solver launched only from the trajectory cannot discover the better minimizer in that basin.

notation.meaning: reachable set of the trajectory rule
unreached portion of an improving attraction basin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability failure causing deterministic transformed trajectories to miss improving basins.

source_refs.locator: 3. Methods of Generalized Descent p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every trial point generated from the incumbent \(x^c\) lie in \(R\), and suppose \(V\subseteq X\setminus\overline R\) lies in the attraction basin of a local minimizer \(x^b\) with \(f(x^b)<f(x^c)\). Then no trajectory launch belongs to \(V\), so repeated local searches restricted to those launches cannot reach \(x^b\) through \(V\). Stagnation may therefore occur even when objective values along the generated path decrease locally. A global convergence claim requires a reachability, density, exhaustive-restart, or valid lower-bound condition that rules out such hidden improving basins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trajectory stagnates globally when its reachable set misses an open part of every route into a better basin, even if it continues making local progress.
knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory Stagnation Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Methods of Generalized Descent p. 53

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Missing one relatively open subset V of an attraction basin does not prevent other reachable launches from entering the same basin and finding its minimizer. A valid failure result needs the whole relevant launch region or every route into the improving basin to be unreachable, with a direct supporting locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Detection of an integral-path tangent bifurcation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric and spectral diagnostic for tangent bifurcations in global terrain paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Along an integral path, monitor Gauss curvature and compare the path-flow direction with the tangent subspace of the level sets. Decreasing Gauss curvature together with collinearity of the flow and tangent subspace identifies a tangent bifurcation. It generally appears as a jump to a distant point on a neighboring level curve; between the two points, the constrained minimum defining the path is degenerate and \(H\) has repeated eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent bifurcation is detected by decreasing Gauss curvature and collinearity between the integral-path flow and the level-set tangent subspace. It typically produces a jump to a distant point on a neighboring level curve, with a degenerate path-defining constrained minimum and repeated eigenvalues of H between the points.
assumptions_latex: \text{Points are followed along an integral path with level-set tangent subspaces.}
\text{Gauss curvature, path-flow vectors, and the eigenvalues of }H\text{ are monitored.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\text{Gauss curvature decreases}\bigr)\land\bigl(\text{path flow is collinear with the level-set tangent subspace}\bigr)\Longrightarrow\text{a tangent bifurcation is detected.}

children.title: Homotopy Global Methods
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for parameterized continuation approaches to global search.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regular continuation path can be followed to a zero of \(H(\cdot,1)\), but global optimization additionally requires an endpoint-selection or exhaustive-path condition linking terminal zeros to global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic regular continuation scheme; the intended global-selection mechanism remains source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \((x_0,\lambda_0)=(x_0,0)\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), predict a point on the solution manifold \(H(x,\lambda)=0\) using a tangent satisfying \(D_xH\,\dot x+D_\lambda H\,\dot\lambda=0\), then correct it by solving \(H(x_{k+1},\lambda_{k+1})=0\). Adapt the step size and continue until \(\lambda_{k+1}=1\). If \(D_xH(x(\lambda),\lambda)\) is nonsingular along the path, local continuation is well-defined. Output a terminal point only after applying the method's prescribed rule for selecting globally minimizing endpoints or exhausting all relevant paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homotopy methods track solutions from an easy parameter value to the target problem; regular tracking alone does not ensure that the selected endpoint is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Homotopy Global Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when two fixed points of a self-map belong to the same fixed-point class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological definition underlying homotopy-based continuation methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces, let $I=[0,1]$, and let $f,g:X\to Y$ be continuous maps. The maps $f$ and $g$ are homotopic if there exists a continuous map $H:X\times I\to Y$ such that $H(x,0)=f(x)$ and $H(x,1)=g(x)$ for every $x\in X$. The map $H$ is called a homotopy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let X and Y be topological spaces, let I be the unit interval, and let f and g be continuous maps from X to Y. The maps are homotopic if there is a continuous map H from X × I to Y with H(x, 0) = f(x) and H(x, 1) = g(x) for every x in X. Such a map H is called a homotopy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\simeq g\iff \exists H:X\times I\to Y\text{ continuous such that }\forall x\in X,\ H(x,0)=f(x)\ \text{and}\ H(x,1)=g(x).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-started continuation for finding a fixed point of a smooth map from the closure of a compact convex domain into its interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded, open, and convex, let \(\overline D\) be compact, and suppose \(\partial D\) consists of finitely many smooth hypersurfaces. Let \(f:\overline D\to D\) have continuous first and second derivatives, and set \(C=\{x\in\overline D:f(x)=x\}\). For \(x\notin C\), let \(H(x)\) be the point where the ray from \(f(x)\) through \(x\) meets \(\partial D\). Starting from a regular point \(x^0\in\partial D\), follow the component of \(H^{-1}(x^0)\) containing \(x^0\). Along this component, where \(\operatorname{rank}H'(x)=n-1\), select \(z(x)\ne0\) with \(H'(x)z(x)=0\) and track \(x'(t)=z(x(t))\), \(x(0)=x^0\). The continuation curve satisfies \(H(x(t))=x^0\), cannot meet \(\partial D\) at a point other than \(x^0\), and contains a fixed point of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct the radial boundary map associated with f and, from a regular boundary point, track the corresponding level-set component using a null direction of its derivative. Under the stated smoothness and rank conditions, this continuation curve cannot return to another boundary point and contains a fixed point of f.
assumptions_latex: D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is bounded, open, and convex}
\partial D\text{ consists of finitely many smooth hypersurfaces}
f:\overline D\to D\text{ has continuous first and second derivatives}
x^0\in\partial D\text{ is regular for the followed level set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(x(t))=x^0,\quad x'(t)=z(x(t)),\quad H'(x)z(x)=0,\quad x(0)=x^0,\quad \text{and the continuation curve contains some }x^*\text{ with }f(x^*)=x^*

children.title: Local-Minimum Escape Transformations
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for transformations designed to escape known local minima.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers both the unconstrained annealing diffusion and its projected barrier specialization for minimizing over Ax=b and x>0.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(x\ge 0\), assume \(A\) has full row rank and set \(P=I-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A\). Starting from an equality-feasible point, evolve, for fixed \(\mu>0\), the diffusion
\[dX(t)=P[-\nabla f(X(t))+\mu X(t)^{-1}]\,dt+\sqrt{2T(t)}P\,dB(t),\]
where \((X^{-1})_i=1/X_i\), and progressively reduce \(\mu\) after sufficiently long evolution periods. The projection makes the drift and noise tangent to \(Ax=b\), the barrier term addresses positivity, and the cooling noise permits escape from local minima. For the unconstrained diffusion \(dX=-\nabla f(X)dt+\sqrt{2T(t)}dB(t)\), under appropriate conditions on \(f\) and \(T\), its transition law converges as \(t\to\infty\) to a probability measure supported on the global minimizers; the projected barrier scheme is asserted to reach a global minimum under its corresponding conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank equality matrix, project gradient, barrier, and Brownian dynamics onto the null space of the constraints. Run the diffusion at a fixed positive barrier parameter, then reduce that parameter and repeat. Projection preserves an initially satisfied equality constraint, the barrier handles positivity, and cooling noise helps escape local minima. Under appropriate objective and cooling conditions, the unconstrained annealing diffusion has a limiting law supported on global minimizers; the constrained projected scheme has the analogous stated global-convergence guarantee under its corresponding conditions.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\text{ has full row rank}
B(t)\text{ is standard Brownian motion in }\mathbb{R}^n
T(t)\ge 0\text{ satisfies the appropriate cooling conditions}
f\text{ satisfies the appropriate regularity and global-convergence conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: AX(t)=b\text{ along the projected dynamics, and under the stated appropriate conditions the annealing limit is supported on }\operatorname*{argmin}f\text{ (with the projected barrier continuation asserted to approach a constrained global minimizer).

children.title: Tunneling Transformations
children.top_down_role: Landscape transformations designed to move search beyond a known local minimizer.

assumptions_latex: The transformed search excludes \(x^c\) and points where \(f(x)=f(x^c)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every negative value of \(T_p\) identifies a point strictly better than \(x^c\); thus minimizing the transform can provide an escape from the incumbent level set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pole-based tunneling transform for detecting points below an incumbent local-minimum level.

source_refs.locator: 3. Methods of Generalized Descent p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\setminus\{x^c\}\) with \(f(x)\neq f(x^c)\), define \[T_p(x;x^c)=\frac{f(x)-f(x^c)}{\lVert x-x^c\rVert^p}.\] Because the denominator is positive, \(T_p(x;x^c)<0\) if and only if \(f(x)<f(x^c)\). Consequently, any feasible point with negative transformed value is a directly verifiable escape point. The pole at \(x^c\) discourages return to the incumbent, while the transformation preserves the sign of improvement; it does not by itself guarantee that a local minimization of \(T_p\) will find a negative value when one exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pole-based transform has negative value exactly at points better than the current local minimizer, so finding a negative transformed value certifies an escape.
knowledge_statements.title: Tunneling Transformations

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Methods of Generalized Descent p. 53

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign equivalence of the displayed quotient is elementary, but calling the singularity a pole that discourages return is not valid for every p>0; its limiting behavior depends on p and the local growth of f. The specific tunneling transformation and admissible exponent require direct source confirmation.

children.title: Filled-Function Transformations
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-landscape families designed to suppress attraction to known local minima.

assumptions_latex: \(x^c\) is a nonglobal local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local minimization of a filled function cannot terminate at a nonincumbent point in the old basin and, when it reaches a point below the incumbent level, supplies an escape start for minimizing \(f\).

notation.meaning: attraction basin of the incumbent under the fixed local solver
filled function based at the incumbent
strict lower sublevel set of the incumbent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational filled-function definition relative to a fixed local solver and incumbent basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B(x^c)\) be the attraction basin of \(x^c\) for a fixed local solver and let \(S_{x^c}=\{x\in X:f(x)<f(x^c)\}\). A function \(P(\cdot;x^c):X\to\mathbb{R}\) is a filled function at \(x^c\) if \(x^c\) is a strict local maximizer of \(P\), \(P\) has no local minimizer in \(B(x^c)\setminus\{x^c\}\), and every local minimizer of \(P\) reachable from a descent launch outside the incumbent satisfies or leads to \(S_{x^c}\). The transformation fills the incumbent basin while preserving an avenue toward a strictly lower objective level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A filled function turns the current minimizer into a local maximum, removes competing minima from its basin, and directs transformed descent toward a lower objective level.
knowledge_statements.title: Filled-Function Transformations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Filled-function definitions impose source-dependent properties, and the clause that every reachable local minimizer 'satisfies or leads to' the lower sublevel set is not mathematically defined. A direct definition or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Escape-Basin Selection
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing which neighboring basins become reachable.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact and partitioned into attraction basins for a fixed deterministic local solver.
A finite candidate set \(Y_k\subset X\) and valid basin lower estimates are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Discarding only basins whose valid lower estimate is at least \(f(x^c)\) preserves every improving basin; fair selection among the remaining candidates eventually launches in each represented improving basin.

notation.meaning: finite candidate launch set at iteration k
estimated or identified basin containing y
valid lower estimate for a basin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fair basin selection using valid lower estimates and transformed candidate launches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), remove every \(y\in Y_k\) whose basin is already explored or satisfies \(L(B(y))\geq f(x^c)\). From the remaining candidates select \[y_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y_k}L(B(y)),\] breaking ties by a fair rule. Apply the local solver at \(y_k\); if it returns \(x^{\mathrm{new}}\) with \(f(x^{\mathrm{new}})<f(x^c)\), replace the incumbent. Mark \(B(y_k)\) explored and augment \(Y_k\) using the prescribed escape transformation. Stop globally only when every unvisited basin has a valid lower estimate at least \(f(x^c)\); otherwise return an uncertified incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select an unexplored basin with the best valid lower estimate, launch local search there, and certify globality only after all remaining basin bounds exceed the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Escape-Basin Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed algorithm assumes identifiable attraction basins and valid lower bounds for each basin, neither of which is defined or sourced. Its fairness and eventual-coverage conclusion also requires a precise rule governing candidate-set augmentation and basin representation.

children.title: Transformation Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where transformed landscapes fail to reveal useful escape directions.

assumptions_latex: A local escape transformation is searched only inside a neighborhood contained in the attraction basin of the right-hand local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformation may certify no local escape while the left-hand local minimizer has strictly smaller objective value; hence incomplete transformed search cannot certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete double-well failure caused by restricting transformed search to the incumbent basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sufficiently small \(\delta>0\), the tilted double-well function \(f(x)=(x^2-1)^2+\delta x\) has two strict local minimizers \(x_L<0<x_R\), with \(f(x_L)<f(x_R)\). Let a tunneling or filled-function subproblem be solved only on a closed neighborhood \(N_R\) contained in the attraction basin of \(x_R\) and disjoint from the strict sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)<f(x_R)\}\). Then no transformed trial restricted to \(N_R\) can reveal \(x_L\), although \(x_R\) is nonglobal. Failure of this restricted transformation therefore supplies no global certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tilted double well defeats an escape transformation confined to the worse well: local failure to escape does not exclude a better minimum elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Transformation Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tilted double well does exhibit two unequal local minima for a suitable explicit range of delta, but that range is not stated and the claimed behavior is not tied to a defined tunneling or filled-function transformation. A direct source or a transformation-specific formulation is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the subenergy component of a TRUST tunneling transformation relative to a fixed reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed reference point \(\bar x^*\), let \(\widehat f(\bar x)=f(\bar x)-f(\bar x^*)\). The subenergy tunneling transformation is
\[
E_{\mathrm{sub}}(\bar x,\bar x^*)=\log\!\left(\frac{1}{1+\exp\!\left(-\bigl(\widehat f(\bar x)+a\bigr)\right)}\right).
\]
The constant \(a\) affects the asymptotic behavior of the transformation but not its monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed reference point x*, subtract f(x*) from f(x), apply the displayed logistic-logarithmic transformation, and denote the result by the subenergy tunneling transformation. The constant a changes its asymptotic behavior but not its monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E_{\mathrm{sub}}(\bar x,\bar x^*)=\log\!\left(\frac{1}{1+\exp\!\left(-\bigl(\widehat f(\bar x)+a\bigr)\right)}\right),\quad a\text{ changes asymptotics but not monotonicity}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basin-hopping transformation and preservation of the global minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The minimum notation denotes performing local energy minimization from the specified starting configuration, not taking a pointwise minimum over an independently specified set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be an energy landscape and let \(L(x)\) denote the local minimum reached by an energy minimization initialized at \(x\). The basin-hopping transformation is \(\widetilde E(x)=E(L(x))\). It is constant on each basin of attraction \(B_m=\{x\in X:L(x)=m\}\), producing plateaus indexed by local minima, and it preserves the underlying global minimum: \(\min_{x\in X}\widetilde E(x)=\min_{x\in X}E(x)\), with globally minimal plateaus corresponding to basins whose associated minimum is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign to every starting configuration the energy of the local minimum reached by local minimization. The transformed landscape is constant over each basin of attraction, forming interpenetrating staircase-like plateaus. Its lowest plateau value equals the original global minimum value, and the associated underlying minimum remains globally optimal.
assumptions_latex: L(x)\text{ is the local minimum returned by energy minimization initialized at }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde E(x)=E(L(x)),\quad \widetilde E\vert_{B_m}=E(m),\quad \min_{x\in X}\widetilde E(x)=\min_{x\in X}E(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tabu search with adaptive search memory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General tabu-search mechanism, not restricted to SAT or constraint-programming search.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible monotone-selection recursion with possibly adaptive sampling and a persistent positive-measure coverage condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose $x_0\in A$ and set $k=0$. At iteration $k$, generate $\xi_k$ according to $P_k$ on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B)$, set
\[
x_{k+1}=D(x_k,\xi_k),
\]
choose $P_{k+1}$, and continue. Here $D:A\times\mathbb R^n\to A$ satisfies
\[
f(D(x,\xi))\le f(x),\qquad \xi\in A\Longrightarrow f(D(x,\xi))\le f(\xi).\tag{H1}
\]
For adaptive sampling, $P_k$ may be the conditional distribution, given $\sigma_{k-1}$, of a $\sigma_k$-measurable trial vector. The coverage condition is that, almost surely, every Borel set $B\subset A$ with $\mu(B)>0$ satisfies
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-P_k(B))=0.\tag{H2}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible point, sample a trial vector, use D to select a feasible point no worse than the incumbent and, when the trial is feasible, no worse than the trial, then update the sampling distribution. The distributions may depend on past search information. Every positive-measure Borel subset of the feasible region must have zero probability of being missed at every iteration forever.
assumptions_latex: f(D(x,\xi))\le f(x)\text{ and }\bigl[\xi\in A\Rightarrow f(D(x,\xi))\le f(\xi)\bigr].
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}=D(x_k,\xi_k)\in A,\quad f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k),\quad k\ge0,\text{ with condition (H2) imposing persistent coverage.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Divergent local sampling mass implies almost-sure recurrent near-optimal visits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The lower sampling-probability bound is uniform over all possible preceding sampled points and objective observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(f\) has finitely many global minimizers, let \(x_*\) be a global minimizer with \(m=f(x_*)\), and suppose \(f\) is continuous in a neighborhood of \(x_*\). Define \(B_A(x_*,\varepsilon)=\{x\in A:\|x-x_*\|\le\varepsilon\}\) and let \(q_j(\varepsilon)\) be the infimum of \(P_j(B_A(x_*,\varepsilon))\) over all possible preceding sampled points and corresponding objective evaluations. If \(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}q_j(\varepsilon)=\infty\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), then, for every \(\delta>0\), \(\mathbb P\bigl(x_j\in W(\delta)\ \mathrm{infinitely\ often}\bigr)=1\), where \(W(\delta)=\{x\in A:f(x)-m\le\delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suppose the objective has finitely many global minimizers and is continuous near a chosen minimizer. If, for every radius, the sampling probabilities of the corresponding feasible neighborhood have history-uniform lower bounds whose sum diverges, then with probability one the random-search sequence enters every positive near-optimal level set infinitely often.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is continuous in a neighborhood of }x_*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\delta>0:\quad \mathbb P\!\left(x_j\in\{x\in A:f(x)-m\le\delta\}\ \mathrm{i.o.}\right)=1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-sure recurrence near a level set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional progress-or-approach criterion for stochastic search sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $C=\{x:f(x)=\alpha\}\ne\varnothing$, let $\rho(x,C)=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|$, and for fixed $\delta>0$ define
\[
F_k=\{\rho(x_k,C)\ge\delta\},\qquad
A_k=\{f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)-\varepsilon\}.
\]
Suppose that for every $\delta>0$ there exist $\varepsilon(\delta)>0$ and numbers $p_k(\delta)\in[0,1]$ such that, for all $0\le m\le k$,
\[
P\!\left(A_k\cup\overline F_k\,\middle|\,\bigcap_{j=m}^{k-1}(\overline A_j\cap F_j)\right)\ge p_k,
\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}p_k=\infty.
\]
Then
\[
P\!\left(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\rho(x_k,C)=0\right)=1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let C be a nonempty objective level set. If, whenever the iterates have remained at least delta away from C without achieving an epsilon objective decrease, the next step has conditional probability at least p_k of either making that decrease or coming within delta of C, and the p_k values have divergent sum, then almost surely the iterates approach C arbitrarily closely along a subsequence.
assumptions_latex: \forall\delta>0\ \exists\varepsilon(\delta)>0,\ p_k(\delta)\in[0,1]\text{ satisfying the stated conditional lower bound for all }0\le m\le k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\left\{\liminf_{k\to\infty}\rho(x_k,C)=0\right\}=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Divergent conditional hitting probabilities imply optimal-region convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient history-dependent hitting condition for a random-search sequence in the preceding framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the random-search sequence and optimality region $R_{\varepsilon,M}$, define
\[
\alpha_k(R_{\varepsilon,M})=
\inf_{\substack{x_i\in A\setminus R_{\varepsilon,M}\\ i=1,\ldots,k-1}}
P_k\bigl(R_{\varepsilon,M}\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}\bigr).
\]
If
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_k(R_{\varepsilon,M})=\infty,
\]
then
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}P\{x_k\in R_{\varepsilon,M}\}=1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each iteration, take the infimum of the conditional probability of hitting the optimality region over histories whose preceding points all remain outside that region. If the sum of these worst-case conditional hitting probabilities diverges, then the probability that the kth point lies in the optimality region tends to one.
assumptions_latex: (x_k)\text{ is the random-search sequence in the surrounding framework}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{k\to\infty}P\{x_k\in R_{\varepsilon,M}\}=1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cluster-directed random-search procedure; the extract supplies no convergence or global-optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To minimize \(f\) over \(A\), randomly sample \(N^*\) trial points throughout \(A\), retain a prescribed number \(M\) having the lowest observed objective values, cluster the retained points, rank the clusters by their lowest objective values, and construct a subregion \(A_j\) containing the retained points of each cluster. Repeat these operations within the subregions in rank order, optionally considering only the best few clusters. A prescribed objective-value bound may be used to stop further improvement attempts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the whole region randomly, retain the best M observations, cluster and rank them, form a subregion for each cluster, and recursively repeat the process in selected subregions. The search may consider only the best few clusters or stop at a prescribed objective threshold; no convergence guarantee is stated.
assumptions_latex: N^*\text{ trial points are sampled randomly in }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Sampling is recursively redirected toward subregions associated with the best observed clusters.}
