knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-Set Sandwich and Equality Under Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the previously defined sets $W(\varepsilon)$ and $M_r$ from the Markov monotonous-search analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set $\Delta=\Delta(\varepsilon)=\sup\{\rho(x,x_*):x\in W(\varepsilon)\}$. Then $\bigcup_{0<r<\Delta}M_r\subset W(\varepsilon)\subset M_\Delta\subset B_\Delta(x_*)$. If $f$ is continuous on $B_\Delta(x_*)$ and $\Delta<\operatorname{diam}(A)$, then $W(\varepsilon)=M_\Delta$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let Delta be the greatest distance from the optimizer among points in the specified objective region. The union of all comparison sets with radius below Delta lies inside that region, which lies inside the radius-Delta comparison set and hence inside the closed Delta-ball. If the objective is continuous throughout that ball and Delta is smaller than the domain diameter, the objective region equals the radius-Delta comparison set.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the equality conclusion, }f\text{ is continuous on }B_\Delta(x_*)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcup_{0<r<\Delta}M_r\subset W(\varepsilon)\subset M_\Delta\subset B_\Delta(x_*),\qquad f\in C(B_\Delta(x_*)),\ \Delta<\operatorname{diam}(A)\implies W(\varepsilon)=M_\Delta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Baseline feasible-set and objective assumptions for global random search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A collected assumption regime; individual results may use only a subset or replace C4 by the stronger uniform condition C4'.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x\in A}f(x)\), assume the finite value \(m=\min_{x\in A}f(x)\) is attained, possibly at multiple points. A common regime is: (C1) \(A\subset\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge1\), is closed and bounded; (C2) \(0<\operatorname{vol}(A)<\infty\); (C3) \(A\) is a finite union of sets defined by finitely many inequalities \(g_i(x)\le0\) with continuously differentiable \(g_i\); (C4) for some minimizer \(x_*\), constants \(c>0,\varepsilon_0>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{vol}(A\cap B(x_*,\varepsilon))\ge c\varepsilon^d\) for every \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\); (C5) sampling from distributions on \(A\) and relevant subsets has acceptable complexity; (C6) \(f\) is exactly evaluable on \(A\); (C7) the set of minimizers is finite, sometimes additionally a singleton; (C8) \(f\) is bounded and piecewise continuous on \(A\); and (C9) for some \(\delta_0>0\), every \(W(\delta)=\{x\in A:f(x)\le m+\delta\}\), \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), is closed and \(f\) is continuous on \(W(\delta_0)\). Neither convexity nor connectedness of \(A\) is required. The stronger substitute (C4') requires \(\operatorname{vol}(A\cap B(x,\varepsilon))\ge c\varepsilon^d\) for every \(x\in A\) and \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\). Continuity of \(f\) on \(A\), together with C1, implies C8 and C9.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimizing an attained objective over a feasible subset of Euclidean space, a standard random-search regime assumes a compact positive-volume feasible set with regular finite-inequality geometry, nonvanishing feasible volume near at least one minimizer, tractable sampling, exact evaluations, finitely many minimizers, and bounded piecewise continuity plus continuity and closedness near the optimal level. The feasible set need not be convex or connected. A stronger boundary-thickness condition may be imposed uniformly at every feasible point, and global continuity on the compact feasible set implies the two objective-regularity conditions.
assumptions_latex: d\ge1,\quad A\subset\mathbb R^d,\quad m=\min_{x\in A}f(x)\text{ is attained}
\text{Conditions C1--C9 as stated, with C4 optionally replaced by C4'}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These conditions define the baseline regularity regime for the ensuing global random-search analysis.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concentration of the adaptive sampling distribution at a unique minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional convergence for the stated population-limit update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(x^*\) is the unique global minimum point and \(f\) is continuous at \(x^*\). For \(N_k\to\infty\), define
\[
R_{k+1}(dx)=\frac{\int_A R_k(dy)f(y)Q(y,dx)}{\int_A R_k(dy)f(y)}.
\]
Then, as \(k\to\infty\), the unconditional distribution of \(\xi_{kj}\) converges to the distribution concentrated at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the objective has a unique global minimum point and is continuous there, the population-limit adaptive sampling distribution converges to a point mass at that point.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is the unique global minimum point}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Law}(\xi_{kj})\longrightarrow\delta_{x^*}\quad\text{as }k\to\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variable neighborhood search with local descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized variable-neighborhood search using ordered neighborhoods and improvement-triggered reset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a random initial point and apply local descent to obtain a local minimizer \(x^*\). Set \(k=1\). While \(k\le k_{\max}\), define \(N_k(x^*)\), sample \(\widetilde x\in N_k(x^*)\), and apply local descent from \(\widetilde x\) to obtain a local minimizer \(x'\). If \(x'\) is better than \(x^*\), set \(x^*\leftarrow x'\) and \(k\leftarrow1\); otherwise set \(k\leftarrow k+1\). Terminate when \(k>k_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin from a locally minimized random point. Sample and locally minimize points from an ordered sequence of neighborhoods around the incumbent. Improvement replaces the incumbent and resets the neighborhood index; failure advances it. Stop when every prescribed neighborhood level has failed consecutively.
assumptions_latex: \text{local descent produces a local minimizer from each sampled start}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm terminates when }k>k_{\max}\text{ and returns the incumbent local minimizer }x^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower hitting-time bounds for symmetric Markov monotonous search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-dependent lower bounds under condition F1 and the maximum metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a symmetric Markov monotonous search, set
\[
\tau'_\varepsilon=\min\{n\ge1:x_n\in B_\varepsilon(x_*)\},\qquad n'(x,\varepsilon,\gamma)=\min\{n\ge1:\mathbb P_x(x_n\in B_\varepsilon(x_*))\ge\gamma\},
\]
and let $D=\rho(x,x_*)$. Assume that $f$ satisfies F1 and $\rho=\rho_\infty$. If $A=\mathbb R^d$ and $\varepsilon<D$, or if $A=\mathbb I^d$ and $\varepsilon<D\le1/4$, then
\[
\mathbb E_x\tau_\varepsilon\ge\mathbb E_x\tau'_\varepsilon\ge\ln(D/\varepsilon)+2,
\]
\[
n(x,\varepsilon,\gamma)\ge n'(x,\varepsilon,\gamma)\ge\gamma\bigl(\ln(D/\varepsilon)+2\bigr).
\]
If $A=\mathbb I^d$ and $\varepsilon<1/4<D$, then
\[
\mathbb E_x\tau_\varepsilon\ge\mathbb E_x\tau'_\varepsilon\ge\ln(\sqrt D/\varepsilon)+1-\ln2,
\]
\[
n(x,\varepsilon,\gamma)\ge n'(x,\varepsilon,\gamma)\ge\gamma\bigl(\ln(\sqrt D/\varepsilon)+1-\ln2\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under F1 and the maximum metric, a symmetric Markov monotonous search obeys logarithmic lower bounds on expected hitting time and confidence time. The formula depends on whether the search is on Euclidean space or in the near- or far-distance regime of the unit cube.
assumptions_latex: \text{The search is Markov monotonous and symmetric}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_x\tau_\varepsilon\ge\mathbb E_x\tau'_\varepsilon\text{ and }n(x,\varepsilon,\gamma)\ge n'(x,\varepsilon,\gamma)\text{ with the stated domain-dependent bounds}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conceptual adaptive random-search algorithm and its stated practical kernel realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(f(x)<0\) for every \(x\in A\). Choose \(P_0\), and at iteration \(k\) draw \(\xi_{k1},\ldots,\xi_{kN_k}\) from \(P_k\). After evaluating the objective, update
\[
P_{k+1}(dx)=\sum_{j=1}^{N_k}\frac{|f(\xi_{kj})|}{\sum_{t=1}^{N_k}|f(\xi_{kt})|}Q_k(\xi_{kj},dx).
\]
The stated practical kernels have the form
\[
Q_k(y,dx)=c_k(y)\beta_k^{-n}\varphi\!\left(\beta_k^{-1}(x-y)\right)\mu(dx),
\]
where \(c_k(y)\) normalizes the kernel on \(A\), \(\beta_k>0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\beta_k<\infty\), and \(\varphi\) is a continuous symmetric finite density on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, sample from the current distribution and form the next distribution as an objective-magnitude-weighted mixture of localized kernels centered at the sampled points. The stated kernels are normalized on the domain and have summable positive bandwidths.
assumptions_latex: \varphi\text{ is a continuous symmetric finite density on }\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{k+1}(dx)=\sum_{j=1}^{N_k}\frac{|f(\xi_{kj})|}{\sum_{t=1}^{N_k}|f(\xi_{kt})|}Q_k(\xi_{kj},dx)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the metric domains and ball-volume facts used for Markov monotonous search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization space is a pair $(A,\rho)$ consisting of a feasible region and a metric. For $A=\mathbb R^d$, let $\rho=\rho_p$ be the usual $\ell_p$ metric, $1\le p\le\infty$. For $A=\mathbb I^d=[0,1)^d$, replace each coordinate distance by $\varrho(s,t)=\min\{|s-t|,1-|s-t|\}$ and aggregate with the corresponding $\ell_p$ norm; then $(\mathbb I^d,\rho_p)$ is the $d$-torus. With $B_\varepsilon(x)=\{y\in A:\rho(x,y)\le\varepsilon\}$, its Lebesgue volume is independent of $x$, and $\varphi(\varepsilon):=\operatorname{vol}(B_\varepsilon(x))=c(d,\rho)\varepsilon^d$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. In $\mathbb R^d$ this equality holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, whereas on the torus $\varphi(\varepsilon)=1$ when $\varepsilon>\operatorname{diam}(A)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimization space is a feasible region equipped with a metric. The relevant spaces are Euclidean space with an l-p metric and the unit cube with wrap-around coordinate distances, which forms a torus. Metric-ball volume is center-independent and equals a metric-dependent constant times the d-th power of the radius for sufficiently small radii; this holds at every radius in Euclidean space, while a torus ball has full volume beyond the diameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vol}(B_\varepsilon(x))\text{ is independent of }x,\qquad \operatorname{vol}(B_\varepsilon(x))=c(d,\rho)\varepsilon^d\text{ for sufficiently small }\varepsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Markov Monotonous Search and Accept-or-Stay Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the method family and a transition-kernel construction that ensures almost-sure objective monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A random sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $A$ is a Markov random search when, for every $n$, the conditional distribution of $x_{n+1}$ given $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ equals its conditional distribution given $x_n$. It is a Markov monotonous search when additionally $f(x_{n+1})\le f(x_n)$ almost surely for every $n$. Let $W_x=\{y\in A:f(y)\le f(x)\}$. Given Markov transition kernels $P_n$, define
\[
R_n(x,\cdot)=\delta_x(\cdot)P_n(x,W_x^c)+P_n(x,\cdot\cap W_x).
\]
Then $R_n(x,W_x)=1$, so a chain governed by these kernels is Markov monotonous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Markov random search chooses its next-point distribution using only the current point. It is Markov monotonous when objective values never increase almost surely. An accept-or-stay kernel achieves this by accepting a proposal no worse than the current point and otherwise retaining the current point.
assumptions_latex: P_n(x,\cdot)\text{ is a probability measure for every }n\ge 1\text{ and }x\in A
P_n(\cdot,U)\text{ is Borel measurable for every Borel set }U
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_n(x,W_x)=1,\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(f(x_{n+1})\le f(x_n)\right)=1\quad\text{for every }n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solis–Wets convergence to an optimality region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of optimality-region membership probabilities under monotone selection and persistent coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f$ be measurable, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be measurable, and let $(x_k)$ be generated by the Solis–Wets framework. Suppose
\[
f(D(x,\xi))\le f(x),\qquad \xi\in A\Longrightarrow f(D(x,\xi))\le f(\xi),\tag{H1}
\]
and, almost surely, for every Borel set $B\subset A$ with $\mu(B)>0$,
\[
\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-P_k(B))=0.\tag{H2}
\]
Then, for the optimality region $R_{\varepsilon,M}$ defined using the essential infimum,
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}P\{x_k\in R_{\varepsilon,M}\}=1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a measurable objective and measurable feasible region, a sequence generated by the Solis–Wets framework has probability tending to one of lying in the prescribed essential-infimum optimality region, provided its selection rule is monotone and its sampling distributions cannot miss any positive-measure Borel subset forever.
assumptions_latex: (x_k)\text{ is generated by the Solis--Wets framework}.
f(D(x,\xi))\le f(x)\text{ and }\bigl[\xi\in A\Rightarrow f(D(x,\xi))\le f(\xi)\bigr].
R_{\varepsilon,M}\text{ is the preceding essential-infimum optimality region}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{k\to\infty}P\{x_k\in R_{\varepsilon,M}\}=1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the adaptive random sampling and stopping structure of global random search; the listed convergence modes are possible forms of analysis, not automatic guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A global random-search algorithm generates random observation points $(x_j)_{j\ge 1}$, with $x_j\sim P_j$. For $j\ge 2$, $P_j$ may depend on $x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1}$ and on their possibly noisy objective-function evaluations. The stopping index $N\in\{1,2,\ldots,\infty\}$ may be deterministic or random and may depend on observed evaluations. Since the observation points are random, a convergence result for a particular algorithm may be formulated as almost-sure convergence, convergence in probability, or a confidence-qualified guarantee with probability at least $1-\gamma$, where $\gamma>0$; the extract does not assert that every such algorithm converges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global random-search algorithm uses random decisions to select observation points. Later sampling distributions may adapt to earlier points and possibly noisy evaluations, and stopping may be deterministic or random and data-dependent. Depending on the algorithm and assumptions, convergence results may be almost sure, in probability, or confidence-qualified; convergence is not guaranteed merely by this definition.
assumptions_latex: P_j\text{ may depend on }x_1,\ldots,x_{j-1}\text{ and their observed objective values for }j\ge 2
N\in\{1,2,\ldots,\infty\}\text{ may be deterministic or random and evaluation-dependent}
\gamma>0\text{ when a confidence-qualified convergence statement is made}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The scheme is a global random-search method; any established convergence result may use almost-sure, in-probability, or confidence-qualified language.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon accept-or-stay Markov search and its symmetric radial proposal specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $x_1=x$. For $n=1,\ldots,N-1$, sample $\eta\sim P_n(x_n,\cdot)$ and set $x_{n+1}=\eta$ if $f(\eta)\le f(x_n)$, otherwise set $x_{n+1}=x_n$. The method is called Markov symmetric monotonous search when $P_n(x,dy)$ has a density $p_n(x,y)=g_n(\rho(x,y))$ with $g_n$ nonincreasing. For $A=\mathbb R^d$, such a density must in particular satisfy $\int_0^\infty r^{d-1}g_n(r)\,dr<\infty$. The radial form is translation invariant in $\mathbb R^d$ and invariant under coordinatewise addition modulo $1$ on $\mathbb I^d$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a given point, repeatedly sample a proposal from the current transition law, accept it if it does not increase the objective, and otherwise stay put. The search is symmetric when each proposal density is a nonincreasing function only of metric distance; in Euclidean space the radial profile must be integrable with the d-dimensional radial weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_{n+1})\le f(x_n)\ \text{for every generated step, and radial proposal densities define the symmetric specialization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: I-optimal density and squared-logarithmic hitting-time bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the optimal radial density under constant asymmetry and records the subsequent unit-cube complexity guarantee under a uniform asymmetry lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume $F^f\equiv F_0>0$. For $A=\mathbb I^d$, let
\[
\delta_1=\min\{\delta(x),\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb I^d)/2\}\le1/4,
\]
and for $A=\mathbb R^d$ let $\delta_1=\delta(x)$. If $\varepsilon<\delta_1/\sqrt[d]{4}$, set
\[
a=2\sqrt[d]{2},\qquad b=\frac{4\delta_1}{a},\qquad \lambda=d\ln(\delta_1/\varepsilon)+2-\ln4.
\]
Then
\[
g^\star(r)=\frac1{c(d,\rho)\lambda}\begin{cases}
(a\varepsilon)^{-d},&0<r\le a\varepsilon,\\
r^{-d},&a\varepsilon<r\le b,\\
b^{-d},&b<r\le2\delta_1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\]
is I-optimal and
\[
I\bigl(\delta(x),\varepsilon;f,g^\star\bigr)=\frac{2^d\lambda^2}{F_0}.
\]
Furthermore, on $\mathbb I^d$, if $\delta(x)$ is known, $F^f(r)\ge F_0>0$ for all $r>0$, $\varepsilon<1/(4\sqrt[d]{4})$, and $\delta_1(x)<1/4$, there exists a corresponding density $g^\star$ such that
\[
\mathbb E_x\tau_\varepsilon\le I\bigl(\delta(x),\varepsilon;f,g^\star\bigr)+1
\le\frac{2^dd^2}{F_0}\ln^2\varepsilon+1
=O(\ln^2\varepsilon)\quad(\varepsilon\to0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the asymmetry coefficient is a positive constant, the I-optimal radial density is constant near zero, proportional to r to the power −d at intermediate radii, constant on a final interval, and zero outside its support; its exact I-value is 2^d lambda squared divided by F0. Under the separate uniform positive-asymmetry assumptions on the unit cube, a suitable density yields an expected hitting time of squared-logarithmic order as epsilon tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: F^f\equiv F_0>0\text{ for the exact I-optimal characterization}
\delta(x)\text{ is known},\ F^f(r)\ge F_0>0\ \forall r>0,\ \varepsilon<1/(4\sqrt[d]{4}),\ \delta_1(x)<1/4\text{ for the unit-cube complexity bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\bigl(\delta(x),\varepsilon;f,g^\star\bigr)=2^d\lambda^2/F_0,\qquad \mathbb E_x\tau_\varepsilon=O(\ln^2\varepsilon)\text{ under the stated respective assumptions}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximization-oriented random search with an incumbent-preserving update map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\mu_n\}_{n\ge0}\) be probability distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\). Choose \(x_0\in S\), draw \(y_{n+1}\sim\mu_n\), and set \(x_{n+1}=D(x_n,y_{n+1})\), where \(D:S\times\mathbb R^d\to S\) satisfies \(f(D(x,y))\ge f(x)\) and, if \(y\in S\), \(f(D(x,y))\ge f(y)\). Then \(\{f(X_n)\}\) is nondecreasing almost surely. If, in addition, \(\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}(1-\mu_n(A))=0\) for every set \(A\) with \(\varphi(A)>0\), then \(f(X_n)\to f^*\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each trial is combined with the incumbent so that the resulting feasible point is no worse than the incumbent and, for feasible trials, no worse than the trial. Objective values are almost surely nondecreasing. Under the stated positive-measure sampling condition, they converge almost surely to the global optimum value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(X_{n+1})\ge f(X_n)\ \text{a.s.},\qquad f(X_n)\to f^*\ \text{a.s. under the coverage condition}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concentration and Stochastic Ordering of Adaptive Search Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(S_\epsilon\) is an \(\epsilon\)-optimal level set for the maximization problem, and \(\varphi\) is the uniform distribution on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\epsilon>0\), the temperature-indexed distribution \(\pi_T\) satisfies \[\lim_{T\downarrow0}\pi_T(S_\epsilon)=1.\] Moreover, for \(T\le T'\), conditional on membership in any level set \(S_\epsilon\), the objective-value distribution induced by \(\pi_T\) stochastically dominates the corresponding distribution induced by \(\pi_{T'}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As temperature tends to zero, the sampling distribution concentrates on every epsilon-optimal set. knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-parent population search using normalized auxiliary weights and transition-kernel mixtures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration $j$, construct a nonnegative auxiliary function $f_j$ using all objective evaluations obtained so far. Provided $\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}f_j(x_i^{(j)})>0$, define $p_l^{(j)}=f_j(x_l^{(j)})/\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}f_j(x_i^{(j)})$ and generate each next-generation point from $P_{j+1}(\cdot)=\sum_{l=1}^{n_j}p_l^{(j)}Q_j(x_l^{(j)},\cdot)$. Under independent mixture sampling, parent $x_l^{(j)}$ is selected $n_{j+1}p_l^{(j)}$ times on average. Selection variability may be reduced by assigning it $\lfloor n_{j+1}p_l^{(j)}\rfloor$ selections and allocating the remaining selections according to the normalized fractional parts.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Modes of convergence for random vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General probability-theoretic definitions and their implication hierarchy, with only contextual relevance to random-search analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(X_i)_{i\ge 1}$ and $X$ be random vectors on $(\Omega,\sigma,P)$ with values in $\mathbb R^n$. Almost-sure convergence is defined by
\[
P\{\omega:\lim_{i\to\infty}X_i(\omega)=X(\omega)\}=1.
\]
Convergence in probability is defined by
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0,\qquad \lim_{i\to\infty}P\{\|X_i-X\|>\varepsilon\}=0.
\]
If $F_i$ and $F$ are the distribution functions of $X_i$ and $X$, convergence in distribution means that $F_i(y)\to F(y)$ at every continuity point $y$ of $F$. Moreover,
\[
X_i\xrightarrow{a.s.}X\Longrightarrow X_i\xrightarrow{P}X\Longrightarrow X_i\xrightarrow{d}X.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-sure convergence means sample-path convergence outside a null set. Convergence in probability means that the probability of an error larger than any fixed positive tolerance tends to zero. Convergence in distribution means convergence of the distribution functions at every continuity point of the limiting distribution. Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution.
assumptions_latex: X_i,X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n\text{ are random vectors on }(\Omega,\sigma,P).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_i\xrightarrow{a.s.}X\Longrightarrow X_i\xrightarrow{P}X\Longrightarrow X_i\xrightarrow{d}X.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed $x$, $\varepsilon$, and $f$, an admissible density $g^\star$ is called I-optimal if it minimizes the integral functional:
\[
g^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{g}I\bigl(\delta(x),\varepsilon;f,g\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed x, target accuracy epsilon, and objective f, an I-optimal density is an admissible search density minimizing the integral functional I.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ ranges over admissible search densities}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{g}I\bigl(\delta(x),\varepsilon;f,g\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected evaluations to hit a target region in stochastic-walk search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniform-sampling hitting time and bounds for uniformly bounded sampling densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu(A)<\infty\), let \(R=R_{\epsilon,M}\), and let Algorithm SW generate trial \(x_k\) according to
\[
P_k(dx\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1})=p_k(x\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1})\mu(dx).
\]
If every \(p_k\) is uniform on \(A\), then the expected number \(K\) of objective evaluations needed to reach \(R\) is
\[
K=\frac{\mu(A)}{\mu(R)}.
\]
If \(0<Q_-\le p_k(x)\le Q_+<\infty\) for all \(x\in A\) and all \(k\), then \(L_-\le K\le L_+\), where
\[
L_- = \frac{\mu(A)}{\mu(R)}+\frac{\mu(A)}{\mu(A\setminus R)}\frac{\beta_-}{1-\beta_+}\left(\frac{1}{\beta_+^2}-1\right),
\]
\[
L_+ = \frac{\mu(A)}{\mu(R)}+\frac{\mu(A)}{\mu(A\setminus R)}\frac{\beta_+}{1-\beta_-}\left(\frac{1}{\beta_-^2}-1\right),
\]
with
\[
\beta_- =\mu(R)\inf_{y\in R,\,x\in A\setminus R}p_k(y-x),\qquad
\beta_+ =\mu(R)\sup_{y\in R,\,x\in A\setminus R}p_k(y-x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite-measure domain, uniform sampling reaches a target region after an expected number of evaluations equal to the domain-to-target measure ratio. For sampling densities bounded above and below, the theorem gives explicit lower and upper bounds in terms of the target measure and extremal transition probabilities.
assumptions_latex: p_k\text{ is uniform on }A\text{ for the exact formula}
0<Q_-\le p_k(x)\le Q_+<\infty\quad\forall x\in A,\ \forall k\text{ for the bounds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=\frac{\mu(A)}{\mu(R_{\epsilon,M})}\quad\text{in the uniform case},\qquad L_-\le K\le L_+\quad\text{in the bounded-density case}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective asymmetry coefficient, asymmetry function, and nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the volume-based asymmetry quantities used in Markov monotonous search and states a local smoothness condition yielding nondegeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $M_r$ and $B_r(x_*)$ be the objective-dependent region and comparison ball used by the search analysis. Define
\[
F^f(r)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}(M_r)}{\operatorname{vol}(B_r(x_*))},\qquad V^f(r)=\operatorname{vol}(M_r)=F^f(r)\operatorname{vol}(B_r(x_*)).
\]
The objective $f$ is called nondegenerate if
\[
\liminf_{r\to0}F^f(r)>0.
\]
If $(A,\rho)$ is $(\mathbb R^d,\rho_2)$ or $(\mathbb I^d,\rho_2)$, $f$ is twice continuously differentiable near $x_*$, and $\nabla^2f(x_*)$ is nonsingular with eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ and $\lambda_{\min}=\min_i\lambda_i>0$, then
\[
\lim_{r\to0}F^f(r)=\sqrt{\prod_{i=1}^d\frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_i}}>0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymmetry coefficient compares the volume of the objective-dependent region with that of a comparison ball, while the asymmetry function is the region's volume. An objective is nondegenerate when the coefficient has a positive lower limit at zero. In Euclidean space or the unit cube, local twice continuous differentiability and the stated positive nonsingular Hessian condition give the displayed positive spectral limit.
assumptions_latex: f\in C^2\text{ in a neighborhood of }x_*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{r\to0}F^f(r)=\sqrt{\prod_{i=1}^d\lambda_{\min}/\lambda_i}>0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A derivative-free randomized population search; the extract does not guarantee that an improving feasible trial will be found or that the procedure converges globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), initialize \(C\) with \(N=25n\) randomly sampled evaluated pairs \((x_i,f_i)\). Repeatedly select a pair \((x_m,f_m)\in C\) having the largest objective value and seek a feasible trial \((x_t,f_t)\) satisfying \(f_t<f_m\). Randomly choose \(R_1,\ldots,R_{n+1}\) from \(C\), let \(x_g\) be the centroid of \(R_1,\ldots,R_n\), and try \(x_t=2x_g-x_{n+1}\). Repeat until a feasible improving trial is obtained; if the cumulative success rate is below \(50\%\), use \(x_t=(x_g+x_{n+1})/2\) instead. Replace the worst pair by the accepted trial and stop when all points in \(C\) are sufficiently close.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize 25n random evaluated points. Repeatedly replace the worst point with a feasible improving point obtained by reflecting one randomly selected point through the centroid of n others, using their midpoint when the cumulative success rate is below 50 percent. Stop when the population is sufficiently concentrated. The extract gives no assurance that a required improving point will be found or that the final cluster is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Every accepted replacement satisfies }x_t\in A\text{ and }f_t<f_m;\text{ if the stopping test is reached, the points of }C\text{ are sufficiently close.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines uniform procedure dominance over a function class and identifies moment-based asymptotic and record-c.d.f. stochastic criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of functions on $A$, and let $\Phi_f(\mathcal P)$ be a criterion oriented so that smaller values are better. Procedure $\mathcal P$ dominates $\mathcal P'$ on $\mathcal F$ if $\Phi_f(\mathcal P)\leq\Phi_f(\mathcal P')$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $\Phi_{f^*}(\mathcal P)<\Phi_{f^*}(\mathcal P')$ for at least one $f^*\in\mathcal F$. For random-search records, the stated comparison criteria are the asymptotic $p$-th moment of $f_*[X]-m$ for fixed $p>0$ and the finite-sample c.d.f. of $f_*[X]$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A procedure dominates another when it is no worse for every objective in the class and strictly better for at least one. Random-search procedures may be compared through asymptotic positive moments of record error or through finite-sample stochastic ordering of record values.
assumptions_latex: $\mathcal F$ is a class of functions on $A$.
$\Phi_f$ is a comparison criterion whose smaller value represents better performance.
For the moment criterion, $p>0$ is fixed and the relevant moments exist.
For record error, $m=\min_{x\in A}f(x)$ is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\succ\mathcal P'\iff\left[(\forall f\in\mathcal F)\ \Phi_f(\mathcal P)\leq\Phi_f(\mathcal P')\right]\land\left[(\exists f^*\in\mathcal F)\ \Phi_{f^*}(\mathcal P)<\Phi_{f^*}(\mathcal P')\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Near-Optimal Hitting Probability and Evaluation Count
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample performance of independent pure random search for a fixed near-optimal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_\varepsilon=\{x:f(x)<f^*+\varepsilon\}\) have sampling probability \(p_\varepsilon=\mu(A_\varepsilon)\). For \(n\) independent draws, \[\Pr\!\left(\min_{1\le i\le n}f(X_i)<f^*+\varepsilon\right)=1-(1-p_\varepsilon)^n.\] If \(0<p_\varepsilon<1\), confidence at least \(1-\alpha\) is attained exactly when \((1-p_\varepsilon)^n\le\alpha\), equivalently \[n\ge\left\lceil\frac{\log\alpha}{\log(1-p_\varepsilon)}\right\rceil.\] The first hitting time has mean \(1/p_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pure random search hits an epsilon-optimal set with probability one minus the corresponding miss probability; expected waiting time is the reciprocal of its sampling mass.
assumptions_latex: \(0<p_\varepsilon<1\) for the displayed finite-count and mean formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(U_n<f^*+\varepsilon)=1-(1-p_\varepsilon)^n,\qquad \mathbb E[\tau_\varepsilon]=p_\varepsilon^{-1}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For points $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in A$ and a convex reference set $B\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, define

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum multivariate spacing is the supremal scale of a translated copy of a convex reference body that fits in the domain without containing any sampled point. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates idealized PAS iterations from implementable evaluation complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: PAS presumes exact sampling from \(\lambda(\cdot\cap R_n)/\lambda(R_n)\). If this is implemented by independent uniform proposals on \(X\) rejected outside \(R_n\), the expected proposals for one accepted update equal \(\lambda(X)/\lambda(R_n)\), which can diverge near the optimum. Logarithmic accepted-iteration bounds therefore do not imply logarithmic evaluation complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PAS's idealized rate assumes an exact improving-region sampler; rejection implementations may have reciprocal-volume evaluation cost.
assumptions_latex: Conditional sampling is implemented by uniform proposals on \(X\) and rejection outside \(R_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected proposals per accepted update equal \(\lambda(X)/\lambda(R_n)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(V(x)=\lambda(\{z:f(z)<f(x)\})/\lambda(X)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Iteration Bound for Pure Adaptive Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected hitting-time bound for maximization by PAS on a convex Lipschitz problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every global maximization problem over a convex feasible region \(S\subset\mathbb R^d\) of diameter at most \(\Delta\), with objective Lipschitz constant at most \(\lambda\), and with absolutely continuous associated distribution \(H\), the PAS hitting time \(N^{PAS}(y)\) satisfies, for every \(f_*\le y<f^*\), \[\mathbb E[N^{PAS}(y)]\le 1+d\ln\!\left(\frac{\lambda\Delta}{f^*-y}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex feasible region of bounded diameter, for a Lipschitz objective with absolutely continuous gap distribution, the expected number of Pure Adaptive Search iterations needed to reach value y or better is at most one plus the dimension times the logarithm of the Lipschitz diameter divided by the remaining optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[N^{PAS}(y)]\le 1+d\ln\!\left(\frac{\lambda\Delta}{f^*-y}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pure Adaptive Search and Its Weak Variant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional sampling from strict or non-strict improving sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $x_1\sim P$ on $A$. For $j\geq1$, define
\[
y_{oj}=\min_{1\leq i\leq j}f(x_i),\qquad S_j=\{x\in A:f(x)<y_{oj}\}.
\]
Whenever $P(S_j)>0$, pure adaptive search draws $x_{j+1}$ from the conditional distribution
\[
P_{j+1}(U)=\frac{P(U\cap S_j)}{P(S_j)}
\]
for every Borel set $U\subseteq A$. Thus each new point is a strict record, and the generated points are dependent in general. If $P$ is uniform on $A$, the conditional distribution is uniform on $S_j$. Weak pure adaptive search instead samples using the non-strict sublevel set $W_{x_j}=\{x\in A:f(x)\leq f(x_j)\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pure adaptive search samples each next point from the original distribution conditioned on strictly improving the current record. Each accepted sample is therefore a new record, and the samples are generally dependent. The weak variant uses the corresponding non-strict sublevel set.
assumptions_latex: P(S_j)>0\text{ whenever the conditional step is executed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{j+1}(U)=\frac{P(U\cap S_j)}{P(S_j)},\quad S_j=\{x\in A:f(x)<y_{oj}\};\qquad W_{x_j}=\{x\in A:f(x)\leq f(x_j)\}\text{ for the weak variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose $x_0\in D$. At iteration $k$, sample $s_k$ according to a probability measure $\mu_k$ on $\mathbb R^n$. Require that for every measurable $D_1\subseteq D$ with $\lambda^{(n)}(D_1)>0$ and every $\delta>0$, there exist $\widehat\varepsilon(\delta)>0$ and $\widehat p(D_1,\delta)>0$ such that, for all integers $k\ge n\ge0$, $P\!\left(B_k\cup F_k\mid\bigcap_{j=n}^{k-1}(\bar A_j\cap F_j)\right)\ge\widehat p$, where $A_k=\{f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)-\widehat\varepsilon\}$, $B_k=\{\exists\gamma\ge0:x_k+\gamma s_k\in D_1\}$, and $F_k=\{\varrho(x_k,X^\star)\ge\delta\}$. Then choose $\gamma_k\in\arg\min\{f(x_k+\gamma s_k):\gamma\ge0,\ x_k+\gamma s_k\in D\}$ and set $x_{k+1}=x_k+\gamma_k s_k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a feasible point, sample each search direction from an adaptive probability measure satisfying the stated uniform positive-probability coverage condition, and obtain the next iterate by globally minimizing the objective along the feasible forward ray.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability adaptation over a finite set of RCL parameters for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m\} be the available RCL parameters. Initially set p(\alpha_i)=1/m. At each GRASP iteration sample \alpha_i according to p. After warm-up, let F(S^*) be the best objective value found and A_i the average objective value obtained using \alpha_i. Periodically compute q_i=(F(S^*)/A_i)^\delta and update p(\alpha_i)=q_i/\sum_{j=1}^m q_j.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reactive GRASP initially samples each candidate alpha value uniformly, records the solution quality obtained with each value, and periodically increases the selection probability of values having better average performance relative to the incumbent best value.
assumptions_latex: \text{Warm-up iterations provide an average }A_i\text{ for every }i.
q_i=\left(F(S^*)/A_i\right)^\delta\text{ is real and defined for every }i,\quad \sum_{j=1}^m q_j>0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(\alpha_i)=\frac{q_i}{\sum_{j=1}^m q_j},\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m p(\alpha_i)=1,\text{ with larger }q_i\text{ yielding larger }p(\alpha_i).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-sample guarantee on a compact metric space, including a Lipschitz specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(A,\rho)$ be a compact metric space, let $f:A\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $X_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset A$. Define $d_n=\sup_{a\in A}\min_{1\le i\le n}\rho(a,x_i)$, $m=\min_{a\in A}f(a)$, and $y_{on}=\min_{1\le i\le n}f(x_i)$. Then $y_{on}-m\leq\omega_\rho(f;d_n)$, where $\omega_\rho(f;t)=\sup\{|f(u)-f(v)|:u,v\in A,\rho(u,v)\leq t\}$. If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz, then $y_{on}-m\leq Ld_n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous objective on a compact metric space, the best sampled value exceeds the global minimum by at most the modulus of continuity at the sample dispersion. For an L-Lipschitz objective, the gap is at most L times the dispersion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_{on}-m\leq\omega_\rho(f;d_n),\qquad f\in\operatorname{Lip}(A,L,\rho)\Rightarrow y_{on}-m\leq Ld_n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite metric-ball covering of a feasible region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coverage by feasible-region-truncated metric balls and its equal-radius specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ and let $\rho$ be a metric on $A$. For $x_i\in A$ and $\varepsilon_i\geq0$, define $B(x_i,\varepsilon_i,\rho)=\{z\in A:\rho(x_i,z)\leq\varepsilon_i\}$. The balls cover $A$ when $A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nB(x_i,\varepsilon_i,\rho)$. In the equal-radius case, $\varepsilon_i=\varepsilon>0$ for every $i$, so $A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nB(x_i,\varepsilon,\rho)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite collection of metric balls covers the feasible region when their union contains every feasible point. Equal positive radii give the equal-radius covering case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nB(x_i,\varepsilon_i,\rho),\qquad \varepsilon_i=\varepsilon>0\ \forall i\implies A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nB(x_i,\varepsilon,\rho).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform sequence with respect to a probability distribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformity defined by empirical integration, with sufficient test classes and an anchored-rectangle characterization on the unit cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P$ be a probability distribution on $A$. A sequence $X_\infty=\{x_1,x_2,\ldots\}\subset A$ is uniform with respect to $P$ if, for every Riemann-integrable $f$ on $A$, $\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n f(x_j)\to\int_A f(x)P(dx)$. If the $x_j$ are random, the convergence is required almost surely. Uniformity follows if this convergence holds for the stated determining classes, including continuous functions or indicators of all Jordan-measurable subsets. When $A=[0,1]^d$ and $P$ is uniform, uniformity is equivalent to $\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_{[0,b)}(x_j)\to\prod_{i=1}^d b_i$ for every $b\in(0,1]^d$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence is uniform for P when empirical averages of every Riemann-integrable function converge to its P-integral; random sequences require almost-sure convergence. The stated continuous-function and Jordan-set tests are sufficient. On the unit cube with uniform measure, uniformity is equivalent to the correct limiting frequency in every rectangle anchored at the origin.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a probability distribution on }A
A=[0,1]^d\text{ and }P=\mu\text{ for the anchored-rectangle equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n f(x_j)\to\int_A f\,dP;\qquad A=[0,1]^d,\ P=\mu\Rightarrow\left[X_\infty\text{ uniform}\iff\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_{[0,b)}(x_j)\to\prod_{i=1}^d b_i\ \forall b\in(0,1]^d\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequence-driven covering search with unequal adaptive balls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluates a prescribed point sequence while skipping covered candidates and adapting radii through the kth order statistic of accepted objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $k\geq1$, first evaluate $z_1,\ldots,z_k$ from $Z_\infty=(z_i)_{i\geq1}$, set $x_l=z_l$ and $\varepsilon_l=\delta/L$ for $l=1,\ldots,k$, and let $y^*_{k,k}=\max_{1\leq l\leq k}f(x_l)$. For each subsequent $z_{i+1}$, skip it if $\rho(z_{i+1},x_l)\leq\varepsilon_l$ for some accepted point. Otherwise accept it as $x_j$ and evaluate $f(x_j)$. If $f(x_j)\geq y^*_{k,j-1}$, keep $y^*_{k,j}=y^*_{k,j-1}$ and set $\varepsilon_j=(f(x_j)-y^*_{k,j}+\delta)/L$. If $f(x_j)<y^*_{k,j-1}$, redefine $y^*_{k,j}$ as the kth smallest value among $f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_j)$ and reset $\varepsilon_l=\delta/L+\max\{0,f(x_l)-y^*_{k,j}\}/L$ for every $l=1,\ldots,j$. Continue until the stopping condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the first k points of a prescribed sequence. Skip later candidates lying in an existing exclusion ball and evaluate uncovered candidates. Radii depend on the current kth-smallest accepted value and are all recomputed whenever that order statistic decreases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho(z_{i+1},x_l)\leq\varepsilon_l\text{ for some }l\implies z_{i+1}\text{ is skipped},\qquad \varepsilon_l=\frac{\delta+\max\{0,f(x_l)-y^*_{k,j}\}}{L}\text{ after recomputation}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectrally restricted random primal sampling motivated by zero-gap primal-dual structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the duality gap is zero, an optimal primal solution lies in the minimum-eigenvalue eigenspace. Motivated by this, set \(\mu=-\lambda_1(A)e\), independently draw \(\alpha_k\sim N(0,1)\), and for each \(i=1,\ldots,p\) form \[y^i=\sum_{k=1}^r\alpha_k v_k(A+\mu I),\qquad x^i=\frac{\sqrt n\,y^i}{\lVert y^i\rVert}.\] Then \[S_{\mathrm E}=\{(x^i,\mu):i=1,\ldots,p\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the duality gap is zero, an optimal primal solution lies in the minimum-eigenvalue eigenspace. The sampling rule therefore forms independent Gaussian linear combinations of eigenvectors associated with the r smallest eigenvalues of the shifted matrix, normalizes each combination to radius square root n, and pairs it with the fixed spectral dual point.
assumptions_latex: \text{The motivating primal-dual pair has zero duality gap}
v_k(A+\mu I)\ \text{corresponds to the }k\text{-th smallest eigenvalue}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathrm E}=\left\{\left(\frac{\sqrt n\,y^i}{\lVert y^i\rVert},\mu\right):i=1,\ldots,p\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cubic-grid coverage implies enlarged coverage of the unit cube
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-grid certificate for Euclidean coverage after an explicit uniform enlargement of the radii.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A=[0,1]^d$ with the Euclidean metric, let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in A$, let $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_n\geq0$, and let $k\geq1$. Define $C_k=\{(i_1/k,\ldots,i_d/k):i_j\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\}$. If $C_k\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nB_{\varepsilon_i}(x_i)$, then, for $r=\sqrt d/(2k)$, $A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nB_{\varepsilon_i+r}(x_i)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the given balls cover every point of the regular step-1/k grid in the unit d-cube, enlarging each radius by sqrt(d)/(2k) makes the balls cover the whole cube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nB_{\varepsilon_i+\sqrt d/(2k)}(x_i).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case empirical-measure error and its standard rectangle specializations on the unit cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $X_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset A$, a probability distribution $P$, and a family $\mathcal M$ of measurable subsets of $A$, define $D_n(\mathcal M,X_n,P)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal M}\left|\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_U(x_j)-P(U)\right|$. On $[0,1]^d$ with Lebesgue measure, star discrepancy uses anchored rectangles $[0,b)$, whereas extreme discrepancy uses general axis-aligned half-open rectangles $[a,b)$. For every $n$, $D_n^*(X_n)\leq D_n(X_n)\leq2^dD_n^*(X_n)$, so the two quantities have the same asymptotic order of decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrepancy is the largest absolute difference between empirical frequency and target probability over a chosen family of sets. Star discrepancy uses rectangles anchored at the origin, while extreme discrepancy uses general axis-aligned rectangles. Extreme discrepancy is between star discrepancy and 2^d times star discrepancy, so they have the same asymptotic decay order.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a probability distribution on }A
A=[0,1]^d\text{ and }P=\mu\text{ for the star and extreme specializations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_n(\mathcal M,X_n,P)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal M}\left|\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_U(x_j)-P(U)\right|,\qquad D_n^*(X_n)\leq D_n(X_n)\leq2^dD_n^*(X_n)

children.title: Stratified Random Search
children.top_down_role: Random search organized through a partitioned sampling domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise finite-design guarantee once every stratum is represented.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) exactly partition \(X\), choose \(x_j\in S_j\), and set \(\delta=\max_j\operatorname{diam}(S_j)\). For an objective with modulus of continuity \(\omega_f\), \[0\le\min_jf(x_j)-f^\star\le\omega_f(\delta).\] For an \(L\)-Lipschitz objective the bound is \(L\delta\), independently of how representatives were randomized within their strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One representative from every exact stratum gives an error bounded by the objective's modulus of continuity at the largest stratum diameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_jf(x_j)-f^\star\le\omega_f(\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Stratum-Diameter Error Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a genuine covering partition and fixes boundary allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite stratification of compact metric space \(X\) is a family of nonempty measurable sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) satisfying \(X=\bigcup_jS_j\) and \(S_i\cap S_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\), with boundaries assigned explicitly. A one-per-stratum design chooses \(x_j\in S_j\); a randomized design draws \(X_j\) from a distribution supported on \(S_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stratified design exactly partitions the entire domain and selects or samples at least one representative from every stratum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point, including boundary points, belongs to a represented stratum.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Stratified Design

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for worst-case continuous-objective coverage claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A partition only up to reference-measure zero need not cover every possible minimizer. If an omitted point is positively separated from all represented sets, a continuous objective can have its unique minimum there while sampled values remain separated from the optimum. Even for an exact partition, the diameter certificate fails if a stratum receives no representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting a separated null-set point or leaving a stratum unrepresented can destroy worst-case optimization coverage.
assumptions_latex: A point is omitted and positively separated from represented sets, or some exact stratum has no representative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency for every continuous objective and the diameter certificate need not hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Omitted-Set and Unrepresented-Stratum Failures

assumptions_latex: The compact region \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is partitioned into measurable strata \(S_{n,1},\ldots,S_{n,m_n}\).
Each stratum has positive reference measure and its conditional sampling distribution has support equal to that stratum.
The maximal stratum diameter tends to zero as the total number of evaluations grows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every continuous \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), the best sampled value converges almost surely to \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One conditionally independent draw per shrinking measurable stratum, with best-so-far output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At stage \(n\), construct a partition \(X=\bigcup_{j=1}^{m_n}S_{n,j}\) up to null sets. Independently for each \(j\), draw \(X_{n,j}\) from the reference measure conditioned on \(S_{n,j}\), evaluate \(f(X_{n,j})\), and return the best point among all samples generated through stage \(n\). If \(\delta_n=\max_j\operatorname{diam}(S_{n,j})\to0\), then every point of \(X\) lies arbitrarily close to a sampled stratum representative. Uniform continuity of \(f\) on compact \(X\) consequently yields convergence of the best sampled value to the global minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the domain into increasingly fine strata, sample once within each stratum, and retain the best evaluation; shrinking strata ensure consistency for continuous objectives.
knowledge_statements.title: Stratified Random Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. Moreover, a partition only up to null sets need not cover a minimizer located in an omitted null set, so the stated assumptions do not establish the claimed consistency for every continuous objective. The statement also contains proof text. The algorithm kind otherwise fits the leaf.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cube Containment from Intersection with a Euclidean Ball
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dimension-dependent enlargement bound for a cubic cell intersecting a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $d\in\mathbb{N}$, let $B_r(O)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ be a Euclidean ball of radius $r$, and let $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ be a cube of edge length $h$. For every $z\in C\cap B_r(O)$, one has $C\subseteq B_{r+h\sqrt d}(O)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a d-dimensional cube of edge length h contains a point that also lies in a Euclidean ball of radius r centered at O, then the entire cube lies in the concentric ball of radius r plus h times the square root of d.
assumptions_latex: B_r(O)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is a Euclidean ball of radius }r
C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\text{ is a cube of edge length }h
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\subseteq B_{r+h\sqrt d}(O)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper allocation characterizes stochastic dominance of stratified sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes proportional allocation as sufficient for stochastic dominance over independent sampling and gives a witness showing that any nonproportional allocation destroys uniform dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mathcal R_k$ be a fixed partition of $A$ into $k\leq n$ subsets, let $\mathcal F=C^p(A)$ for some $0\leq p\leq\infty$, and let $\mathcal P_{k,L}$ be the stratified procedure with $l_i\geq0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k l_i=n$. If $l_i=nq_i$ for every $i$, where $q_i=P(A_i)$, then $\mathcal P_{k,L}$ stochastically dominates the independent procedure $\mathcal P_1$ on $\mathcal F$ under criterion (3.43). If $l_i\neq nq_i$ for at least one $i$, then $\mathcal P_{k,L}$ does not stochastically dominate $\mathcal P_1$; moreover, there exist $f^*\in\mathcal F$ and $t$ such that $F_{k,L}(f^*,t)<F_1(f^*,t)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed partition and sample budget, allocating samples in exact proportion to stratum probability makes stratified random search stochastically dominate independent sampling over the stated function class. If any allocation is nonproportional, uniform dominance fails, and a function and threshold witness the adverse cdf inequality.
assumptions_latex: $\mathcal R_k$ is a fixed partition of $A$ into $k\leq n$ subsets.
$F_{k,L}(f,t)$ and $F_1(f,t)$ are the record-value c.d.f.s specified by criterion (3.43).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[(\forall i)\ l_i=nq_i\right]\Rightarrow\mathcal P_{k,L}\text{ stochastically dominates }\mathcal P_1;\qquad\left[(\exists i)\ l_i\neq nq_i\right]\Rightarrow\left[(\exists f^*\in\mathcal F)(\exists t)\ F_{k,L}(f^*,t)<F_1(f^*,t)\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic moment ratio for stratified and independent random search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an almost-sure asymptotic ratio of positive record-error moments as the number of strata grows while the sample count per stratum remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that $P$ and the class $\mathcal F_*$ of continuous functions $f(x)=\varphi(x-x_*)$ having a unique global minimizer $x_*(f)$ satisfy condition (2.42) for $F=F_f$ with some $\alpha>0$. Suppose $x_*$ has distribution $R$ on $A$, where $R$ is equivalent to Lebesgue measure. If $n=kl$, $l$ is fixed, and $k\to\infty$, then for every $p>0$, with $R$-probability one, $$\frac{\mathbb E\left(f_*[X_{k,l}]-m\right)^p}{\mathbb E\left(f_*[X_{1,n}]-m\right)^p}=l^{p/\alpha}\frac{\Gamma(l+1)}{\Gamma(p/\alpha+l+1)}+o(1),\qquad n\to\infty.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under condition (2.42) and the stated distributional assumption on the unique minimizer, keeping l samples per stratum while increasing the number of strata makes the ratio of stratified to independent record-error moments converge almost surely to an explicit gamma-function expression.
assumptions_latex: $f\in\mathcal F_*$ is continuous, has the form $f(x)=\varphi(x-x_*)$, and has a unique global minimizer $x_*$.
$x_*\sim R$, and $R$ is equivalent to Lebesgue measure on $A$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\mathbb E\left(f_*[X_{k,l}]-m\right)^p}{\mathbb E\left(f_*[X_{1,n}]-m\right)^p}=l^{p/\alpha}\frac{\Gamma(l+1)}{\Gamma(p/\alpha+l+1)}+o(1)\quad(n\to\infty),\qquad R\text{-a.s.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines conditional sampling on a measurable partition, proportional allocation, the product sampling law, and independent sampling as the one-stratum case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P$ be a probability measure on $A$, and let $A=\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i$ be a partition into pairwise disjoint connected measurable sets with $q_i=P(A_i)>0$. Define $P_i(B)=P(B\cap A_i)/q_i$ for measurable $B\subseteq A$. Given integers $l_i\geq0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^k l_i=n$, a stratified sample is $X_{k,L}=(x_{i,j})$, where the variables are mutually independent and $x_{i,j}\sim P_i$ for $1\leq j\leq l_i$. Its joint law is $Q_{k,L}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^k P_i^{\otimes l_i}$. It is proper if $l_i=nq_i$ for every $i$. For $k=1$, the construction is independent sampling from $P$. For an objective $f$, $f_*[X]=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\geq m:=\min_{x\in A}f(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stratified sample draws mutually independent points from the conditional distribution within each positive-probability stratum. It is proper when the number assigned to each stratum is proportional to its probability mass. With one stratum the construction becomes ordinary independent sampling from P, and the best sampled value cannot be below the global minimum.
assumptions_latex: $A=\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i$, with the $A_i$ connected, measurable, pairwise disjoint, and $P(A_i)=q_i>0$.
The variables $x_{i,j}$ are mutually independent and satisfy $x_{i,j}\sim P_i$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{k,L}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^kP_i^{\otimes l_i},\qquad \operatorname{proper}(X_{k,L})\iff(\forall i)\ l_i=nq_i,\qquad k=1\Rightarrow Q_{1,n}=P^{\otimes n},\qquad f_*[X]\geq m.

children.title: Quasirandom Search
children.top_down_role: Global exploration based on low-discrepancy sampling designs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts declared fill-distance or star-discrepancy rates into objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a design prefix has fill distance \(h_n\le Ca_n\), then for modulus of continuity \(\omega_f\), \[0\le\min_{i\le n}f(u_i)-f^\star\le\omega_f(Ca_n).\] On \([0,1]^d\), the bound \(h_n\le2(D_n^*)^{1/d}\) gives error at most \(\omega_f(2(D_n^*)^{1/d})\). For an \(L\)-Hölder objective of exponent \(\alpha\), this is at most \(L2^\alpha(D_n^*)^{\alpha/d}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasirandom prefix's covering or discrepancy rate converts through the objective's modulus of continuity into a deterministic optimization-error rate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous on the compact unit cube.
The stated fill-distance or discrepancy bound holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_n-f^\star\le\omega_f(h_n)\le\omega_f(2(D_n^*)^{1/d})\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quasirandom Coverage-to-Optimization Rate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard quantitative design class for quasirandom search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \((u_i)_{i\ge1}\subset[0,1]^d\) is low discrepancy with respect to anchored boxes when its prefix star discrepancies satisfy \(D_n^*=O(n^{-1}(\log n)^d)\). More generally, \(D_n^*\to0\) is equivalent to uniform distribution of the sequence on the unit cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-discrepancy sequences have rapidly vanishing anchored-box discrepancy; vanishing star discrepancy characterizes uniform distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(D_n^*\) is the star discrepancy of the first \(n\) points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Low discrepancy implies \(D_n^*\to0\) and uniform distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Discrepancy Sequence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits conclusions drawn merely from labeling a design randomized or low discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Random shifting or scrambling supports pathwise optimization convergence only when the selected construction preserves a deterministic or almost-sure vanishing-discrepancy or vanishing-covering guarantee. Randomization alone supplies no such guarantee. Likewise, discrepancy affects pointwise optimization only through a valid discrepancy-to-covering conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization alone does not ensure coverage, and discrepancy must be converted geometrically before it bounds optimization error.
assumptions_latex: Only randomization or an unquantified discrepancy label is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No pathwise optimization-error guarantee follows without a construction-specific coverage implication.
knowledge_statements.title: Construction-Specific Randomization Boundary

assumptions_latex: The deterministic or randomized point sequence has covering radius tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incumbent values satisfy \(\min_{1\le i\le n}f(U_i)\to\min_{x\in X}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Covering radius in the chosen norm
Best objective value through evaluation n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic low-dispersion sequences or randomized variants used as global-search evaluation sites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select a space-filling sequence \((U_i)_{i\ge1}\subset[0,1]^d\), such as a low-discrepancy sequence, optionally after a random digital shift or scrambling that preserves its coverage order. Evaluate \(f(U_n)\) sequentially and output an index \(i_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le i\le n}f(U_i)\). If its covering radius \(h_n\to0\), then for a minimizer \(x^\star\) there is a sampled point within distance \(h_n\) of \(x^\star\). Hence continuity gives \(f(U_{i_n})\to f(x^\star)\). Randomization changes the sampling law but not this conclusion whenever \(h_n\to0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate a space-filling low-discrepancy sequence and retain its best point; vanishing covering radius guarantees convergence for continuous objectives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Low-discrepancy sequences and finite point-set families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Star-discrepancy rates distinguishing infinite sequences from families of finite sampling designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An infinite sequence $X_\infty\subset[0,1]^d$ is low-discrepancy if the star discrepancy of its first $n$ points satisfies $D_n^*(X_\infty)=O((\log n)^d/n)$ as $n\to\infty$. A family of $n$-point sets $\{X_n\}_n$ is low-discrepancy if $D_n^*(X_n)=O((\log n)^{d-1}/n)$ as $n\to\infty$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite d-dimensional sequence is low-discrepancy when the star discrepancy of its first n points is O((log n)^d/n). A family of finite n-point designs is low-discrepancy when its star discrepancy is O((log n)^(d−1)/n).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_n^*(X_\infty)=O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^d}{n}\right),\qquad D_n^*(X_n)=O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^{d-1}}{n}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Van der Corput and Halton Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the radical-inverse construction, the one-dimensional van der Corput sequence, and its coordinatewise extension to a Halton sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\ge 2\) be an integer. For \(k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), let \(k=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_j(k)b^j\) be its unique base-\(b\) digit expansion, with \(a_j(k)\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}\) and only finitely many nonzero digits. Define \(\phi_b(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_j(k)b^{-j-1}\). The van der Corput sequence in base \(b\) is \((\phi_b(k))_{k\ge0}\). Given pairwise relatively prime integer bases \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\ge2\), the Halton sequence is \(\bigl((\phi_{p_1}(k),\ldots,\phi_{p_n}(k))\bigr)_{k\ge0}\subset[0,1)^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radical inverse reflects the base-b digits of each nonnegative integer across the radix point. These values form the van der Corput sequence; applying the construction coordinatewise with pairwise relatively prime bases produces a Halton sequence in the unit cube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k=\bigl(\phi_{p_1}(k),\ldots,\phi_{p_n}(k)\bigr)\in[0,1)^n\quad\text{for every }k\ge0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radical-inverse, Halton, van der Corput, and Hammersley constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Digit-reversal constructions using pairwise relatively prime integer bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer $R\geq2$, write $K\in\mathbb N_0$ in base $R$ as $K=\sum_{j=0}^M a_jR^j$, with $0\leq a_j\leq R-1$, and define $\phi_R(K)=\sum_{j=0}^M a_jR^{-j-1}$. For pairwise relatively prime bases $R_1,\ldots,R_d\geq2$, the Halton sequence is $x_{j+1}=(\phi_{R_1}(j),\ldots,\phi_{R_d}(j))$, $j\geq0$; its one-dimensional case is a van der Corput sequence. For fixed $n$, the Hammersley point set is $x_{j+1}=(j/n,\phi_{R_1}(j),\ldots,\phi_{R_{d-1}}(j))$, $0\leq j<n$, using pairwise relatively prime bases. Halton sequences are infinite, whereas Hammersley point sets depend on $n$ and are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radical-inverse map reverses an integer's base-R digits across the radix point. Halton sequences combine radical inverses in pairwise coprime bases; the one-dimensional construction is the van der Corput sequence. Hammersley sets add the coordinate j/n and form finite n-point designs.
assumptions_latex: R_1,\ldots,R_d\text{ are pairwise relatively prime integers at least }2
n\in\mathbb N\text{ for the Hammersley construction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{j+1}^{\mathrm{Halton}}=(\phi_{R_1}(j),\ldots,\phi_{R_d}(j)),\qquad x_{j+1}^{\mathrm{Hammersley}}=(j/n,\phi_{R_1}(j),\ldots,\phi_{R_{d-1}}(j))

children.title: Randomized Covering Search
children.top_down_role: Randomized schemes designed to improve geometric coverage of the domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable probabilistic condition implying almost-sure candidate-pool density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C_n\) consists of \(m_n\) iid draws from a full-support probability measure \(\mu\) on compact \(X\). For every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), choose a finite cover by \(K_\varepsilon\) balls of radius \(\varepsilon/2\), and let \(p_\varepsilon>0\) be the smallest \(\mu\)-mass of those balls. If \(\sum_nK_\varepsilon(1-p_\varepsilon)^{m_n}<\infty\) for every such \(\varepsilon\), then \(q_n\to0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-support candidate pools become dense almost surely when pool sizes make the probabilities of missing finite ball covers summable.
assumptions_latex: Draws within each pool are iid from a full-support measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_n\to0\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: Smallest ball mass in the chosen cover

knowledge_statements.title: Random Candidate-Pool Density Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp support boundary for randomized covering search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every candidate pool is almost surely contained in a closed proper subset \(S\subsetneq X\), every selected site belongs to \(D_{n_0}\cup S\). If some \(x\in X\) has positive distance from that set, then \(\inf_n h(D_n)>0\). Maximin selection therefore cannot repair missing support in the candidate generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Farthest-candidate selection cannot cover regions that the candidate generator never proposes.
assumptions_latex: \(C_n\subset S\) almost surely for a closed proper subset \(S\subsetneq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive distance from \(D_{n_0}\cup S\) forces fill distance to remain positive.

notation.meaning: Support subset of all candidate pools

knowledge_statements.title: Missing Candidate Support Prevents Coverage

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense Candidate Pools Yield Approximate Farthest-Point Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for maximin candidate selection to generate a dense evaluated design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be compact, \(r_n(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,D_n)\), and choose \(x_{n+1}\in C_n\) satisfying \(r_n(x_{n+1})\ge\sup_{x\in C_n}r_n(x)-\eta_n\). If \(q_n=\sup_{x\in X}\operatorname{dist}(x,C_n)\to0\) and \(\eta_n\to0\), then the evaluated-design fill distance \(h(D_n)=\sup_{x\in X}r_n(x)\) tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate farthest-candidate selection becomes dense when candidate pools become dense and selection error vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Candidate Pools Yield Approximate Farthest-Point Coverage

assumptions_latex: The feasible region \(X\) is compact in a metric space \((X,\rho)\).
At iteration \(n\), a finite random candidate set \(C_n\subset X\) is generated.
Candidate sets become sufficiently dense so that their fill distance tends to zero almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(f\) is continuous, the best evaluated value converges almost surely to \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to the current design
Random candidate set at iteration n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random candidate generation followed by a maximin coverage rule and incumbent selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial finite design \(D_{n_0}\subset X\). For \(n\ge n_0\), generate a finite random candidate set \(C_n\), select \(X_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C_n}r_n(x)\), evaluate \(f(X_{n+1})\), and set \(D_{n+1}=D_n\cup\{X_{n+1}\}\). Output a minimizer of \(f\) over \(D_n\). If the resulting fill distance \(h(D_n)=\sup_{x\in X}\min_{z\in D_n}\rho(x,z)\) tends to zero almost surely, then compactness and continuity imply that the incumbent objective value converges almost surely to the global minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate random candidates, evaluate the candidate farthest from prior sites, and retain the best point; vanishing fill distance yields global consistency.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Randomized covering search with fixed-radius exclusion balls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Samples from the currently uncovered region and removes a fixed-radius ball after each evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set $Z_1=A$ and $j=1$. At iteration $j$, sample $x_j$ from $P_{Z_j}$, evaluate $y_j=f(x_j)$, and compute $y_{oj}=\min_{1\leq i\leq j}y_i$. If the stopping condition is false, set $Z_{j+1}=Z_j\setminus B(x_j,\varepsilon,\rho)$, replace $j$ by $j+1$, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with the full feasible region. Sample from the currently uncovered set, evaluate the objective, update the best observed value, and—unless stopping—remove the fixed-radius ball around the sample before continuing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_{oj}=\min_{1\leq i\leq j}f(x_i),\qquad Z_{j+1}=Z_j\setminus B(x_j,\varepsilon,\rho)\text{ when stopping does not occur}.

children.title: Coverage Discrepancy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coverage quality under differing dimension, sample-budget, or design conditions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cube-specific curse-of-dimensionality boundary for point designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \(n\)-point design in \([0,1]^d\) has maximum-norm fill distance \(h_n\ge\tfrac12 n^{-1/d}\). Therefore coverage-only certification of a Lipschitz error of order \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(\varepsilon^{-d})\) sites in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any n-point cube design has fill distance at least one half n to the minus one over d.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Covering Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fill Distance, Dispersion, and Star Discrepancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes three standard design-quality statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D_n=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\subset[0,1]^d\), define \(h_n=\sup_x\min_i\|x-u_i\|_\infty\), \(\operatorname{disp}(D_n)=\sup\{\lambda(B):B\text{ is an axis-parallel box},\ B\cap D_n=\varnothing\}\), and \(D_n^*=\sup_{a\in[0,1]^d}|n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf1_{[0,a)}(u_i)-\lambda([0,a))|\). These measure metric covering, largest empty-box volume, and anchored-box distributional error, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fill distance, dispersion, and star discrepancy measure metric covering, empty boxes, and anchored-box distributional error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three statistics encode distinct coverage information and require valid conversions before substitution.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill Distance, Dispersion, and Star Discrepancy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supplies valid cube-specific conversions among coverage statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite \(D_n\subset[0,1]^d\), with axis-parallel boxes and the maximum norm, \[h_n^d\le \operatorname{disp}(D_n)\le 2^dD_n^*.\] Consequently, \(h_n\le2(D_n^*)^{1/d}\), and either vanishing dispersion or vanishing star discrepancy implies vanishing fill distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the unit cube, fill distance is controlled through empty-box dispersion, which is in turn controlled by star discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_n^d\le\operatorname{disp}(D_n)\le2^dD_n^*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Valid Discrepancy-to-Covering Comparisons

assumptions_latex: The domain is \(X=[0,1]^d\), equipped with the maximum norm.
The evaluation design after \(n\) samples is \(D_n\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic error certificate is \(0\le\min_{z\in D_n}f(z)-f^\star\le Lh_n\); thus any regime with \(h_n\to0\) is globally consistent.

notation.meaning: Volume of the largest empty axis-parallel box

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage measures as deterministic regimes controlling global-search error for Lipschitz objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_n\) be the first \(n\) evaluation sites. Its covering regime is described by \(h_n\), while its axis-parallel dispersion is the largest empty-box volume \(v_n\). A design is coverage-consistent when \(h_n\to0\); a rate \(h_n=O(a_n)\) defines an \(a_n\)-coverage regime. If \(x^\star\) minimizes \(f\), choose \(z_n\in D_n\) with \(\lVert z_n-x^\star\rVert_\infty\le h_n\). Lipschitz continuity then gives \(0\le\min_{z\in D_n}f(z)-f^\star\le Lh_n\). Consequently, coverage radius directly determines a worst-case optimization-error regime, whereas discrepancy or dispersion requires a geometric conversion before implying such a bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering radius directly bounds Lipschitz optimization error; discrepancy or empty-box volume affects optimization only after conversion to a covering guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Discrepancy Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. The central mathematical claim is an explicit optimization-error certificate, so generic property is not the best exact kind; certificate is more appropriate. The relation between empty-box dispersion or discrepancy and covering radius is left unspecified, and the statement contains proof text.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rejected Builder claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proposed universal inequality \(\operatorname{disp}(D_n)\le(2h_n)^d\) is false: an empty axis-parallel box may be highly elongated, so its volume is not controlled by the \(d\)-th power of its shortest scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dispersion is not universally bounded by (2h) to the d; elongated empty boxes invalidate that direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Builder's claimed two-sided comparison between \(h_n^d\) and dispersion cannot be accepted.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Reverse Dispersion Bound
