children.title: Markovian Global Search
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for stochastic transition-based search families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Markov condition for a stochastic global-search state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state process \((X_n)\) is Markov with kernels \(K_n\) when, for every measurable \(A\), \[\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid X_0,\ldots,X_n)=K_n(X_n,A)\quad\text{a.s.}\] Every archive, temperature, or adaptive parameter affecting the next transition must be included in \(X_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The current state must contain all transition-relevant information for the search to be Markov.
assumptions_latex: \((X_n)\) takes values in a measurable state space.
The conditional transition laws are represented by kernels \(K_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditional-law equality characterizes transition sufficiency of the declared Markov state.
knowledge_statements.title: Transition-State Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity Does Not Imply Global Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between equilibrium and best-so-far optimization convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Existence of, or convergence to, an invariant distribution \(\pi\) does not by itself imply that \(X_n\) or \(\min_{i\le n}f(X_i)\) approaches a global minimum. If \(\pi(A_\varepsilon)=0\) for \(A_\varepsilon=\{x:f(x)<f^\star+\varepsilon\}\), a stationary chain has probability zero of occupying \(A_\varepsilon\) at any fixed time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equilibrium convergence is not an optimization guarantee without continued access to near-optimal regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Invariant-distribution convergence alone is insufficient for global-search convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Does Not Imply Global Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Miss-probability bound under persistent conditional access to a measurable target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A be measurable and \tau_A=\inf\{n\ge1:X_n\in A\}. If, for n=0,\ldots,T-1, \Pr(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)\ge p_n almost surely on \{\tau_A>n\}, then \Pr(\tau_A>T)\le\prod_{n=0}^{T-1}(1-p_n)\le\exp(-\sum_{n=0}^{T-1}p_n).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional lower bounds on reaching a target set give product and exponential bounds on the probability of missing it through a finite horizon.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional lower bounds hold before the first hit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\tau_A>T)\le\prod_{n<T}(1-p_n)\le e^{-\sum_{n<T}p_n}.

notation.meaning: first positive-time visit to the target set
conditional lower bound on the next-step hit probability

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Conditional Hitting Bound

assumptions_latex: The feasible state space \(X\) is measurable and the objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is measurable.
For each incumbent level, the transition kernels assign uniformly persistent probability to every better sublevel set.
The algorithm records the best state visited.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the persistent-hitting condition, the recorded best value converges almost surely to \(f^\star=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Best objective value through time n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-homogeneous or inhomogeneous Markov transitions with best-so-far recording.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(X_0\in X\). Given \(X_n=x\), draw \(X_{n+1}\) from \(K_n(x,\cdot)\), evaluate \(f(X_{n+1})\), and update \(B_{n+1}=\min\{B_n,f(X_{n+1})\}\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(A_\varepsilon=\{x:f(x)<f^\star+\varepsilon\}\). A sufficient global-search condition is the existence of numbers \(p_{n,\varepsilon}\in[0,1]\) satisfying \(K_n(x,A_\varepsilon)\ge p_{n,\varepsilon}\) for all \(x\), with \(\sum_n p_{n,\varepsilon}=\infty\). Then the chain hits each \(A_\varepsilon\) almost surely, and the recorded values converge to \(f^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move through the domain using stochastic transition kernels and record the best state; persistent probability of hitting every near-optimal set ensures global convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Markovian Global Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The kernel minorization and divergent-sum hitting claim requires an authoritative theorem-level source and precise filtration or conditional formulation. None is provided, and the statement includes inferential proof text. The algorithm kind fits the Markovian search container.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General proposal-and-acceptance scheme for Markovian global search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General iterative scheme parameterized by an initial distribution, transition kernels, and acceptance probabilities; optional record dependence extends beyond the strict current-pair Markov property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sample $x_1\sim P_1$ on $A$, evaluate $y_1=f(x_1)$, and set $n=1$. At iteration $n$, repeatedly sample $z_n\sim Q_n(x_n,\cdot)$ until $z_n\in A$, evaluate $f(z_n)$, and set $x_{n+1}=z_n$ with probability $p_n$ and $x_{n+1}=x_n$ with probability $1-p_n$. Set $y_{n+1}=f(z_n)$ upon acceptance and $y_{n+1}=y_n$ otherwise, then stop or continue according to the stopping criterion. The kernel $Q_n$ may depend on $n$ and $x_n$, and $p_n$ may depend on $n,x_n,z_n,y_n,$ and $f(z_n)$. The scheme also permits dependence on $(x_{on},y_{on})$; nontrivial such dependence is not Markovian with respect to $(x_n,y_n)$ alone. Particular choices of $P_1,Q_n,$ and $p_n$ yield particular global random-search algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample an initial feasible point. At each iteration, draw proposals from a state-dependent transition distribution until a feasible proposal is obtained, evaluate it, and accept it with a prescribed probability; otherwise retain the current point. Update the stored objective value consistently and repeat until stopping. The initial, proposal, and acceptance distributions determine the particular method. Optional use of the incumbent record lies outside strict dependence on the current point-value pair alone.
assumptions_latex: P_1\text{ is a probability distribution on }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{n+1}=\begin{cases}z_n,&\text{with probability }p_n,\\x_n,&\text{with probability }1-p_n.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Markovian dependence in global random search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes current-state and record-state definitions from rules that use both states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_1,f(x_1),\ldots,x_n,f(x_n))$ be the conditional distribution used to generate $x_{n+1}$. The algorithm is Markovian in the current-state sense when, for every $n\ge 1$, this distribution equals $P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_n,f(x_n))$. Alternatively, with $y_{on}=\min_{i\le n}f(x_i)$ and $f(x_{on})=y_{on}$, a record-state Markovian rule satisfies $P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_1,f(x_1),\ldots,x_n,f(x_n))=P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_{on},y_{on})$. A rule that depends nontrivially on both $(x_n,y_n)$ and $(x_{on},y_{on})$ is not Markovian with respect to the current pair alone, although its structure is closely related.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global random search is current-state Markovian if its next-point distribution depends on the search history only through the current point and objective value. A record-state alternative depends only on the best point and value observed so far. Nontrivial simultaneous use of the current and record pairs falls outside the strict current-pair definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_1,f(x_1),\ldots,x_n,f(x_n))=P_{n+1}(\cdot\mid x_n,f(x_n))

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state barrier example showing failure under summable uphill acceptance probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the path graph \(a-b-c\), with proposals moving to adjacent vertices, \(f(a)=0\), \(f(b)=H>0\), \(f(c)=-1\), and \(X_0=a\). If \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\exp(-H/T_n)<\infty\), then \(\Pr(X_n=a\text{ for every }n)>0\). Thus simulated annealing can remain forever at the nonglobal local minimum \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the probabilities of crossing a necessary energy barrier are summable, simulated annealing can remain in a nonglobal well with positive probability.
assumptions_latex: The proposal graph is the path \(a-b-c\), with positive adjacent-edge proposals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(X_n=a\text{ for all }n)>0.\)

notation.meaning: energy barrier separating the initial well from the global minimum

knowledge_statements.title: Premature-Cooling Trap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state symmetric-proposal Metropolis kernel underlying simulated annealing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite, let \(Q(x,y)=Q(y,x)\) be an irreducible proposal kernel, and fix \(T>0\). For \(y\ne x\), set \(P_T(x,y)=Q(x,y)\min\{1,\exp(-(f(y)-f(x))/T)\}\), with the diagonal chosen to make \(P_T\) stochastic. Then \(P_T\) is reversible with respect to \(\pi_T(x)=Z_T^{-1}\exp(-f(x)/T)\). Consequently \(\pi_T\) is its unique stationary distribution and \(\pi_T(X^\star)\to1\) as \(T\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed temperature, finite-state Metropolis search with a symmetric irreducible proposal has a Gibbs stationary law that concentrates on global minimizers as temperature vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_T(x)\propto e^{-f(x)/T}\) is the unique stationary distribution and \(\pi_T(X^\star)\to1\) as \(T\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Temperature Gibbs Reversibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state symmetric Metropolis annealing with a barrier-depth cooling threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite and let the symmetric proposal kernel induce a connected graph. Define \(H(\gamma)=\max_{z\in\gamma}f(z)\), \(H(x,A)=\min_{\gamma:x\leadsto A}H(\gamma)\), and \(\Gamma^\star=\max_{x\notin X^\star}(H(x,X^\star)-f(x))\). For the time-inhomogeneous Metropolis chain with \(T_n=c/\log(n+n_0)\), if \(c>\Gamma^\star\) and \(n_0>1\), then \(\Pr(X_n\in X^\star)\to1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite connected landscape, logarithmic cooling slower than the deepest nonglobal energy barrier yields convergence in probability to the global-minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: The symmetric proposal kernel is irreducible and assigns positive probability to every graph edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr(X_n\in X^\star)=1.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state annealing iteration allowing asymmetric proposals; symmetric Metropolis annealing is the special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite, let \(T_n>0\), and let \(Q\) be an irreducible proposal kernel with mutual support: \(Q(x,y)>0\iff Q(y,x)>0\). Given \(X_n=x\), draw \(Y_n\sim Q(x,\cdot)\) and, when \(Q(x,Y_n)>0\), accept \(Y_n=y\) with probability \[\alpha_n(x,y)=\min\left\{1,\exp\left(-\frac{f(y)-f(x)}{T_n}\right)\frac{Q(y,x)}{Q(x,y)}\right\};\] otherwise retain \(x\). Record a least-objective incumbent among visited states. For symmetric \(Q\), the proposal ratio cancels. This definition makes no convergence claim for an arbitrary cooling schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-state simulated annealing uses temperature-dependent Metropolis-Hastings moves and records the best visited state.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is irreducible and has mutual support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rule defines finite-state simulated annealing and reduces to ordinary Metropolis annealing for symmetric \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Metropolis-Hastings Simulated Annealing

assumptions_latex: The proposal kernel \(Q(x,\cdot)\) is irreducible on the feasible state space \(X\).
The positive temperature sequence \((T_n)\) decreases toward zero according to a schedule satisfying an appropriate global-convergence condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under a valid cooling condition, the probability of occupying any fixed nonoptimal energy level tends to zero, and best-so-far values approach the global minimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metropolis simulated annealing; the precise sufficient cooling schedule depends on state-space assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(X_0\in X\) and temperatures \(T_n\downarrow0\). Given \(X_n=x\), propose \(Y_n\sim Q(x,\cdot)\) and accept it with probability \(\alpha_n(x,Y_n)=\min\{1,\exp(-(f(Y_n)-f(x))/T_n)\}\); otherwise set \(X_{n+1}=x\). Record the best state visited and stop according to a prescribed evaluation budget or convergence diagnostic. At fixed \(T\), the acceptance rule favors low objective values while allowing uphill moves. Global convergence requires sufficiently slow cooling relative to the energy barriers and irreducibility properties of the chosen state-space model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use Metropolis moves whose willingness to accept objective increases decreases with temperature; sufficiently slow cooling can concentrate the search on global minima.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simulated annealing acceptance and cooling principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative method description; the extract does not provide hypotheses sufficient for a formal convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Simulated annealing samples a neighbor randomly. A neighbor with a better objective value replaces the incumbent with probability \(1\), whereas a worse neighbor is accepted with a probability strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). Slight deteriorations are accepted more readily than large deteriorations, and the probability of accepting worsening moves decreases over time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulated annealing randomly samples a neighbor, always accepts an improvement, and may accept a worsening move. Smaller deteriorations are accepted more readily, while cooling makes worsening moves progressively less likely.
assumptions_latex: A solution space, objective value, and neighborhood relation are defined.
The acceptance mechanism assigns positive probability to worsening moves and reduces that probability over time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted worsening moves provide a mechanism for leaving local minima, while cooling increasingly favors nonworsening moves.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm for maximizing c(Q) over Q in a feasible family; the acceptance formula is preserved as extracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \alpha_0>0,\ 0<\beta<1,\ Q^0\in\mathcal F,\ i=0. Given Q^i, generate Q'\in N(Q^i). If c(Q')>c(Q^i), set Q^{i+1}=Q'. Otherwise set Q^{i+1}=Q' with probability p=\exp(c(Q')-c(Q^i))/\alpha_i and set Q^{i+1}=Q^i with probability 1-p. Then set \alpha_{i+1}=\alpha_i(1-\beta), increment i, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible solution and positive temperature, sample a neighbor, accept every improvement, accept a nonimprovement with the stated exponential probability, and reduce the temperature geometrically by the factor 1−β each iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_{i+1}=\alpha_i(1-\beta)\quad\text{with the stated probabilistic update of }Q^{i+1}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence in probability of simulated-annealing objective values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-specific convergence to the global maximum value under the proposal-density and cooling assumptions stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{X_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\) be generated by the stated simulated-annealing algorithm, and let \(f^*\) be the global maximum of \(f\) on \(S\). Suppose each proposal distribution \(R(x,\cdot)\) is absolutely continuous with density \(r(x,\cdot)\), the family of densities is uniformly bounded away from zero, and, for every starting point \(x_0\), the cooling schedule converges to zero in probability. Then, for every \(\epsilon>0\) and \(x_0\in S\), \[\Pr\!\left(f(X_n)<f^*-\epsilon\mid X_0=x_0\right)\longrightarrow 0.\] Thus \(f(X_n)\) converges in probability to \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the simulated-annealing proposal densities are uniformly bounded away from zero and the cooling schedule converges to zero in probability from every starting point, then the sampled objective values converge in probability to the global maximum value.
assumptions_latex: \{X_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\text{ is generated by the stated simulated-annealing algorithm on }S.
\forall x\in S,\;R(x,\cdot)\text{ is absolutely continuous with density }r(x,\cdot).
\text{The densities }r(x,\cdot)\text{ are uniformly bounded away from zero.
\forall x_0\in S,\quad T_n\xrightarrow{\Pr}0\text{ under the process initialized at }X_0=x_0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall \epsilon>0\;\forall x_0\in S,\quad \Pr\!\left(f(X_n)<f^*-\epsilon\mid X_0=x_0\right)\longrightarrow0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization form with a fixed number of trials per temperature and best-so-far output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial solution \(S\), an initial temperature \(T>0\), a reduction factor \(r\in(0,1)\), and a positive integer \(L\), repeat until the process is frozen: perform \(L\) trials in which a random neighbor \(S'\) is sampled and \(\Delta=f(S')-f(S)\) is computed; accept \(S'\) whenever \(\Delta\leq 0\), and when \(\Delta>0\), accept it with probability \(e^{-\Delta/T}\). After the trials, set \(T\leftarrow rT\). Return the best solution encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each temperature, sample L random neighbors. Always accept a nonworsening neighbor and accept a worsening one with probability exp(-deterioration/temperature). Multiply the temperature by a factor between zero and one after each batch, stop when frozen, and return the best solution found.
assumptions_latex: A random-neighbor sampler and a freezing criterion are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The heuristic returns the best visited solution after Metropolis acceptance and geometric cooling \(T_{k+1}=rT_k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Metropolis-type acceptance rule, a standard additive proposal construction, the infinite-inverse-temperature boundary, and commonly used—but not required—kernel conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x_n\in A$, propose $z_n$ according to $Q_n(x_n,\cdot)$ and set $\Delta_n=f(z_n)-f(x_n)$. For finite $\beta_n\ge0$, accept $z_n$ with probability $p_n=\min\{1,\exp(-\beta_n\Delta_n)\}$: if $\Delta_n\le0$, then $p_n=1$, whereas if $\Delta_n>0$, then $p_n=\exp(-\beta_n\Delta_n)>0$. A standard construction sets $z_n=x_n+\xi_n$ and resamples $\xi_n$ until $z_n\in A$. In the limiting case $\beta_n=\infty$ for every $n$, strict uphill moves are rejected and the scheme becomes Markov monotonous search. Frequently used additional choices include symmetric transition densities and $q_n(x,z)\ge c>0$ for all $n$ and $x,z\in A$; for discrete $A$, the corresponding condition is $Q_n(x,z)\ge c>0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulated annealing always accepts a non-worsening proposal and accepts a worsening proposal with probability equal to the exponential of minus the inverse-temperature parameter times the objective increase. Finite inverse temperature therefore gives worsening moves positive acceptance probability. A standard implementation adds a random perturbation and resamples when it is infeasible. Infinite inverse temperature gives monotone search. Symmetry and uniform positivity of the transition kernel are common additional choices, not defining requirements of the acceptance rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_n=\begin{cases}1,&\Delta_n\le0,\\e^{-\beta_n\Delta_n},&\Delta_n>0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An extraction-grounded adaptive random-direction heuristic labeled as modified simulated annealing. The extract specifies neither a stopping rule nor a convergence guarantee and contains undefined initial-history quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a random \(\alpha_0\in A\), set \(i=0\), \(q_0=H(\alpha_0)\), and \(\beta=\pi\). At iteration \(i\), choose a random unit vector \(v_i\in A\) whose angle with \(v_{i-1}\) does not exceed \(\beta\), and find \(\widetilde a>0\) minimizing \(F(a)=H(\alpha_i+a v_i)\). Let \(q_{i+1}=H(\alpha_i+\widetilde a v_i)\). If \(q_{i+1}\ge q_i\), replace \(\beta\) by \(\beta+\pi/8\) and resample a direction. Otherwise set \(\beta\leftarrow\beta-(\pi/8)\operatorname{sign}((q_i-q_{i+1})-(q_{i-1}-q_i))\), cap it above at \(2\pi\), accept \(\alpha_{i+1}=\alpha_i+\widetilde a v_i\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a random point with angular bound pi. Sample a random unit direction constrained by the angle to the preceding direction, minimize the objective along its positive ray, and reject any non-improving trial while widening the angular bound. After an improving trial, adjust the bound according to whether the latest improvement increased or decreased relative to the previous improvement, cap it at 2 pi, accept the new point, and repeat. No termination or convergence claim is provided.
assumptions_latex: \widetilde a\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a>0}H(\alpha_i+a v_i)\text{ exists whenever the line-search step is executed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q_{i+1}<q_i\text{ for every accepted step, and the accepted iterate and angular bound are updated by the stated rules; no stopping or convergence guarantee is asserted.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard Genetic Algorithm Cycle as Written
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The source's population-update pseudocode, preserving its apparent time-index inconsistency rather than silently correcting it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(t:=0\), initialize and evaluate \(P(t)\), and test the termination criterion. While termination has not occurred, set \(t:=t+1\), form \(Q(t):=\operatorname{SelectParents}(P(t))\), recombine and stochastically mutate \(Q(t)\), evaluate \(Q(t)\), and assign \(P(t+1):=\operatorname{Survive}(P(t),Q(t))\). As written, the first iteration refers to \(P(1)\) immediately after only \(P(0)\) has been initialized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize and evaluate population P(0). While the stopping test is false, increment the time index, select parents from the indexed population, recombine and stochastically mutate them, evaluate the resulting offspring, and select survivors to form the next indexed population. The pseudocode has an apparent off-by-one inconsistency: its first loop iteration uses P(1), although only P(0) was initialized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(t+1):=\operatorname{Survive}(P(t),Q(t));\quad\text{however, the procedure is not fully defined as written unless }P(1)\text{ is available at the first iteration or the indexing is corrected.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A differential-evolution population update for objective minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\in(0,2)\), \(CR\in(0,1)\), \(P\ge4\), and \(n\ge1\). For each target index \(i\), choose \(\bar i\) uniformly from \(\{1,ldots,n\}\) and choose distinct \(k_1,k_2,k_3\in\{1,ldots,P\}\setminus\{i\}\). Form \(\mathbf t=mathbf x_{k_1}+F(\mathbf x_{k_2}-mathbf x_{k_3})\). For each \(j\ne\bar i\), restore \(t^{(j)}=x_i^{(j)}\) when a draw from \(\mathcal U(0,1)\) exceeds \(CR\); coordinate \(\bar i\) remains from the donor vector. If \(f(\mathbf t)<f(\mathbf x_i)\), set \(\mathbf x_i\leftarrow\mathbf t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each target, create a donor from one population vector plus a scaled difference of two others. Coordinate crossover retains at least one donor coordinate, and the trial replaces the target only under strict objective improvement.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ge4\), permitting three distinct indices different from the target index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each target vector is replaced exactly when its differential-mutation and crossover trial has strictly smaller objective value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Particle-swarm iteration with inertia and attraction toward personal and shared reference positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(P>0\), \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(\omega,\phi_1,\phi_2,\beta_{\max}>0\). Initialize \(\mathbf x_i\sim\mathcal U(S)\), \(\mathbf p_i=mathbf x_i\), and \(\mathbf v_i\sim\mathcal U(W)\), and choose \(\mathbf p^\star\in\arg\min_i f(\mathbf x_i)\). While the local stopping rule is false, for each particle draw \(\beta_1,\beta_2\) from \((0,\beta_{\max})\), set \(\mathbf v_i\leftarrow\omega\mathbf v_i+beta_1\phi_1(\mathbf p_i-mathbf x_i)+beta_2\phi_2(\mathbf p^\star-mathbf x_i)\), and then set \(\mathbf x_i\leftarrow\mathbf x_i+mathbf v_i\). Retain as \(\mathbf p_i\) whichever of its old value and the new \(\mathbf x_i\) has smaller objective value. After processing the particles, rebuild the state and choose \(\mathbf p^\star\in\arg\min_i f(\mathbf x_i)\) from the current particle positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Particles move using inertia, attraction to their own retained best positions, and attraction to a shared reference selected from the current particle positions. Personal positions retain the better point, and the process continues until the local stopping rule holds.
assumptions_latex: Positions and velocities can be sampled from \(S\) and \(W\), respectively.
The objective \(f\) is minimized and the displayed finite argmin sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm generates successive states \(\{\mathbf X,\mathbf V,\mathbf P,\mathbf p^\star\}\) until the stated local stopping rule is satisfied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation accounting for fixed-size synchronous offspring generations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If initialization evaluates \(N\) individuals and each of \(T\) generations evaluates exactly \(N\) new offspring without reevaluating retained individuals, the total number of evaluations is \(N(T+1)\). More generally, if generation \(t\) evaluates \(e_t\le N\) offspring, the total is \(N+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}e_t\le N(T+1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full fixed-size generational method performs N(T+1) evaluations, with the displayed upper bound for partial offspring evaluation.
assumptions_latex: The initial population has size \(N\) and is evaluated once.
Retained unchanged individuals are not reevaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated exact count and upper bound hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Per-Generation Evaluation Count

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generational Replacement Is Not Necessarily Elitist
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes synchronous replacement from elite preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under pure replacement \(P_{t+1}=O_t\), the current best value can increase because a best member of \(P_t\) need not occur in \(O_t\). Monotonicity of the current-population minimum therefore requires elitist survival or an external archive; it does not follow from generational organization alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whole-population replacement can lose the current best individual, so synchronous generations do not imply elitism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Current-population best values need not be nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.title: Generational Replacement Is Not Necessarily Elitist

assumptions_latex: The population size is a fixed integer \(N\ge1\).
Selection and variation define probability kernels on the population space \(X^N\).
Every generated individual is evaluated by the objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update defines a Markov chain on \(X^N\), and elitist survival makes the recorded best objective value nonincreasing across generations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous population replacement with optional elitism and a fixed evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(P_0\in X^N\) and evaluate all members. At generation \(t\), sample parents \(M_t\) from a selection kernel depending on the evaluated population, generate \(N\) offspring \(O_t\) through a variation kernel, and evaluate them. A generational replacement rule sets \(P_{t+1}=O_t\); an elitist rule instead applies a survivor kernel to \(P_t\cup O_t\) while retaining at least one current best individual. Stop after a prescribed number of generations or evaluations and output the best individual ever evaluated. Conditional on \(P_t\), the selection, variation, and replacement kernels determine the distribution of \(P_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select parents, generate and evaluate an entire offspring population, then replace the current generation; elitism preserves the best value found.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generational Genetic Algorithm with Feasibility Rejection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic genetic-algorithm iteration using a prescribed population threshold and rejection of infeasible offspring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(P^0=\{x^1,\ldots,x^{\bar p}\}\), set \(k=0\). Assign fitness using \(f(x)\) to each \(x\in P^k\). To construct \(P^{k+1}\), repeatedly either select a survivor from \(P^k\), or select two parents, create an offspring by crossover, and mutate it with probability \(\gamma\). If the offspring is infeasible, discard it and repeat the selection step; otherwise declare it a survivor. Place each survivor in \(P^{k+1}\) until \(|P^{k+1}|\geq\bar p\). Then increment \(k\) and either stop or repeat the fitness step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate the current population's fitness and build the next generation by retaining selected survivors or producing offspring through parent selection and crossover. Mutate offspring with probability gamma, discard infeasible offspring, and add feasible survivors until the population threshold is reached. Then stop or begin another generation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |P^{k+1}|\geq\bar p\ \Longrightarrow\ k\leftarrow k+1\text{, followed by termination or another fitness evaluation.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity and Marginal Approximation for Fixed-Size Generational Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Markov-chain stationarity and large-population marginal approximation under a uniform minorization condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume conditions C1--C9 of Section 2.1.1 and suppose that $Q(z,dx)\ge c_2\mu(dx)$ for $\mu$-almost every $z\in A$, with $c_2>0$. Then, for every $n\ge1$, the population sequence $a_k=(x_1^{(k)},\ldots,x_n^{(k)})$, $k\ge1$, is a homogeneous Markov chain having a stationary distribution $R_n(dx_1,\ldots,dx_n)$ whose coordinates are symmetrically dependent. Moreover, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $n_*\ge1$ such that, whenever $n\ge n_*$, the marginal $R_{(n)}(dx)=R_n(dx,A,\ldots,A)$ satisfies $\|R_{(n)}-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\varepsilon$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under conditions C1–C9 and a positive uniform minorization of the transition kernel by μ, every fixed-size population process is a homogeneous Markov chain with a stationary, symmetrically dependent population distribution. As the population size grows, its one-coordinate stationary marginal becomes arbitrarily close in total variation to P.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists R_n\text{ stationary for }(a_k)_{k\ge1},\quad \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists n_*\ \forall n\ge n_*:\ \|R_n(\cdot,A,\ldots,A)-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\varepsilon.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential greedy replacement for minimization using current and perturbed populations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(P\ge 1\), a current population \(\mathbf X=(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_P)\), and a perturbed population \(\mathbf Y=(\mathbf y_1,\ldots,\mathbf y_P)\), process \(p=1,\ldots,P\) sequentially. Choose \(c\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le P}f(\mathbf x_i)\). If \(f(\mathbf y_p)<f(\mathbf x_c)\), set \(\mathbf x_c\leftarrow\mathbf y_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process the perturbed points sequentially. Each point replaces a currently worst population member exactly when it has a strictly smaller objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf X=(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_P)\) and \(\mathbf Y=(\mathbf y_1,\ldots,\mathbf y_P)\)
The objective \(f\) is minimized and is defined at all processed points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequentially modified population is returned as \(\mathbf X\leftarrow\operatorname{Select}(\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generational stochastic search in which ordered parent pairs are fitness-weighted and descendants are sampled through two-parent transition kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration $j$, construct $f_j:A\times A\to(0,\infty)$ from prior objective evaluations and define $p_{il}^{(j)}=f_j(x_i^{(j)},x_l^{(j)})/\sum_{u=1}^{n_j}\sum_{v=1}^{n_j}f_j(x_u^{(j)},x_v^{(j)})$. Generate the next population from $P_{j+1}(\cdot)=\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}\sum_{l=1}^{n_j}p_{il}^{(j)}Q_j(x_i^{(j)},x_l^{(j)},\cdot)$, where $Q_j(y,z,\cdot)$ is a probability measure on $A$. The function $f_j$ determines parent-pair selection and $Q_j$ determines their recombination and mutation into descendants; one admissible weighting is $f_j(y,z)=\exp\{-\alpha_j[f(y)+f(z)]\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign positive weights to ordered pairs of current parents and sample each descendant from the resulting mixture of two-parent transition kernels. The pair-weight function controls parent selection, while the transition kernel controls recombination and mutation; exponential weighting by the sum of the parents' objective values is one natural choice.
assumptions_latex: Q_j(y,z,\cdot)\text{ is a probability measure on }A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between retention and global reachability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Elitist survival preserves the best evaluated value but does not ensure discovery of better points. If a strict suboptimal class of population states is closed under selection, variation, and survival, a search initialized in that class cannot reach a global minimizer outside it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elite preservation cannot overcome a variation mechanism trapped in a suboptimal population class.
assumptions_latex: A strict suboptimal set of population states is closed under the selection, variation, and survival kernels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Initialization in that closed class prevents global convergence to minimizers outside it.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b_t=\min\{f(x):x\text{ has been evaluated through iteration }t\}\). Then \(b_{t+1}\le b_t\). If survival retains a candidate attaining the current population minimum, then \(\min_{x\in P_{t+1}}f(x)\le\min_{x\in P_t}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An archive is always monotone, while monotonicity of the current population requires elitist survival.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General evolutionary search template encompassing generational and steady-state replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize and evaluate a finite population \(P_0\). At iteration \(t\), sample one or more parents with probabilities determined by a selection rule, apply recombination kernel \(C\) and mutation kernel \(M\) to obtain offspring, evaluate the offspring, and form \(P_{t+1}\) using a specified survival rule. The survival rule may replace the whole population or only selected members and may preserve elites. Continue until an evaluation budget or stated stopping predicate is met, then output \(x_{\mathrm{best}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{f(x):x\text{ was evaluated}\}\). Global-convergence claims additionally require an exploration condition ensuring continued access to every relevant region of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterate fitness-based selection, recombination, mutation, evaluation, and survival, returning the best candidate ever evaluated; convergence needs persistent global exploration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population-based evolutionary search, its principal variation operators, and the extraction's sampling-density boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An evolutionary algorithm searches using a population of candidate solutions rather than a single point. At each iteration, fitness-dependent reproduction copies candidates into a new population, crossover exchanges binary sections between two candidates, and mutation randomly changes a small part of a candidate. Mutation enables movement into previously unexplored regions. The method may be well suited to highly nonlinear discrete problems; for continuous variables, a finite random population may be too sparse to reach a global minimizer. A larger initial population is described as increasing the probability of finding the desired solution while increasing computational time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evolutionary algorithms search with a population. They use fitness-dependent reproduction, crossover of binary sections, and random mutation. Mutation helps explore new regions. The extract identifies highly nonlinear discrete problems as a favorable setting and warns that finite sampling may be too sparse in continuous domains; larger populations may improve discovery probability but require more computation.
assumptions_latex: \text{The search maintains a population of candidate solutions.}
\text{Fitness is determined by an objective or penalty-function value.}
\text{The described crossover operator applies to binary-encoded sections.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Reproduction, crossover, and mutation generate population search, with an extraction-stated tradeoff between sampling coverage and computational cost.}

children.title: Population Diversity Control
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms preserving exploratory variation within a search population.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A checkable survivor operator enforcing minimum metric separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order a finite evaluated candidate pool by nondecreasing objective value with deterministic tie breaking. Scan in that order and accept \(x\) only if \(\rho(x,z)>r\) for every previously accepted survivor \(z\), stopping at the survivor capacity. The accepted set is pairwise more than \(r\) apart and contains the best-ranked candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy survivor selection retains the best candidate and rejects later candidates lying within a chosen radius of an accepted survivor.
assumptions_latex: The candidate pool is finite and totally ordered by fitness and tie breaking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted survivors are pairwise separated by more than \(r\), and the first-ranked candidate is retained.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Distance-Separated Survivor Selection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diversity Alone Does Not Ensure Global Exploration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates population spread from reachability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive within-population diversity statistic does not imply access to every region of \(X\). A transition can preserve pairwise separation while keeping all members in a strict suboptimal invariant subset \(S\subset X\). Hence diversity control alone implies neither irreducibility nor global convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A population can remain diverse inside a suboptimal invariant region, so diversity is not a substitute for global reachability.
assumptions_latex: A strict suboptimal subset \(S\) is closed under the population transition.
The diversity requirement is feasible within \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diversity requirement can hold indefinitely without reaching a global minimizer outside \(S\).
knowledge_statements.title: Diversity Alone Does Not Ensure Global Exploration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct metric-space summaries used by diversity controls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) in \((X,\rho)\), define \[\delta_{\min}(P)=\min_{i<j}\rho(x_i,x_j),\quad \Delta(P)=\frac{2}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i<j}\rho(x_i,x_j),\quad R(P)=\max_i\rho(x_i,c(P)).\] These statistics are generally inequivalent; for example, duplicate points and one distant outlier can give \(\delta_{\min}(P)=0\) while \(R(P)\) is large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum separation, mean pairwise distance, and radius measure different aspects of diversity and are not interchangeable.
assumptions_latex: The center rule \(c(P)\) is declared when radius is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed statistics are well-defined and generally inequivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Common Population-Diversity Statistics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Packing Feasibility of a Separation Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility test for a minimum-distance population constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a metric space (X,\rho) and r\ge0, define M_r(X)=\sup\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \rho(x,z)>r\text{ for all distinct }x,z\in S\}. A population of N members satisfying \delta_{\min}(P)>r exists if and only if N\le M_r(X). Consequently, no enforcement operator can guarantee such a population when N>M_r(X).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-separation threshold is feasible exactly when the domain's packing number at that radius is at least the requested population size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists P\in X^N:\delta_{\min}(P)>r\iff N\le M_r(X).

notation.meaning: maximum attainable cardinality of an r-separated subset

knowledge_statements.title: Packing Feasibility of a Separation Threshold

assumptions_latex: The population is \(P=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\in X^N\) in a metric space \((X,\rho)\).
A diversity statistic and admissible range are fixed before the update.
The control operator can reject, repair, or replace candidates without altering already recorded evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted population satisfies the prescribed diversity constraint, while any elitist implementation can simultaneously retain a best-so-far individual.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A checkable pairwise-distance diversity constraint with rejection or repair enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(N\ge2\), define the mean pairwise diversity \(\Delta(P)=\frac{2}{N(N-1)}\sum_{1\le i<j\le N}\rho(x_i,x_j)\). At iteration \(t\), a population satisfies the diversity-control condition when \(\Delta(P_t)\ge\delta_t\), where \(\delta_t\) is a prescribed nonnegative threshold. Given a proposed population \(P'_t\), accept it only if the condition holds; otherwise apply a specified repair or replacement operator until the inequality holds or a declared failure limit is reached. An elitist repair must retain at least one member attaining the best objective value previously recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Require population mean pairwise distance to exceed a chosen threshold, repairing or rejecting populations that violate it while optionally preserving an elite.
knowledge_statements.title: Population Diversity Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is cited. A prescribed threshold can be infeasible for the metric space and population size, so repair need not produce an accepted population; the conclusion needs an explicit feasibility or conditional-success hypothesis. The record also mixes a diversity condition with an enforcement algorithm, making the selected condition kind only partially aligned.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population replacement combining nearest-neighbor competition with a dissimilarity threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(P\ge1\), \(\mathbf X=(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_P)\), \(\mathbf Y=(\mathbf y_1,\ldots,\mathbf y_P)\), and \(D_{\mathrm{cut}}\ge0\), process \(p=1,ldots,P\) sequentially. Choose \(c\in\arg\min_{1\le i\le P}d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf y_p)\). If \(d(\mathbf x_c,\mathbf y_p)>D_{\mathrm{cut}}\), choose instead \(c\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le P}f(\mathbf x_i)\). Replace \(\mathbf x_c\) by \(\mathbf y_p\) if and only if \(f(\mathbf y_p)<f(\mathbf x_c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbed point competes with its nearest population member when it lies within the threshold; otherwise it competes with a currently worst member. It replaces that member only under strict objective improvement.
assumptions_latex: The distance \(d\) and objective \(f\) are defined at all processed points, and \(f\) is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequentially modified \(\mathbf X\) is the threshold-dependent selection \(\operatorname{Select}(\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dissimilarity-Based PBH Selection with Population Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-controlled population updating that can append sufficiently dissimilar improving candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current population \(\mathbf X=(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_P)\), candidates \(Y\), and \(D_{\mathrm{cut}}\ge0\), process each \(\mathbf y\in Y\) using the current value of \(P\). Choose \(c\in\arg\min_{1\le i\le P}d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf y)\). If \(d(\mathbf x_c,\mathbf y)>D_{\mathrm{cut}}\), choose \(c\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le P}f(\mathbf x_i)\); when \(f(\mathbf y)<f(\mathbf x_c)\), set \(P\leftarrow P+1\) and append \(\mathbf x_P=mathbf y\). Otherwise, if the nearest member is within the threshold and \(f(\mathbf y)<f(\mathbf x_c)\), replace \(\mathbf x_c\leftarrow\mathbf y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearby improving candidate replaces its nearest member. A candidate beyond the threshold is appended, rather than substituted, when it improves on the current worst objective value.
assumptions_latex: The initial population size satisfies \(P\ge1\) and may increase during processing.
The distance \(d\) and objective \(f\) are defined at all processed points, and \(f\) is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update combines local replacement with conditional population growth for sufficiently dissimilar candidates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dynamic Niching Selection for Population Diversity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cluster-geometry specialization of population-diversity control; the broader genetic and local-search procedure is outside this node's ownership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a pool containing locally optimized offspring and unchanged parents, order candidates by increasing energy. Traverse the ordered pool and admit a candidate to the next fixed-size generation when its geometry is sufficiently distinct from previously selected candidates, thereby opening a dynamic niche. A geometrically similar candidate may also be admitted while the niche remains below its capacity and its energy is sufficiently separated from existing niche members. Reserve a niche for mutants to maintain exploration, and continue until the population is full. Niches exist only during selection, may change between generations, and are determined by prescribed geometry-dependent widths and capacity limits rather than by a fixed number of niches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order the pool of locally optimized offspring and unchanged parents by increasing energy. Select candidates into the next fixed-size generation using geometry-based dynamic niches. A distinct candidate opens a niche; a similar candidate is accepted only while that niche has capacity and its energy is sufficiently separated from those already admitted. A reserved mutant niche maintains some exploration. The niches exist only during selection, their number can vary between generations, and their criteria depend on the cluster class.
assumptions_latex: \text{A finite candidate pool of locally optimized cluster geometries and their energies is available.}
\text{Geometric-similarity criteria, niche widths, niche capacities, and an energy-separation threshold are specified.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The selection mechanism produces a fixed-size population with explicit geometric-diversity controls, but it supplies neither a global-optimality guarantee nor a reliable stopping certificate.}

children.title: Selection-Pressure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Behavior associated with weak, balanced, or aggressive population selection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Premature-convergence boundary when nonbest parents receive zero probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If selection assigns zero probability to every nonbest candidate and variation from current best candidates is confined to a strict reachable subset, then a global minimizer outside that subset has zero discovery probability. Increasing selection pressure is therefore not necessarily a monotone improvement in global-search reliability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting only current best candidates can eliminate material needed to reach better basins when variation lacks independent global support.
assumptions_latex: Nonbest candidates receive zero parent-selection probability.
Variation from current best candidates is confined to a strict reachable subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global minimizer outside that subset cannot be discovered.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Pressure Can Destroy Exploration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Pressure Is Invariant to Objective-Gap Magnitude
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes rank-based from magnitude-sensitive selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed ranks, tournament-selection probabilities are unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of objective values. Thus tournament pressure cannot distinguish populations with identical rankings but different objective gaps, whereas magnitude-based rules generally can.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tournament selection responds to ranks, not to the sizes of objective gaps.
assumptions_latex: The transformation preserves the candidates' total rank order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tournament-selection probabilities are unchanged when only objective-gap magnitudes change.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Pressure Is Invariant to Objective-Gap Magnitude

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank-based pressure parameterization for tournaments sampled with replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rank \(N\) candidates from best to worst. Draw \(k\ge1\) ranks independently and uniformly with replacement and select the best sampled rank. Then \[p_r(k)=\left(\frac{N-r+1}{N}\right)^k-\left(\frac{N-r}{N}\right)^k.\] Thus \(k=1\) is uniform selection, while the best-rank probability \(1-(1-1/N)^k\) increases with \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tournament size parameterizes rank pressure: size one is uniform, and larger tournaments increasingly favor better ranks.
assumptions_latex: \(N\ge1\) candidates have a deterministic total rank order.
Tournament draws are independent, uniform, and with replacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed formula gives the rank-selection probabilities, and the best-rank probability is nondecreasing in \(k\).
knowledge_statements.title: Tournament-Selection Pressure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-independent comparison of rank-based parent-selection pressure; informal regime labels still require a declared family or threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Rank \(N\) candidates from best to worst, and let \(p_r^A\) and \(p_r^B\) be their parent-selection probabilities under rules \(A\) and \(B\). Rule \(A\) has at least as much rank-selection pressure as \(B\) when \[\sum_{r=1}^{m}p_r^A\geq\sum_{r=1}^{m}p_r^B\qquad(m=1,\ldots,N).\] Dominance is strict if at least one inequality is strict. Uniform rank selection is a neutral reference, deterministic selection of rank one is maximal in this order, and rules unrelated by these inequalities have incomparable rank-pressure profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-based rule exerts greater selection pressure when it assigns at least as much probability to every top-ranked prefix.
assumptions_latex: The population has \(N\geq1\) candidates with a deterministic total rank order.
Each rule defines a probability distribution over ranks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cumulative-prefix inequalities define a partial order of rank-selection pressure; best-only selection is maximal, while some rules are incomparable.

notation.meaning: Probability that rule A selects rank r

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Distribution Ordering of Selection Pressure

assumptions_latex: A population contains candidates with finite objective values \(f_1,ldots,f_N\).
Parent selection uses Boltzmann weights with inverse-selection parameter \(\beta\ge0\).
All candidates with finite objective values receive positive selection probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\beta=0\) selection is uniform; finite \(\beta>0\) gives soft selection; and \(\beta\to\infty\) concentrates probability on the current minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boltzmann selection provides a precise weak-to-strong pressure parameterization for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For objective values \(f_1,ldots,f_N\), define \(p_i(\beta)=\exp(-\beta f_i)/\sum_{j=1}^N\exp(-\beta f_j)\). The selection-pressure ratio between candidates \(i\) and \(j\) is \(p_i(\beta)/p_j(\beta)=\exp(\beta(f_j-f_i))\). The regime \(\beta=0\) is neutral selection, since \(p_i(0)=1/N\). Finite \(\beta>0\) is soft fitness-biased selection, with every candidate retaining positive probability. As \(\beta\to\infty\), total probability concentrates uniformly on the indices attaining \(\min_j f_j\), defining the limiting maximal-pressure regime. Thus increasing \(\beta\) monotonically amplifies every fixed favorable objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boltzmann selection ranges from uniform sampling at zero pressure to concentration on current best candidates as inverse temperature grows.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Pressure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for choosing Boltzmann selection as the representation of this regime leaf. Both the assumptions and statement contain malformed LaTeX, writing `ldots` instead of \(\ldots\). Because the record parameterizes and characterizes regimes rather than imposing a condition, representation or property is a better exact kind than condition.

children.title: Statistical-Model-Based Search

children.title: Random-Process Models
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for process-based statistical search models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: An Incomplete Search State Need Not Be Markov
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-sufficiency boundary for adaptive process models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a next-step rule uses transition-relevant information not measurable with respect to the declared current state, then the declared state process need not be Markov. Including all such information in an augmented state restores the Markov representation when the conditional laws are kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search state is Markov only when it contains every history variable used by the transition rule.
assumptions_latex: At least one transition-relevant history variable is absent from the declared state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declared state can fail to be Markov, while a transition-sufficient augmented state is Markov.
knowledge_statements.title: An Incomplete Search State Need Not Be Markov

knowledge_statements.scope_note: State augmentation for a history-dependent discrete-time search process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the next-step law of \(S_{n+1}\) be a probability kernel \(Q_n(\cdot\mid H_n)\) depending on \(H_n=(S_0,\ldots,S_n)\). Defining \(Z_n=H_n\) yields a Markov process whose transition kernel appends a draw from \(Q_n(\cdot\mid Z_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A history-dependent search becomes Markov after its state is augmented with all transition-relevant history.
assumptions_latex: Search variables and finite histories have measurable state spaces.
Each next-step conditional law is represented by a probability kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented history process \((Z_n)\) is Markov.

notation.meaning: Complete search history through iteration n

knowledge_statements.title: History-State Markovization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Kernel Construction of a Discrete-Time Search Process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness in law from an initial distribution and history-dependent transition kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (S,\mathcal S) be a measurable space, let \mu_0 be a probability measure on it, and for each n\ge0 let Q_n(\cdot\mid s_0,\ldots,s_n) be a probability kernel from (S^{n+1},\mathcal S^{\otimes(n+1)}) to (S,\mathcal S). Then there is a unique probability measure on (S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) whose initial law is \mu_0 and whose successive conditional laws are Q_n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An initial law and measurable history-dependent kernels uniquely determine the law of a discrete-time search process.
assumptions_latex: (S,\mathcal S) is a measurable state space.
\mu_0 is a probability measure on (S,\mathcal S).
Each Q_n is a probability kernel on the declared finite-history space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A unique path-space probability law realizes the specified process}.
knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Construction of a Discrete-Time Search Process

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty and \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is the objective.
\((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) carries an increasing filtration \((\mathcal F_n)_{n\geq 0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The process model specifies the conditional law used to generate and assess the next search state.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time stochastic-process model for adaptive global search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random-process search model is an adapted stochastic process \((Z_n)_{n\geq 0}\), where \(Z_n\) contains the sampled points, observed objective values, and incumbent after iteration \(n\). Its evolution is specified by probability kernels \(K_n\) satisfying \[\mathbb P(Z_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K_n(Z_n,A)\] for every measurable state set \(A\). The kernel may depend on all accumulated information, so the model includes independent random search, history-dependent sampling, and stochastic transitions followed by local optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-process model represents global search as an adapted sequence whose conditional transition law may depend on all observations and incumbents collected so far.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Process Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the process-model container, but no citation is supplied. The measurable state space of Z_n is not specified, and K_n(Z_n,A) is Markov in the stated state even though the prose says the kernel may depend on all accumulated information; a source and a precise state/history formulation are required.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_K\) be intervals governed by a comparative-probability relation satisfying (A1.1)--(A1.5). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation on the field of finite unions of intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let comparative probability on intervals satisfy (A1.1)--(A1.5), and extend it to the field of finite unions of intervals by (A1.6). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axioms for a weak preference relation \(\succcurlyeq\), with strict and indifferent parts \(\succ\) and \(\sim\), on intervals or associated measurable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary intervals, assume: (i) completeness, \(Y_1\succcurlyeq Y_2\) or \(Y_2\succcurlyeq Y_1\); (ii) transitivity; (iii) \(Y\succ\varnothing\iff\mu(Y\cap U)>0\), and \(Y\sim Y\cup X\) whenever \(\mu(X)=0\); (iv) if \(Y_1\cap Y_2=Y_1\cap Y_3=\varnothing\) and \(\bar Y_1\cap\bar Y_2\ne\varnothing\), \(\bar Y_1\cap\bar Y_3\ne\varnothing\), then \(Y_2\succcurlyeq Y_3\iff \bar Y_1\cup Y_2\succcurlyeq\bar Y_1\cup Y_3\); and (v) if \(Y_1\succ Y_2\succ\varnothing\), then there exist \(z_1,z_2\) with \(y_1'<z_i<y_1''\) for \(i=1,2\) such that \((y_1',z_1)\sim(z_2,y_1'')\sim Y_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The comparative-probability relation is complete and transitive, detects positive Lebesgue measure, ignores null-set additions, is invariant under the stated common-set union operation, and satisfies an interval solvability condition for every set strictly between an interval and the empty set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Axioms (A1.1)--(A1.5) hold for }\succcurlyeq.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-dependent comparison of the smallest sampled subintervals containing two points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\delta(n,x)\) denote the smallest subinterval containing \(x\) after \(n\) minimization steps. For the Wiener-process P-algorithm,
\[\frac12\left(\frac{f(x)-m+\epsilon}{f(z)-m+\epsilon}\right)^2\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\delta(n,x)}{\delta(n,z)}\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\delta(n,x)}{\delta(n,z)}\le2\left(\frac{f(x)-m+\epsilon}{f(z)-m+\epsilon}\right)^2.\]
For the smooth-function-model P-algorithm,
\[\frac12\sqrt{\frac{f(x)-m+\epsilon}{f(z)-m+\epsilon}}\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\delta(n,x)}{\delta(n,z)}\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\delta(n,x)}{\delta(n,z)}\le2\sqrt{\frac{f(x)-m+\epsilon}{f(z)-m+\epsilon}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymptotic ratio of the smallest subintervals containing two points is bounded within a factor of two of a model-dependent power of their regularized objective gaps: power two for the Wiener model and power one-half for the smooth-function model.
assumptions_latex: \delta(n,x)\text{ is the smallest subinterval containing }x\text{ after }n\text{ steps}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\delta(n,x)}{\delta(n,z)}\text{ satisfies the stated liminf and limsup bounds for each model.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the equivalent simplified priority score and next-observation location.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration $n$, select an interval $(x_{i-1}^n,x_i^n)$ maximizing
\[
\gamma_i^n=\frac{(x_i^n-x_{i-1}^n)^2\tau_i(1-\tau_i)}{y_i^n\tau_i+y_{i-1}^n(1-\tau_i)-y_{0n}+\epsilon}.
\]
Because $\Phi$ is increasing, this selection is equivalently obtained by maximizing
\[
\gamma_i^n=\frac{x_i^n-x_{i-1}^n}{\sqrt{y_i^n-y_{0n}+\epsilon}+\sqrt{y_{i-1}^n-y_{0n}+\epsilon}}.
\]
The next objective observation is taken in the selected interval at $t_i=x_{i-1}^n+\tau_i(x_i^n-x_{i-1}^n)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the interval with the largest P-algorithm priority score, equivalently its simplified square-root form, and evaluate the objective at the model maximizer t_i in that interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i_n\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i\gamma_i^n,\qquad x_{n+1}=t_{i_n}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique interval maximizer of the P-algorithm model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the maximizer used to choose the next P-algorithm observation within a sampled interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On the interval $[x_{i-1}^n,x_i^n]$, the function $P_n(x)$ has a unique local maximum, attained at $t_i=x_{i-1}^n+\tau_i(x_i^n-x_{i-1}^n)$, where
\[
\tau_i=\frac{\Delta_{ni}}{\Delta_{n,i-1}+\sqrt{\Delta_{n,i-1}^2+(y_i^n-y_{i-1}^n)\Delta_{n,i-1}}},\qquad
\Delta_{ni}=y_{i-1}^n-y_{0n}+\epsilon.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On each sampled interval, the P-algorithm model has a unique local maximum at the stated interpolation point t_i, with interpolation coefficient tau_i given by the displayed formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in[x_{i-1}^n,x_i^n]}^{\mathrm{local}}P_n(x)=\{t_i\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validity of a Second-Order Random-Field Kernel
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient covariance-kernel condition for a real second-order field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric function \(k:D\times D\to\mathbb R\) is the covariance kernel of a real second-order random field indexed by \(D\) if and only if, for every \(n\ge1\), \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in D\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\sum_{i,j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric function is a valid covariance kernel exactly when every finite Gram matrix is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\) is a covariance kernel if and only if all its finite Gram matrices are positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Validity of a Second-Order Random-Field Kernel

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean and Covariance Do Not Determine a General Field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability boundary between Gaussian and general second-order fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two second-order random fields can have identical mean and covariance functions but different finite-dimensional distributions. Thus \((m,k)\) alone need not determine a field law or its conditional laws; it does determine a Gaussian field law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean and covariance determine a Gaussian field but generally do not determine a non-Gaussian field or its posterior.
assumptions_latex: The compared fields have finite second moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality of first and second moments need not imply equality of field laws outside an identifying family such as the Gaussian family.
knowledge_statements.title: Mean and Covariance Do Not Determine a General Field

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise conditional law under independent Gaussian observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a Gaussian field with mean \(m\) and covariance \(k\). For \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), let \(y=F_X+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) is independent of \(F\). If \(K+\Sigma\) is nonsingular, then \[F(x)\mid y\sim N\!\left(m(x)+k_X(x)^\top(K+\Sigma)^{-1}(y-m_X),\ k(x,x)-k_X(x)^\top(K+\Sigma)^{-1}k_X(x)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian-field conditioning gives explicit posterior means and variances from the covariance and noise matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is Gaussian with mean \(m\) and covariance \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed normal distribution is the conditional pointwise law of \(F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Gaussian-Field Conditioning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation-invariant spatial dependence for a second-order real random field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order field on D\subseteq\mathbb R^d is weakly stationary when \mathbb E[F(x)]=\mu and \operatorname{Cov}(F(x),F(x+h))=C(h) whenever both sites lie in D. Its semivariogram satisfies \gamma(h)=\tfrac12\mathbb E[(F(x+h)-F(x))^2]=C(0)-C(h). Isotropy imposes the additional restriction C(h)=c(\|h\|).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weakly stationary field, covariance depends only on displacement and the semivariogram equals covariance loss from zero lag; isotropy additionally removes directional dependence.
assumptions_latex: Both x and x+h belong to D.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma(h)=C(0)-C(h),\qquad C(h)=c(\|h\|)\text{ under isotropy}.

notation.meaning: stationary covariance function at displacement h

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Stationarity and Variogram Relation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Laws Determine a Random Field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Law-level characterization of a real-valued random field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an index set D, the law of F=(F(x))_{x\in D} on (\mathbb R^D,\mathcal C), where \mathcal C is the cylinder \sigma-algebra, is uniquely determined by all finite-dimensional distributions \mathcal L(F(x_1),\ldots,F(x_n)). Conversely, every projectively consistent family of such finite-dimensional probability laws defines a unique field law on \mathcal C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-field law is exactly encoded by a projectively consistent collection of finite-dimensional distributions.
assumptions_latex: The finite-dimensional laws are permutation-compatible and consistent under marginalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{There is a unique law on }(\mathbb R^D,\mathcal C)\text{ with the prescribed finite-dimensional distributions}.

notation.meaning: cylinder sigma-algebra on the coordinate space

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Laws Determine a Random Field

assumptions_latex: The objective is observed at finitely many sampled locations, possibly with noise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioning the field on observations yields a spatial surrogate distribution over objective values on \(D\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spatial stochastic surrogate for an unknown continuous objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random-field model for an objective on \(D\) is a collection \(\{F(x):x\in D\}\) of jointly distributed random variables. In a second-order model, \[m(x)=\mathbb E[F(x)],\qquad k(x,x')=\operatorname{Cov}(F(x),F(x'))\] specify its mean and spatial dependence. Given observations \(Y_i=F(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), conditioning on \(\{(x_i,Y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) produces a posterior or conditional field whose pointwise distributions quantify predicted objective values and uncertainty throughout \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-field model assigns jointly distributed objective values across the domain and conditions that spatial model on sampled, possibly noisy observations.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Field Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global incumbent-value convergence of the Gaussian random-field P-algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded convergence theorem whose numbered model conditions are defined in the surrounding source; the conclusion concerns incumbent objective values, not necessarily convergence of iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:A\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, where \(A\subset\mathbb R^n\) is compact. Suppose the Gaussian family \(\{\xi_x:x\in A\}\) has characteristics satisfying (6.14), (6.18), (6.16), and (6.19), with
\[
0<\gamma^-\leq\gamma_k\leq\gamma^+<\infty,
\qquad
z_{ok}<\min_{x\in A}m_k(x,\cdot).
\]
Condition (6.16) may instead be replaced by continuity in \(x\) of the weights \(w_i^k(x,\cdot)\) and the following concentration condition: if \(z\) is a cluster point of a sequence \((z_i)\subset A\), then for every \(\epsilon\) satisfying \(\delta_0<\epsilon<1\) and every \(\delta>0\), there exists \(N\) such that, for all \(k\geq N\),
\[
\sum_{i\in I(z,\delta)}w_i^k\!\left(z,(z_j)_{j=1}^k\right)>1-\epsilon,
\qquad
I(z,\delta)=\{i\leq k:\lVert z-z_i\rVert<\delta\}.
\]
Then
\[
y_{ok}:=\min_{1\leq i\leq k}y_i\longrightarrow\min_{x\in A}f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous objective on a compact feasible set, the P-algorithm's best observed value converges to the global minimum when the stated Gaussian-model, bounded-parameter, threshold, and weight-concentration conditions hold.
assumptions_latex: A\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is compact and }f:A\to\mathbb R\text{ is continuous}
\{\xi_x:x\in A\}\text{ is a Gaussian family satisfying (6.14), (6.18), (6.16), and (6.19), or the stated replacement for (6.16)}
\forall z,\epsilon,\delta\text{ as stated},\ \exists N\ \forall k\geq N:\ \sum_{i\in I(z,\delta)}w_i^k\!\left(z,(z_j)_{j=1}^k\right)>1-\epsilon
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y_{ok}=\min_{1\leq i\leq k}y_i\longrightarrow\min_{x\in A}f(x)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity property of the unique interior maximizer of a smooth random-field acquisition criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

 i=1,\ldots,k)\right|_{x=x_{n+1}}<0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the acquisition criterion has a unique interior maximizer for every threshold and the posterior mean and standard deviation are twice differentiable, the derivative of the maximizing point with respect to the threshold has a negative inner product with the posterior-standard-deviation gradient at that point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting Exploitation and Exploration of the Probability Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes two limiting regimes of a random-field probability criterion; arg-extrema are understood as compatible selected optimizers when nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
\widetilde y_{on}=\min_{x\in A}m_n(x\mid x_i,y_i,
 i=1,\ldots,n)
\]
and
\[
\frac{\widetilde y_{on}-m_n(x\mid x_j,y_j,
 j=1,\ldots,k)}{s_n(x\mid x_j,y_j,
 j=1,\ldots,k)}\to0
\quad\text{as }x\to\arg\min_{z\in A}m_n(z\mid\cdot).
\]
Then
\[
\arg\max_{x\in A}\phi(x,\widetilde y_{on})=\arg\min_{x\in A}m_n(x\mid\cdot).
\]
Moreover, as \(\widetilde y_{on}\to-\infty\),
\[
\left\|\arg\max_{x\in A}\phi(x,\widetilde y_{on})-\arg\max_{x\in A}s_n(x\mid x_j,y_j,
 j=1,\ldots,k)\right\|\to0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the target equals the minimum posterior mean and the standardized target gap vanishes near a posterior-mean minimizer, maximizing the probability criterion selects that minimizer. As the target tends to minus infinity, the criterion's maximizer approaches a point of maximal posterior uncertainty.
assumptions_latex:
\frac{\widetilde y_{on}-m_n(x\mid x_j,y_j,
 j=1,\ldots,k)}{s_n(x\mid x_j,y_j,
 j=1,\ldots,k)}\to0\text{ as }x\to\arg\min_{z\in A}m_n(z\mid\cdot)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \arg\max_{x\in A}\phi(x,\widetilde y_{on})=\arg\min_{x\in A}m_n(x\mid\cdot),\qquad \operatorname{dist}\!\left(\arg\max\phi,\arg\max s_n\right)\to0\text{ as }\widetilde y_{on}\to-\infty

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step P-algorithm rule for statistical-model-based global minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y_{on}=\min_{1\le i\le n}y_i\) and choose \(\widetilde y_{on}<y_{on}\), for example \(\widetilde y_{on}=y_{on}-\varepsilon_n\) with \(\varepsilon_n>0\). A method compatible with the stated rationality axioms selects
\[
x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in A}\Pr\!\left\{\xi(x)\le \widetilde y_{on}\mid \xi(x_i)=y_i,\ i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.
\]
Under a conditionally Gaussian model, at points where \(s_n(x)>0\), the same maximizers are obtained from
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in A}\frac{\widetilde y_{on}-m_n(x\mid\mathcal D_n)}{s_n(x\mid\mathcal D_n)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the next observation point by maximizing the posterior probability that the objective falls below a target smaller than the best observed value. For a conditional Gaussian model with positive posterior standard deviation, this is equivalent to maximizing the standardized target-minus-mean criterion.
assumptions_latex: \text{The method satisfies the referenced rationality axioms}
\xi(x)\mid\mathcal D_n\text{ is Gaussian for the standardized representation}
s_n(x\mid\mathcal D_n)>0\text{ at points where the ratio is evaluated}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Multistart Is Not a Global Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates finite confidence from deterministic certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<p<1\), every finite run has positive miss probability \((1-p)^N\). Thus the best returned local minimizer and its local optimality conditions do not certify global optimality. A confidence claim requires a justified lower bound on \(p\), while deterministic certification requires an independent global bound or exhaustive argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite multistart is not a deterministic global certificate, and even probabilistic confidence requires a justified basin-mass bound.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many independent starts are run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incumbent is not certified globally optimal by multistart alone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when repeated starts do not imply eventual global discovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mu(G)=0\), countably many independent starts hit \(G\) with probability zero. Positive marginal mass is also insufficient under arbitrary dependence: if \(X_n=X_1\) for every \(n\), eventual success probability is only \(\mu(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-mass basins are never hit, and dependent repetition can defeat eventual success despite positive marginal basin mass.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the set of starts whose local solves reach a global solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither \(\mu(G)=0\) nor arbitrary dependence supports almost-sure discovery.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact success law for independent starts followed by a fixed local solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\{x\in D:L(x)\in M^\star\}\) be measurable and let \(p=\mu(G)\). For independent \(X_i\sim\mu\), \[\Pr\{\exists i\le N:L(X_i)\in M^\star\}=1-(1-p)^N.\] If \(0<p<1\), failure probability at most \(\alpha\) is ensured by \(N\ge\lceil\log(\alpha)/\log(1-p)\rceil\); if \(p>0\), eventual success has probability one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With global-basin mass p, N independent starts succeed with probability one minus (1-p) to the N.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\exists i\le N:L(X_i)\in M^\star)=1-(1-p)^N\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a run limit \(N\). For \(k=1,\ldots,N\), draw \(X_k\sim\mu\), compute \(Y_k=L(X_k)\), and update \[x_k^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\{Y_1,\ldots,Y_k\}}f(y).\] The algorithm stops after \(N\) local solves, or earlier under a prescribed budget or target-value rule, and outputs \(x_k^*\). If every neighborhood of every global minimizer has positive \(\mu\)-measure and such a neighborhood lies in its local basin, the probability of missing that basin after \(N\) starts tends to zero as \(N\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Low-discrepancy sampling with a clustering radius and objective-dominance screening before local optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(Q=S=\varnothing\), \(k=1\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). Until a prescribed termination condition holds, take the next Sobol point \(q_k\), record \((q_k,f(q_k))\) in \(Q\), and choose a clustering radius \(r_k\), for example \(r_k=\beta k^{-1/n}\).
