If the local solve returns \(y\notin S\), add \(y\) to \(S\). Increment \(k\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process Sobol points sequentially. Start a local solve from a sample only when no sufficiently better earlier sample lies within its clustering radius, and store each newly found local solution. Continue until the prescribed stopping condition holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-Solver Basins and Exact Basin Labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the objects identified by clustering multistart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a deterministic local-solver map \(L:D\to M=L(D)\), the attraction basin of \(y\in M\) is \(B_y=L^{-1}(\{y\})\). The relation \(x\sim_L z\iff L(x)=L(z)\) is an equivalence relation whose nonempty classes are the basins. An exact basin label \(c\) satisfies \(c(x)=c(z)\iff L(x)=L(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic local solver partitions its starting domain into basins, and an exact basin label identifies starts having the same terminal solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safety boundary for geometric duplicate suppression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If one cluster contains \(x,z\) with \(L(x)\ne L(z)\), retaining only one representative can remove one attainable terminal solution. If \(L(z)\) is globally optimal but \(x\) is retained, suppression can lose the only sampled global-basin start. Geometric proximity alone therefore does not establish basin equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merging distinct true basins can suppress the only start leading to a global solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One-representative suppression need not preserve \(L(S)\) or a sampled global-basin hit.

Solving one representative from every nonempty cluster \(c^{-1}(i)\) returns exactly the set \(L(S)\). The reverse implication is unnecessary for safety; its failure only leaves redundant solves.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One solve per nonempty cluster recovers exactly \(L(S)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic clustering multistart scheme; cluster geometry is intentionally parameterized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\) and no incumbent. At stage \(k\), sample a finite set \(S_k\subset D\), rank its points by objective value, and assign each point to a cluster using the prescribed distance or connectivity rule. For each selected representative \(r\) not assigned to an explored cluster, compute \(y=L(r)\), record \(y\), and augment \(\mathcal C_k\) with the cluster associated with its attraction basin. Update the incumbent to the recorded point of smallest objective value. Stop at the sampling or local-solve budget and return that incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clustering multistart groups sampled points into prospective basins and launches local optimization only from representatives of basins not already explored.

The statement also moves from clusters defined by an arbitrary distance or connectivity rule to a cluster associated with an attraction basin without defining or justifying that correspondence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-better suppression multistart with estimated-minima stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized multistart method that suppresses local searches near better samples and stops when the estimated number of minima is nearly exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose $N^*,\gamma,\sigma$ and initialize the discovered stationary-point set $X^*$. Draw $N^*$ random points, retain the fraction $\gamma$ with lowest objective values, and set $k=\gamma N^*$. For each new retained point $x_i$, start a local optimizer unless there exists a sampled point $x_j$ such that $f(x_j)<f(x_i)$ and $\|x_j-x_i\|\le r_k$. Add every newly encountered stationary point to $X^*$. If the estimated number of minima $\widehat w$ and the number $w$ of distinct minima found satisfy $\widehat w-w<0.5$, stop; otherwise sample another point, increment $k$, and repeat the suppression and local-search step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain the best fraction of a random sample. Start local optimization from a retained point only when no better sampled point lies within the current critical radius. Record new stationary points, and stop when the estimated total number of minima exceeds the number already found by less than one half.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian-metric single-linkage clustering for multistart search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basin-oriented clustering using local Hessian geometry, an approximate nearest-neighbor threshold under uniform sampling, and gradient-direction checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cluster seeded by a local minimum $x_i^*$, define $D(x,x')=[(x-x')^T H(x_i^*)(x-x')]^{1/2}$. In the single-linkage variant, an unclustered point $x$ is added when its distance to its nearest cluster neighbor $x'$ is less than $$r=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+n/2)|H(x_i^*)|^{1/2}\mu(A)}{\pi^{n/2}}\left(1-\alpha^{1/(N-1)}\right)\right]^{1/n},$$ and the applicable gradient-direction check passes. For a seed $x_i^*\in X^*$, the negative gradient must point toward $x_i^*$; for a seed in $X^{(1)}$, the gradient must point in the same direction as at the seed. A separate variant replaces successively larger hyperspheres by ellipsoidal approximations of level sets around the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use a positive-definite local Hessian to define distance from a cluster seed. In the single-linkage variant, admit a point when its nearest-neighbor distance is below a threshold approximated from uniform-sampling statistics and the appropriate gradient-direction check succeeds. Another variant grows ellipsoidal level-set approximations instead of hyperspheres.
assumptions_latex: \text{The threshold uses an approximation based on uniformly distributed sample points in }A.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(x,x')<r\ \land\ \text{the applicable gradient-direction condition holds}\ \Longrightarrow\ x\ \text{is added to the cluster.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A clustering-multistart scheme alternating local concentration, density-mode estimation, and random sample renewal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate \(N^*\) points uniformly in \(A\). Apply several steps of a local optimizer from these points and retain the best fraction \(\gamma=0.25\), denoted \(z_1,\ldots,z_M\). Estimate the density \(\psi\) determined by these points and compute its modes \(m_1,\ldots,m_K\). If \(K=1\), perform final local optimization from \(m_1\). If \(K>1\), generate \(N'=(N-K)/2\) new points uniformly in \(A\), set \(N^*=K+N'\), form the next sample from the \(K\) modes and the new points, and repeat the concentration and mode-estimation stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly sample the region, partially optimize the samples, and retain the best quarter. Estimate their density and find its modes. If one mode remains, optimize locally from it; otherwise combine the modes with newly generated uniform points and repeat.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=1\Rightarrow\text{final local optimization begins at }m_1;\qquad K>1\Rightarrow\text{the modes and renewed random points form the next sample.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability-stopped clustering multistart for rapid incumbent improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling-and-clustering procedure designed to improve the best sampled value and stop from a probabilistic accuracy assessment rather than enumerate every attraction basin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose $N^*,M,f_0,\alpha,\epsilon$ and initialize the discovered minima $X^*$ and their starting points $X_s$ as empty. Sample $M$ points, run local search from the best, and obtain $\widehat f^*$. Stop immediately if $P(F(\widehat f)<\epsilon\mid\widehat F=\widehat f)>\alpha$. Otherwise, repeatedly sample $N^*$ points in $A$, retain the best $\gamma N^*$ points, cluster them from the best point $x_b$, retain each cluster's best point and radius, and compare the clusters with prior stages. Run local search from $x_b$ when the evidence suggests a previously unidentified attraction region, updating $X^*$ and $X_s$. After $N$ accumulated samples, stop and accept $\widehat f^*$ if $$P(F_f(\widehat f)<\epsilon\mid y_1,\ldots,y_N,\widehat F=\widehat f)>\alpha;$$ otherwise repeat sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First sample and locally refine the best point. If the conditional probability assessment indicates the desired accuracy with confidence exceeding alpha, accept the estimate. Otherwise repeatedly retain and cluster the best sampled points, starting a local search only when clustering suggests a new attraction region. Stop when the updated conditional probability exceeds alpha.
assumptions_latex: \text{The stated conditional probabilities can be estimated.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(F_f(\widehat f)<\epsilon\mid y_1,\ldots,y_N,\widehat F=\widehat f)>\alpha\ \Longrightarrow\ \widehat f^*\ \text{is accepted as the final estimate.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-neighbor critical radii for clustering multistart
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Statistical calibration of clustering radii under a uniformity null hypothesis for reduced samples within connected level-set components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sample size $N$ and neighbor order $j=1,\ldots,k$, set $$r_j=\left(\frac{\beta_{j,1-\alpha}}{\lambda}\right)^{1/n},$$ where $\beta_{j,1-\alpha}$ is the $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of $\operatorname{Be}(j,N-j)$. Under $H_0$, that the reduced sample points remain uniformly distributed within the connected components of $$\{x\in A:f(x)\le y_{\gamma N}\},$$ with $y_{\gamma N}$ the $\gamma N$-th smallest sampled objective value, the type-I error for this choice of critical radii is approximately $\alpha$. Natural seed points initiate the clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose each critical clustering radius from the stated beta-distribution quantile. Under the null hypothesis that retained sample points remain uniform within each connected component of the retained level set, the resulting type-I error is approximately alpha.
assumptions_latex: H_0:\ \text{the reduced sample points are uniformly distributed in each connected component of }\{x\in A:f(x)\le y_{\gamma N}\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_j=\left(\beta_{j,1-\alpha}/\lambda\right)^{1/n}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the type-I error under }H_0\text{ is approximately }\alpha.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A density-based mechanism for clustering sampled points and detecting possible lower-dimensional concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Grow a cluster from a natural seed by adding unclustered points lying in successively larger concentric hyperspheres while the point density in each intervening shell remains greater than the average density in the reference region. Choose successive radii so that one point in a shell is sufficient to attain the limiting density. Let \(d\in\{n,n+1\}\), where the optional \((n+1)\)-st coordinate is \(f(x)\), and let \(n'\leq d\) be the effective dimension selected by the clustering algorithm. For covariance eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_d\), use the stated reference volume \(V=\prod_{i=1}^{n'}4\sqrt{\lambda_i}\). An inferred value \(n'<d\) may indicate that the sampled minima lie in a lower-dimensional space.

The reference volume uses covariance eigenvalues in an inferred effective dimension. An effective dimension below the ambient dimension may reveal lower-dimensional concentration of the sampled minima.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Clusters grow while shell density exceeds reference density, and }n'<d\text{ may indicate lower-dimensional concentration.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A clustering multistart procedure consists of three potentially iterative stages: sample points in the region of interest; transform the sample so that points become grouped around local minima; and cluster the transformed points to recognize neighborhoods of those minima. If these stages successfully identify every relevant local-minimum neighborhood and one local optimization from each cluster reaches its associated minimum, the local runs determine all such local minima and therefore include a global minimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hypersphere-grown clustering multistart with cluster merging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-sample clustering algorithm that grows clusters through function-monotone hypersphere neighborhoods and conditionally launches local searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Uniformly sample $N^*$ new points in $A$, add them to the accumulated sample of size $N$, and retain the $\gamma N$ smallest-value points. Select the best unclustered point as seed and father. Grow hyperspheres $S_i$ of radii $r_i$, $i=1,\ldots,k$, while each contains a new reduced-sample point with objective value larger than the father; assign all qualifying points in the last such sphere to the cluster, and recursively use each assigned son as father. If a point $x_1$ rejected from cluster $C_a$ seeds $C_b$, merge $C_a$ and $C_b$ when some $x_2\in C_a$ satisfies $\|x_1-x_2\|\le2r_1$ and, for the segment midpoint $z$, $f(x_2)<f(z)<f(x_1)$. Start local search from a new cluster's seed only when the cluster has at least two points and no prior local search began within it. Stop after two consecutive cycles find no new minimum; otherwise resample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain the best sampled points and form clusters by recursively growing hyperspheres from low-valued father points to higher-valued neighboring sons. Merge two clusters when nearby points and their midpoint satisfy the stated objective ordering. Launch at most one local search from a cluster and only when it has at least two points. Stop after two cycles without a new minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Two consecutive cycles with no newly found minimum}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{termination.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A multistart procedure that repeatedly concentrates and thins samples before launching local minimizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sample \(N\) points in \(A\), concentrate them about candidate minima, and identify the resulting clusters. If a stopping condition holds, such as one point remaining in each cluster or the same number of clusters occurring in two consecutive clusterings, proceed to local minimization. Otherwise rank the clusters and their points by the lowest objective values, retain every \(m\)-th point in each cluster, and repeat the concentration and clustering stages. At termination, determine local minima starting from the best point in each cluster.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the region, concentrate the points near minima, and cluster them. Until a stated stopping condition holds, rank and thin each cluster by retaining every mth point, then repeat. Finally run local minimization from the best point in each terminal cluster.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A local-minimization run is initiated from the best point of each terminal cluster.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sample-clustering mechanism used to identify distinct basins in clustering multistart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For points \(x_1,\ldots,x_M\), let \(r_1\) be the average nearest-neighbor distance and \(r_2\) the average distance among the points. Starting from a point as a candidate center, average into its center any examined point lying within the radius-\(r_1\) hypersphere; return an examined point lying between the radius-\(r_1\) and radius-\(r_2\) hyperspheres for subsequent treatment; and initiate another candidate center from a point lying outside the radius-\(r_2\) hypersphere. Assign remaining points to the resulting clusters using a nearest-neighbor rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use an inner radius based on average nearest-neighbor distance and an outer radius based on average point separation. Merge close points into an updated center, return intermediate points for later treatment, let sufficiently distant points initiate new centers, and finally assign remaining points by a nearest-neighbor rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterative clustering multistart for discovering potentially global local minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized multistart procedure that clusters concentrated samples to avoid redundant local searches while accumulating distinct local minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a batch size $N^*$ and retained fraction $\gamma$. Maintain the discovered local minima $X^*$ and sampled points $X^{(1)}$ already known to lead to members of $X^*$. Repeatedly augment the sample by $N^*$ points, retain the fraction $\gamma$ with lowest objective values, apply one steepest-descent step to each retained point, and cluster the transformed sample using $X^*$ and then $X^{(1)}$ as seeds. For each unclustered lowest-value point $x^{(1)}$, run a local search to a local minimum $x^*$; add a new $x^*$ to $X^*$, or, if $x^*\in X^*$, add $x^{(1)}$ to $X^{(1)}$. Resample whenever a new local minimum is found. When every transformed point is assigned without discovering a new minimum, return $y^*=\min_{x^*\in X^*}f(x^*)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain the local minima found so far and points already known to lead to them. Repeatedly sample, retain the best fraction, take a steepest-descent step, and cluster using known minima and their associated starts as seeds. Launch local search from the best remaining unclustered point, recording either a new minimum or another start leading to a known minimum. Resample after finding a new minimum; otherwise stop when all transformed points are clustered and return the smallest local-minimum value found.
assumptions_latex: \text{A local-search procedure and a clustering procedure are available.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute an initial local minimizer \(x_0\). At stage \(k\), generate a trial point \(z_k\) by the prescribed basin-escape or global-sampling rule and compute \(y_k=L(z_k)\). Accept \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) only if \(f(y_k)<f(x_k)\); otherwise retain \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) or generate another trial. Thus every genuine transition satisfies \[f(x_{k+1})<f(x_k).\] Stop under a transition, evaluation, or stagnation rule and return the best recorded local minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Termination over Finitely Many Reachable Local Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accepted-transition bound for a finite reachable value set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{f(y):y\text{ is a reachable local minimizer}\}\) be finite. If every accepted state is a reachable local minimizer and every genuine transition strictly decreases its value, at most \(|V|-1\) transitions are accepted. The terminal state is optimal among reachable local minimizers exactly when no reachable local minimizer has a smaller value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finitely many reachable local-minimum values, strict improvement accepts at most one fewer transitions than the number of such values.
assumptions_latex: Every accepted state is a reachable local minimizer.
Accepted transitions strictly decrease the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(|V|-1\) transitions are accepted.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton prediction and level-set correction used to trace a valley uphill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initiate uphill motion along an eigenvector corresponding to the smallest positive eigenvalue of \(H\). Use predictor steps \(\Delta_p=\alpha\Delta_N\), where \(\Delta_N=J^{-1}F\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). When the prescribed angular drift measure satisfies \(\theta\ge\Theta\) (with \(\Theta=5^\circ\) in the stated implementation), correct back to the terrain feature by solving \(\min g^{T}g\) subject to \(F^{T}F=L\), where \(L\) is the current level. A corrector is converged when \(F^{T}F-L=0\) and \(Hg-\lambda g=0\); it may be computed by an SQP subproblem using a Lagrangian-Hessian approximation \(M=H^{T}H-\lambda H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move uphill from the smallest-positive-curvature direction using scaled Newton predictors. When angular drift exceeds the threshold, solve a level-set constrained gradient-norm problem, typically by SQP, until feasibility and stationarity hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^{T}F-L=0,\qquad Hg-\lambda g=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterative Topographical Global Optimization Algorithm I-TGO2
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Batchwise accumulation and repeated filtering of graph minima for local-minimization initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose iteration count \(I\), per-iteration point count \(N_I\), nearest-neighbor count \(k\), and initialize \(G=\varnothing\). During each of the \(I\) iterations, while \(|G|\leq N_I\), sample \(N_I\) random points in \(A\), determine their graph minima, add those minima to \(G\), recompute the graph minima of \(G\), and retain only them. Finally, recompute the graph minima of \(G\), possibly with a reduced value of \(k\), and use the retained points as starting points for local minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the iteration count, batch size, and nearest-neighbor count. In each iteration, while the retained set has at most the specified number of points, sample a new random batch in the domain, keep its graph minima, merge them with the retained set, and filter the merged set to its graph minima. Finally, optionally reduce the neighbor count, filter once more, and use the remaining graph minima to initialize local minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ contains the final graph-minimum points selected as starting points for local minimization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smoothing-Based Sequential Improvement of Protein Conformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Application-specific global–local search framework for protein conformations using smoothed and unsmoothed energy models. The extract contains duplicated phase numbering and inconsistent backward references; this statement records only the unambiguous operations and does not impose an unsupported desmoothing order within Phase II.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate \(k\) conformations sequentially, repeatedly sampling each current dihedral angle and retaining the sampled value having the lowest smoothed partial-conformation energy. Select \(\ell<k\) samples for full-dimensional local minimization of the smoothed energy, then locally minimize the unsmoothed energy from the resulting smooth minimizers and use the best \(m\) results to initialize \(\mathcal L\). In each improvement iteration, select a conformation from \(\mathcal L\) and a small subset of its dihedral angles; globally optimize the smoothed energy over that subset while holding the remaining angles fixed; apply full-dimensional smooth local minimization to the best \(\widehat m\) resulting configurations; merge the new local minimizers into \(\mathcal L\); and retire the selected conformation. The framework also prescribes full-dimensional unsmoothed local minimization of the generated smooth minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build protein conformations one dihedral angle at a time by sampling candidate angles and retaining the one with the lowest smoothed partial energy. Fully refine selected samples in the smooth model, refine the resulting minimizers in the unsmoothed model, and initialize a list with the best results. Each improvement iteration selects a listed conformation and a small subset of its angles, performs global optimization over that subset in the smooth model, fully refines the best configurations, merges new local minimizers into the list, and retires the selected conformation. Generated smooth minimizers are also subjected to full-dimensional refinement in the unsmoothed model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L\ \text{is maintained as a list of locally refined conformations and updated through smooth subset-global searches and full-dimensional local minimizations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessary conditions for a local minimum of separable resource allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to the continuous separable resource-allocation model of the extract; its feasibility constraints are not restated in the extracted theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a feasible point $x$ is a local minimum, then there exists $\lambda$ such that, for every $i$, $f_i'(x_i)=\lambda$ when $x_i>0$, and $f_i(0)\ge \lambda$ when $x_i=0$. Moreover, $f_i''(x_i)\ge 0$ at every positive component except possibly one component $x_r>0$. If $f_r''(x_r)<0$, then $|f_r''(x_r)|\le f_i''(x_i)$ for every other positive component $x_i\ne x_r$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible local minimum admits a common multiplier lambda across its positive components, while each zero component satisfies the stated boundary inequality. All positive components have nonnegative curvature except possibly one; if one has negative curvature, its magnitude cannot exceed the curvature at any other positive component.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is feasible for the continuous separable resource-allocation model}
f_i'\text{ and }f_i''\text{ exist at the points where they are used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda\;\Bigl[\forall i:x_i>0\Rightarrow f_i'(x_i)=\lambda;\;\forall i:x_i=0\Rightarrow f_i(0)\ge\lambda\Bigr],\quad \#\{i:x_i>0,\ f_i''(x_i)<0\}\le1,\quad f_r''(x_r)<0\Rightarrow\forall i\ne r\;(x_i>0\Rightarrow |f_r''(x_r)|\le f_i''(x_i)).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=2J^{T}F\), let \(L\) range over a collection \(\Lambda\) of levels of \(F^{T}F\), and, for every \(L\in\Lambda\), select local solutions of \(\min g^{T}g\) subject to \(F^{T}F=L\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V=\bigcup_{L\in\Lambda}\operatorname{locmin}\{g^{T}g:F^{T}F=L\}\text{ characterizes a terrain feature.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Downhill phase of a global terrain method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region iteration used to descend toward stationary or singular points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\Delta_N=J^{-1}F\), form \(\Delta=-\beta\Delta_N+(\beta-1)g\), where \(\beta=1\) if \(\|\Delta_N\|\le R\), \(\beta=0\) if \(\|\Delta_N\|>R\) and \(\|F\|\ge R\), and otherwise \(\beta\in[0,1]\) is the unique value satisfying \(\|\Delta\|=R\). Accept the iterate only when it reduces \(\|F\|\); otherwise reduce \(R\) and repeat. Terminate when \(\|F\|\le\varepsilon\) or \(\|F\|/\|\Delta_N\|\le\zeta\), switching to quadratic acceleration in the latter case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Blend the Newton and gradient directions according to the trust-region radius, accept only steps reducing the residual norm, and shrink the radius after rejection. Stop at the residual tolerance or switch to quadratic acceleration when the Newton step is disproportionately large.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|F\|\le\varepsilon\quad\text{or}\quad \|F\|/\|\Delta_N\|\le\zeta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bookkeeping and direction selection for terrain connections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Avoidance of repeated stationary or singular points during terrain exploration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Store each discovered point \(z_i^{*}\), its type, its values of \(\varphi\) and \(F^{T}F\), and its relevant eigen-connections. Before leaving \(z_i^{*}\), choose a nearest previously stored point \(z_j^{*}\in\arg\min_{k\ne i}\|z_i^{*}-z_k^{*}\|\), set \(d_i=z_i^{*}-z_j^{*}\), and select the sign of the relevant eigenvector \(v_i\) so that the initial movement is directed away from \(z_j^{*}\), equivalently choosing the sign for which \((\pm v_i)^{T}d_i<0\) under the stated convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Record discovered solutions and their eigen-connections. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial eigensystem computation by inverse iteration and deflation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computation of selected Hessian eigenpairs for choosing uphill or downhill terrain phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from an eigenvector estimate, alternate \(v_{k+1}=\lambda_kH^{-1}v_k\) and \(\lambda_{k+1}=\frac{v_{k+1}^{T}v_{k+1}}{v_{k+1}^{T}H^{-1}v_{k+1}}\) until \(\|v_{k+1}-\lambda_kH^{-1}v_k\|<\varepsilon\). After obtaining an eigenpair, deflate the symmetric matrix by orthonormal projection onto the complement of the eigenvectors already found, apply inverse iteration in the reduced space, and lift each new eigenvector to \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\). Continue until the desired number of eigenpairs is obtained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute only the needed Hessian eigenpairs by inverse iteration. After each pair, project onto the orthogonal complement of the eigenvectors already found, repeat in the reduced space, and lift the result back to the original space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible region $A$ and an objective function $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$, global optimization seeks $x^*\in A$ such that $f(x^*)=\min_{x\in A}f(x)$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete global descent function at a local minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for discrete global descent relative to the neighborhood system U_1 and the exceptional set X_c.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x^* be a U_1-local minimizer of f on X. A function G:X\to\mathbb{R} is a discrete global descent function of f at x^* if: (D1) x^* is a strict U_1-local maximizer of G on X; (D2) G has no U_1-local minimizers in X(x^*)\setminus X_c; and (D3) for every \widetilde{x}\in X\setminus X_c, \widetilde{x} is a U_1-local minimizer of f on X with f(\widetilde{x})<f(x^*) if and only if \widetilde{x} is a U_1-local minimizer of G on X.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a U1-local minimizer x* of f on X, G is a discrete global descent function at x* when x* is a strict U1-local maximizer of G, G has no U1-local minimizers in X(x*) outside Xc, and the U1-local minimizers of G outside Xc are exactly the U1-local minimizers of f having objective value strictly below f(x*).
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a }U_1\text{-local minimizer of }f\text{ on }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is a discrete global descent function of }f\text{ at }x^*\iff \mathrm{(D1)}\wedge\mathrm{(D2)}\wedge\mathrm{(D3)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), generate an exploration trial \(z_k\), compute \(y_k=L(z_k)\), and choose \[x_k^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\{x_{k-1}^*,y_k\}}f(x).\] If a measurable global-minimizer basin \(B\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(z_k\in B\mid\mathcal F_{k-1})\geq\delta\) almost surely for a constant \(\delta>0\) and every \(k\geq1\), then \[\mathbb P(z_k\notin B\text{ for }k=1,\ldots,N)\leq(1-\delta)^N.\] Consequently, the search reaches \(B\) with probability one. Because \(L(z)\) is globally minimizing for \(z\in B\) and the update retains the better point, a globally minimizing incumbent is retained after the first such visit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every exploration step has a uniform positive conditional probability of entering a global-minimizer basin, globalized local search reaches that basin almost surely and then retains a global solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonpersistent Exploration Gives No Global Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the local solver maps each start to a minimizer in its attraction basin. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty feasible set, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and let \(f^*=\inf_{x\in D}f(x)\) be finite. Feasibility of \(\bar x\in D\) gives \(f^*\leq f(\bar x)\), while validity of the independent bound gives \(L\leq f^*\). Hence \[0\leq f(\bar x)-f^*\leq f(\bar x)-L.\] Therefore \((\bar x,L)\) certifies absolute \(\varepsilon\)-global optimality whenever \(f(\bar x)-L\leq\varepsilon\). For a declared scale \(s>0\), it certifies scaled relative tolerance \(\varepsilon\) whenever \((f(\bar x)-L)/s\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible heuristic point and a rigorous lower bound give a computable upper bound on the incumbent's true optimality gap, which certifies absolute or explicitly scaled relative tolerances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unverified Primal or Lower-Bound Data Cannot Certify a Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness boundary for heuristic-primal/certified-bound hybrids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inequality \(L\le f^*\le f(\bar x)\) requires both verified feasibility of \(\bar x\) and rigorous validity of \(L\). If either condition is absent, the computed difference \(f(\bar x)-L\) need not upper-bound the true primal suboptimality and cannot certify global optimality or safe pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical candidate or nonrigorous bound does not yield a global-gap certificate; primal feasibility and lower-bound validity must both be verified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\notin D\ \text{or}\ L\nleq f^*\implies f(\bar x)-L\text{ is not a certified gap in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Unverified Primal or Lower-Bound Data Cannot Certify a Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone Strengthening of the Certified Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic bound-management invariant already owned by general bound-gap and global-search leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given verified feasible points \(x_1,\ldots,x_p\) and rigorous lower bounds \(L_1,\ldots,L_q\le f^*\), define \(U=\min_i f(x_i)\) and \(L=\max_jL_j\). Then \(L\le f^*\le U\), and adding valid primal or lower-bound information cannot increase \(U-L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combining the best verified incumbent and strongest rigorous lower bound monotonically tightens the certified gap.
assumptions_latex: Each \(L_j\) is a rigorous lower bound on \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\le f^*\le U,\quad U-L\text{ cannot increase as valid information is added}.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Strengthening of the Certified Gap

children.title: Polynomially Solvable Nonconvex Islands

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-to-Global Geometry Does Not Imply Polynomial Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between solution geometry and bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even if every local minimizer in a class is global, polynomial-time solvability does not follow without a polynomial-time method for finding such a point and a polynomially specified output or approximation criterion. Thus invexity, pseudoconvexity, or another local-to-global property is not by itself a bit-complexity theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local-equals-global geometry establishes validity of solutions, not a polynomial-time method for finding or encoding them.
assumptions_latex: Complexity is measured for encoded instance families in a specified computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{all local minima global}\not\Rightarrow\text{polynomial-time global optimization}.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Geometry Does Not Imply Polynomial Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic mechanism yielding a polynomially solvable nonconvex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every rationally encoded \(I\in\mathcal C\) can be transformed in polynomial time and polynomial output size into a convex instance \(T(I)\), with preservation of the global value and polynomial-time recovery of an optimizer or approximation of the declared accuracy. If the target convex class is polynomially solvable in that same output model, then \(\mathcal C\) is polynomially solvable despite the nonconvex original formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact polynomial-size reduction to a tractable convex class transfers polynomial solvability to the original nonconvex class.
assumptions_latex: Forward transformation and recovery have polynomial complexity.
The transformation preserves feasibility and optimal value in the declared output model.
The target convex class is polynomially solvable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I\mapsto T(I)\text{ exact and polynomial}\Rightarrow\mathcal C\text{ is polynomially solvable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Convexification Transfer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonquadratic tractable island; quadratic subclasses remain in the quadratic-landscape sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb Q[x]\) be given densely and let \(a,b\in\mathbb Q\), \(a\le b\). The problem \(\min_{x\in[a,b]}p(x)\) is exactly solvable in polynomial bit complexity in the dense encoding length of \((p,a,b)\) when an optimizer may be returned as a rational endpoint or as a real algebraic number represented by a square-free defining polynomial and isolating interval. An algorithm isolates the real roots of \(p'\) in \([a,b]\) and compares the objective at those roots and the endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational univariate polynomial, even when nonconvex and of arbitrary degree, can be minimized exactly on a rational interval in polynomial bit complexity using algebraic-number output.
assumptions_latex: Real algebraic optimizers use defining-polynomial and isolating-interval encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in[a,b]}p(x)\text{ and an algebraically encoded minimizer are computable in polynomial bit complexity.}
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Time Exact Univariate Polynomial Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact, Decision, and Approximate Polynomial Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates computational claims requiring different output encodings and accuracy guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rationally encoded minimization class \(\mathcal C\), polynomial-time exact optimization returns an attained optimizer and value in a specified finite representation in time polynomial in the input length. Polynomial-time threshold decision decides whether \(v^*(I)\le q\) for a rational threshold \(q\). Polynomial-time additive approximation, with positive rational \(\varepsilon\) encoded in binary, returns a feasible \(x_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(f_I(x_\varepsilon)\le v^*(I)+\varepsilon\) in time polynomial in the input length and the bit length of \(\varepsilon\). These are distinct predicates unless reductions between their output models are established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact optimization, threshold decision, and additive approximation are different polynomial-solvability claims and require explicit output and accuracy models.
assumptions_latex: Instances, thresholds, and tolerances are finitely encoded.
Approximation is asserted only for finite optimal value and requires a feasible returned point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{PolyExact}(\mathcal C),\ \operatorname{PolyDecision}(\mathcal C),\ \operatorname{PolyApprox}(\mathcal C)\text{ are not interchangeable without explicit reductions.}
knowledge_statements.title: Exact, Decision, and Approximate Polynomial Solvability

assumptions_latex: Instances are encoded by rational data and input length is measured in bits.
A structural restriction defines a subclass of otherwise nonconvex optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The subclass is a polynomially solvable nonconvex island exactly when global optimization over it has polynomial worst-case bit complexity.

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity definition; no particular tractable subclass is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structurally restricted class \(\mathcal C\) is a polynomially solvable nonconvex island if its members may have nonconvex objectives or feasible regions, yet there exist an exact global-optimization algorithm and a polynomial \(p\) such that every rationally encoded instance \(I\in\mathcal C\) is solved using at most \(p(|I|)\) bit operations. For approximation formulations, the corresponding requirement is a runtime polynomial in \(|I|\) and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) that returns a feasible point with a stated \(\varepsilon\)-global guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex island is polynomially solvable when its structural restrictions permit exact global optimization in time polynomial in the rational input length.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomially Solvable Nonconvex Islands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is a reasonable role for this taxonomy container, but no source is supplied. Exact continuous global optimization in the bit model requires an explicit output or decision formulation, and the asserted dependence polynomial in log(1/epsilon) is not a generic approximation requirement for nonconvex classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the minimization form and records the denominator-sign boundary stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fractional linear program minimizes \(\frac{\mathbf c^T\mathbf x+\gamma}{\mathbf d^T\mathbf x+\delta}\) subject to \(A\mathbf x\geq\mathbf b\). The denominator must have constant sign on the feasible domain; in the stated regime, \(\mathbf d^T\mathbf x+\delta>0\) throughout. If it changes sign on the domain, the problem is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional linear program minimizes a ratio of affine functions over a polyhedral feasible set. The denominator is assumed positive throughout the feasible domain; the extract states that a denominator changing sign makes the problem unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\mathbf x\in D}\frac{\mathbf c^T\mathbf x+\gamma}{\mathbf d^T\mathbf x+\delta}

children.title: Quadratic Complexity Landscape
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for tractable and hard quadratic subclasses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard side of the quadratic landscape through weighted MAX-CUT.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph with nonnegative rational edge weights and weighted Laplacian \(L\succeq0\), \[\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}x^{\mathsf T}Lx=\max_{x\in[0,1]^n}x^{\mathsf T}Lx.\] The common value is the maximum cut weight. Therefore deciding whether \[\min_{x\in[0,1]^n}-x^{\mathsf T}Lx\le-\tau\] is NP-hard. Hardness thus holds even for concave quadratic minimization over a unit box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted MAX-CUT reduces exactly to concave quadratic minimization over a box.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights and threshold \(\tau\) are nonnegative rational data.
\(L\) is the corresponding weighted graph Laplacian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in[0,1]^n}-x^{\mathsf T}Lx\text{ is NP-hard in threshold-decision form}.
knowledge_statements.title: Concave Box-Quadratic NP-Hardness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial side of the rational quadratic complexity boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational \(Q\succeq0,c,A,b\), assume \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) is nonempty, bounded, and supplied with polynomially encoded inner and outer radius bounds. Then an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal solution of \[\min_{x\in P}\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\] can be computed in time polynomial in the input length and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational convex quadratic minimization over a well-described bounded rational polyhedron admits polynomial-time weak optimization.
assumptions_latex: The polyhedron is nonempty and bounded with polynomially encoded geometric bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Runtime is polynomial in the input length and }\log(1/\varepsilon).
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Weak Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-Region Exactness Does Not Extend to General QCQP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the single-ball hidden-convexity regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scalar-shift characterization above relies on one quadratic norm constraint. Replacing the ball by an arbitrary intersection of quadratic inequalities does not preserve that characterization; quadratic syntax alone implies neither zero duality gap nor polynomial solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tractability of the one-ball trust-region problem does not extend automatically to general QCQP.
assumptions_latex: The comparison class permits multiple arbitrary quadratic constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{trust-region exactness}\not\Rightarrow\text{general QCQP exactness or tractability}.
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Exactness Does Not Extend to General QCQP

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-Region Hidden Convexity and Exact Dual Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical tractable indefinite quadratic subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric \(Q\) and \(\Delta>0\), let \[p^*=\min_{\|x\|_2\le\Delta}x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x.\] Then \[p^*=\max_{\substack{\lambda\ge0,\ Q+\lambda I\succeq0\\c\in\operatorname{Range}(Q+\lambda I)}}\{-c^{\mathsf T}(Q+\lambda I)^{\dagger}c-\lambda\Delta^2\}.\] Thus the possibly indefinite single-ball problem has zero Lagrangian duality gap, including the stated singular-case range condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indefinite trust-region quadratic has an exact scalar-shift dual representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*=\max_{\lambda\ge0}\{-c^{\mathsf T}(Q+\lambda I)^{\dagger}c-\lambda\Delta^2\}\text{ under PSD and range conditions}.
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Hidden Convexity and Exact Dual Bound

assumptions_latex: Quadratic programs have rational data and are measured in the Turing bit model.
The feasible region is either a rational convex set with convex quadratic objective or a box with an indefinite quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive-semidefinite quadratic minimization is polynomially solvable under standard convex representations, whereas general indefinite box-constrained quadratic minimization is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model boundary between convex and general indefinite quadratic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) with rational symmetric \(Q\). If \(Q\succeq0\) and the rational convex feasible set admits polynomial-time separation, an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal solution can be computed in time polynomial in the input length and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). Without positive semidefiniteness, global minimization is NP-hard even for bounded box constraints. Thus the sign structure of \(Q\), together with the feasible-set representation, separates a standard polynomially solvable quadratic subclass from the general hard landscape.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex quadratic minimization is polynomially approximable under standard oracle assumptions, while allowing an indefinite quadratic over a box makes global minimization NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Complexity Landscape

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity-bound record is appropriate for this leaf, but both sides of the claimed boundary need authoritative citations. Polynomial-time weak optimization from separation requires additional representation, boundedness, and oracle-access conditions, while NP-hardness of indefinite box-constrained quadratic minimization needs a specific theorem or reduction locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation complexity parameterized by negative Hessian eigenvalues
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearly constrained quadratic programming over a compact feasible region, using the source section's range-normalized approximation criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\tfrac12 x^T Hx+c^Tx:Ax\ge b\}\), where the feasible region is compact. Let \(t\) be the number of negative eigenvalues of \(H\). For \(\epsilon\in(0,1]\), an \(\epsilon\)-approximate solution can be found in \[O\!\left(\left\lceil\frac{n(n+1)}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right\rceil^{t}\ell\right)\] steps, where \(\ell\) is the time required to solve a convex quadratic program of the same size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linearly constrained quadratic program with compact feasible region, an epsilon-approximate solution can be found with a step bound exponential in the number of negative Hessian eigenvalues and proportional to the cost of solving a same-size convex quadratic program.
assumptions_latex: t\text{ is the number of negative eigenvalues of }H
\ell\text{ is the time to solve a same-size convex quadratic program}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(n,\epsilon,t)=O\!\left(\left\lceil\frac{n(n+1)}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\right\rceil^{t}\ell\right)

children.title: General Nonconvex Hardness
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for worst-case hardness of broad continuous global classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvexity Alone Does Not Establish Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on complexity conclusions from geometry alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonconvexity of an objective or feasible set does not itself imply NP-hardness. For example, \(\min_{x\in[-2,2]}(x^2-1)^2\) is nonconvex but has the explicit global optimum \(0\) at \(x=\pm1\). Hardness concerns encoded instance families and requires a reduction or hard-subclass containment argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonconvexity is a geometric property, not a hardness proof.
assumptions_latex: Complexity is measured over encoded families of instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{nonconvexity alone}\not\Rightarrow\text{NP-hardness}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvexity Alone Does Not Establish Hardness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction principle for exact-value or threshold-decision global optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be NP-hard. Suppose a polynomial-time, polynomial-output-size map \(R\) sends each instance \(I\in\mathcal H\) to an instance \(R(I)\in\mathcal G\) and a rational threshold such that deciding whether the global optimum of \(R(I)\) meets that threshold decides \(I\). Then the threshold-decision version of global optimization over \(\mathcal G\) is NP-hard; consequently an exact polynomial-time optimizer or value algorithm for every instance of \(\mathcal G\) would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A broad global-optimization class inherits NP-hardness from any polynomially embedded hard subclass.
assumptions_latex: The reduction and its output encoding have polynomial size.
The stated optimal-value threshold decides the source instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal H\le_p\mathcal G\Rightarrow\mathcal G\text{ is NP-hard}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Hard-Subclass Inheritance

assumptions_latex: Optimization instances are rationally encoded and complexity is measured in the Turing model.
The problem class contains box-constrained indefinite quadratic minimization as a polynomially representable subclass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact global optimization over the broad class is NP-hard, so a polynomial-time exact algorithm would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subclass-containment hardness statement in the rational Turing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G\) be a continuous nonconvex minimization class containing every rational box-constrained indefinite quadratic program, with a polynomial-size embedding of each such quadratic instance. Because globally minimizing that subclass is NP-hard, computing \(f^*\) exactly for arbitrary \(I\in\mathcal G\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time reductions. Consequently, unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), no algorithm solves every instance in \(\mathcal G\) exactly in time polynomial in \(|I|\). This worst-case statement does not preclude efficient algorithms for restricted subclasses or useful instance-dependent behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any broad nonconvex class that polynomially contains indefinite box-constrained quadratic optimization inherits its NP-hardness, although restricted subclasses may remain tractable.
knowledge_statements.title: General Nonconvex Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subclass-containment implication is correctly scoped and a complexity bound fits the container, but its premise relies on an uncited NP-hardness result for box-constrained indefinite quadratic minimization. A specific authoritative theorem or reduction locator is required before the broad-class conclusion can be retained.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }\mathbf X=\mathbf V\mathbf V^T\succ\mathbf0,\ \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf X)\le\mathbf e,\ \mathbf D=\operatorname{Diag}(\sqrt{X_{11}},\ldots,\sqrt{X_{nn}}),\ \widehat{\mathbf x}=\mathbf D\sigma(\mathbf V^T\mathbf u),\ \mathbf u\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\text{unit ball}).\text{ Then }\lim_{\mathbf X\to\widetilde{\mathbf X}}\mathbb E[\widehat{\mathbf x}^T\mathbf Q\widehat{\mathbf x}]=\lim_{\mathbf X\to\widetilde{\mathbf X}}\frac{2}{\pi}\mathbf Q\bullet\left(\mathbf D\arcsin[\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf X\mathbf D^{-1}]\mathbf D\right)\ge\frac{2}{\pi}g^*(\mathbf Q)+\left(1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right)g_*(\mathbf Q).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite factorization X=VV^T with diagonal at most one, randomized sign rounding using a uniformly sampled unit-ball vector has a limiting expected quadratic value equal to the corresponding arcsine expression and at least the stated convex combination of the relaxed upper and lower values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\mathbf X\to\widetilde{\mathbf X}}\mathbb E[\widehat{\mathbf x}^T\mathbf Q\widehat{\mathbf x}]=\lim_{\mathbf X\to\widetilde{\mathbf X}}\frac{2}{\pi}\mathbf Q\bullet\left(\mathbf D\arcsin[\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf X\mathbf D^{-1}]\mathbf D\right)\ge\frac{2}{\pi}g^*(\mathbf Q)+\left(1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right)g_*(\mathbf Q)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Inapproximability of Polynomial Optimization over Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional weak-approximation lower bounds for continuous quadratic and polynomial programming over polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Assume }\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}.\quad \text{(i) For every }\epsilon<\tfrac13,\text{ continuous quadratic programming over polytopes has no polynomial-time weak }\epsilon\text{-approximation algorithm.}\quad \text{(ii) There exists }\delta>0\text{ such that polynomial programming over polytopes has no polynomial-time weak }(1-n^{-\delta})\text{-approximation algorithm.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming P is not equal to NP, continuous quadratic programming over polytopes has no polynomial-time weak epsilon-approximation algorithm for any epsilon below one third. Moreover, for some positive constant delta, polynomial programming over polytopes has no polynomial-time weak approximation with parameter 1 minus n to the negative delta.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The polynomial-time weak-approximation algorithms specified in parts (i) and (ii) do not exist.}

knowledge_statements.title: Classes Admitting Fully Polynomial Approximation Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoded nonnegative minimization problems with multiplicative approximation guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An encoded minimization problem belongs to the class admitting a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme if there is an algorithm that, for every instance \(I\) and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), returns a feasible point \(x_\varepsilon\in X_I\) satisfying \[f_I(x_\varepsilon)\le (1+\varepsilon)f_I^*,\qquad f_I^*:=\inf_{x\in X_I}f_I(x),\] and whose running time is bounded by a polynomial in both the binary encoding length \(|I|\) and \(1/\varepsilon\). This multiplicative convention assumes \(f_I^*\ge0\); when \(f_I^*=0\), it requires the algorithm to return a feasible point of value zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An FPTAS is one algorithm that computes a multiplicative approximation in time polynomial in both the instance length and reciprocal accuracy; a zero optimum must be attained exactly.
assumptions_latex: Instances and requested accuracies have finite binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_I(x_\varepsilon)\le(1+\varepsilon)f_I^*\) in time \(\operatorname{poly}(|I|,1/\varepsilon)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: FPTAS bounds for fixed-dimensional mixed-integer polynomial maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial maximization over the mixed-integer points of a rational polytope in fixed total dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n=n_1+n_2\). Let \(P\) be specified by binary-encoded rational inequalities, let \(f\) be specified by rational monomial coefficients encoded in binary and exponents encoded in unary, and let \(1/\epsilon\) be encoded in unary. If \(f\ge 0\) on \(P\cap(\mathbb R^{n_1}\times\mathbb Z^{n_2})\), a polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible \((x_\epsilon,z_\epsilon)\) such that \(\lvert f(x_\epsilon,z_\epsilon)-f(x_{\max},z_{\max})\rvert\le \epsilon f(x_{\max},z_{\max})\). Without nonnegativity, a polynomial-time algorithm returns a feasible point satisfying \(\lvert f(x_\epsilon,z_\epsilon)-f(x_{\max},z_{\max})\rvert\le \epsilon\lvert f(x_{\max},z_{\max})-f(x_{\min},z_{\min})\rvert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In fixed dimension, nonnegative mixed-integer polynomial maximization over a rational polytope admits an FPTAS. For a general polynomial, a weak FPTAS bounds the error by epsilon times the feasible objective range.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is given by binary-encoded rational inequalities}
f\text{ has binary-encoded rational coefficients and unary-encoded exponents}
f\ge 0\text{ on the feasible region for the relative-error guarantee}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated polynomial-time relative-error and objective-range-error approximation guarantees hold.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoded nonnegative minimization problems with fixed-accuracy polynomial running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An encoded minimization problem belongs to the class admitting a polynomial-time approximation scheme if, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), there is an algorithm that returns, on every instance \(I\), a feasible point \(x_\varepsilon\) such that \[f_I(x_\varepsilon)\le(1+\varepsilon)f_I^*,\qquad f_I^*:=\inf_{x\in X_I}f_I(x),\] and runs in time polynomial in the encoding length \(|I|\). The polynomial may depend arbitrarily on the fixed value of \(\varepsilon\), so this definition does not require polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_I(x_\varepsilon)\le(1+\varepsilon)f_I^*\) in time \(p_\varepsilon(|I|)\) for a polynomial \(p_\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimax certificate for a restricted-index approximation ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an indexed minimization problem approximated by optimizing over a polynomial-time-solvable subset of indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq K\), let \(\min_{i\in I}\phi_i(x)\) be polynomial-time computable, and suppose the ratios below are defined with positive denominators. Define \(\rho=\min_x \frac{\min_{k\in K}\phi_k(x)}{\min_{i\in I}\phi_i(x)}\). For \(\rho_0\ge 0\), the bound \(\rho\ge\rho_0\) is equivalent to \(\phi_k(x)-\rho_0\min_{i\in I}\phi_i(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\) and \(k\in K\), or equivalently \(\max_{i\in I}(\phi_k(x)-\rho_0\phi_i(x))\ge0\). Hence it suffices to establish, for every \(k\in K\), \(\min_x\max_{i\in I}(\phi_k(x)-\rho_0\phi_i(x))\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an indexed minimization problem approximated by restricting the index set to a tractable subset, a nonnegative lower bound on the approximation ratio can be certified by a minimax inequality for every original index. The ratio formulation requires positive, nonzero restricted optimum values.
assumptions_latex: \min_{i\in I}\phi_i(x)\text{ is computable in polynomial time}
\min_{i\in I}\phi_i(x)>0\text{ on the domain of the ratio}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall k\in K:\ \min_x\max_{i\in I}\bigl(\phi_k(x)-\rho_0\phi_i(x)\bigr)\ge0\right]\Longrightarrow \rho\ge\rho_0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The approximation guarantee is specifically for maximization; PTAS and FPTAS differ in runtime dependence on the error parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization instance of encoding length \(n\) and optimal cost \(f_{\max}\), \(\mathcal A\) is an \(\epsilon\)-approximation algorithm if it runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and returns a feasible solution of cost \(f_{\mathcal A}\ge(1-\epsilon)f_{\max}\). knowledge_statements.title: Inapproximability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap-reduction boundary excluding a PTAS for encoded minimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be NP-complete. Suppose a polynomial reduction maps every input \(z\) to a minimization instance \(I_z\) with nonnegative objective and polynomial-time verifiable feasible solutions, and there are constants \(0<a<b\) such that \[z\in L\Rightarrow f_{I_z}^*\le a,\qquad z\notin L\Rightarrow f_{I_z}^*\ge b.\] Then any polynomial-time \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation with fixed \(\varepsilon<b/a-1\) would decide \(L\): its returned objective is below \(b\) in the first case and at least \(b\) in the second. Consequently, unless \(P=NP\), this problem class admits no PTAS.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant multiplicative gap reduction from an NP-complete problem rules out a PTAS unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is NP-complete and the reduction is polynomial-time.
Returned solutions are feasible and their objective values are polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\ne NP\Rightarrow\) no PTAS exists for the reduced problem class.

notation.meaning: optimal value of the reduced instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions required for a meaningful multiplicative hardness factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Multiplicative approximation ratios for minimization are not invariant under adding a constant to the objective: replacing \(f\) by \(f+C\) preserves minimizers but changes \((f(x)+C)/(f^*+C)\). If negative or zero optima are allowed, \(f(x)\le\rho f^*\) may be meaningless or require exact optimization. A multiplicative inapproximability threshold must therefore specify a nonnegative objective normalization and handle zero-optimum instances explicitly; otherwise an additive metric or another declared guarantee is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative hardness needs a fixed nonnegative normalization and explicit treatment of zero optima.
assumptions_latex: The claimed approximation guarantee is multiplicative for minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A multiplicative hardness factor is meaningful only relative to a specified objective normalization and zero-optimum convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Ratio Normalization Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic gap reduction excluding sufficiently accurate additive approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an NP-complete language reduces in polynomial time to minimization instances such that \[z\in L\Rightarrow f_I^*\le a(I),\qquad z\notin L\Rightarrow f_I^*\ge a(I)+\Delta(I),\] where \(a(I)\) and the positive rational \(\Delta(I)\) are polynomial-time computable and polynomially encoded. If returned feasible objective values are polynomial-time computable, then an algorithm guaranteeing additive error strictly less than \(\Delta(I)/2\) would distinguish the two cases. Unless \(P=NP\), no such polynomial-time algorithm exists on the reduced class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomially encoded objective gap rules out additive approximation fine enough to distinguish it unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The reduction, thresholds, and returned objective values are polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\ne NP\Rightarrow\) no polynomial-time additive approximation with error below \(\Delta(I)/2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Additive-Gap Inapproximability Boundary

children.title: Information-Based Complexity
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by finite access to black-box continuous functions.

children.title: Evaluation Complexity
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for function-information budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case cost measured by calls to a specified information oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function class \(\mathcal F\), domain \(X\), oracle \(\mathcal O\), and error tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), the deterministic evaluation complexity is \[N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F,\mathcal O):=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F} n_A(f,\varepsilon),\] where the infimum ranges over algorithms using adaptive oracle calls, \(n_A(f,\varepsilon)\) is the number of calls before termination, and the returned point \(x_A\in X\) must satisfy \(f(x_A)-\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\le\varepsilon\) for every \(f\in\mathcal F\). The oracle model must specify whether a call returns values, derivatives, bounds, or other information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation complexity is the least worst-case number of specified oracle calls needed to return a globally epsilon-optimal point.
assumptions_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) is finite for every \(f\in\mathcal F\).
Algorithms receive information only through the declared oracle \(\mathcal O\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F,\mathcal O)\) is the optimal worst-case oracle budget for additive error \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: number of oracle calls made by algorithm A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence oracle-call complexity for randomized global optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function class \(\mathcal F\), oracle \(\mathcal O\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and risk \(\delta\in(0,1)\), define \[N_{\mathrm{rand}}(\varepsilon,\delta;\mathcal F,\mathcal O):=\inf\left\{n:\exists A\text{ using at most }n\text{ oracle calls such that }\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb P_A\!\left(f(x_A)-\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\le\varepsilon\right)\ge1-\delta\right\}.\] The probability includes all randomness declared in the algorithm and oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomized evaluation complexity is the smallest uniform oracle budget attaining the requested global error with the prescribed confidence for every function in the class.
assumptions_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) is finite for every \(f\in\mathcal F\).
The oracle and all sources of randomness are explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{rand}}\) is the optimal fixed-confidence worst-case oracle budget.

notation.meaning: probability induced by the algorithm and declared oracle randomness

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Evaluation Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic oracle lower-bound criterion based on indistinguishable objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deterministic algorithm making at most \(n\) adaptive calls to \(\mathcal O\). If \(f_0,f_1\in\mathcal F\) produce identical oracle responses along their common induced transcript and no point is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal for both, the algorithm returns the same point for both objectives and fails on at least one. Consequently, \(N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F,\mathcal O)>n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If n oracle calls cannot distinguish two objectives with disjoint epsilon-solution sets, no deterministic n-call algorithm solves the whole class.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and adaptive.
The objectives produce identical declared-oracle responses along the induced transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F,\mathcal O)>n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Indistinguishable-Transcript Evaluation Lower Bound

children.title: Dimensional Coverage Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for dimensional growth in global coverage requirements.

children.title: Dimension-Dependent Evaluation Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth of global-search evaluation requirements with ambient dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Evaluation Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform-grid upper bound for Lipschitz optimization on a cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\). Evaluate \(f\) on a Cartesian grid whose coordinate spacing is at most \(\varepsilon/L\), and return a sampled point \(\widehat x\) of smallest value. Every point of the cube lies within \(\varepsilon/L\) of a grid point, hence \[f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in[0,1]^d}f(x)\le\varepsilon.\] The number of value evaluations is at most \(\bigl(1+\lceil L/\varepsilon\rceil\bigr)^d\), displaying exponential growth in ambient dimension when \(L/\varepsilon>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform grid solves d-dimensional Lipschitz optimization to additive accuracy epsilon using on the order of the reciprocal accuracy raised to d evaluations.
assumptions_latex: Only exact function-value evaluations are counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\le\bigl(1+\lceil L/\varepsilon\rceil\bigr)^d\) and \(f(\widehat x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant in the max norm

children.title: Curse-of-Dimensionality Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information limits demonstrating unavoidable dimensional growth.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic Lipschitz Oracle Covering Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case value-oracle lower bound with returned-point accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_d\) be all unit-Lipschitz functions on \([0,1]^d\) under \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\). If a deterministic exact-value algorithm makes \(N\) queries, may return one additional unsampled point, and guarantees \(f(\widehat x)-\min f\le\varepsilon\) for every \(f\in\mathcal F_d\), then its query points together with \(\widehat x\) must form a \(2\varepsilon\)-net. Hence, for \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\), \[N+1\ge\mathcal N([0,1]^d,\|\cdot\|_\infty,2\varepsilon)\ge(4\varepsilon)^{-d},\] and therefore \(N\ge(4\varepsilon)^{-d}-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic black-box Lipschitz optimization requires exponentially many evaluations in dimension because queries and output must cover the cube.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and receives exact function values only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\ge(4\varepsilon)^{-d}-1.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Lipschitz Oracle Covering Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adversarial family underlying the covering lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After a zero-valued transcript at query points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) and returned point \(\widehat x\), suppose some \(z\) has distance greater than \(2\varepsilon\) from all these points. Then \[f_0(x)=0,\qquad f_z(x)=-\max\{0,2\varepsilon-\|x-z\|_\infty\}\] are unit-Lipschitz and agree at every query, but \(f_z(\widehat x)=0\) while \(\min f_z=-2\varepsilon\). The algorithm therefore cannot guarantee error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncovered region supports a negative Lipschitz bump invisible to every query but deeper than the promised error.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and uses exact values.
An uncovered point lies more than \(2\varepsilon\) from queries and output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The same transcript is compatible with output error }2\varepsilon>\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: adversarial negative bump centered at z

knowledge_statements.title: Invisible Lipschitz Bump
Curse-of-Dimensionality Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case value-oracle lower bound for multidimensional Lipschitz optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the class \(\mathcal F_d\) of all \(1\)-Lipschitz functions on \([0,1]^d\) under \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\), any deterministic algorithm that uses only exact function values and guarantees \(f(\widehat x)-\min f\le\varepsilon\) for every \(f\in\mathcal F_d\) must sample enough points to form an \(\varepsilon\)-net of the cube. Consequently, for \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), its worst-case number of evaluations satisfies \[N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F_d)\ge \mathcal N([0,1]^d,\|\cdot\|_\infty,\varepsilon)\ge\left\lfloor\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\right\rfloor^d.\] Thus fixed-accuracy worst-case complexity grows exponentially with \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Black-box optimization of arbitrary Lipschitz functions requires exponentially many evaluations in dimension because samples must cover the whole cube.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and receives exact values only.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F_d)\ge\lfloor(2\varepsilon)^{-1}\rfloor^d\).

notation.meaning: unit-Lipschitz functions on the d-dimensional cube
radius-r covering number of a metric space

children.title: Effective-Dimension Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem structures where intrinsic dimension differs from ambient dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Dimension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation growth governed by a known low-dimensional active representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) be compact and suppose \(f(x)=g(Px)\), where the known linear map \(P:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\) has rank \(k\ll d\), and \(g\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(Y=P(X)\). If a radius-\(\varepsilon/L\) net of \(Y\) is evaluated through feasible representatives \(x_y\in X\) satisfying \(Px_y=y\), the best representative \(\widehat x\) obeys \[f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\le\varepsilon.\] The required evaluations are at most \(\mathcal N(Y,\|\cdot\|,\varepsilon/L)\), which scales with intrinsic dimension \(k\), rather than ambient dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the objective factors through a known rank-k projection, covering-based evaluation complexity depends on k rather than the ambient dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is compact and every net point has a computable feasible representative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\le\mathcal N(P(X),\|\cdot\|,\varepsilon/L)\) suffices for additive error \(\varepsilon\).

children.title: Regularity–Information Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for complexity changes induced by stronger analytic information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General conversion of a supplied modulus of continuity into evaluation complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be compact and let every \(f\in\mathcal F\) satisfy \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le\omega(d(x,y))\), where the known function \(\omega:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) is nondecreasing and \(\omega(0)=0\). If \(r>0\) satisfies \(\omega(r)\le\varepsilon\), evaluate \(f\) on an \(r\)-net of minimum cardinality \(\mathcal N(X,d,r)\) and return its best point. Then \[f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\le\varepsilon,\qquad N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F,\mathcal O_{\mathrm{value}})\le\mathcal N(X,d,r).\] Hölder regularity \(\omega(t)=Lt^\alpha\) permits \(r=(\varepsilon/L)^{1/\alpha}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A known common modulus converts an admissible covering radius into an evaluation bound; the Hölder case uses radius epsilon over L raised to one over alpha.
assumptions_latex: The known nondecreasing \(\omega\) bounds every objective in the class.
Exact function values are available and \(r>0\) satisfies \(\omega(r)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon;\mathcal F,\mathcal O_{\mathrm{value}})\le\mathcal N(X,d,r)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Known-Modulus Covering Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Uniform Finite Evaluation Bound Without a Common Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-information impossibility for unrestricted continuous objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an infinite compact metric space and \(\varepsilon>0\). For every deterministic algorithm making finitely many exact value queries and returning \(\widehat x\in X\), there are continuous \(f_0,f_1:X\to\mathbb R\) that give identical values at every query on their common induced transcript but have disjoint \(\varepsilon\)-optimal solution sets. Hence \[N(\varepsilon;C(X),\mathcal O_{\mathrm{value}})=\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity alone gives no uniform finite black-box budget because a continuous improving well can remain hidden away from all queried points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an infinite compact metric space.
Only exact function values are observed.
The admissible class is all real-valued continuous functions on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon;C(X),\mathcal O_{\mathrm{value}})=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform Finite Evaluation Bound Without a Common Modulus
Regularity–Information Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder regularity converts spatial resolution into an evaluation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R\) satisfy the Hölder condition \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty^\alpha\) with \(0<\alpha\le1\). Evaluating a Cartesian grid of spacing at most \((\varepsilon/L)^{1/\alpha}\) and returning its best point guarantees additive global error at most \(\varepsilon\). The evaluation count satisfies \[N(\varepsilon)\le\left(1+\left\lceil(L/\varepsilon)^{1/\alpha}\right\rceil\right)^d.\] Thus stronger known regularity increases the admissible spacing and reduces the required information, while uncertainty about \(L\) or \(\alpha\) prevents direct use of this budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Known Hölder smoothness determines the grid resolution and yields evaluation growth proportional to epsilon raised to minus d over alpha.
assumptions_latex: Exact function values and the regularity parameters are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon)\le\bigl(1+\lceil(L/\varepsilon)^{1/\alpha}\rceil\bigr)^d\).
