children.title: Deterministic Convergence-Finiteness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convergence families for partitioning and relaxation-based global methods.

children.title: Exhaustive-Partition Convergence
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for convergence driven by exhaustive spatial refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive-Partition Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic convergence under exhaustive refinement of a compact domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) be compact and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. For each \(k\), let \(\mathcal P_k\) be a finite partition of \(X\), choose one representative \(x_Q\in Q\) from every \(Q\in\mathcal P_k\), and define \(U_k:=\min_{Q\in\mathcal P_k}f(x_Q)\). If the mesh satisfies \[\max_{Q\in\mathcal P_k}\operatorname{diam}(Q)\longrightarrow0,\] then \(U_k\to f^*:=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\). Moreover, every accumulation point of representatives attaining \(U_k\) is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling every cell of partitions whose maximum diameter vanishes makes the best sampled value converge to the global minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty and compact, and \(f\) is continuous.
Each partition is finite and its mesh tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_k\to f^*\), and every cluster point of best representatives belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coverage or Shrinkage Failure Can Hide the Optimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for exhaustive-refinement convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If children fail to cover their parent, an omitted subset may contain the unique global minimizer. Coverage alone is also insufficient: take the constant partition \(\mathcal P_k=\{[0,1]\}\), always choose representative \(x_k=1\), and let \(f(x)=x\). The region never shrinks and the sampled value remains \(1\ne f^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence can fail through either omitted coverage or nonshrinking retained regions.
assumptions_latex: Representatives are sampled only from generated regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Coverage preservation and shrinkage are both necessary for the generic guarantee}.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage or Shrinkage Failure Can Hide the Optimizer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree formulation complementary to the seed's vanishing-mesh partition sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finitely branching recursive partition of compact \(X\) is exhaustive if each parent is the union of its children and every infinite nested descendant chain \(Q_0\supset Q_1\supset\cdots\) satisfies \(\operatorname{diam}(Q_k)\to0\). For nested finite level partitions, \(\max_{Q\in\mathcal P_k}\operatorname{diam}(Q)\to0\) implies this branchwise condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exhaustive recursive partition preserves coverage and shrinks every infinite descendant chain.
assumptions_latex: Every nonterminal region has finitely many children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_0\supset Q_1\supset\cdots\Rightarrow\operatorname{diam}(Q_k)\to0.

notation.meaning: region on an infinite descendant chain

knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive Recursive Partition

children.title: Bound-Consistency Convergence
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for convergence governed by shrinking relaxation error.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validity Without Consistency Does Not Close the Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convergence when shrinking-region bounds retain fixed error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=[0,1]\), let \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(L(Q)=\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)-1\). Every \(L(Q)\) is valid, but \(\inf_Q f-L(Q)=1\) for every nonempty \(Q\). Thus even when the incumbent equals \(f^*=0\), the certified lower–upper gap remains at least one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid regional bounds may remain uniformly too low on arbitrarily small regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\text{ is valid but not refinement-consistent, and its gap does not vanish}.
knowledge_statements.title: Validity Without Consistency Does Not Close the Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Refinement Consistency of Regional Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-accuracy condition distinct from the sibling requirement of exhaustive spatial refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_Q^*:=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\cap Q\}\) and let \(L(Q)\le f_Q^*\) for every region with \(F\cap Q\ne\varnothing\). The bounds are uniformly refinement-consistent if there is \(\omega(t)\downarrow0\) as \(t\downarrow0\) such that \[0\le f_Q^*-L(Q)\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}Q).\] Equivalently, \[\sup_{F\cap Q\ne\varnothing,\,\operatorname{diam}Q\le t}(f_Q^*-L(Q))\longrightarrow0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regional bounds are uniformly consistent when their worst feasible-region error vanishes with region diameter.
assumptions_latex: \(L(Q)\) is a valid lower bound for every feasible region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{F\cap Q\ne\varnothing,\operatorname{diam}Q\le t}(f_Q^*-L(Q))\to0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Refinement Consistency of Regional Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Consistency Is Equivalent to Arbitrary-Sequence Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier characterization distinguishing uniform consistency from tests restricted to nested branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Q\) be a family of feasible regions and define \(e(Q)=f_Q^*-L(Q)\ge0\). Then \[\sup\{e(Q):Q\in\mathcal Q,\ \operatorname{diam}Q\le t\}\to0\quad(t\downarrow0)\] if and only if \(e(Q_k)\to0\) for every sequence \((Q_k)\subseteq\mathcal Q\) satisfying \(\operatorname{diam}(Q_k)\to0\). This equivalence does not reduce the universal sequence condition to nested shrinking sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform bound consistency is exactly consistency along every shrinking-region sequence; checking only nested branches is a weaker condition unless additional structure is imposed.
assumptions_latex: Every considered region has a valid finite lower bound and finite regional optimum.
Diameters are measured in a fixed metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\operatorname{diam}Q\le t}e(Q)\to0\iff[\operatorname{diam}(Q_k)\to0\Rightarrow e(Q_k)\to0\text{ for every sequence }(Q_k)]\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Consistency Is Equivalent to Arbitrary-Sequence Consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best-Bound Convergence under Uniform Bound Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-and-bound convergence driven by valid uniformly consistent regional bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be compact, let \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let each finite active family \(\mathcal A_k\) cover every feasible point not safely fathomed. For \(Q\in\mathcal A_k\), let \(L(Q)\le f_Q^*:=\inf_{x\in F\cap Q}f(x)\), with \(f_Q^*-L(Q)\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) and \(\omega(t)\to0\). Suppose \(Q_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{Q\in\mathcal A_k}L(Q)\) is processed, \(\operatorname{diam}Q_k\to0\), and a feasible \(z_k\in F\cap Q_k\) is generated with \(f(z_k)-f_{Q_k}^*\to0\). If fathoming never removes every region containing a global minimizer, then, with \(L_k=\min_{Q\in\mathcal A_k}L(Q)\) and best feasible incumbent \(U_k\), \[L_k\to f^*,\qquad U_k\to f^*,\qquad U_k-L_k\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Best-bound processing, preserved optimal coverage, shrinking selected regions, uniformly consistent bounds, and adequate feasible points force both global bounds to the optimum.
assumptions_latex: Active regions preserve coverage of at least one global minimizer under safe fathoming.
Regional lower bounds are valid and uniformly refinement-consistent.
A minimum-bound region is selected and selected-region diameters tend to zero.
Feasible points generated in selected regions become regionally optimal in value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_k\to f^*,\quad U_k\to f^*,\quad U_k-L_k\to0.

notation.meaning: active global lower bound and incumbent upper bound

knowledge_statements.title: Best-Bound Convergence under Uniform Bound Consistency
Bound-Consistency Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of branch-and-bound bounds under locally consistent relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each partition element \(Q\subset X\), let \(L(Q)\le\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)\) be a valid lower bound. Assume local consistency: for every nested sequence \(Q_1\supset Q_2\supset\cdots\) with \(\operatorname{diam}(Q_k)\to0\), \[\inf_{x\in Q_k}f(x)-L(Q_k)\longrightarrow0.\] In an exhaustive branch-and-bound process on compact \(X\), let \(L_k\) be the least lower bound among active elements and let \(U_k\) be the best feasible objective found. If incumbent points are generated in every indefinitely refined region, then \(L_k\to f^*\), \(U_k\to f^*\), and \(U_k-L_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid lower bounds that become exact on shrinking regions make exhaustive branch-and-bound upper and lower bounds converge to the same global optimum.
assumptions_latex: Partitioning is exhaustive and lower bounds are valid and locally consistent.
Incumbents are generated in every indefinitely refined region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\to f^*\), \(U_k\to f^*\), and \(U_k-L_k\to0\).

notation.meaning: global active lower bound and incumbent upper bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nested-Chain Consistency under a Uniform Diameter Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed consequence of uniform refinement consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e(Q)=f_Q^*-L(Q)\ge0\). If there exists a common modulus \(\omega(t)\downarrow0\) such that \(e(Q)\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) for every feasible region \(Q\), then every nested chain \(Q_1\supseteq Q_2\supseteq\cdots\) with \(\operatorname{diam}Q_k\to0\) satisfies \(e(Q_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform diameter-error modulus implies consistency along every shrinking nested chain.
assumptions_latex: Every regional lower bound is valid.
A single diameter-error modulus applies to the entire region family.
The nested chain has diameter tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e(Q)\le\omega(\operatorname{diam}Q),\ \omega(t)\to0\Longrightarrow e(Q_k)\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Chain Consistency under a Uniform Diameter Error Bound

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns uniform regional lower-bound consistency, its arbitrary shrinking-sequence characterization, and the failure of validity alone. The proposed nested-chain consequence is deferred as a duplicate and does not solve the missing converse. Exhaustive spatial refinement and finite termination remain sibling subjects, while the fully specified convergence theorem is still absent.

children.title: Finite Tolerance Termination
children.top_down_role: Navigation container for finite completion at positive global tolerance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping test once rigorous lower and upper bounds are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be attained by a certified feasible point and \(L\le f^*\) be rigorous. If \[U-L\le\varepsilon_{\rm abs}+\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\max\{1,|U|\},\] then \[U-f^*\le\varepsilon_{\rm abs}+\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\max\{1,|U|\}.\] All relaxation and numerical errors must already be included in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible upper bound and rigorous lower bound certify the declared absolute-plus-relative tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U-L\le\varepsilon_{\rm abs}+\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\max\{1,|U|\}\Rightarrow U-f^*\le\varepsilon_{\rm abs}+\varepsilon_{\rm rel}\max\{1,|U|\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute–Relative Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between finite tolerance crossing and exact finite completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g_k=1/(k+1)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) is crossed at a finite index, but \(g_k\ne0\) for every finite \(k\). Thus gap convergence alone gives no zero-tolerance finite-termination guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent gap crosses every positive tolerance but may never become zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_k\to0\quad\text{but}\quad\nexists k<\infty:g_k=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Tolerance Is Essential

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Crossing of Every Positive Certified Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract positive-tolerance theorem independent of branching implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_k=f(x_k)\) for feasible incumbents \(x_k\), let \(L_k\le f^*\) be rigorous global lower bounds, and let \(g_k=U_k-L_k\). If \(g_k\to0\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some finite \(K\) satisfies \[0\le f(x_K)-f^*\le U_K-L_K\le\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified global gap converging to zero crosses every fixed positive tolerance after finitely many iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists K<\infty:f(x_K)-f^*\le U_K-L_K\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Crossing of Every Positive Certified Gap
Finite Tolerance Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite branch-and-bound completion for every positive absolute tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider branch-and-bound minimization of a continuous function on a compact domain. Suppose branching is finite, every infinite nested branch has diameters tending to zero, regional lower bounds are valid and locally consistent, and feasible incumbents are generated consistently on shrinking regions. Let \(U_k\) be the incumbent value and \(L_k\) the smallest active lower bound. If the algorithm selects an active region attaining \(L_k\) and stops when \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\), then for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) it stops after finitely many iterations and returns \(x_k\) satisfying \[f(x_k)-f^*\le U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under exhaustive branching and consistent bounds, branch-and-bound reaches any positive global optimality tolerance after finitely many iterations.
assumptions_latex: The feasible domain is compact and the objective is continuous.
Branching is finitely branching and exhaustive.
Lower bounds and incumbent generation are locally consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\Rightarrow\) finite termination with \(f(x_k)-f^*\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Finiteness in Special Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exact global minimization of a concave function over a polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty compact polytope with finite vertex set \(V(P)\), and let \(f:P\to\mathbb R\) be concave. Then \[\min_{x\in P}f(x)=\min_{v\in V(P)}f(v).\] Consequently, when the vertices can be enumerated and function values are evaluated exactly, evaluating every vertex and returning a vertex of least value terminates after exactly \(|V(P)|\) evaluations with an exact global minimizer. This finite exactness relies on polyhedral finiteness and concavity; it does not extend to an arbitrary compact convex feasible set having infinitely many extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave function on a compact polytope has a global minimum at a vertex, so finite vertex enumeration is exact.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope with finite vertex set.
\(f\) is concave on \(P\) and can be evaluated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in P}f(x)=\min_{v\in V(P)}f(v)\), giving exact termination after \(|V(P)|\) evaluations.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite exhaustive family of exactly resolvable regions yields finite exact global completion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex-isolating slack perturbation for a polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion concerning f is conditional on concavity, an assumption required mathematically but not restated explicitly in the extracted span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^Tx\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\) be a nonempty polytope and define
\[
g(x)=\min_{\substack{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ |J|=n\\ \{a_j:j\in J\}\text{ linearly independent}}}\sum_{j\in J}(b_j-a_j^Tx).
\]
Then \(g\) is concave and, for fixed \(x\), is computable in polynomial time by greedy minimum-weight basis selection. Moreover, \(g(v)=0\) for every vertex \(v\) of \(S\), while \(g(x)>0\) for every nonvertex \(x\in S\). If \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) is concave, then the global minimizers of \(f+g\) are exactly the globally minimizing vertices of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the sum of constraint slacks over all bases of n linearly independent constraint normals. The resulting function is concave, is polynomial-time evaluable by a greedy minimum-weight basis algorithm, and is zero exactly at the vertices of the polytope. For a concave objective f, adding this perturbation preserves the globally minimizing vertices and removes all nonvertex global minimizers.
assumptions_latex: S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_j^Tx\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\text{ is a nonempty polytope}
f:S\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is concave for the minimizer-preservation conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is concave and polynomial-time evaluable},\quad \{x\in S:g(x)=0\}=\operatorname{vert}(S),\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}(f(x)+g(x))=\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in\operatorname{vert}(S)}f(v).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corollary strengthening Theorem 3.6.2; all hypotheses of that theorem remain assumptions rather than being replaced by its conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X_n)_{n\ge1}\) be sampling points adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_n)\). Suppose that for every open neighborhood \(U\) of the minimizer set \(S^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\), there is \(p_U>0\) such that \(\mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in U\mid\mathcal F_n)\ge p_U\) almost surely for every \(n\). Then every such \(U\) is visited infinitely often almost surely. Consequently, the nonincreasing best-value sequence \(f_n^\star=\min_{1\le k\le n}f(X_k)\) satisfies \(f_n^\star\downarrow f^\star\) almost surely, where \(f^\star=\min_{x\in X}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent positive probability of sampling every minimizer neighborhood forces infinitely many visits and makes the best observed objective value converge almost surely to the global minimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary and Isotropic Gaussian Covariance Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of stationarity and isotropy together with the covariance-kernel characterization used in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gaussian process is stationary (homogeneous) when its mean is constant and $\operatorname{Cov}(f(x_1),f(x_2))=R(x_1-x_2)$. After centering, one may take the mean to be zero. It is isotropic when $R(x)$ depends only on $\|x\|$. By Bochner's characterization, a continuous positive-definite $R$ on $\mathbb R^d$ is the Fourier transform of a finite positive measure; if $R(0)>0$, then $R/R(0)$ is a characteristic function. Examples of isotropic covariance functions listed in the extract are $\sigma^2e^{-\|x\|^2/2}$, $3\sigma^2e^{-\|x\|}$, and $\sigma^2/(1+\|x\|^2)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gaussian process is stationary when it has constant mean and covariance depending only on the displacement between two points, and it is isotropic when that covariance depends only on displacement length. Positive-definite stationary covariances admit the Bochner Fourier representation, with normalization yielding a characteristic function.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a Gaussian process on }\mathbb R^d
R\text{ is continuous and positive definite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{i\langle x,t\rangle}\,d\mu(t)\text{ for a finite positive measure }\mu;\quad R(x)=\rho(\|x\|)\text{ in the isotropic case}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and existence representation for Gaussian stochastic processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic process $f$ on $S$ is Gaussian when every finite vector $(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_k))$ has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean and covariance are $u(x)=\mathbb E[f(x)]$ and $R(x_1,x_2)=\mathbb E[(f(x_1)-u(x_1))(f(x_2)-u(x_2))]$. Conversely, if $u:S\to\mathbb R$ is finite-valued and $R:S\times S\to\mathbb R$ is nonnegative, symmetric, and positive semidefinite, then the Gaussian finite-dimensional distributions determined by $u$ and $R$ are Kolmogorov-consistent and define a Gaussian process having mean $u$ and covariance $R$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A process is Gaussian when every finite collection of its values is jointly Gaussian. Its mean and covariance determine those finite-dimensional laws; conversely, a finite mean function and a nonnegative symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance kernel determine a consistent Gaussian process.
assumptions_latex: R:S\times S\to\mathbb R\text{ is nonnegative and symmetric}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a Gaussian process }f\text{ with }\mathbb E[f(x)]=u(x)\text{ and }\operatorname{Cov}(f(x_1),f(x_2))=R(x_1,x_2)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and principal distributional and path properties used for one-dimensional random objective modeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a one-dimensional parameter domain contained in $[0,\infty)$, a Wiener process with scale $\sigma^2$ is a centered Gaussian process satisfying $R(x_1,x_2)=\sigma^2\min\{x_1,x_2\}$. Hence, whenever $x,x+h$ are in the domain and $h\ge0$, $f(x+h)-f(x)\sim N(0,\sigma^2h)$. If $x_1<x_2<x_3<x_4$, the increments $f(x_2)-f(x_1)$ and $f(x_4)-f(x_3)$ are independent, and its sample paths are continuous with probability one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional Wiener process is a zero-mean Gaussian process whose covariance is sigma squared times the smaller of its two arguments. Its increments are centered normal with variance proportional to interval length, increments on disjoint ordered intervals are independent, and its paths are almost surely continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x+h)-f(x)\sim N(0,\sigma^2h),\quad f(x_2)-f(x_1)\perp f(x_4)-f(x_3),\quad P(f\text{ has continuous paths})=1

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Limit Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weibull-domain limit for minima under a regularly varying lower tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) be independent copies of \(Y\), let \(m=\inf\{y:\mathbb P(Y\le y)>0\}\) be finite, and set \(M_n=\min_{1\le i\le n}Y_i\). If \(\mathbb P(Y\le m+t)=ct^\alpha+o(t^\alpha)\) as \(t\downarrow0\), where \(c>0\) and \(\alpha>0\), then \(n^{1/\alpha}(M_n-m)\Rightarrow W\), where \(W\) is nonnegative and satisfies \(\mathbb P(W>z)=\exp(-cz^\alpha)\) for every \(z\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent observations whose probability mass near a finite lower endpoint has a power-law expansion, the scaled sample minimum converges in distribution to a nonnegative Weibull-type random variable.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) are independent copies of \(Y\) with finite lower endpoint \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^{1/\alpha}(M_n-m)\Rightarrow W\), where \(\mathbb P(W>z)=e^{-cz^\alpha}\) for \(z\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Endpoint Atoms Produce a Degenerate Minimum Limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between continuous Weibull scaling and exact endpoint hits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p=\mathbb P(Y=m)>0\) and \(M_n\) is the minimum of \(n\) iid copies, then \(\mathbb P(M_n=m)=1-(1-p)^n\to1\). Consequently, for every deterministic \(a_n>0\), \((M_n-m)/a_n\to0\) in probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive mass at the lower endpoint makes the minimum hit the endpoint exponentially quickly and collapses every positive rescaling to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_i\) are iid with finite lower endpoint \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(M_n=m)=1-(1-p)^n\to1.

notation.meaning: probability mass at the lower endpoint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantile-normalized Weibull limit under a regularly varying lower tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(t)=\mathbb P(Y\le m+t)\), where \(m\) is a finite lower endpoint and \(G(0)=0\). Suppose \(G(tx)/G(t)\to x^\alpha\) as \(t\downarrow0\) for every \(x>0\), with \(\alpha>0\), and choose \(a_n\downarrow0\) so that \(nG(a_n)\to1\). For iid copies and \(M_n=\min_{i\le n}Y_i\), \[(M_n-m)/a_n\Rightarrow W_\alpha,\qquad \mathbb P(W_\alpha>z)=e^{-z^\alpha},\ z\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular variation of the lower tail yields a Weibull minimum limit under one-over-n lower-tail quantile scaling.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_i\) are iid with finite lower endpoint \(m\) and \(\mathbb P(Y=m)=0\).
\(G(t)=\mathbb P(Y\le m+t)\) is regularly varying at zero with index \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{M_n-m}{a_n}\Rightarrow W_\alpha,\qquad \mathbb P(W_\alpha>z)=e^{-z^\alpha}.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Convergence Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability value-error rate for independent pure random search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) be independent copies of a random variable with finite lower endpoint \(m\), and let \(M_n=\min_{1\le i\le n}Y_i\). Suppose that \(\mathbb P(Y\le m+t)\ge ct^\beta\) for every \(0<t\le t_0\), where \(c>0\), \(t_0>0\), and \(\beta>0\). For \(0<\delta<1\), if \(r_{n,\delta}=(\log(1/\delta)/(cn))^{1/\beta}\le t_0\), then \(\mathbb P(M_n-m>r_{n,\delta})\le\delta\). Consequently, for \(0<\varepsilon\le t_0\), any integer \(n\ge c^{-1}\varepsilon^{-\beta}\log(1/\delta)\) gives \(\mathbb P(M_n-m\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\), and \(M_n-m=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/\beta})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the probability of sampling within error t of the lower endpoint is at least proportional to t raised to beta, independent random search has error of stochastic order n to the minus one over beta and the displayed finite-confidence evaluation bound.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) are independent copies of a random variable with finite lower endpoint \(m\).
For some \(c>0\), \(t_0>0\), and \(\beta>0\), \(\mathbb P(Y\le m+t)\ge ct^\beta\) whenever \(0<t\le t_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_n-m=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/\beta})\), with the stated finite-confidence evaluation bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Sample-Minimum Error under Power-Law Mass
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment-rate counterpart of the high-probability bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(0\le Y-m\le B\) almost surely and \(\mathbb P(Y\le m+t)\ge ct^\beta\) for \(0<t\le t_0\). Then for iid sample minima, \[\mathbb E[M_n-m]\le \Gamma\!\left(1+\frac1\beta\right)(cn)^{-1/\beta}+B e^{-nc t_0^\beta}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded sampled-value range converts the lower-tail mass condition into expected error of order n to the minus one over beta.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_i\) are iid and \(0\le Y_i-m\le B\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[M_n-m]=O(n^{-1/\beta}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Sided Lower-Tail Bounds Give a Sharp Polynomial Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching stochastic upper and lower rate under two-sided power-law tail control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(t)=\mathbb P(Y\le m+t)\) and suppose \(ct^\beta\le G(t)\le Ct^\beta\) for \(0<t\le t_0\), where \(0<c\le C\). For \(M_n=\min_{i\le n}Y_i\), fixed \(z>0\), and all sufficiently large \(n\), \[\left(1-\frac{Cz^\beta}{n}\right)^n\le \mathbb P\bigl(n^{1/\beta}(M_n-m)>z\bigr)\le e^{-cz^\beta}.\] Hence \(M_n-m=\Theta_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/\beta})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-sided power-law control makes the n-to-the-minus-one-over-beta rate both achievable and unimprovable in stochastic order.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_i\) are iid with finite lower endpoint \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_n-m=\Theta_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/\beta}).

notation.meaning: matching upper and lower stochastic order

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sample Tail Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and exponential finite-sample tails for an independent sample minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be independent copies of a random variable with distribution function \(F\) and finite lower endpoint \(m\), and set \(M_n=\min_{1\le i\le n}Y_i\). For every \(\varepsilon\ge0\), \(\mathbb P(M_n-m>\varepsilon)=(1-F(m+\varepsilon))^n\le\exp(-nF(m+\varepsilon))\). If \(F(m+\varepsilon)>0\) and \(0<\delta<1\), every integer \(n\ge\log(1/\delta)/F(m+\varepsilon)\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(M_n-m\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent sampled values, the probability that the minimum misses an epsilon-neighborhood of the lower endpoint is exactly the nth power of the one-sample miss probability and is bounded exponentially.
assumptions_latex: \(F(y)=\mathbb P(Y\le y)\), and \(m\) is the finite lower endpoint of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(M_n-m>\varepsilon)=(1-F(m+\varepsilon))^n\le e^{-nF(m+\varepsilon)}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for multiplying one-sample miss probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1=\cdots=Y_n=Y\) almost surely, with \(p_\varepsilon=\mathbb P(Y\le m+\varepsilon)\in(0,1)\). Then \[\mathbb P\!\left(\min_{i\le n}Y_i-m>\varepsilon\right)=1-p_\varepsilon,\] rather than \((1-p_\varepsilon)^n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-budget tail law without identical sampling distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be independent, let \(m\) be a common lower bound, and write \(p_i(\varepsilon)=\mathbb P(Y_i\le m+\varepsilon)\). Then \[\mathbb P\!\left(\min_{i\le n}Y_i-m>\varepsilon\right)=\prod_{i=1}^n(1-p_i(\varepsilon))\le \exp\!\left(-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(\varepsilon)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent nonidentical draws, cumulative near-optimal hit mass controls the finite-budget miss probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(\min_{i\le n}Y_i>m+\varepsilon)=\prod_{i=1}^n(1-p_i(\varepsilon))\le e^{-\sum_i p_i(\varepsilon)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absence of a Distribution-Free Convergence Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily slow convergence of iid sample minima over continuous lower-tail laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every deterministic sequence \(r_n\downarrow0\), there exist a continuous distribution with lower endpoint \(0\) and integers \(n_k\uparrow\infty\) such that, for iid sample minima \(M_n\), \[\mathbb P(M_{n_k}>r_{n_k})\ge e^{-2}\quad\text{for all }k.\] Hence no deterministic rate tending to zero uniformly bounds the sample-minimum error in probability over all continuous distributions with a fixed finite lower endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a quantitative lower-tail assumption, minimum convergence can be slower than any proposed universal rate along a subsequence.
assumptions_latex: The distribution ranges over continuous laws with lower endpoint zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists F,\exists n_k\uparrow\infty:\ \mathbb P_F(M_{n_k}>r_{n_k})\ge e^{-2}.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Extreme Order Statistics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-sample distribution of lower order statistics used by random-search inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be independent random variables with common distribution function \(F\), and write \(Y_{1:n}\le\cdots\le Y_{n:n}\) for their order statistics. For every \(y\in\mathbb R\) and \(1\le k\le n\), \(\mathbb P(Y_{k:n}\le y)=\sum_{j=k}^n\binom{n}{j}F(y)^j(1-F(y))^{n-j}\). In particular, \(\mathbb P(Y_{1:n}>y)=(1-F(y))^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an independent identically distributed sample, the distribution function of the kth order statistic is a binomial tail, and the minimum exceeds a threshold precisely with the displayed nth-power probability.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are independent random variables with common distribution function \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(Y_{1:n}>y)=(1-F(y))^n\), and \(\mathbb P(Y_{k:n}\le y)=\sum_{j=k}^n\binom{n}{j}F(y)^j(1-F(y))^{n-j}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Density Representation of an Ordered Sample
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint and marginal densities under absolute continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are iid with density \(f\) and distribution function \(F\), then the ordered vector has density \(n!\prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i)\) on \(y_1<\cdots<y_n\), and \[f_{Y_{k:n}}(y)=\frac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}F(y)^{k-1}(1-F(y))^{n-k}f(y)\] for almost every \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under absolute continuity, the ordered vector has the symmetrized product density and each order statistic has the standard beta-weighted marginal density.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are iid with an absolutely continuous distribution having density \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{Y_{1:n},\ldots,Y_{n:n}}(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=n!\prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i)\mathbf1_{\{y_1<\cdots<y_n\}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Beta and Quantile Representations of Continuous Order Statistics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-free transform and quantile representation for continuous iid samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be iid with continuous distribution function \(F\). For \(1\le k\le n\), \(F(Y_{k:n})\sim\operatorname{Beta}(k,n+1-k)\). Equivalently, if \(U_{k:n}\) is the \(k\)-th order statistic of \(n\) iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) variables and \(F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{y:F(y)\ge u\}\), then \(Y_{k:n}\overset d=F^{-1}(U_{k:n})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-sample order statistic transforms to a beta variable and is distributed as a population quantile evaluated at a uniform order statistic.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are iid with continuous distribution function \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(Y_{k:n})\sim\operatorname{Beta}(k,n+1-k),\qquad Y_{k:n}\overset d=F^{-1}(U_{k:n}).
knowledge_statements.title: Beta and Quantile Representations of Continuous Order Statistics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-endpoint regularity assumptions for sample extremes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract's bounded-support clause prints F(t)=1 for t≤M. This conflicts with support [m,M] and the preceding lower-endpoint condition; the mathematically coherent boundary condition F(t)=1 for t≥M is recorded as an apparent source or extraction correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the c.d.f. of a real random variable \(\eta\). The basic conditions are \(m=\operatorname{ess\,inf}\eta> -\infty\), \(F(t)=0\) for \(t<m\), \(F(t)>0\) for \(t>m\), and continuity of \(F\) on a neighborhood of \(m\). Stronger conditions used separately are bounded support \([m,M]\), with \(-\infty<m<M<\infty\) and \(F(t)=1\) for \(t\ge M\), and continuity of \(F\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-tail analysis assumes a finite essential lower endpoint, positive distribution mass arbitrarily above it, and continuity of the c.d.f. near that endpoint. Stronger regimes assume bounded support or global continuity.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is continuous on a neighborhood of }m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These conditions define the lower-endpoint regularity regime; stronger alternatives impose bounded support or global continuity.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strict decreases of the kth order statistic as the sample grows; k=1 recovers the ordinary lower-record quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge k\), let \(\eta_{1,n}\le\cdots\le\eta_{n,n}\) be the order statistics of \(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_n\). Set \(L^{(k)}(0)=0\), \(L^{(k)}(1)=k\), and, whenever the defining set is nonempty, \[L^{(k)}(r+1)=\min\{j>L^{(k)}(r):\eta_j<\eta_{k,j-1}\}.\] Define the kth record values and waiting times by \[\eta^{(k)}_{(r)}=\eta_{k,L^{(k)}(r)},\qquad \Delta^{(k)}(r)=L^{(k)}(r)-L^{(k)}(r-1),\] and let \(\mathcal N^{(k)}(n)\) be the number of kth record values among the first \(n\) observations. For \(k=1\), these quantities coincide with the ordinary lower-record quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As observations arrive, the kth order statistic is nonincreasing. A kth record moment is an index where it strictly decreases; the corresponding order statistic is the kth record value, successive record indices determine waiting times, and their count up to n is the kth record count. Ordinary lower records are the case k=1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limit distribution of a ratio of lower order statistics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic distribution of the normalized gap ratio between the first and kth sample order statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the finite-lower-endpoint and regular-variation hypotheses yielding the \(\Psi_\alpha\) limit law, for every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), \[D_{n,k}=\frac{\eta_{1,n}-m}{\eta_{k,n}-m}\xrightarrow{d}D_k\qquad(n\to\infty),\] where \(D_k\) has c.d.f. \[F_k(u)=1-\left[1-\left(\frac{u}{1+u}\right)^\alpha\right]^{k-1},\qquad u\ge0.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Record moments, values, counts, and waiting times
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for lower records; reversing the strict comparison defines upper records. A record sequence can terminate if a later strict record does not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \((\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\), set \(L(1)=1\) and \(\eta(1)=\eta_1\). Whenever the defining set is nonempty, define \[L(n+1)=\min\{j>L(n):\eta_j<\eta_{L(n)}\},\qquad \eta(n)=\eta_{L(n)}.\] The variables \(L(n)\) are lower record moments and \(\eta(n)\) are their lower record values. Let \(\mathcal N(N)\) denote the number of record values among \(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_N\), so that \(\mathcal N(L(n))=n\), and define \(\Delta(n)=L(n)-L(n-1)\) as the waiting time between consecutive record moments. Replacing \(<\) by \(>\) defines upper records.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower record occurs when an observation is strictly below the preceding record. Its index is the record moment, its value is the record value, the number seen by a sample horizon is the record count, and the difference between consecutive record moments is the waiting time. Reversing the comparison gives upper records.
assumptions_latex: (\eta_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a sequence of real random variables}
\text{A recursive record moment is defined only when its defining set is nonempty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(n+1)=\min\{j>L(n):\eta_j<\eta_{L(n)}\},\quad \eta(n)=\eta_{L(n)},\quad \Delta(n)=L(n)-L(n-1),\quad \mathcal N(L(n))=n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moment asymptotics for lower order statistics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-moment and cross-moment asymptotics for lower order statistics in a lower-endpoint extreme-value domain of attraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=\operatorname{ess\,inf}\eta> -\infty\) and \(F\in D(\Psi_\alpha)\) with \(\alpha>1\). Suppose that \(k\) is fixed, or that \(k=k_n\to\infty\) while \(k^2/n\to0\). Then, for every \(\beta>0\), \[\mathbb E(\eta_{k,n}-m)^\beta\sim(\kappa_n-m)^\beta\frac{\Gamma(k+\beta/\alpha)}{\Gamma(k)}.\] For integers \(1\le j\le k\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[(\eta_{j,n}-m)(\eta_{k,n}-m)\right]\sim(\kappa_n-m)^2\lambda_{jk},\qquad \lambda_{jk}=\frac{\Gamma(k+2/\alpha)\Gamma(j+1/\alpha)}{\Gamma(k+1/\alpha)\Gamma(j)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the stated lower-endpoint extreme-value domain, power moments and cross-moments of lower order statistics have the given gamma-ratio asymptotics when k is fixed or grows slowly enough that k squared divided by n tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: 1\le j\le k\text{ for the cross-moment formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E(\eta_{k,n}-m)^\beta\sim(\kappa_n-m)^\beta\frac{\Gamma(k+\beta/\alpha)}{\Gamma(k)},\qquad \mathbb E[(\eta_{j,n}-m)(\eta_{k,n}-m)]\sim(\kappa_n-m)^2\frac{\Gamma(k+2/\alpha)\Gamma(j+1/\alpha)}{\Gamma(k+1/\alpha)\Gamma(j)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular-variation limit law for the sample minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit distribution of the normalized first order statistic near a finite lower endpoint; the referenced c.d.f. definitions are retained symbolically because they are not expanded in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=\operatorname{ess\,inf}\eta> -\infty\), let \(F\) be the c.d.f. of \(\eta\), and define \(V(v)=F(m+1/v)\) for \(v>0\). If \(V\) is regularly varying at infinity with index \(-\alpha\), where \(0<\alpha<\infty\), so that \[\lim_{v\to\infty}\frac{V(tv)}{V(v)}=t^{-\alpha}\qquad\text{for every }t>0,\] then, for a \(1/n\)-quantile \(\kappa_n\) of \(F\), \[\lim_{n\to\infty}F_{1,n}\!\left(m+(\kappa_n-m)z\right)=\Psi_\alpha(z),\] where \(F_{1,n}\) is the c.d.f. of the first order statistic and \(\Psi_\alpha\) is the referenced limiting c.d.f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the distribution near its finite lower endpoint has the stated regularly varying form, then the sample minimum, centered at the endpoint and scaled by the 1/n-quantile distance, converges to the limiting distribution Psi-alpha.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{n\to\infty}F_{1,n}\!\left(m+(\kappa_n-m)z\right)=\Psi_\alpha(z).

knowledge_statements.title: Record-Value Processes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-free lower-record process for continuous independent sampled values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed with a continuous distribution. Define \(I_1=1\) and \(I_j=\mathbf 1_{\{Y_j<\min_{1\le i<j}Y_i\}}\) for \(j\ge2\), and let \(R_n=\sum_{j=1}^n I_j\). Then \((I_j)_{j\ge1}\) are mutually independent, \(\mathbb P(I_j=1)=1/j\), \(\mathbb E[R_n]=\sum_{j=1}^n1/j\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(R_n)=\sum_{j=1}^n(1/j)(1-1/j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous independent identically distributed observations, lower-record indicators are independent with success probability one over the observation index, so the expected number of records is the nth harmonic number.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) are independent and identically distributed with a continuous distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indicators \((I_j)_{j\ge1}\) are mutually independent with \(\mathbb P(I_j=1)=1/j\), and \(\mathbb E[R_n]=\sum_{j=1}^n1/j\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Multiplicative Representation of Lower Record Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-free record-value representation after probability-integral transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) be iid with continuous distribution function \(F\), and let \(L_r\) denote the \(r\)-th lower-record value. Then \[F(L_r)\overset d=\prod_{k=1}^rW_k,\] where \(W_1,W_2,\ldots\) are independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variables. Equivalently, \(-\log F(L_r)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(r,1)\); conditionally on a transformed current record \(u\), the next transformed record is uniform on \((0,u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After probability-integral transformation, successive lower record values multiply by independent uniforms, or add independent exponentials on the negative-log scale.
assumptions_latex: The observations are independent and identically distributed with continuous distribution function \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(L_r)\overset d=\prod_{k=1}^rW_k\) and \(-\log F(L_r)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(r,1)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Multiplicative Representation of Lower Record Values

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Record-Count Strong Law and Central Limit Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic growth and fluctuations of the number of lower records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the continuous iid assumptions of the seed, let \(R_n=\sum_{j=1}^nI_j\), \(H_n=\sum_{j=1}^nj^{-1}\), and \(V_n=\sum_{j=1}^nj^{-1}(1-j^{-1})\). Then \[\frac{R_n}{\log n}\to1\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad \frac{R_n-H_n}{\sqrt{V_n}}\Rightarrow N(0,1).\] Thus the number of lower records grows logarithmically, with fluctuations of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The number of continuous iid lower records is asymptotic to log n almost surely and is asymptotically normal after centering and scaling.
assumptions_latex: The observations are independent, identically distributed, and continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_n/\log n\to1\) almost surely and \((R_n-H_n)/\sqrt{V_n}\Rightarrow N(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Record-Count Strong Law and Central Limit Theorem

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Based Optimality Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact confidence interval for an optimum under a known shifted lower-tail model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_i=m+Z_i\), where \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) are independent, nonnegative random variables with known continuous distribution function \(G\), and let \(M_n=\min_{1\le i\le n}Y_i\). For \(0<\delta<1\), define \(q_{n,\delta}=G^{-1}(1-\delta^{1/n})\), where \(G^{-1}(u)=\inf\{t:G(t)\ge u\}\). Then \(\mathbb P(m\in[M_n-q_{n,\delta},M_n])=1-\delta\). This coverage statement requires the specified shift model and known \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated known continuous shift model, subtracting the specified quantile from the sample minimum produces an exact confidence interval for the unknown lower endpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_i=m+Z_i\), where \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) are independent, nonnegative, and have known continuous distribution function \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(m\in[M_n-q_{n,\delta},M_n])=1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Known continuous distribution function of excess above the optimum
Confidence radius determined by the excess distribution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of sample-minimum optimality inference without lower-tail scale information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\ge1\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and finite \(r>0\). For independent \(Y_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}[m,m+H]\) with \(H>r\) and \(M_n=\min_iY_i\), \[\mathbb P\bigl(m\notin[M_n-r,M_n]\bigr)=(1-r/H)^n.\] This probability can exceed \(\delta\) by taking \(H\) sufficiently large. Thus no radius depending only on \((n,\delta)\) yields a distribution-free finite lower confidence endpoint for \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without lower-tail scale information, even uniform distributions can place the sample minimum farther than any fixed confidence radius above the true endpoint.
assumptions_latex: The admissible class includes continuous uniform distributions with unrestricted width \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{H>r}\mathbb P(m\notin[M_n-r,M_n])=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: No Fixed-Radius Distribution-Free Endpoint Interval

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Efficiency of a Consistent Linear Order-Statistic Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-k efficiency relative to the minimum asymptotic quadratic risk among consistent coefficient vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed $k$ and a consistent linear estimator $\widehat m_{n,k}(a)$ with $a^\prime\mathbf1=1$, define
$\operatorname{eff}(\widehat m_{n,k}(a))=\dfrac{\min_{c\in\mathbb R^k:\,c^\prime\mathbf1=1}c^\prime\Lambda c}{a^\prime\Lambda a}$. If $\Lambda$ is invertible, then $\operatorname{eff}(\widehat m_{n,k}(a))=1/[(\mathbf1^\prime\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf1)(a^\prime\Lambda a)]$, and $0\le\operatorname{eff}(\widehat m_{n,k}(a))\le1$. For $\widehat m_{n,k}=\eta_{1,n}$, $\operatorname{eff}=1/[(\mathbf1^\prime\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf1)\Gamma(1+2/\alpha)]$. An estimator optimized using an incorrect value of $\alpha$ can have low efficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Efficiency is the minimum asymptotic quadratic risk among consistent linear estimators divided by the estimator's own risk. It lies between zero and one, has the stated inverse-matrix form, and can deteriorate when the tail index used to construct the estimator is wrong.
assumptions_latex: \Lambda\text{ is invertible for the closed-form expression}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{eff}(\widehat m_{n,k}(a))=\frac{1}{(\mathbf1^\prime\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf1)(a^\prime\Lambda a)}\in[0,1],\qquad \operatorname{eff}(\eta_{1,n})=\frac{1}{(\mathbf1^\prime\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf1)\Gamma(1+2/\alpha)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Sample Efficiency and Its Replication Estimate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample relative efficiency of an endpoint estimator and its independent-replication approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed $n$ and $k$, define the finite-sample efficiency of $\widehat m$ as $\big[(\kappa_n-m)^2/(\mathbf1^\prime\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf1)\big]/\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat m)$; this quantity may be slightly greater than $1$. Given $R$ independent replications $\widehat m_1,\ldots,\widehat m_R$ of the estimator from samples of size $n$, define $\operatorname{eff}_R(\widehat m)=\dfrac{(\kappa_n-m)^2/(\mathbf1^\prime\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf1)}{R^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^R(\widehat m_j-m)^2}$. As $R\to\infty$, this replication-based efficiency tends to the finite-sample efficiency defined using $\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat m)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sample efficiency divides a reference risk by the estimator's actual mean-square error and can slightly exceed one. Replacing the MSE by the average squared error over independent replications yields an estimate converging to that efficiency.
assumptions_latex: \widehat m_1,\ldots,\widehat m_R\text{ are independent replications from samples of size }n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{eff}_R(\widehat m)\to\frac{(\kappa_n-m)^2}{(\mathbf1^\prime\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf1)\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat m)}\quad\text{as }R\to\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Confidence Interval and Test for the Endpoint m
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic confidence and type-I-error guarantees based on the first and kth order statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $r_{k,\delta}=\left((1-\delta^{1/k})^{-1/\alpha}-1\right)^{-1}$. Under the referenced sample-extreme limit law, $[\eta_{1,n},\,\eta_{1,n}+r_{k,\delta}(\eta_{k,n}-\eta_{1,n})]$ is a one-sided confidence interval for $m$ whose asymptotic confidence level is $1-\delta$. The corresponding test of $H_0:m\le K$ rejects when $(\eta_{1,n}-K)/(\eta_{k,n}-\eta_{1,n})\ge r_{k,\delta}$, and its type-I error probability asymptotically does not exceed $\delta$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled gap between the first and kth order statistics defines a one-sided confidence interval for the endpoint m with asymptotic confidence level one minus delta. The corresponding threshold test of m at most K has asymptotic type-I error no greater than delta.
assumptions_latex: \text{The limit law cited as Proposition 2.1 holds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\!\left(m\in[\eta_{1,n},\eta_{1,n}+r_{k,\delta}(\eta_{k,n}-\eta_{1,n})]\right)\to1-\delta,\qquad \limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{H_0}(\mathrm{reject})\le\delta.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consistency, Bias, and MSE of Linear Order-Statistic Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic properties of fixed-coefficient linear estimators of the endpoint m.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed $k$, let $\widehat m_{n,k}(a)=\sum_{i=1}^k a_i\eta_{i,n}$. Under the referenced moment expansions, $\kappa_n-m\to0$, and finite variances of the order statistics, $\widehat m_{n,k}(a)$ is consistent for $m$ if and only if $a^\prime\mathbf 1=1$. Moreover, $\mathbb E\widehat m_{n,k}(a)=m\,a^\prime\mathbf 1-(\kappa_n-m)a^\prime b+o(\kappa_n-m)$. If $a^\prime b=0$ and $\alpha>1$, its bias is $o(\kappa_n-m)=o(n^{-1/\alpha})$. For a consistent estimator, $\mathbb E(\widehat m_{n,k}(a)-m)^2\sim(\kappa_n-m)^2a^\prime\Lambda a$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed linear combination of the first k order statistics is consistent exactly when its coefficients sum to one. Orthogonality to the leading bias vector removes the leading bias term, and the mean-square error has the stated quadratic-form asymptotics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat m_{n,k}(a)\text{ is consistent}\iff a^\prime\mathbf1=1;\qquad a^\prime b=0\implies\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat m_{n,k}(a))=o(n^{-1/\alpha}),\qquad \operatorname{MSE}(\widehat m_{n,k}(a))\sim(\kappa_n-m)^2a^\prime\Lambda a.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Likelihood Estimator under a Known Weibull Tail Index
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and asymptotic performance of the likelihood estimator of the lower endpoint $m$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that the sample has the asymptotic Weibull distribution and that the tail index $\alpha\ge 2$ is known. For fixed $n,k$, define $\beta_j(\widehat m)=(\eta_{k,n}-\eta_{j,n})/(\eta_{j,n}-\widehat m)$ for $j<k$. The maximum-likelihood estimator $\widehat m$ is a solution satisfying $\widehat m\le\eta_{1,n}$ of $(\alpha-1)\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\beta_j(\widehat m)=k$; if no such solution exists, set $\widehat m=\eta_{1,n}$. If additionally condition (2.45) holds, $k\to\infty$, and $k/n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, then $\widehat m$ is asymptotically normal and efficient among asymptotically normal estimators, and, with $\kappa_n$ the $1/n$-quantile of $F$, $\mathbb E(\widehat m-m)^2\sim(1-2/\alpha)(\kappa_n-m)^2k^{-1+2/\alpha}$ for $\alpha>2$, while $\mathbb E(\widehat m-m)^2\sim(\kappa_n-m)^2\ln k$ for $\alpha=2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a known Weibull tail index at least two, the maximum-likelihood estimate of the lower endpoint solves the stated likelihood equation below the smallest order statistic, with the smallest order statistic used when no admissible solution exists. Under the additional tail condition and an intermediate-order regime, the estimator is asymptotically normal and efficient, with the stated mean-square-error asymptotics.
assumptions_latex: \text{The sample follows the asymptotic Weibull model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat m\text{ is asymptotically normal and efficient, with the stated piecewise MSE asymptotics.}

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Record Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed record-free windows as distribution-free global-optimality evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) be independent and identically distributed with a continuous distribution. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(k\ge1\), the probability of no new lower record at indices \(n+1,\ldots,n+k\) is \(n/(n+k)\). For fixed \(k\), this probability converges to \(1\) as \(n\to\infty\), independently of the common continuous distribution. Therefore, absence of a record during a fixed subsequent window is not a distribution-free finite-sample certificate that the current record is near the lower endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuous independent identically distributed observations, a fixed future window contains no new lower record with probability n over n plus k; this approaches one and cannot certify near-optimality by itself.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) are independent and identically distributed with a continuous distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\text{no new lower record at indices }n+1,\ldots,n+k)=n/(n+k)\).

notation.meaning: Length of the subsequent record-free window

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite Mean Waiting Time for the Next Record
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heavy-tailed waiting time following any fixed observation index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the continuous iid assumptions, let \(T_n=\inf\{k\ge1:Y_{n+k}<\min_{1\le i\le n+k-1}Y_i\}\). Then \(\mathbb P(T_n>k)=n/(n+k)\) for \(k\ge0\), and \(\mathbb E[T_n]=\infty\). Moreover, the probability of a new lower record in the next \(k\) observations is \(k/(n+k)\), so attaining probability at least \(1-\delta\) requires \(k\ge n(1-\delta)/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The next-record waiting time has infinite mean, and a nonvanishing chance of another record requires a window proportional to the accumulated sample size.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) are iid with a continuous distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(T_n>k)=\frac{n}{n+k},\qquad \mathbb E[T_n]=\infty.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Stopping Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence stopping rule based on known near-optimal sampling mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon>0\), \(0<\delta<1\), and suppose independent samples satisfy \(\mathbb P(f(X_i)\le f^\star+\varepsilon)\ge p_\varepsilon\), where \(0<p_\varepsilon\le1\) is known. Set \(N=1\) if \(p_\varepsilon=1\), and otherwise set \(N=\left\lceil\log(\delta)/\log(1-p_\varepsilon)\right\rceil\). Independently sample and evaluate \(X_1,\ldots,X_N\), then return any \(\widehat x_N\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le i\le N}f(X_i)\). The rule satisfies \(\mathbb P(f(\widehat x_N)\le f^\star+\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the sample count from the known lower bound on the probability of an epsilon-optimal draw, sample independently that many times, and return the best sampled point; its value is epsilon-optimal with the prescribed confidence.
assumptions_latex: Independent samples satisfy \(\mathbb P(f(X_i)\le f^\star+\varepsilon)\ge p_\varepsilon\), where \(0<p_\varepsilon\le1\).
The tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), risk \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and valid lower bound \(p_\varepsilon\) are supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(f(\widehat x_N)\le f^\star+\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Known lower bound on the one-sample epsilon-optimal probability
Best sampled point returned by the rule

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Uniform Fixed-Confidence Budget Without Near-Optimal Mass
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Impossibility of distribution-free finite stopping when near-optimal sampling probability can be arbitrarily small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and a finite sample budget \(N\). If admissible independent-sampling models allow \(p_\varepsilon=\mathbb P(f(X)\le f^\star+\varepsilon)\) to be arbitrarily small and positive, then some admissible model has \((1-p_\varepsilon)^N>\delta\). Hence no finite \(N\) gives a uniform \((1-\delta)\)-confidence guarantee without a positive uniform lower bound on near-optimal sampling mass or equivalent structural information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If epsilon-optimal points may have arbitrarily small sampling probability, every fixed finite budget fails the requested confidence on some admissible problem.
assumptions_latex: The admissible class has no positive uniform lower bound on \(p_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\text{admissible models}}\mathbb P(f(\widehat x_N)>f^\star+\varepsilon)>\delta\) for every finite \(N\).
knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform Fixed-Confidence Budget Without Near-Optimal Mass

knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Graph Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorable directed-acyclic representation of nonlinear objective and constraint expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each finite model expression, create leaf nodes for variables and constants and an internal node for every primitive operation. Add directed edges from operand nodes to the operation that consumes them, and optionally identify syntactically identical common subexpressions. In a topological ordering, every internal node \(v\) computes \(z_v=\phi_v(z_{u_1},\ldots,z_{u_{r_v}})\), where \(u_1,\ldots,u_{r_v}\) are its predecessors. The resulting finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) is acyclic, and each designated root has the same value as its original objective or constraint expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite factorable nonlinear expression can be represented by a directed acyclic graph whose leaves are inputs, internal nodes are primitive operations, and roots reproduce the original model expressions.
assumptions_latex: The nonlinear model is a finite expression built from variables, constants, and primitive operators of fixed finite arity.
Syntactically identical common subexpressions may be shared rather than duplicated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model admits a finite directed acyclic expression graph whose designated root values equal the original expressions.

children.title: Automatic Structure Detection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound rule-based detection need not recognize all valid structure and need not be representation invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a detector apply a finite library of sound local composition rules to a supplied expression graph. It may return \(\mathrm{unknown}\) even when the represented function is convex, monotone, or separable, and algebraically equivalent graphs may receive different labels. For example, a library that recognizes affine primitives but performs no symbolic cancellation can label the constant \(0\) affine while returning unknown for the equivalent expression \(x^2-x^2\). Thus soundness excludes false positive labels but does not imply completeness or representation invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rule-based structure detection can be sound yet incomplete and sensitive to the chosen algebraic graph.
assumptions_latex: The detector uses sound local rules but does not perform complete symbolic equivalence or cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An \(\mathrm{unknown}\) label does not imply absence of structure, and recognized labels may depend on the supplied graph.

children.title: Reformulation Lifecycle

knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Lifecycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifecycle invariant for bound-dependent lifted reformulations in deterministic global optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an original problem \(P_0\) and current variable box \(B_k\), construct a lifted reformulation \(P_k=T(P_0,B_k)\), recording maps between original and lifted variables. After branching or bound tightening produces \(B_{k+1}\subseteq B_k\), update every bound-dependent domain, envelope, and generated constraint before solving. Accept the update only if projection preserves feasible points, \(\operatorname{proj}_x F(P_{k+1})=F(P_0)\cap B_{k+1}\), and objective values agree on corresponding feasible points. Otherwise discard and rebuild the affected reformulation objects. Output the updated model and its variable-constraint mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build the lifted model from current bounds, refresh every bound-dependent object after tightening, and accept it only when projection and objective values remain faithful to the original problem.
assumptions_latex: \(P_0\) has explicitly bounded variables on each processed region.
The transformation \(T\) identifies every object depending on variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{k+1}\) is accepted only if \(\operatorname{proj}_x F(P_{k+1})=F(P_0)\cap B_{k+1}\) with preserved objective values.

notation.meaning: Variable box at lifecycle stage k.

children.title: Variable-Bound Maintenance
children.top_down_role: Storage and propagation of current variable bounds within a modeling system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical merge operation for independently valid bounds on one current region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every feasible point in the current region satisfies both \(\ell_i^{(1)}\leq x_i\leq u_i^{(1)}\) and \(\ell_i^{(2)}\leq x_i\leq u_i^{(2)}\). Then \(\ell_i'=\max\{\ell_i^{(1)},\ell_i^{(2)}\}\) and \(u_i'=\min\{u_i^{(1)},u_i^{(2)}\}\) define another valid bound interval. If \(\ell_i'>u_i'\), the current region is infeasible. Repeated interval merging is associative, commutative, and idempotent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independently valid bounds are merged by interval intersection; an empty intersection certifies regional infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Both input intervals contain every feasible value of \(x_i\) in the same current region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_i\in[\ell_i',u_i']=[\ell_i^{(1)},u_i^{(1)}]\cap[\ell_i^{(2)},u_i^{(2)}]\quad\text{for every feasible point}.

notation.meaning: Merged authoritative interval for variable i.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection of Valid Variable Bounds
Variable-Bound Maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency condition for bounds shared by branching, propagation, and reformulation components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each variable \(x_i\), maintain authoritative bounds \([\ell_i^k,u_i^k]\) at region state \(k\). A bound update is admissible when \(\ell_i^k\leq \ell_i^{k+1}\leq u_i^{k+1}\leq u_i^k\) and no feasible point of the current region is removed. Before another relaxation is solved, every bound-dependent constraint, auxiliary-variable range, and solver copy must reference the same version \(k+1\). Empty intervals certify infeasibility only when the tightening operation is valid for the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounds may tighten monotonically, but all solver and reformulation copies must use the same version; a validly derived empty interval certifies regional infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Initial bounds satisfy \(\ell_i^0\leq u_i^0\) for every \(i\).
Each tightening rule is valid for all feasible points in the current region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All active model objects use \([\ell_i^{k+1},u_i^{k+1}]\), and \(\ell_i^{k+1}>u_i^{k+1}\) validly certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: Authoritative bounds for variable i at version k.

children.title: Lifted-Model Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency between original expressions and lifted auxiliary representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective agreement between an original model and its exact or relaxed lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)\) be the original objective, let \(y=\phi(x)\), and let \(q(x,y)\) be the lifted objective. Exact objective consistency requires \(q(x,\phi(x))=f(x)\) for every original feasible \(x\). For a minimization relaxation containing every feasible graph point, the weaker condition \(q(x,\phi(x))\leq f(x)\) is sufficient for lower-bound validity. A projected incumbent must nevertheless be evaluated using \(f\), unless objective equality has been validated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact lift preserves objective values on the defining graph. A minimization relaxation may underestimate them, but projected incumbents require the original objective unless equality is verified.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi(x)\) is defined at every original feasible point.
The lifted relaxation contains \((x,\phi(x))\) for every original feasible \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(x,\phi(x))=f(x)\text{ for exact objective consistency};\qquad q(x,\phi(x))\leq f(x)\text{ suffices for minimization lower-bound validity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Objective Consistency
Lifted-Model Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection and graph-consistency requirements for auxiliary variables in lifted models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the original feasible set be \(F=\{x:g(x)\leq0,\ h(x)=0\}\) on a box \(B\), and introduce auxiliaries \(y=\phi(x)\). A lifted formulation with feasible set \(L_B\) is exact when \(\operatorname{proj}_x L_B=F\cap B\) and every lifted feasible point satisfies \(y=\phi(x)\). A lifted relaxation \(R_B\) is consistent when \(\{(x,\phi(x)):x\in F\cap B\}\subseteq R_B\); any point returned as an original feasible incumbent must additionally satisfy the exact defining equalities for its auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact lift projects to the original feasible set and satisfies all defining equations; a relaxed lift must contain every lifted original feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is defined on the current box \(B\).
Projection retains precisely the original variables \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness gives \(\operatorname{proj}_x L_B=F\cap B\); relaxation consistency gives \(\operatorname{graph}(\phi|_{F\cap B})\subseteq R_B\).

notation.meaning: Exact lifted feasible set on B.

children.title: Bound-Synchronization Failures
children.top_down_role: Implementation failures caused by stale or inconsistent bound information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp containment condition for reusing bound-dependent relaxations after bound changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(\widehat B)\) be an outer relaxation certified for every graph point whose original variables lie in \(\widehat B\). Reusing it on a current region \(B\) is valid whenever \(B\subseteq\widehat B\), although regeneration on \(B\) may strengthen it. If \(B\nsubseteq\widehat B\), the certificate for \(Q(\widehat B)\) gives no validity guarantee on \(B\setminus\widehat B\); reuse may exclude feasible graph points and produce an invalid lower bound. Enlargement therefore requires regeneration or an independent extension certificate, whereas tightening within the generating box preserves validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation generated on one box remains valid on contained tighter regions, but reuse outside that box is unsafe without revalidation.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(\widehat B)\) is certified as an outer relaxation only on \(\widehat B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\subseteq\widehat B\) implies outer validity is preserved on \(B\); if \(B\nsubseteq\widehat B\), validity does not follow from the original certificate.

notation.meaning: Relaxation generated and certified on box \(\widehat B\).

knowledge_statements.title: Validity-Domain Containment Boundary
Bound-Synchronization Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of relaxation validity when bound-dependent envelopes use incompatible regional bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w=xy\), McCormick inequalities generated from a box \(B=[\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\) are valid on \(B\). If a worker processes a region \(B'\) but installs inequalities generated from an incompatible box \(\widehat B\) with \(B'\nsubseteq\widehat B\), validity can fail. For example, \(B'=[0,1]^2\) and \(\widehat B=[0,\tfrac12]^2\) produce \(w\leq\tfrac12x\); the graph point \((x,y,w)=(1,1,1)\) belongs to \(B'\) but violates this inequality. Thus the resulting lower bound need not be valid for \(B'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An envelope built for bounds that do not contain the processed region can cut off true graph points, making the resulting regional lower bound invalid.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation contains bound-dependent McCormick inequalities for \(w=xy\).
The processed region is not contained in the box used to generate those inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation may exclude feasible graph points, so its optimum is not necessarily a valid lower bound on the processed region.

notation.meaning: Region currently processed by a worker.
Box used to generate stale or incompatible envelopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Incumbent Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-point certificate for objective upper bounds in minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\}\). A candidate \(\bar x\) becomes a primal incumbent only after validation establishes \(\bar x\in F\), including variable bounds, inequalities, and equalities under the prescribed feasibility tolerances. Its value \(U=f(\bar x)\) then satisfies \(p^*\leq U\). Among validated candidates \(x^1,\ldots,x^m\), retain \(U_m=\min_j f(x^j)\) and an attaining point. An unvalidated or infeasible candidate supplies no certified upper bound, regardless of its objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any validated feasible point gives an upper bound for a minimization problem; the best validated candidate is retained as the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: The global problem is a minimization problem with feasible set \(F\).
Objective values are evaluated consistently with the original model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in F\) implies \(p^*\leq f(\bar x)\), and \(U_m=\min_{1\leq j\leq m}f(x^j)\) is the incumbent bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem on region \(B\), let \(F_B\) be its feasible set and let \(R_B\) be a solver-compatible linear, convex, or conic relaxation in the same variable space satisfying \(F_B\subseteq R_B\). If the relaxation objective \(\underline f\) obeys \(\underline f(x)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in F_B\), then any certified relaxation optimum \(L_B=\inf_{x\in R_B}\underline f(x)\) satisfies \(L_B\leq\inf_{x\in F_B}f(x)\). An infeasible relaxation certifies regional infeasibility, while an unbounded or numerically uncertified solve does not provide a finite certified lower bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certification of a relaxation lower bound independently of a potentially inexact primal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization relaxation with primal optimal value \(v_R\) and a dual satisfying weak duality. For every validated dual-feasible point \(\bar y\) with finite dual objective \(d(\bar y)\), \(d(\bar y)\leq v_R\). If the relaxation is a valid lower-bounding model for the original regional problem with value \(p_B^*\), then \(d(\bar y)\leq v_R\leq p_B^*\). Thus \(d(\bar y)\) is a certified regional lower bound even when a returned primal point is approximate. A relaxation-primal feasible objective generally bounds \(v_R\) from above and is not, by itself, a lower-bound certificate for \(p_B^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validated dual-feasible objective certifies a regional lower bound by weak duality; an approximate primal objective generally does not.

children.title: Warm-Start State Transfer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-neutral transfer of supported internal initialization state, excluding incumbent-solution transfer and relaxation-basis reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given predecessor state \(s_p\) and successor model \(Q_c\), map only state fields for which the receiving interface supplies a compatible successor object and representation. Discard every unmapped or incompatible field, submit the accepted partial state \(s_c\) only as initialization data, and validate all feasibility, bounds, termination tests, and certificates from computations performed on \(Q_c\). Rejection of any or all transferred fields leaves correctness unchanged and permits an ordinary initialization.

Map state components by persistent variable and constraint identifiers, discard components whose dimensions or mathematical meanings changed, project primal values onto the bounds of \(Q_c\), and retain dual or basis information only when its solver-specific compatibility conditions hold.
